[UX-W007, “From the Viplan method to the Viplan methodology”]

A distinct Italian programme: structure, interaction, and compatibility#

Sergio Barile, Jaqueline Pels, Francesco Polese, and Marialuisa Saviano introduce the Italian Viable Systems Approach as a methodological framework for business and social phenomena, including marketing. They acknowledge Beer as part of its background while drawing on a broader set of systems traditions. Their text explicitly describes the approach as a meta-level orientation, rather than a ready set of operative models for each problem. [SG-W014, printed pp. 62–63]

Their structure–system distinction separates a description of components and organized relations from the dynamics of their actual interaction. The account also identifies decision-making and operations, selective openness to resources, and dependence on other actors. The relevant context includes actors whose resources and influence bear on the undertaking's viability. Their broader propositions about all viable systems are premises of their approach. [SG-W014, pp. 63–65]

Consonance and resonance make one selected distinction particularly concrete. Consonance refers to potential compatibility among entities that might interact. Resonance concerns the harmonious interaction that actually develops. A favorable structural possibility is consequently distinguished from its realization in activity. The source relates this distinction to selecting relationships and engaging actors who control relevant resources. [SG-W014, pp. 65–66]

Viability, identity and organizational purpose#

The central VSM account is connected: local units respond using local knowledge; coordination addresses interference; cohesion and resource bargaining relate activities to the undertaking; audit supplies examination; intelligence brings changing wider conditions into view; policy addresses identity and direction. Channels and interpretation connect these functions.

These sources ask whose identity an organization preserves, how purposes are agreed, and what its measurements support. They locate decisions and responsibilities among participants with different information, capacities and authority.

S23 Le Moigne: purposeful modeling and organized activity#

A theory of modeling and its changing layers#

Jean-Louis Le Moigne's La théorie du système général: Théorie de la modélisation develops a connected account of contextual purpose, representation, organized processes, memory, coordination and adaptation. The relevant material concerns both how a model can economize inquiry and how a modeled arrangement can change the demands on its participants.

The 2006 presentation of the 1994 edition includes earlier layers, later rereadings, a postface and appendices. [UX-W027]

The 2006 preface positions the enterprise as a theory of systemic modeling rather than a universal ontology declaring what every natural system really is. The model is constructed for a project in a context. Ends, means, representations and reasoning can recursively revise one another. Finalization therefore includes the ongoing formation of purposes, rather than merely execution toward an eternally fixed goal. Choosing those purposes remains an epistemic and ethical responsibility. [UX-W027, PDF 13–15, 35–47]

The book does not present this as a finished formal calculus. It acknowledges incomplete tools for organization and memory, borrows extensively and permits plural methods. Its polemics challenge the dominance of analytical science. Classical methods remain available where appropriate; the objection is to their exclusive authority over every modeling task. [UX-W027, PDF 27, 35–47, 63]

A representation is selected for a question#

Le Moigne's precepts concern relevance to intentions, attention to a larger context, purposes and deliberate aggregation. A model includes selected traits and relations, rather than reproducing its object in every respect. Complexity consequently concerns the representation and its question, not simply a count of variables possessed by an object independently of every observer. The choice of what to aggregate can simplify inquiry or conceal what makes the question difficult. [UX-W027, PDF 51–69]

His “General System” is a modeling artifact, distinct from the aspiration to describe a single universal System-Universe. Context, project, activity, structure and changing identity enter the definition of the modeled object. His triangulation asks what it is, what it does and what it becomes. The point is to keep several aspects in relation, rather than infer function solely from a parts list or treat one instantaneous picture as the complete history. [UX-W027, PDF 70–94]

Systemography then constructs a particular model with reference to this general modeling device and to the observed object. Empirical correspondence is partial and purpose-dependent. Internal consistency and usefulness are different questions: a coherent formal construction can fail to address the intended situation. Conversely, a limited model can be useful without being a complete causal reconstruction. [UX-W027, PDF 95–110]

The observer and the representation-making process can themselves become objects of modeling. Intentions, values and disciplinary conventions affect what is selected and what a measure is taken to mean. Le Moigne's discussion of economic indicators, for example, refuses to let one aggregate stand for every dimension of well-being. That is an argument for explicit purposes and interpretive accountability. [UX-W027, PDF 107–110]

Functional use can require less internal knowledge#

The calculator illustration challenges the claim that useful understanding always requires dissecting every internal component. A user can interpret operations, improve use, carry out some upkeep or connect a calculator with another device through knowledge of its behavior. Complete electronics knowledge is not required for each such task. This is a specified economy in what a particular user must know for a particular operation. [UX-W027, PDF 58]

A black-box description can support use while leaving the internal physical relations needed for diagnosis unspecified. Its adequacy depends on the task. [UX-W027, PDF 58–63]

Le Moigne economizes modeling by choosing relatively weakly connected regions while retaining their relevant environmental relations. [UX-W027, PDF 105–106]

Processors make transport and transformation explicit#

The process framework distinguishes changes in time, space and form: storage, transport and transformation. Matter, energy and information can be processed, while a processor can itself become the object of another process. The vocabulary permits recursion. The modeler selects the processes needed for the question. [UX-W027, PDF 111–125]

Networks of processors represent activities and their relations. A processor can be multifunctional, and the boundaries of a selected subnetwork must retain its connections to surroundings. The network is an account of organized transformations, not merely a picture of boxes. A matrix showing instantaneous connections cannot by itself replace a description of delays or the sequence in which connections are used. [UX-W027, PDF 126–149]

Le Moigne's ideal neutral connector is a modeling convention. Actual transport requires activity, which can be represented by its own processor. Elsewhere he expressly treats a real communication channel as a processor. The distinction between a schematic relation and the machinery that realizes it is part of the book's account. [UX-W027, PDF 134–136, 256]

Transduction similarly requires specific energy. Events must be turned into signals and signals into events through actual operations. Le Moigne proposes distinguishing maintenance or logistical processors to represent the provision and upkeep of processors themselves. In a simplified diagram maintenance can be aggregated into the operating subsystem, an explicit representational choice. [UX-W027, PDF 164, 171 note 2, 196]

A separate decision box is not always required#

The book's nine levels move through passive, active, regulated, informed, deciding, memorizing, coordinating, imagining and self-finalizing descriptions. They are a pedagogical modeling construction. Information attributed to a modeled object also differs from the modeler's own knowledge of it. [UX-W027, PDF 150–173]

The Watt-governor discussion makes a more concrete claim. A predictable algorithmic operation can be embodied in operating structure rather than retained in an additional artificial decision processor. A separate decision box may be a useful representation but is not always necessary. [UX-W027, PDF 162]

When the relevant logic is not completely specified, the account instead retains heuristics, memory of earlier events and a question of when to stop. The child's ability to continue spelling without knowing where to finish illustrates the missing termination judgment. Decisions can require history and purpose, rather than only a transformation of the present input. Le Moigne acknowledges that imagination and self-finalization are only preparatorily represented by this architecture. [UX-W027, PDF 162, 168–171]

The book considers differentiated projects and nonhierarchical possibilities while admitting limits to its formal tools. Its categories help pose who coordinates what, using which information and capabilities. [UX-W027, PDF 164–171]

Programmes reduce description by retaining a rule#

The trajectory discussion replaces a large sequence of state pictures with an initial picture and a schedule of parameter changes. An animation need not store every frame independently if a representation and programme specify how the parts move. The economy lies in the selected description and its reusable rule. [UX-W027, PDF 176–190, especially 182]

Organization is then described through structure together with memorized programmes. Memory here is a modeling hypothesis and need not correspond to a literal genome or a distinct physical memory organ. The description can preserve a functional relation across different material realizations. [UX-W027, PDF 191–196]

Common programmes, codes and representations can simplify a network of decision communications. Instead of requiring each participant to obtain a separately tailored instruction through a complicated chain, participants can access a shared resource. Le Moigne describes a common representation of operations and a pool of available programmes as possible supports for coordination. [UX-W027, PDF 203 –206]

He immediately preserves a crucial distinction: storing a programme does not make it execute. Memory and deciding are different processes. A code must be established and remain common, representations must be maintained, participants need access, and current purposes must guide selection. [UX-W027, PDF 203–204]

The book also recognizes disagreement about both means and ends. A shared store is not a proof that participants share values or accept the same action. Coalition and conflict questions remain. The interpretation of common memory as more democratic or more economical is attributed to the sources discussed, rather than established as a measured general effect. [UX-W027, PDF 199–208]

Stability can come from absorption, correction or anticipation#

Stability is relative to selected purposes and criteria. Le Moigne distinguishes maintaining behavior through an existing structure, changing programmes, modifying the structure, and changing purposes or environmental relations. Treating all of these as the same feedback operation obscures the different activities involved. [UX-W027, PDF 217–237]

He explicitly corrects an overbroad claim for feedback by presenting three routes to regulation. The first absorbs or decouples disturbances through buffers, shields, insulation or similar arrangements. The second corrects deviations through a returning loop. The third anticipates and compensates for disturbances. The modeler is advised to consider these alternatives rather than automatically installing a feedback account. [UX-W027, PDF 223–224]

Shells and buffers attenuate disturbances before they reach the operating process, reducing the occasions for a corrective response. [UX-W027, PDF 223–224]

Adaptation can require stored resources and spare capacity. Le Moigne describes stable regions in which a trial response can be attempted, evaluated and retained or rejected. If almost everything changes faster than the trial, its consequences become difficult to learn. Excessive coupling can remove those regions and consume the slack needed for new connections. Stability and learning are therefore connected under specified timing conditions, rather than simple opposites. [UX-W027, PDF 225–226]

Le Moigne distinguishes effectiveness relative to purposes from input/output efficiency: maintaining a stable outcome or reducing an input can serve different purposes. [UX-W027, PDF 228–234]

Sparse links can require complicated programmes#

Le Moigne's differentiation–coordination discussion identifies a concrete tension. A very sparse tree uses few links but can require elaborate indirect sequences to accomplish interactions for which a direct connection is absent. A complete mesh supplies more possible routes but can exceed cognitive and relational capacity. The economical link diagram and the economical programme need not coincide. [UX-W027, PDF 260–277, especially 268]

The proposed design task is consequently to organize the relation between network and programme. New connections can enlarge what coordinators can do, while too many overwhelm them. Missing links can force fragile detours. Resources, purposes, communication capacities and timing must be specified. [UX-W027, PDF 268]

Variety is not necessarily absorbed only at the top. Local arrangements can deal with distinctions before they reach a wider coordinator, and the rate of relevant change matters as well as the number of possibilities. As the Ashby account in S03 explains, not every state distinction requires an individually commanded response, and mere possession of alternatives is not sufficient for appropriate regulation. [UX-W027, PDF 269–271; S03]

The warning about using human beings to absorb the unmodeled residue is particularly direct. An apparently complete technical arrangement can depend on a person's continuing cognitive and relational work to cope with what it omits. Naming a coordination subsystem does not specify that capacity or establish that the job can be done at the required rate. [UX-W027, PDF 270]

His discussions of Simon, Galbraith and Voge are attributed connections within this framework. They help explain conditional assembly, information demand and autonomy with solidarity. [UX-W027, PDF 270– 277]

Formal definitions and quantitative claims#

Some formal definitions in the book are loose. A bijection alone does not establish an isomorphism preserving the relevant structure, and the printed descriptions of homomorphism and polymorphism contain inconsistent mapping language. [UX-W027, PDF 101]

The Voge passage also places two different quantities near one another: a proposed connection count and a number of possible configurations. They cannot serve as lower and upper bounds on the same measure without further definitions. Similarly, the toy performance expression whose normalized contact fraction peaks halfway does not establish universally optimal fifty-percent connectivity. [UX-W027, PDF 147–148, 215]

The book acknowledges the absence of sufficiently general metrics and rejects one scalar measure of organization. Its entropy, variety, information, value and energy analogies concern different quantities. Schematic curves do not establish that every noise input improves organization. [UX-W027, PDF 215, 240 –259, especially 247, 251]

The chapters on evolution and creative time retain changing agendas, historical codes and values. Le Moigne labels important claims as hypotheses and leaves finalization unfinished. The concluding contrast between design, analysis and simulation concerns different intentional uses of models. [UX-W027, PDF 278–301]

Morin through Le Moigne#

Le Moigne explicitly reconstructs organization through capacities to transform, produce, relate and maintain identity, drawing on Morin's La Méthode, volume 1. He connects producing with self-producing and describes active organization in relation to surroundings. [RGC-W028 through UX-W027, PDF 39–42, 209–214]

The second volume is related through autonomy that requires dependence and through auto-eco-reorganization. Self-maintenance involves environmental relations; greater organization does not imply escape from them. [RGC-W029 through UX-W027, PDF 209–214, 276–290]

Critics: accessibility and the need for internal mechanisms#

Motulsky's 1978 review praises a documented and coherent synthesis while finding the entry difficult. Examples are insufficient for an introductory reader, parts resist isolation, and the exposition makes nonlinear demands. The review concerns the 1977 first edition, rather than the later 2006 additions. [RGC-W024, 217–218]

Braudeau's critical discussion addresses a different issue. For the physical delimitation and explanation of the water–soil system, he objects to an anti-Cartesian or black-box orientation that can leave internal mechanisms inadequately specified. He retains triangulation and operating, information and pilot models while recasting the description around a structural representative volume. The account shows how a model useful for one purpose may omit physical relations necessary for another. [RGC-W026, §3.1, printed pp. 16–25/PDF pp. 18–27]

Braudeau's stronger assertion that a black-box approach prevents an account of organization must be read alongside Le Moigne's explicit internal networks, programmes and permission to use classical methods where appropriate. [RGC-W026; UX-W027, PDF 63, 126–149, 191–216]

The author's later retrospective#

Le Moigne's 2015 chronicle derives from a revised 2014 oral account, with an editorial introduction by Dominique Genelot. It describes the formation and later development of the modeling programme. As autobiography, it identifies how the author understood his own questions. [RGC-W025]

The recollection of industrial optimization is especially pertinent. Fragile estimates entered elaborate models, while a single profit criterion organized the calculation. Le Moigne's concern was both the reliability of inputs and the choice of what was being optimized. Sophisticated computation cannot by itself decide whether omitted factors are negligible or whether one objective captures the purposes of the organization's members. The account is a criticism of the problem formulation. [RGC-W025, PDF 2]

He later distinguishes the published model from the situated, tentative process of constructing it. Merely replacing the word “model” with “modeling” can leave that work unexamined. His retrospective relates practical action, epistemic justification and ethical reflection, and treats algorithmic methods as possible heuristics within a wider inquiry. The testimony supports an account of his methodological intention while leaving model adequacy to the purposes, evidence and criticism relevant to each application. [RGC-W025, PDF 5–6]

S24 Capra and Luisi: living organization, meaning and integrative design#

A broad synthesis with several kinds of claim#

Fritjof Capra and Pier Luigi Luisi's The Systems View of Life connects biological organization, cognition, social relationships and ecology. Its concluding design material brings these themes into questions of energy, materials, buildings and institutions. The breadth is substantive: the authors explain relationships among self-maintenance, embodied capability, meaning and wider dependencies. [WME-W006; SG-W011, introduction]

The authors describe scientific models as limited, approximate and subject to empirical examination. Their historical narrative about a movement from mechanism toward systems also contains philosophical, ethical and political commitments. A scientific model, a history of ideas and a proposed response to ecological interdependence have different warrants. The book itself says ecological connections do not logically entail ethical norms, while proposing a psychological route through identification with a wider world. [WME-W006, introduction, especially PDF 44; SG-W011]

Relations change what components can do#

The organismic account distinguishes organization from an added nonphysical life force. Properties arise through the way components are related and active together. Objects, quantities and structures remain important, even though a parts list alone can omit the relations responsible for a capability. The account is therefore not accurately described as rejecting every form of analysis. [WME-W006, chs. 1, 4, especially PDF 117–142]

The hemoglobin illustration gives the claim a mechanism: the arrangement of subunits changes their binding behavior, so the assembled organization is not described adequately by assigning each isolated subunit an unchanged role. The authors use this to discuss emergence and downward causation without requiring an extra mystical force. Their discussion leaves philosophical differences between stronger and weaker accounts of emergence open. [WME-W006, ch. 8, PDF 245–250]

Repeated patterns can also economize specification. Symmetry permits the description of a repeated arrangement without independently specifying every instance. Homochirality narrows combinatorial variants in molecular arrangements. These are particular ways in which organized constraints alter possibilities. [WME-W006, PDF 265–266]

The mathematical chapter supplies attractors, basins, sensitivity, bifurcations and generative rules as a repertoire for inquiry. It expressly distinguishes a mathematical framework from an empirical scientific explanation: the framework needs a suitable application. The treatment is qualitative and sometimes loose—iteration need not be nonlinear, and a particular logistic-map parameter does not demonstrate chaos for all parameters. [WME-W006, ch. 6, PDF 167–203]

Autopoiesis maintains an organization through exchange#

The biological account centers on a network of reactions that produces components, including the boundary supporting those reactions. Organization can persist while particular components and structural details change. The maintained cell is an ongoing production process rather than a fixed collection of matter. Nutrients and energy enter, waste leaves, and the network's activity sustains the conditions for further activity. [WME-W006, ch. 7, PDF 205–230]

Operational closure concerns the organization of processes. It is not thermodynamic independence. The identity of the self-maintaining organization still depends on resources and conditions outside it. A

history of structural coupling also affects the responses available: the present arrangement embodies a history rather than starting without constraints at each encounter. [WME-W006, ch. 7]

The book distinguishes self-organization, autopoiesis and autopoiesis associated with cognition. An organized pattern can form without satisfying the self-producing conditions, and an artificial self-producing structure can raise further questions about whether it counts as alive. The text explicitly reports a necessary-but-not-sufficient qualification to autopoiesis, although it subsequently returns to broader equivalence language in the biological domain. [WME-W006, PDF 219–221, 258]

Reproduction is also distinguished from the identity of an already living individual. Its importance for continuation of lineages does not mean that every living individual must reproduce. The framework asks first how a unit maintains the organization capable of participating in reproduction. Whether a larger aggregate itself satisfies the same criteria remains a further question. [WME-W006, PDF 221]

Assembly, maintenance and historical origin differ#

The molecular chapters distinguish thermodynamically favored assembly, energy-throughput-dependent dynamics and kinetically constrained pathways. Confinement, binding, catalysis and signaling can alter what happens. Their description depends on what lies inside the selected boundary: enzymes treated as internal rules in one account can be externally supplied preparations in another. [WME-W006, ch. 8, PDF 231–279]

The authors explicitly acknowledge manual additions and micromanipulation in reconstitution experiments. Such experiments can show that a prepared collection performs an activity under laboratory conditions. They do not establish that the same collection spontaneously assembled without supplied components, nor that it describes the actual historical path by which life originated. The origin-of-life chapter openly presents that historical problem as unsolved. [WME-W006, PDF 243; ch. 10, PDF 329–367]

Minimal cells are consequently relative to the functions and environment being specified. A prepared vesicle may depend on externally supplied enzymes, ribosomes or nutrients. Some replicating core/shell systems discussed in the book are expressly not living. [WME-W006, PDF 350–361]

The proposed explanation for unusual molecular entrapment in vesicles is likewise labeled speculative. Similar power-law appearances do not establish one causal mechanism or complete metabolism. The book also acknowledges small tested subsets in protein research. [WME-W006, PDF 357–366]

Genetic instructions retain a reading apparatus#

The chapters on evolution connect gene and protein networks, regulatory feedback, epigenetic processes, symbiosis, structural constraints and historical contingency. One particularly relevant distinction is between stored sequence and the system that uses it. DNA instructions require a protein-reading apparatus and a cellular setting. The text's compact-disc/player analogy makes the relation accessible: a record does not generate the activity independently of the machinery that interprets it. [WME-W006, ch. 9, especially PDF 314–316]

Patrick Bateson's guest essay also distinguishes broad developmental epigenetics from molecular silencing and warns that observed effects across generations can wash out. Such observations are not automatically proof of enduring evolutionary genetic change. The guest's qualifications remain distinct from stronger surrounding rhetoric. [WME-W006, guest essay PDF 303–310]

The human-evolution chapter then proposes connections among tools, hands, brains, language, dependency and social relations. Large brains have metabolic and birth costs in the account; capability is

not described as an unqualified benefit. Merrill’s criticism of this historical sequence and its chronology is discussed below. [WME-W006, ch. 11, PDF 368–386]

Cognition is broader than consciousness in this account#

The cognition chapters define mind through embodied process and interaction rather than an isolated store of representations. A living system's structure and history condition how it perceives and acts. “Cognition” is used broadly for that relation; consciousness and reflective experience are more specific questions. The authors even disagree explicitly about applying “mind” to organisms without brains. [WME-W006, ch. 12, PDF 387–427, especially 391]

Michel Bitbol's guest essay proposes that phenomenal experience is a methodological prerequisite for science and that functional third-person descriptions do not explain its sheer presence. He favors constraints among first-, second- and third-person inquiry. This is an identifiable philosophical position within the book. The text describes its clinical examples as hints and acknowledges a lack of evidence for a stronger surrounding hypothesis. [WME-W006, PDF 410–416]

Interpreting a signal can depend on embodied capability and history without establishing every metaphysical conclusion discussed later. Spiritual transformation, religion and scientific explanation are treated in different registers. The recorded disagreement with a purely material emergence account further prevents presenting the book as a single undisputed doctrine of consciousness. [WME-W006, ch. 13, especially PDF 449–450]

Social organization adds meaning, rules and power#

The main integrative architecture relates form or organization, matter or embodiment, and process; meaning adds a further dimension for human action. A social network is not explained solely by its topology. Its connections involve language, cultural constraints, purposes and power. The authors explicitly say that understanding the chemistry of a cellular network does not supply the material mechanisms of a social one. Domain knowledge remains necessary. [WME-W006, ch. 14, PDF 466–484]

This is also where they qualify the transfer of autopoiesis. Higher-order cases are described as unclear and speculative. A social system whose members are living cells or organisms is not thereby proved to be an autopoietic network in its own right. The book reconstructs Maturana and Varela's restriction of the term to cellular production and their wider use of operational closure. [WME-W006, PDF 482–483]

Luhmann's alternative, reconstructed by the authors, treats communications as producing further communications and sustaining social roles and boundaries. Such boundaries are cultural and symbolic, rather than necessarily a membrane in physical space. Rules can be broken; molecules do not choose whether physical relations apply. [WME-W006, PDF 483–491]

The social-theory reconstructions are also mediated. Giddens and Habermas enter through other interpreters, while the power account involving John Kenneth Galbraith is distinct from Jay Galbraith's organizational information-processing work. [WME-W006, ch. 14]

Designed rules and emergent work both matter#

Organizations contain designed structures—formal rules, routines and assigned authority—and emergent networks through which people learn and solve practical difficulties. The book treats both as necessary. Formal stability can support reliable activity, while communities of practice retain tacit knowledge and adaptive capability. Work-to-rule illustrates how much functioning can depend on activity omitted from formal instructions. [WME-W006, PDF 498–507]

Informal relations are not automatically flexible or beneficial. The authors' old-boys-network example supplies a counterexample within their own discussion. Nor is a crisis guaranteed to improve an organization: it can lead to breakdown as well as breakthrough. Creating conditions for participation and meaningful response is a proposed way to support change. [WME-W006, PDF 502–505]

The account retains relationships, communication, skills, learning, formal rules and power. The authors argue that meaningful impulses can require less change effort than coercive direction. The workshops described elsewhere similarly require funding, substantial participation, teaching, practical upkeep and dialogue; positive participant reports are different from controlled outcome evaluations. [WME-W006, chs. 13–14]

Ecology supplies dependencies and tolerance limits#

Ecological persistence involves energy flows, cycling, decomposition, overlapping functions and continuing interactions. Redundancy can help preserve activity when one contributor is disrupted, while disturbances outside tolerance limits can collapse it. Diversity has the proposed strategic value within a connected community; assembling diverse parts without suitable relations can also generate friction. [WME-W006, ch. 16, PDF 541–574]

Stephan Harding's Daisyworld guest essay illustrates how temperature regulation can arise through feedback between organisms, growth and albedo without foresight or a coordinating committee. The simulated regulation is a property of the specified model. Later variants reportedly retain resilience over a range and then collapse when available habitat capacity is exhausted. [WME-W006, guest essay PDF 259 –263]

The book is explicit that ordinary ecosystem autopoiesis remains open, particularly the requirement of a self-made boundary. Its argument about Gaia is a proposed higher-order case. It also states that ecology does not itself supply justice, democracy or other human values. Those commitments require human judgment alongside ecological understanding. [WME-W006, PDF 550–560]

Ecological education is itself organized work. The integrated curriculum described requires difficult scheduling, summer preparation and coordination among teachers, parents and administrators. Integration changes the pattern of effort rather than making preparation disappear. [WME-W006, PDF 568]

Integrative design can change several loads together#

The closing engineering account reconstructs Amory Lovins and colleagues' integrative design. The proposed method brings architects, engineers and designers together early to consider relationships among subsystems and seek several benefits from a change. The objective differs from improving isolated components under unchanged assumptions about the loads they must serve. [WME-W006, ch. 18, PDF 660–670]

The building example gives a causal sequence. Better windows, lighting and office equipment reduce the peak cooling demand. A cooling system can then be renovated at a smaller required capacity, helping offset other retrofit costs. The authors report the Empire State Building project as cutting peak cooling load by a third and saving $17 million in cooling-system capital. The onsite window work and installed equipment remain part of realization. [WME-W006, PDF 667]

The piping example changes the physical resistance of the route. Replacing long, narrow, sharply turning pipes with shorter, wider and straighter routes reduces pumping demand. Smaller pumps, motors and electrical systems can then become possible. The text reports at least eighty-six percent electricity savings

in the cited loop and lower associated capital requirements. The result depends on the loop's flows and installation constraints. [WME-W006, PDF 667–668]

The lightweight-car account describes another cascade: lower mass and altered aerodynamic demand can reduce loads on other systems. It also retains the conditions of material production, propulsion and supporting infrastructure. The book acknowledges energy for separating hydrogen and says a more efficient vehicle cannot alone resolve all urban, social and environmental problems associated with car dependence. Its forecasts, prices and transition dates remain historical proposals rather than current recommendations. [WME-W006, PDF 662–666]

The smart-grid proposal retains substantial coordination machinery: communication, forecasting, geographical and technological diversity, storage, metering and governance. Its simulations concern specified combinations and conditions. [WME-W006, PDF 668–674]

Cascades and service cycles retain providers#

The coffee-farm cluster connects several transformations: residues support mushrooms, further residues feed animals or worms, manure enters biogas production, and remaining material fertilizes soil. The arrangement tries to make one activity's output useful to another. It depends on organisms, water, a digester, management, labor and appropriate flows. Calling it a cascade specifies a productive relation; calling it “zero waste” remains a design aspiration rather than thermodynamic independence. [WME-W006, PDF 689–692, fig. 18.2]

The distinction between biological and technical nutrients similarly depends on preserving material quality and avoiding contamination. Repeated use requires suitable separation and processing. A service-and-flow arrangement in which a manufacturer retains ownership can create reasons to recover components, but also needs collection, disassembly, reverse logistics and an enduring provider. Changing ownership does not execute those activities. [WME-W006, PDF 693–695]

Passive building features—orientation, shape, insulation and windows—can reduce heating, cooling or lighting loads. Their performance depends on climate, use, materials and realization. The relevant information is how an arrangement changes the physical loads and the work assigned to active equipment. [WME-W006, PDF 695–696]

The agricultural and ecological proposals also retain local knowledge, collective work and sometimes greater labor intensity. More jobs can be part of the authors' social objective, while lower material throughput is another objective. They are not identical with minimizing all work. The concluding call for cooperation among government, business and civil society identifies institutional work still to be done. [WME-W006, PDF 683–688, 701–702]

Institutional purpose and health claims need their own warrants#

Marjorie Kelly's guest essay connects ownership purpose, membership, governance, capital and networks. Its wind, forest, employee, foundation and credit-union illustrations are reported examples of generative ownership and an agenda for further research. [WME-W006, guest essay PDF 636–640]

The health chapter relates care to context, prevention and social conditions. Fabrizio Benedetti's guest essay supplies a narrower distinction: improvement in a placebo group can include natural course and bias, whereas a specific context-induced response needs a different inference. Expectation, learning, reward and anxiety can involve several mechanisms. [WME-W006, ch. 15, especially guest essay PDF 520 –525]

Luisi on life, cognition and autopoiesis#

Luisi's 2016 What Is Life? A Systemic Approach, based on a 2015 conference, explicitly combines biological structure, environment and cognition. The organism's capabilities are specific to its surroundings; cognition is used without requiring an anthropomorphic mind. Outside nutrients and energy sustain the process. [RGC-W013, article and figures]

The paper extends its account to social life and environmental responsibility. These are the author's broader interpretations. [RGC-W013]

The abstract of Bitbol and Luisi's 2004 Autopoiesis with or without Cognition proposes a necessary-but-not-sufficient relation and distinguishes metabolism from environmental interaction. The later book reconstructs the proposal. Luisi's 2022 Reflections on Autopoiesis abstract raises questions about cognition and molecular versus wider autopoiesis. [RGC-W016; WME-W008]

Reception includes specific criticism#

Johny Van Aerde's review reconstructs the book's historical and systemic organization, with particular attention to its biological, cognitive, social and ecological connections. It is an enthusiastic professional response. [WME-W007]

Kübler, Merrill and Anway's collaborative review values the breadth and connected themes while criticizing uneven depth, inaccessible chemistry, schematic mathematics and dated disciplinary material. They specifically contrast the book's account of contingency with a more linear human-evolution narrative, question how examples were selected, and ask for testing and continued revision. [RGC-W014, review section PDF 120–135]

Merrill's separate 24 July 2014 blog review expands the anthropology objection, challenging the proposed links among bipedalism, tools, family arrangements and cultural chronology, as well as reuse of an older narrative. The blog and collaborative review are related critical voices. [RGC-W015; RGC-W014]

S25 Homeokinetics, coordination dynamics and systems philosophy#

Distinct questions about organized persistence#

The sources in this section pursue different projects. Iberall and Soodak propose a physical account of nested complex dynamics. Kelso develops coordination dynamics with empirically identified variables and task-dependent meaning. Gell-Mann distinguishes kinds of complexity. An abridgment of Laszlo’s systems philosophy and reconstructions by Huchingson and Leaning introduce a wider ontological proposal.

Homeokinetics: long actions within nested dynamics#

The Primer on Homeokinetics describes complex systems through a separation of time scales: a long internal action or “factory day” differs from relatively rapid local exchanges among components. Horizontal interactions and vertical relations among nested levels are both needed in the proposed account. Describing a system requires identifying those physical processes at an appropriate observational scale. [WME-W012, printed 2–8]

The authors distinguish a mathematical framework from the physical and engineering path that connects it with an actual system. Discrete descriptions and continuum approximations also have different conditions. Their declared physical reductionism does not mean simply announcing that biology reduces to chemistry and chemistry to physics; the work lies in specifying the intervening organization, exchanges and scales. The primer supplies a programme and examples. [WME-W012, 2–10]

The supplier analogy makes one relevant claim concrete. A factory could not operate within a compact time and place if every subcomponent at every level had to be constructed anew. Previously produced components arrive from other processes. Local operation employs a history and a surrounding organization of supply. The example explains why the time and capability represented by a supplied component cannot be attributed solely to the current act inside the factory. [WME-W012, 8]

Formation, a long maintenance phase, and degradation are separated. The action sustaining a familiar structure may differ from what assembled it or what eventually dissolves it. Low-energy catalytic changes can switch among more energetic action modes. In that account, a signal negotiates a transition while the active process retains the energy and material needed for performance. A small switch is not a source of the whole activity's energy. [WME-W012, 10–15]

The grandfather clock is an especially concrete example. A falling weight supplies gravitational energy, the escapement couples to pendular motion, gearing produces further time scales, and periodic winding replenishes the store. Oiling and a suitable suspension remain necessary. The authors examine transient changes after winding as well as sustained timekeeping. [WME-W012, 11–15]

The oil-can oscillator and other illustrations similarly involve specific couplings and replenishment. The primer is interested in how relatively autonomous motions become coordinated while retaining different scales. The proposed physical explanation requires the forces, energy source and stability conditions. [WME-W012, 11–16]

Its house illustration extends the maintenance distinction accessibly. A house may look like a completed solid object, but repair and replacement require continuing flows of materials, costs and action from its first use. The maintenance engineer sees a persistent flow process where an owner may initially see a finished construction. [WME-W012, 21]

The proposed social physics remains unfinished#

The social passages extend physical language to population, trade, political organization and war. The authors intend condensed and dispersed population phases as literal physical explanations, not merely decorative analogies, and propose civilizational time scales. That intention does not establish the corresponding equations, measurements or historical validity. [WME-W012, 16–23]

The primer's final qualification is unusually explicit. Its account of values and command-control is far from complete or adequately determined, and the hoped-for ultimate neurochemical reduction may be a false hope. [WME-W012, 23]

The abstract of Iberall’s 1985 Outlining Social Physics for Modern Societies proposes flows of matter, energy, momentum, population and value in trade. The later primer develops his nested physical architecture. [WME-W013, abstract; WME-W012]

Kelso: coordination with continuing autonomy#

Kelso's 2008 An Essay on Understanding the Mind engages sympathetically with Iberall but develops a distinct account. Coordination concerns how several processes form a collective pattern while retaining their own tendencies. Its functional information is meaningful in relation to a task and the activity organized, rather than a free-standing count of messages. Relevant order variables and control parameters must be identified empirically. [RGC-W017, 180–190]

The extended Haken–Kelso–Bunz relation includes a difference between the intrinsic frequencies of the participating oscillators, nonlinear coupling and noise. The relative phase can then exhibit regimes that the original symmetric equation did not contain. Kelso expressly warns against assigning the extension's results to the unchanged original equation: symmetry breaking changes fixed points and bifurcation structure, and is crucial to the metastable behavior being discussed. [RGC-W017, 188 and notes 2–3]

Fully locked coordination and complete independence are limiting cases. A metastable regime contains tendencies both to bind together and to act independently. Components can linger in a coordinated relation and then depart, rather than remaining permanently locked in one asymptotically stable pattern. The physical components and their coupling remain necessary. [RGC-W017, 187–193]

Kelso proposes dwell and escape times to describe these tendencies. Dwell time concerns the persistence of a collective tendency; escape time concerns expression of the elements' autonomy. Their ratio is a candidate description of the quality of metastability. The measures require operational definitions, and any transition threshold must be worked out for the particular system. [RGC-W017, 192–193, notes 5–6]

The coordination issue is therefore not solved by maximizing either synchronization or independence. Too little coupling can prevent a useful collective activity; too much locking can remove flexibility. Which relation is satisfactory depends on the task. The essay's comparison across behavioral and neural examples is a programme of identifiable relationships. [RGC-W017, 190–202]

Switching also need not require a localized physical switch. A distributed pattern can lose stability and another pattern become possible through the dynamics of interaction. The explanation retains oscillators, coupling, changing parameters and energy. Absence of one command location does not mean absence of determining processes or continuing work. [RGC-W017, 199–202]

The essay relates stability to reported neural measurements, including BOLD changes as coordinated patterns lose stability. The broader extensions to mind, social activity and meditation remain tentative essay proposals. [RGC-W017, 199, note 10, concluding discussion]

Gell-Mann: a short account can be hard to find and use#

What Is Complexity? distinguishes information measures from time and space required for computation. Algorithmic information content concerns the shortest programme producing a specified string and halting. An incompressible random string can have high content by that definition, yet random gibberish does not capture every ordinary meaning of complexity. Gell-Mann therefore distinguishes a concise description of regularities from the complete specification of the individual entity. [WME-W014, 16–17]

His effective complexity concerns those regularities. The description depends on coarse-graining, prior knowledge, language, coding and the reference machine. Two apparently different measures can answer different questions. A long string containing a very simple repeated relation can have much mutual algorithmic information while its organizing regularity has a brief description. The amount of shared pattern and the length of the rule describing it are not identical. [WME-W014, 16–17]

The adaptive-schema account then connects observation and activity. A system identifies regularities and compresses them into a schema used for description, prediction or prescribed behavior. Comparison with further data and the consequences of action affect competition among schemata. This process can make mistakes: a pattern can be imagined where it is absent, or an actual relation ignored. The account does not treat every acquired rule as correct merely because it is compact. [WME-W014, 17–18]

Prediction and discovery add separate demands. A simple rule with specified boundary conditions can require lengthy computation to produce a detailed prediction. Finding a short rule from data can be difficult even when using it later is straightforward. Gell-Mann relates these questions to logical depth and crypticity, while saying that a more precise mathematical account will appear elsewhere. [WME-W014, 18–19]

Gell-Mann separates a description from the work of discovering it and computing its predictions. Compactness of a rule can coexist with difficult discovery or lengthy execution. [WME-W014]

Laszlo's patterned flows and a mediated larger architecture#

The anonymous abridgment of Laszlo's The Systems View of the World presents enduring structures through patterned flows. A structure channels later activity, while that activity sustains or changes the organization. Human action belongs within wider ecological and social relations rather than an isolated world of self-sufficient individuals. [SG-W038]

Huchingson's article and Leaning's thesis reconstruct the foundational philosophy of Laszlo's Introduction to Systems Philosophy, distinct from the popular The Systems View of the World. [RGC-W018; RGC-W019; RGC-W020; RGC-W021]

Huchingson reconstructs a connected ontology of natural and cognitive systems: ordered wholeness, adaptive stabilization, self-organization and nested relations. Systems can contain other systems, and an enduring identity is formed through relations to an environment. Greater organization permits alternative programmes of action and can support modifying surroundings. The account is a philosophical architecture, not merely a list of examples. [RGC-W020, discussion of reality and environment]

He also reconstructs Laszlo's connection between adaptation, persistence, experience and value. Cognitive systems can pursue imagined conditions, while knowledge arises through observer–world interaction. These are proposed ontological and epistemological relations. Survival or satisfaction does not automatically settle a human ethical choice. [RGC-W020, environment, values and causality sections]

The reconstructions include methodological criticism#

Huchingson's comparison with Whitehead preserves differences. Whitehead's actual occasions are not simply Laszlo's nested composite systems. He asks whether an abstract grid is being imposed on experience, whether the primordial matrix coheres with the universal system categories, and how emergence addresses differences in agency. In particular, a matrix that generates systems while not itself being a system raises a problem for the ontology as presented. [RGC-W020]

The article's later theological reconciliation and information-processing extensions belong to Huchingson. [RGC-W020, critical comparison, conclusion and notes]

Leaning's selected section 3.4.3 reconstructs the same broad programme while questioning its grounds for validation. Presupposing that the world is systematically ordered does not establish that a particular general model adequately describes it. Combining correspondence-based confirmation with theory-laden scientific paradigms also creates methodological tensions that require explanation. The objection concerns justification and empirical productivity. [RGC-W021, §3.4.3, printed pp. 89–92/PDF pp. 92–95]

S26 Rosen through Louie and Siekmann: organization, repair and realization#

Metabolism and repair through Louie and Siekmann#

Robert Rosen's relational biology asks what organized functional relations distinguish living activity. The abstract of his 1958 A Relational Theory of Biological Systems identifies metabolism and repair. A. H. Louie's affirmative 2017 chapter and Ivo Siekmann's critical 2017 preprint reconstruct later formulations as well as this earlier programme. [W102; W104; W103]

Louie develops the architecture of Life Itself and Anticipatory Systems. Rosen was his doctoral supervisor, and Louie continues the intellectual programme. Siekmann offers mathematical and modeling criticism. [RGC-W022; RGC-W023; W104; W103]

Relations specify what processes produce and maintain#

Relational biology abstracts from particular material realizations to examine organized dependencies. It asks what different mechanisms can share in their functional organization. That is more specific than saying everything is connected. A process that transforms material, a process that makes the transforming machinery and a process that maintains that productive capability have different places in the account. Louie also respects molecular biology's successful explanations; his target is the claim that they exhaust every question. [W104, 2–5, 15–24]

Louie's diagrams distinguish a flow from the processor constraining or producing it. For a mapping f from A to B, an input a is transformed to an output b by f. He associates the input with material cause, the processor with efficient cause, and the output with final cause in this formal vocabulary. These terms organize the explanation; “final cause” at an output node does not by itself establish foresight or a conscious purpose. [W104, 15–16]

Two processes can then relate in different ways. In material entailment, the output of one becomes material for the other: one transformation supplies what another processes. In functional entailment, what one produces is the processor of another transformation. The distinction identifies a relation between making something and making the capability that makes something. Ordinary chaining of outputs is different from production of the processors themselves. [W104, 17–18]

For gambits engineering, this is a substantive account of continuing capability. A momentary transformation does not explain how the machinery that performs it remains available. Treating a process as a box with an output can omit the production and replacement activity that sustains that box. Relational biology explicitly puts that activity into the model.

Metabolism and repair address different continuities#

In Siekmann's reconstruction, metabolism is represented by a map f: A → B. It can be interpreted as an enzyme transforming inputs while remaining unchanged during the particular operation. Real enzymes can nevertheless degrade. A repair component Φ produces or replaces the transforming component f, so sustained operation requires more than a currently available metabolic map. [W103, 6–7]

The notation places Φ's output among mappings from A to B. This expresses production of a functional component, not merely production of another quantity of the original metabolic output. The repair component also needs maintenance, which appears to create a regress: a repairer for the repairer, then another repairer for that repairer. The proposed architecture seeks to close the productive relations rather than add an indefinitely external succession of components. [W103, 6–9]

The environmental boundary remains open to resources. Components can replace one another while drawing on matter and energy supplied from outside. Internal production of efficient causes does not mean that every material cause, energy source or surrounding condition is produced within the organism. Both expositions retain the difference between organizational closure and thermodynamic independence. [W103, 7–9; W104, 15–24]

A closed path and full closure differ#

Louie describes hierarchical cycles in which two or more efficient causes enter a closed path. This requires the relevant functional composition, not simply any return arrow in a diagram. A loop of material transformations and a cycle in which processes produce other processors are different relations. [W104, 18–20]

Having such a path among some processes is also different from a claim that every efficient cause relevant to the system is internally entailed. The stronger closure condition demands accounting for all the efficient causes within the selected model. Choosing the system and its modeled functions remains consequential. Neither the circle's appearance nor its name supplies the omitted physical realization, environmental resources or scope. [W104, 20–25; W103, 8–10]

This makes repair organization a positive explanatory proposal even where broader conclusions remain disputed. A system can potentially persist longer than individual components if its organization replaces them in time. To establish an actual instance, the components, their transformations, degradation and resource conditions still need identification. [W103, 7–10]

Siekmann's replication-map objection#

For the simple metabolism–repair architecture, a further replication map β is supposed to repair Φ. The operative condition is β(f) = Φ. Siekmann argues that one can choose a map satisfying that relation and assign it a parameter b* in an associated family of maps. He does not object that writing such a family is mathematically impossible. [W103, 8–9]

His objection concerns what follows. Constructing or parameterizing the map does not show that the natural system produces the corresponding physical process. In particular, deriving the family through evaluation maps does not establish the material identification claimed for it. The distinction is between an available mathematical construction and a realized biological organization. [W103, 8–10]

Siekmann therefore proposes treating closure to efficient causation as a postulate or hypothesis to test in concrete biological systems. This preserves the substantive idea of mutually sustained repair. It disputes the claim that the desired realization follows from the abstract architecture alone. [W103, 9–10]

The biological identification is explicitly postulated#

Louie's affirmative account distinguishes necessary and sufficient conditions for life. A property can include all living systems while also including nonliving ones. Collecting several necessary conditions can narrow the class; declaring their joint sufficiency adds a biological identification that needs to be seen explicitly. The chapter explains this movement before giving its final taxonomy. [W104, 8–11]

Near the conclusion, the “Postulate of Life” identifies an organism with a natural system realizing an (M,R)-system. The ensuing equivalence between life and closure to efficient causation is presented as the “Fundamental Theorem of Relational Biology.” Its formal derivation incorporates that stated postulate. The biological identification enters as a postulate in the derivation, rather than as an independent empirical finding. [W104, 25–27]

Louie's generalization to a union of interacting organisms includes an ecosystem as itself an organism “in some sense.” That is a qualified extension within his framework. [W104, 26]

Anticipation is not the same as life or impredicativity#

Through Louie, an anticipatory system contains an internal predictive model of itself and its environment and acts in the present in accordance with predictions. The antecedent action is the defining feature. A future event need not physically cause the current one; the current model and its use are part of the present organization. [W104, 11–12; RGC-W023 through W104]

The chapter distinguishes the class of living systems, the class of anticipatory systems and the wider class it calls impredicative. It gives a socioeconomic system as a nonliving anticipatory example. Anticipation is therefore not sufficient for life even in this affirmative account. Nor should every automatic response be called anticipation simply because its eventual consequence can be described. [W104, 11–15]

Impredicativity concerns self-referencing definition and the relational dependencies represented. It is not a synonym for an incomprehensible system or a moral ranking of complexity. Louie warns about the misleading status connotations of “simple” and “complex.” The distinction between classes does not itself specify which transitions a dynamical system can undergo. [W104, 12–15]

Modeling relations and purpose-bound mechanisms#

Siekmann explains the category-theoretic modeling relation using algebraic curves and associated algebraic objects. The example shows how mathematical structures and relationships can be related, rather than reducing category theory to arrows between unnamed boxes. A meaningful analogy depends on the structures and relations preserved. [W103, 10–14]

His later argument distinguishes a model's purpose from an exhaustive reconstruction of nature. Applied models make simplifying assumptions to investigate selected behavior. Successful predictions can fail to distinguish several mechanisms, and congruence between a model and every causal feature of the natural system may be unverifiable. The model can still provide insight into the selected aspect. [W103, 17–24]

This leads to a disagreement about the word “mechanistic.” Siekmann argues that a relational model can be a kind of mechanistic model if it specifies how the represented interactions produce the selected behavior. That interpretation does not assert that the whole natural system is nothing but the modeled mechanism. Refining a question can require revising assumptions and adding detail, while the resulting model remains partial. [W103, 18, 23]

The choice to abstract internal material structure is consequently one modeling decision, not proof that such structure never matters. A network can leave interpretation, parameter identification or material feasibility underdetermined. Kinetic and physical constraints can help answer those questions. This is a substantive modeling objection alongside the replication-map argument. [W103, 20–26]

Siekmann points toward compositional reaction networks, biochemical realizations and closure-of-constraints approaches. In his reconstruction they illustrate ways of retaining organized relations while giving components material and kinetic content. They are proposals for further operationalization. [W103, 23–26]

The affirmative and critical accounts thus leave a clearly specified literature question: how does a materially realized organization produce and replace the processes on which its continued operation depends? The sources provide both a rich architecture for asking it and explicit disagreements about which conclusions follow formally and which require biological evidence.

Part 2 Physical realization, regulation, and information#

These accounts describe specified physical behaviors, control problems and representations.

S01 Physical dynamics and passive behavior: mechanisms and operating conditions#

Material arrangement and behavior#

Material arrangement can supply a walking cycle, selective binding, attenuated vibration or a period of stellar support. The accounts below explain these mechanisms using different meanings of stability, function and passivity.

McGeer: walking as a natural dynamic mode#

Tad McGeer's 1990 Passive Dynamic Walking examines a class of two-legged machines that, once started on a shallow downward slope, can settle into a steady gait without active gait control. Gravity supplies the energy through descent. The selected opening distinguishes the problem of dynamic walking from maintaining static equilibrium throughout the motion, and distinguishes several ways active controllers can contribute. The example is informative because the detailed walking cycle need not be imposed as a succession of commanded joint positions. Geometry, mass distribution and the contact dynamics participate in generating it. [W053, abstract and §§1–2]

McGeer's discussion does not simply divide machines into controlled and uncontrolled. The comparison includes feedback toward end-of-step conditions, tracking a specified trajectory, and feedforward schedules supplemented by corrections to the initial conditions of later steps. These locate different tasks for the controller. They help explain why a gait can exploit natural motion without an active controller continuously prescribing its whole trajectory. [W053, §2]

The source reports a test machine as support for the passive effect, while its opening also proposes combining the dynamics with active energy input for a wider range of locomotion. The shallow slope and suitable machine design remain part of the supported accomplishment. A downhill walker is not an equal-task demonstration against every powered walker on level ground or irregular terrain.

Ikemata and Sano: a knee stop can participate in the gait#

Yoshito Ikemata and Akihito Sano's review explains passive walking as a way to study the mechanics of locomotion. The first page describes walking down a gentle slope without motors, sensors or a controller, with gravity as the energy source. Its account of McGeer's knee-equipped walker is mechanically specific: paired inner and outer legs constrain the demonstration to a sagittal plane; a stop prevents the knee bending backward; a curved foot also contributes to the arrangement. During swing the knee can bend and extend naturally, then reach the approximately straight configuration needed for contact and support. [W010, printed p. 2]

The stop therefore has a particular job in a sequence of motions. It permits some movement and restricts another, instead of supplying a general intelligent assessment of every possible footfall. [W010, printed p. 2]

Moon: level-ground walking retains energy input and torque compensation#

Jae-Sung Moon's 2021 paper examines a torso-equipped biped on level ground through a model and simulations. Its opening explicitly identifies the need to replace energy lost when the swing leg contacts the ground. The model divides a step into take-off, passive swing and contact phases. It treats motion in a two-dimensional sagittal plane, neglects scuffing in the model without knees, and assumes a completely inelastic contact without slip or rebound. These assumptions define the analyzed limit cycles. [W066, pp. 608–610, introduction and §II]

The passive swing is partial in a precise sense. Compensating torques can cancel the generalized torque applied to the leg coordinates while retaining a torque for the torso. When the torso is vertical, the relevant inputs can all be zero for that interval. With a torso deviation, corrective input remains. The absence of generalized forcing on selected coordinates consequently does not mean every actuator is inactive or that there is no energetic cost anywhere in the system. The arrangement separates functions through the coupled mechanics and chosen inputs. [W066, §II.3]

The simulations show how exploiting a natural trajectory can coexist with energy injection and stabilization. Their energy levels, collision assumptions and torso compensation specify how the modeled walker moves beyond downhill passive walking.

Lehn: molecular architecture stores distinctions that binding can read#

Jean-Marie Lehn's 1987 Nobel lecture defines supramolecular chemistry around intermolecular bonds and functions of associated chemical species. In the selected recognition discussion, merely binding is insufficient: recognition concerns binding with selection of a substrate and potentially a specified function. The architecture of binding sites, their number and arrangement, and surrounding molecular structure contribute to which association forms and how it persists. Lehn explicitly interprets this as information stored in architecture and read through formation and dissociation of the association. [GL-W009, printed pp. 446–447]

His complementarity includes energetic as well as geometric features. A lock-and-key picture based only on shape would omit part of the account. Thermodynamic and kinetic selectivity matter, and the balance of rigidity and flexibility affects what the receptor can do. A rigidly arranged structure can favor recognition, while exchange, regulation and cooperative changes can need built-in flexibility. The selected discussion thus explains both the capacity provided by a structure and the conditions under which that capacity changes. [GL-W009, p. 447]

Near the lecture's end, Lehn describes designed self-assembly as elaborating molecular components that spontaneously organize into a desired supramolecular architecture. The chemist selects and prepares the components and conditions. His molecular-device and “chemionics” discussion proposes combinations for detection, storage and signal processing. [GL-W009, pp. 483–484]

Rahimi and colleagues: tuning works within a changing frequency relation#

Fatemeh Rahimi, Reza Aghayari and Bijan Samali review tuned mass dampers for structural vibration control. In the selected discussion, a secondary mass and its tuned dynamic relationship with a structure can reduce a targeted response. The review also emphasizes a limitation of a single tuned mass damper: a change in structural frequency or damper parameters can impair effectiveness. The absence of a continuously computing feedback controller does not make the response independent of the frequencies and damping for which it was designed. [GL-W017, selected single-/multiple-TMD discussion]

The reviewed multiple-damper approach distributes natural frequencies over a range. The authors report studies in which this reduces sensitivity to uncertainty and can improve performance relative to an optimal single damper of the same total mass. Those comparisons belong to the studies and simplified forcing/model conditions summarized by the review. Widening a range, changing placement or introducing active/semi-active components creates different arrangements with different demands. [GL-W017, discussion of Xu/Igusa, Yamaguchi/Harnpornchai and subsequent studies]

NASA's stellar explanation: persistence has a fuel-dependent history#

NASA and the Night Sky Network's public explanation of stellar life cycles describes hydrostatic support as pressure opposing gravity. During the main sequence, nuclear reactions provide interior heat and radiation. Before the main sequence, contraction supplies heat before the core supports those reactions. Exhaustion of available core fuel changes what can continue; later phases depend on stellar mass, and eventual loss of sufficient support can lead to collapse. Approximate balance is a phase sustained under changing material conditions, not an assertion of permanent immobility. [GL-W088, institutional explanation]

The account explains naturally occurring organization through opposing effects, supply and changing regime, without an external operator continuously choosing its successive states.

Mechanical responses shaped by geometry#

Bertoldi, Vitelli, Christensen and van Hecke describe a collapsible shell called the buckliball. Its design takes a cue from the Hoberman Twist-O, a toy whose hinged struts let it collapse in one continuous motion. The buckliball uses a patterned elastic shell. Under pneumatic actuation, the shell buckles and folds into a smaller shape. The shell's geometry guides the buckling into the fold the designers want. [GL-W065, fig. 4]

Ling and colleagues' abstract for A survey on synthesis of compliant constant force/torque mechanisms proposes using engineered mechanical response to avoid complicated force-control systems. Nonlinear varying stiffness creates design problems addressed through kinetostatic modeling and optimization. [GL-W073, abstract/highlights]

Van Gerven and Stankiewicz organized process intensification around structure, energy, synergy and time. A later account they coauthored explains what some of those design choices aim to achieve. One aim is to make the conditions encountered by different molecules more uniform. Another is to increase the area over which a driving force acts. The framework applies these questions at scales from molecules to whole processing units. [GL-W074] [SMR-W001, fig. 2 and accompanying text]

S02 Constraints and error prevention: triggers, barriers and mistake-proofing#

What the arrangement changes#

The selected sources concern different ways of changing opportunities for error, exposure or harmful response. Some mechanisms trigger an action; some block an exposure; others remove a hazardous inventory or make an abnormality visible.

Evans and Madrzykowski: the thermal trigger has a response time#

David Evans and Daniel Madrzykowski's 1981 NBS report investigates the thermal response of selected fusible-link sprinklers. The opening explains a physical process: hot combustion products transfer heat to a thermal element; added energy first raises its temperature and then contributes to the phase change in its binding material. Sufficient fusion permits rupture of the link and activation. A rated activation temperature therefore does not alone determine when a sprinkler operates in a developing fire. Heat must reach the element, and the element has a thermal response. [W023, printed pp. 1–2]

The report describes sudden immersion in a hot gas flow as a way to characterize that response. Its exploratory apparatus uses a heat gun, tube, mixing/deflection arrangement and instrumented element. The selected methods state that flow turbulence, known to influence heat transfer, was not measured. Instrumentation itself required attention to mechanical robustness and heat conduction through attached wires. These details are useful because a thermal trigger is not an abstract, instantaneous if-temperature-then-release rule independent of its physical realization. The observed response comes from a specified exposure and measurement arrangement. [W023, pp. 2–3]

The abstract distinguishes two response-characterization methods, one explicitly accounting for phase change, and compares predictions for a selected mattress-fire exposure. Thermal sensing, release, available water and successful suppression remain separate parts of the whole undertaking.

Parmelee: a historical specification for automatic release#

Henry Parmelee's 1874 patent specification describes an attachment to distributing pipes in which heat automatically opens a valve and permits discharge. The selected description includes a perforated sprinkler chamber, a valve held closed by a spring-and-cap arrangement, and fusible supporting material. It also describes a shield intended to protect that material from a flow of water so heat can act on it. The shield makes an interaction within the protective arrangement visible: water from elsewhere can impede the heating needed for another release. [W024, US154076A, description]

The specification also proposes a main-flow arrangement and alarm associated with opening outlets. Thus the automatic trigger belongs to a larger material system of pipes, pressure, distribution and indication. [W024, description; application 24 June 1874, patent 11 August 1874]

Nakajo: mistake prevention retains prospective analysis#

Takeshi Nakajo's 2004 quality-engineering article discusses changing work objects, equipment and procedures to prevent trouble associated with human error. The section describes the practical core of mistake-proofing as improving the work method to suit human characteristics rather than depending solely on changing the person. Objects' shapes and colors, equipment, instructions and the sequence of work can alter what is easy to do or what errors can occur. The article treats these as interventions in the arrangement of work, not simply reminders to be more careful. [W063, §§2.1–2.2, printed pp. 627–628]

The next step is demanding: identify where errors could arise. Nakajo's selected FMEA procedure chooses work for analysis, represents the sequence, divides it into suitable units, identifies possible error modes, evaluates their occurrence and consequences, and plans measures for higher risks. He emphasizes that usefulness depends strongly on identifying appropriate error modes. Units that are too broad obscure what happens; units that are unnecessarily fine waste analysis time. His proposed object-focused cycle asks what object is handled and how its state is changed or recognized. [W063, p. 628]

The same page distinguishes likelihood, seriousness and the effectiveness of measures preventing consequences from spreading. A preventive arrangement can reduce dependence on repeated faultless performance while requiring good decomposition and knowledge during its design.

Amyotte and Khan: removing a hazard is hazard-specific#

Paul Amyotte and Faisal Khan's 2021 synthesis distinguishes inherent safety, passive engineered safety, active engineered safety and procedural safety. Eliminating or reducing a hazard at its source is different from adding a device that prevents or mitigates its effects when called upon. Their stairs example explains the distinction: handrails and careful stair use retain a fall opportunity that a one-story arrangement removes. But the authors immediately complicate the favorable example. Changing an existing building is harder than selecting its design initially, and a location subject to flooding poses other questions about a single story. [W064, §§1.2–1.3]

The same argument is explicitly hazard-specific. Removing a flammability hazard through nitrogen can introduce an asphyxiation hazard. In an operational storage example summarized from other work, smaller inventory and greater distance from a community accompany higher pressure. The authors report an improved overall risk profile for that case, while making the competing changes visible. [W064, §1.2 and §6]

The operational section rejects the idea that early-design emphasis makes existing plants irrelevant to inherently safer design. Modifications can create opportunities, and the discussion retains continuing risk analysis and updating from operational information such as near misses. A design choice can reduce a recurring hazard while leaving a need to understand changed conditions and performance. [W064, §6]

NIOSH: minimal user action is a design aim, not the end of evaluation#

The NIOSH Hierarchy of Controls explanation orders elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls and personal protective equipment. It explains the preference for the first three partly through reduced reliance on significant continuing human interaction. Engineering-control characteristics include blocking a hazard near its source, integrating protection in the original equipment, limiting interference with the control and requiring minimal user action without making the job harder. These are concrete design aims; they are more informative than the claim that a barrier is simply “safer.” [GL-W059, 2024 institutional page, engineering-controls discussion]

The page also distinguishes upfront and operating costs. Engineering controls can cost more initially, while their longer-term cost can be lower, especially across several workers. Substitution requires examining the new risks and interactions of the substitute. Training and regular evaluation remain explicit responsibilities, including checking whether controls continue to reduce exposure. This is an institutional prevention framework and explanation of its rationale. [GL-W059, substitution, cost and train/evaluate passages]

JIPM: local workers make and understand a karakuri arrangement#

The Japan Institute of Plant Maintenance's primary explanation of karakuri kaizen starts with workers identifying difficulties at the site. They combine an available power source with simple mechanisms such as levers, links, cams, gears or inclined paths to make an improvement.
