Gravity, springs, human force and power borrowed from existing machinery are among the sources considered. Reusing a motor's motion or an existing movement is different from claiming that the device operates without energy. The relevant change can be in how an available source performs the task. [UX-W036, definition and method sections]

The explanation includes handling heavy items, presenting parts, moving supplies and reducing awkward work. It also explicitly says realizing an improvement requires understanding the work, the equipment's structure and characteristics, and improvement methods. It treats that effort as a way to develop people as well as devices. The claim that locally made equipment can be repaired locally connects the possible operating benefit to retained skill. [UX-W036, application and personnel/repair sections]

A JIPM technical excerpt illustrates the combination of power sources and mechanisms. Its page 16 describes using an object's weight, human movement or a nearby machine's drive with transmission mechanisms. A gravity-fed roller path moves a part toward a later process; another arrangement borrows one motor's rotation for several motions. [UX-W037, p. 16]

Toyota: stopping changes the work of watching#

Toyota's own explanation of its production system gives jidoka a particular role. A machine can detect an abnormality and stop, or an operator can pull a stop cord; an andon indication brings attention to the exception. Toyota describes this as allowing people to respond when an abnormality occurs instead of continually watching equipment. The arrangement combines detection, stopping and a means of calling for a response. An indicator alone is not the entire mechanism. [GL-W080, jidoka and andon discussion]

The same company account insists on continuing development of human skills and technologies, with people able to think independently and implement kaizen. Its separate just-in-time pillar concerns linking production and making the needed quantity at the needed time. [GL-W080, two-pillars and human-skill passages]

FDA: the interface includes more than a display#

The selected FDA guidance defines the device-user system through users, use environments and user interfaces. Its interface includes packaging, labeling, training materials, physical controls, displays, alarms and operating logic. A task is an interaction or set of interactions toward a desired result. This broad scope prevents an account of error prevention from treating a neat screen or fewer instructions as a complete intervention. Setup, handling and the circumstances of use can affect what a person is actually able to do. [GL-W075, guidance p. 4 and companion explanation]

The guidance's account of use error distinguishes a result differing from what was expected from a failure caused solely by the device. That distinction gives investigation a more precise object than simply blaming an operator. The selected explanation relates design to actual user and environmental characteristics, and calls for confirming that efforts to minimize use-related risk have succeeded. [GL-W075, definitions and overview]

Kabanov, Kupitz and Goetzmann: a grace period retains later judgment#

The 1992 IAEA Bulletin article on advanced reactors describes passive features as relying on naturally available or stored sources of motive power, such as natural circulation, with several levels of passivity.

Some features are actively initiated and then operate passively. The selected discussion also explains a grace period during which automatic responses allow operators time to assess the event and plant state before deciding on action. Delaying immediate intervention is different from eliminating the need for later understanding. [GL-W081, printed p. 34]

The article retains demonstration requirements for new features, potentially including full-scale testing for innovative designs. Its following page labels specified probability targets as design goals that had not been shown achievable for each design. The article provides design reasoning about simplification, accessible energy and operator time. [GL-W081, pp. 34–35]

Source inspection and the removal of hazards#

The Shingo Institute discussion relates source inspection and mistake-proofing to Shigeo Shingo's work: changing the conditions producing a defect and detecting errors at source can prevent defects. Shingo develops the approach in Zero Quality Control: Source Inspection and the Poka-yoke System. [W038, through the Shingo Institute]

Amyotte and Khan's specialist discussion above develops the source-reduction idea associated with Trevor Kletz's What you don't have can't leak, published in 1978 following a 1977 lecture. [W039, through Amyotte and Khan]

Nakajo and Hitoshi Kume drew five principles from about 700 examples at mechanical assembly lines. The first three change the chance that an error occurs. Eliminate the operation that permits the error, substitute a method less prone to it, or make the correct action easier. The other two address what happens if the error occurs. Detect it so it can be acted on, or limit its effects. [W076]

S04 Interconnection and dissipativity: what the formal relation preserves#

From an arrangement to an admissible behavior#

The selected control and network sources make the structure of an arrangement mathematically consequential. They explain different questions: how a governor responds dynamically; what an energy-accounting inequality establishes; how components share a behavior; and when decomposing a network calculation saves computation. The formal words “control,” “passive,” “interconnection” and “decomposition” retain their source-specific meanings here.

Maxwell: stronger correction can destabilize the motion#

James Clerk Maxwell's 1868 On Governors opens by distinguishing devices that increase resistance with speed from governors whose continuing adjustment can restore a normal speed within working limits. That difference concerns the dynamics of the correction, rather than simply the presence of a speed-responsive part. Maxwell then divides disturbances into growth or decay, with or without oscillation. A useful governor must reject growing departures, including oscillations whose amplitudes increase. The intended direction of an adjustment does not settle that question. [W069, opening, printed pp. 270–272]

He describes a limit at which making the regulation faster leads instead to dancing and jerking motion. The example associated with Fleeming Jenkin's governor gives the mathematical problem a mechanical setting: adjustment parameters that appear to increase governing power can change the character of the coupled motion. Its pertinent lesson remains specific: a regulator's nominal corrective action and the stability of the whole process are different claims. [W069, pp. 271–272]

Willems: stored quantity cannot increase beyond supplied quantity#

Jan Willems's 1972 dissipativity theory specifies a dynamical system, an input/output-dependent supply rate, and a nonnegative storage function of state. Dissipativity requires the increase of that storage over every admitted trajectory and time interval to be no greater than the accumulated supply over the interval. Written schematically, S(x1) − S(x0) ≤ ∫w dt. The storage function and supply rate must be identified together with the system and its allowed inputs. [W014, §3, definition 2, printed p. 327]

For a small arithmetic illustration, suppose the initial storage is 5 units and the integrated supply is 3 units over the chosen interval. The inequality permits terminal storage no greater than 8 units. It does not determine whether the actual value is 8,6 or another nonnegative value consistent with the trajectory. If the chosen supply has physical energy units, those units must be used consistently.

The universal quantification also matters. Checking one favorable trajectory is insufficient to establish the required inequality for all admitted inputs, states and intervals. Nor is nonnegative net supply on a closed state-space cycle alone the definition: Willems explicitly says that cyclic condition is inadequate by itself for dissipativity as defined. A proposed connection among components consequently needs more than an appealing energy-flow drawing or a single observed balance. [W014, definition 2 and following discussion]

Available storage is a limit on extraction#

Willems defines available storage by asking how much can be extracted from a given initial state over all allowed future motions and horizons. It is a supremum of the negative accumulated supply. Including the zero-duration choice makes this quantity nonnegative. Theorem 1 states, in the developed setting, that finite available storage for every state is equivalent to dissipativity, that available storage itself is a

possible storage function, and that it is no larger than any nonnegative storage function satisfying the inequality. [W014, definition 3 and theorem 1, pp. 327–328]

The proof's idea is useful to understand. From one state, first follow an allowed path to a second state, then extract what is available there. This combined procedure cannot exceed the best extraction possible from the first state. That comparison gives the dissipation inequality for available storage. Conversely, an existing nonnegative storage function bounds what can be extracted along any such path. The two directions connect the input/output extraction question to the storage bound. [W014, theorem 1 proof]

The article expressly warns that available storage need not equal actual stored energy. Not every internally stored quantity must be accessible through the external terminals under the admitted operations. Treating extraction capacity as the physical total would therefore overstate what the formal result supplies. The distinction is relevant whenever a selected interface is said to reveal all resources inside an arrangement. Likewise, an energy inequality alone does not establish that a chosen gait or a desired asymptotic equilibrium will occur.

Willems 1997: a controller can be another physical system#

In On Interconnections, Control, and Feedback, Willems questions the universal use of a sensor-to-computation-to-actuator signal-flow picture. His door and door-closing mechanism share a physical interaction: force and angle are related through both mechanical systems. Assigning force as cause on one side and effect on the other may be convenient for a conventional controller description, but it is not the only way to describe their interconnection. The paper retains intelligent feedback as useful while proposing a more general framework. [UX-W017, §III, pp. 328–329]

In the behavioral approach, a system's behavior is the set of trajectories compatible with its laws over a time axis and signal space. When two systems share signals, their interconnected behavior consists of trajectories satisfying both sets of laws: an intersection of behaviors. Interconnecting only some terminals can be represented by leaving the others free in the appropriate component. Internal connection variables can later be suppressed through the distinction between manifest and latent variables. The relationship supplied by the interconnection is part of the model, rather than something inferred from an unexplained arrow between boxes. [UX-W017, §IV, pp. 329–330]

This viewpoint lets a mechanical attachment count as a controller without requiring it first to sense, represent and compute in the manner of a digital controller. It does not make every physical attachment adequate. The admissible component behavior and the joint constraint must actually yield the required motions. An intersection can remove possible trajectories while also removing behavior needed for the intended task.

An unrestricted mathematical controller can make the problem trivial#

The 1997 paper itself demonstrates why controller admissibility matters. If arbitrary additional restrictions are permitted in a linear behavioral setting, an interconnection can trivially force a small stable behavior. That formal construction can look stronger than familiar control results because the permitted controller class is so broad. Willems calls attention to the objection and turns to regular interconnection and implementation. A mathematical subset selected by imposing arbitrary laws is not automatically a physical controller that can be connected through the allowed means. [UX-W017, §§VI– VIII, especially p. 332]

Controller admissibility determines which variables can be constrained and which interconnections can be physically realized. The system assumptions and permitted means of connection are therefore part of Willems’s control problem.

Van der Schaft: composition preserves an energetic structure#

Arjan van der Schaft's December 2024 preprint on nonlinear port-Hamiltonian systems describes physical modeling through energy storage, dissipation and power-conserving interconnection. In its selected composition account, components connected through an appropriate power-conserving relation yield another port-Hamiltonian system. The combined stored energy is the sum of component Hamiltonians, with the component dissipation relations retained. The relation at the interface is what permits this accounting; arbitrary coupling is not assumed to have the same property. [GL-W069, §1.1]

Combining the power-preservation relation, storage definition and dissipation condition gives its key inequality: the rate of increase of stored energy is no greater than supplied port power. If the Hamiltonian is bounded below, the system is passive with respect to that supply rate after a suitable storage normalization. “Passive” here is an energetic input/output property. It does not mean that no controller is present or that no external energy arrives. [GL-W069, §1.2, eq. 9]

The preprint also distinguishes zero-input analysis from steady operation with nonzero inflows and outflows, such as a power network. The relevant equilibrium and storage comparison must change accordingly; shifted passivity addresses that different question under further stated conditions. Its treatment of power ports and energy ports also retains different variable roles in later sections. [GL-W069, §§1.2–3]

Van der Schaft and Jeltsema trace port-based modeling to the bond graphs pioneered by Henry Paynter. Each bond carries two quantities whose product is power. Voltage and current serve this purpose in an electrical connection, and force and velocity in a mechanical connection. Using power at the connection gives the model a way to represent exchanges between components from different physical domains. [GL-W070, §1.1]

Willems gives a circuit example with two resistors, a capacitor and an inductor. He writes the laws of the components and connectors, then identifies the variables at the terminals that are joined. To describe what can be observed from outside, he retains the voltage difference across the external terminals and the current entering the circuit. The internal quantities still have to satisfy the component and connection laws. [UX-W019, fig. 8 and accompanying text]

Wu: separating subnetworks retains an interconnection solve#

Felix Wu's 1975 Solution of Large-Scale Networks by Tearing develops a network solution related to Kron's diakoptics. The network is separated into subnetworks, those are solved locally, and an interconnection-level calculation restores the constraints across the cut. The method retains the Kirchhoff relations rather than treating the cut parts as independent complete answers. The selected explanation distinguishes subnetwork computation from the work of joining their results. [SG-W023, selected opening and algorithm discussion]

Wu describes a possible parallel implementation in which satellite computers perform subnetwork work while a central computer performs an interconnection step. The algorithm can also run serially. Parallel execution and total arithmetic work are thus different comparisons. The selected computational discussion compares node-voltage solutions and counts multiplications, accounting for sparse matrices so operations on zero entries are omitted. Matrix ordering and fill-in during elimination materially affect the count. [SG-W023, algorithm remarks and §IV, printed pp. 14–16]

Its parameterized example reports one range in which tearing takes fewer multiplications and a smaller range, 3≤p≤9, in which it takes more. Another stated class of networks also gives no computational saving for the chosen tearing arrangement. The explanation for a possible advantage concerns fill-in relative to the comparator, not decomposition as an intrinsically better operation. The positive and adverse cases

nevertheless preserve the source's explicit conclusion that neither approach is absolutely superior on this counted task. [SG-W023, §IV, printed pp. 16–19]

The local solves can become easier while an interconnection solve and ordering effects remain. Wu supplies a concrete comparison in one technical problem, including an unfavorable result.

S03 Ashby, regulation and models: distinguishable possibilities and constructed capacities#

Behavior, variety and regulation#

Ashby's An Introduction to Cybernetics develops a language for possible behavior, then variety and communication, then regulation and the construction of regulators. The book first asks what system is being described and what distinctions and couplings its description preserves. Its later accounts of regulation rely on those choices. Its final chapters ask how an arrangement can undertake repeated regulation and where its capacities come from. [W001, parts I–III]

A system is a selected state description#

Ashby's pendulum example begins with a failed description. Record the angular position at fixed intervals and it may appear that a position has two different successors. Release the pendulum from ten degrees and its next position differs from the next position when it passes through ten degrees while already moving. The problem is not resolved by insisting that the physical object is the same. Angular position alone omits a distinction that matters to its subsequent behavior. Adding angular velocity supplies the relevant state description for the model under consideration; adding an unrelated variable such as the bob's mass to the original description does not solve that particular omission. [W001, §3/11]

In this usage, a system is a chosen list of variables, with states formed from their possible values. The material object supplies many possible variables; the scientific account selects those relevant to a given interest. This does not license arbitrary simplification. The selected description must support the transition properties claimed for it. If an observed successor depends on an omitted variable, a deterministic account on the reduced state set can fail. Ashby's construction makes finding an adequate description part of investigation, rather than something supplied by pointing at an object and naming it “the system.” [W001, §3/11]

His transformations distinguish a state from the rule under which it changes. A closed transformation sends states in the selected set to states within that set. A single-valued transformation assigns one successor to each state. These are formal properties of the description, not claims that the object is thermodynamically isolated, physically self-sufficient or free of environmental dependence. An input can select among transformations; changing an input then changes the transition applied to the state. Omitting relevant inputs can make the reduced transition uncertain. [W001, chs. 2–4]

Ashby abstracts from material substrate so that the same pattern of transitions can describe differently constituted mechanisms. The behavioral description selects the properties relevant to a particular question. [W001, §§1/2–1/5, 3/11]

Coupling supplies a relation that a parts list lacks#

Ashby considers coupling two machines while retaining their individual transition laws. To do so, each must affect the other through the inputs admitted by those laws. The coupling specifies how one machine's state determines an input of the other. In his elementary construction, both update on a common time scale; the next joint state is determined from the two present states and the selected coupling. The whole can then be described on pairs of component states. A different coupling can produce different joint behavior even when the component transformations are unchanged. [W001, §§4/6–4/10]

The restriction to input and output is consequential. Forcing two objects together so that their mechanisms are damaged would also connect them in ordinary language, but would not preserve the

component laws used in this construction. Likewise, silently changing update timing would change the model being analyzed. Thus “the parts interact” is too incomplete to explain the whole. The manner and conditions of interaction belong to the explanation. The usefulness of an arrangement lies in those actual relations, rather than in a count or inventory of its parts. [W001, §§4/6–4/7]

The book also warns against reading a whole dynamics from a favorable loop label. In its two-variable example, each next value is half the other's present value. Each variable has a positive immediate effect on the other, yet repeated updates converge toward zero. Calling the relation positive feedback is insufficient to prove instability. Conversely, an undesirable state can be stable. Ashby uses a continuing fire as an example: persistence and return after disturbance are not automatically achievements wanted by the observer. The state, disturbance and transition must remain specified before stability becomes a useful judgment. [W001, §§5/9–5/11]

Black-box knowledge does not identify a unique interior#

For Ashby, the experimenter and the black box are coupled: the experimenter's actions change inputs, the box produces observable results, and those results influence subsequent actions. A protocol can support a canonical behavioral description under the assumed determinacy and accessible tests. It does not follow that every relevant transition can be repeatedly tested. A state may become inaccessible after the process passes through it. His examples include an irreversible explosion and an organism that no longer has its original untrained condition. Replacing the specimen introduces an additional assumption about comparability; it is not literally returning the same object to its former state. [W001, §§6/1–6/6]

Even sufficiently described behavior need not determine a unique interior. Ashby's relay networks can realize the same required conducting behavior with different arrangements of contacts. The same object can also have different connection diagrams when studied mechanically and electrically. An insulator can connect two parts mechanically while separating them electrically. Which relation is being investigated therefore matters to the diagram and to any inference about independence. A successful interface description is knowledge of selected behavior, not a transparent picture of every mechanism responsible for it. [W001, §6/7]

Partial knowledge can be complete for a selected operation#

Ashby's parity example gives a precise sense to useful incompleteness. One need not know the exact product of every pair of integers to know whether their product is odd or even. Odd times odd is odd; the other parity combinations give an even product. This little account omits almost everything about numerical magnitude, yet gives a determinate answer to the selected parity question. By contrast, a list of a few exact products is incomplete even within multiplication when it leaves further requested cases unanswered. Partiality and adequacy must therefore be judged with respect to what the account is intended to do. [W001, §6/13]

For a dynamic system, grouping detailed states gives a useful simpler machine only if the grouped transitions remain consistent. Suppose two detailed states receive the same reduced label but move to different reduced labels under the same input. The reduced current label then does not determine the next one. Ashby explicitly contrasts suitable and unsuitable groupings. His homomorphic simplification preserves the operative structure required for the reduced behavior; arbitrary lumping need not. The fewer distinctions are justified by what remains predictable or usable, rather than by their small number alone. [W001, §§6/12–6/14]

This supplies his response to practical largeness. A system is very large relative to an observer when that observer cannot obtain all observations, carry out all calculations or exercise all control with the available resources. More variables or finer discrimination can make the same material object larger in this sense.

The mathematical arguments do not fail because their sets are large, provided their assumptions still hold; their application to a material case remains a separate question. Deliberately chosen aspects can be enough for a practical purpose. Their sufficiency must be established for that purpose, not asserted for every omitted detail. [W001, §§4/17–4/18, 6/14]

What variety counts#

In An Introduction to Cybernetics, W. Ross Ashby gives variety a specified meaning. Consider a sequence containing twelve occurrences of the letters a, b, and c. If order is ignored and only the distinct letters are counted, its variety is three. Counting occurrences, distinguishing types, and retaining an ordered sequence are different descriptions. A numerical statement about variety therefore needs the set of possibilities and the distinctions that define its elements. It is not a count whose object can be left unspecified. [W001, §7/6]

Ashby's semaphore example makes the observer consequential. Two arms with eight positions each can form 64 combinations when their positions are independently set and the arms are individually distinguishable. At a distance, the observer may be unable to distinguish which arm occupies which position. Some combinations then become indistinguishable, leaving 36 distinguishable positions in his example. The physical apparatus has not acquired a different number of arm settings merely because the observer changed. The set of distinctions available in that observation has changed. [W001, §7/6]

This is a useful prerequisite for reading an organizational account that speaks of what a manager or operational unit can distinguish. It directs attention to the relevant possibilities and the means of telling them apart. It does not establish that someone understands a situation merely because a large quantity of data is available.

Counts and bits are different numerical forms#

Ashby uses either the number of distinct elements or its base-two logarithm, with the context specifying which. In the logarithmic form, the unit is the bit. Eight possibilities have a logarithmic variety of three bits; two have one bit. When the distinctions combine independently, the number of combinations multiplies, while these logarithmic quantities add. This explains why a report of “no variety” can mean one remaining possibility: the count is one and its base-two logarithm is zero. Confusing the count with its logarithm changes the meaning of a calculation. [W001, §7/7]

The set need not be a collection of simultaneous states#

A machine is in one state at a time, so why speak of a set of its states? Ashby gives several reasons. A description may concern a population of machines or replicates, each currently in a different state. It may concern one machine's states at different times. Or it may concern the possibilities an observer considers because the machine's actual state is unknown. Those are different grounds for forming a set. A calculation should preserve which ground applies. [W001, §7/23]

This distinction prevents a common misreading. A decrease in the possibilities consistent with an observer's description does not necessarily describe the physical removal of machines or a reduction in the work being performed. Likewise, a collection of observations over time should not be described as though all the recorded states simultaneously existed within one object. Ashby explicitly develops the actual in relation to the possible; that analytical choice is part of the explanation.

How an arrangement can remove distinctions#

Ashby examines a single-valued transformation in which A changes to B, B to C, and C to C. A set initially containing all three possibilities has only two distinct images after one application, B and C. After another application, only C remains. The reason is specific: more than one distinct input can have the same output, while each input has only one output under the transformation. A one-to-one mapping on the inputs actually present would retain their number of distinctions. [W001, §7/22]

This result concerns the stated transformation and set. Losing a distinction need not be beneficial. Ashby's coffee-message illustration shows a case in which convergence toward a common temperature destroys the intended distinction among messages. A person may want an arrangement to remove an unwanted effect or to preserve a useful difference; identifying which is being considered requires the task as well as the count. [W001, §§7/22–7/24]

The response must be appropriate, as well as available#

Ashby's introductory regulation game separates disturbances, responses, and outcomes. One player chooses a row of a table; the responding player, knowing that choice, chooses a column. The selected cell determines the outcome. A desired outcome can always be obtained only when an appropriate entry is available for every relevant row and the responder selects it. Merely having many columns does not establish that they contain what is needed. The arrangement of the table matters. [W001, §§11/3–11/4]

For a particular family of tables, Ashby derives a bound. He assumes that a column contains no repeated outcome, and the responding strategy selects one entry from each row. If there are r rows and c available columns, the selected outcomes cannot have fewer than r/c distinct values. To keep selecting the same outcome, a strategy would need a different column each time; the available columns limit how far it can do so. The bound is a necessary limit under those conditions, rather than a sufficient recipe for constructing every desired regulator. Ashby states the corresponding logarithmic form under the same conditions. [W001, §§11/5–11/7]

This is the setting of his concise statement that response variety can reduce outcome variety. In an organizational application, the set of relevant disturbances, available responses, distinctions, and acceptable outcomes must still be identified. A slogan about matching complexity does not supply those identifications or prove their adequacy. A local arrangement can change what distinctions reach another role, while the capacities and purposes of that arrangement remain substantive questions.

Constraint compares an actual set with alternatives#

Ashby's constraint is a relation between sets: fewer possibilities occur under one condition than under an explicit comparison condition. His traffic signal has three binary lamps, so independent settings would permit eight combinations. The signal uses four. The excluded combinations establish a constraint in that set of simultaneous lamp settings. Each lamp can still be lit or unlit; the restriction concerns which combinations occur together. The presence of constraint must therefore be attached to the joint possibilities under discussion. It cannot be inferred merely from knowing the individual component ranges. [W001, §§7/8–7/11]

He uses an assembled chair to explain why a thing can act as a unit. Four disconnected rigid legs would each have six degrees of freedom of movement; once rigidly joined as a chair, the assembly has six. Knowing the locations of some parts now restricts those of the others. This is his account of coherence as a constraint on their relative possibilities. [W001, §7/16]

The book connects constraint to prediction and compact description. An aircraft cannot occupy an arbitrary new position at each instant; continuity and characteristics of its motion restrict possibilities.

Prediction can exploit such restrictions. Similarly, a long protocol showing consistent machine behavior can be represented more compactly by its transformation and actual inputs. The transformation does not supply the inputs, and a compressed description is not by itself a cheaper physical realization. Ashby is explaining why regularity makes a useful account possible. [W001, §§7/18–7/20]

His learning examples make an environmental condition explicit. An association can be learned only if the observed sequence has relevant regularity; an unchanged maze offers a learnable pattern that an arbitrarily changing maze would not. These are arguments about what supplies the regularity being exploited. [W001, §7/21]

A smaller channel can require a longer process#

Ashby's account of transmission distinguishes what can pass in one step from what a sequence can convey. A channel with two distinguishable values per step can form many distinguishable sequences. Ten binary positions permit up to 1,024 combinations when independent. The restricted alphabet does not impose the same bound on a sequence of ten positions as on one position. A receiver capable of retaining the relevant history can therefore distinguish more possibilities over time than the instantaneous channel alphabet suggests. [W001, §§8/13–8/14]

This is a conditional trade between capacity and duration. It requires usable distinctions, appropriate coding and a receiver/process able to accumulate them. A blocked channel gains no information merely by waiting longer, and distinctions lost before transmission do not reappear by extending the record. Ashby's analysis of delay also retains the intervening stages: if a source affects a receiver only through a chain of parts, some effects reach it later. Redrawing the chain as a single source does not make the delayed internal path instantaneous. The abstraction can change which boundary is described without changing the events. [W001, §§8/14–8/15]

The material environment can participate in such a channel. In his multiplication example, someone unable to complete the task mentally uses pencil and paper. Activity passes from the brain through arm and pencil to marks, then through light and retina back to the brain. This is communication through an external medium between parts of a continuing process. What counts as a channel depends on the behavioral relationship being studied, rather than on whether an anatomical nerve joins the two endpoints. [W001, §9/15]

Redundancy is relative to the message and its realization#

Ashby returns to the traffic lights to ask whether the four required signals could be encoded by two binary lamps rather than three. Four combinations suffice to distinguish stop, prepare to go, go and prepare to stop. Under his stated condition that lamps are expensive, this reduces the lamp cost to two-thirds while preserving those signaling distinctions. [W001, §9/16]

The very same lights supply a different redundancy if examined as a clock-driven sequence. When the four signals always repeat in the same order, the initial phase determines later signals in the sequence. The relevant alternatives are now possible sequences, not simultaneous lamp combinations. The book uses the difference to reject an unqualified question about whether “the lights” are redundant: the same physical object provides different sets with different answers. [W001, §9/16]

Regulation preserves a desired range, not constancy alone#

Ashby's regulation account specifies essential variables and acceptable values. A water bath is not good merely because it stays constant: it must remain in the desired temperature range despite the disturbances considered. In his communication description, a successful barrier prevents differences

among disturbances from producing unacceptable differences in those variables. This does not mean that every part of the system must be deprived of information. The active regulator may need distinctions that its successful action prevents from reaching the protected variables. [W001, §§10/6–10/7]

The tortoise's shell and the fencer illustrate two different ways of obtaining protection. A passive barrier can reduce the effect of blows on protected tissues. Skilled counteraction instead obtains information and varies action to meet the threat. Ashby groups both within the broader regulatory question; he does not define regulation to require a separate active controller in every case. The shell's success remains relative to what it resists, while the fencer's depends on available perception and action. [W001, §10/7]

The response table discussed above represents one family of regulatory limits. The physical or organizational case must supply the table and its assumptions. Ashby explicitly allows the given environment and mechanism to block some disturbance variety before an additional regulatory response acts. In some cases that baseline blocking is enough; in others it leaves work for a responsive regulator. Thus an unconditional equation equating all environmental variety with a required controller size would lose an important part of his own account. Counting relevant disturbances, the preexisting transformation, response distinctions and acceptable outcomes all matter. [W001, §§11/9–11/11]

The book also states where its normative task stops. At the opening of chapter 12, essential variables and their acceptable states are assumed to be given by outside considerations. The problem developed within the book is how to achieve them despite disturbances. The formal machinery does not derive which human purposes should be adopted or who should bear the burden of protecting them. [W001, §12/1]

Sensing, action and timing are separate restrictions#

Ashby distinguishes restrictions on receiving information from restrictions on acting. A driver who cannot see through the windscreen and a rudder that is stuck are different failures of the regulatory path. More information does not supply missing actuation; more possible actions do not identify which one is needed. He also distinguishes knowledge that a disturbance has occurred from knowledge of the system's present state: a signalman can know there is fog while being unable to determine where trains are. These are different required distinctions. [W001, §12/2]

Timing introduces a further condition. The elementary response game gives the regulator time to respond before the outcome is determined. Some regulations can use a warning; others learn of a disturbance through its effects. The thermostat in his water-bath example does not see the cold flask approaching. It receives information after the temperature begins to fall. Calling both processes regulation does not remove the difference in the route or time available for acting. [W001, §§12/3–12/4]

His argument against a perfectly error-controlled regulator is made under a particular static response framing: the response is a determinate function of the present outcome. If that outcome supplies all the disturbance information, holding it exactly constant removes the distinctions available through that channel. Allowing a small deviation can make preventing a much larger deviation possible. A dynamic controller with memory retains additional state that this immediate response table does not represent. [W001, §§12/5–12/7]

An adaptive arrangement must find and retain an acceptable state#

Ashby's hunt-and-stick construction changes what is selected. A regulating component is arranged so that it keeps changing under a “bad” input and can remain at equilibrium under a “good” one. It is coupled to the other component so that an acceptable condition supplies the good input. Any joint equilibrium then has the required property. The regulator vetoes unacceptable equilibria rather than explicitly specifying every detail of the acceptable configuration in advance. [W001, §12/14]

That statement about equilibria is not by itself a guarantee that every trajectory reaches one. The text recognizes trapping in an undesirable stable region and discusses richer transition possibilities. Accessibility of an acceptable state, the absence of other closed classes and the actual coupling remain necessary questions. Enlarging a list of regulatory states does not help if none of the available transitions can obtain the required condition. [W001, §§12/11–12/14]

The homeostat makes the mechanism concrete. Resistor settings, relays and a source of successive values allow changes while the system remains unacceptable; acceptable behavior blocks further changes. Viewed without access to the supplied table of values, the process can appear Markovian. Viewed with those determinants included, a different state description becomes available. Neither description removes the physical switching and supplied values. The explanation locates the variation being selected and the mechanism that retains a satisfactory condition. [W001, §12/15]

His telephone selector gives a simpler determinate example. It tests lines in order and stops at a disengaged line. The sequence supplies the selection without requiring a precomputed answer identifying the first free line. Yet it must encounter an available line if it is to make a successful connection; the construction does not make a free line exist when all are busy. Repeated local testing can replace one kind of prior specification while retaining a criterion, apparatus, time and feasible alternatives. [W001, §12/17]

A reusable rule and a complete response sequence differ#

Chapter 13 asks what happens when similar classes of disturbance recur over a long period. If three disturbances can appear independently on 400 occasions, there are 3^400 possible disturbance sequences. A matching response sequence can have correspondingly many alternatives. Yet a machine with the right input-response rule can generate the appropriate response on each occasion without someone specifying the whole sequence in advance. The rule stays compact because the recurring relationship is reused; the actual disturbance supplies which response is needed each time. [W001, §§13/9–13/10]

This is Ashby's own transition from a regulator's behavior to its construction. The responsible entity can undertake the recurring responses directly or build an arrangement that undertakes them. The small rule does not contain all future disturbance events. It supplies a response relation that operates when events occur. His later mechanics example explicitly retains maintenance. [W001, §§13/10, 14/5]

Design becomes selection among possible machines. In the book's deliberately broad communication account, components, couplings or input specifications distinguish one resulting machine from alternatives. Selection can occur in stages and can be supplemented by other selectors or by processes unrelated to the main system. Ashby distinguishes an abstract amount of selection from how long a search takes. Successive group divisions can find an item much faster than one-at-a-time examination if the required group-membership tests are actually available. His huge-universe example expressly assumes those tests possible; the counting does not construct a detector capable of making them. [W001, §§13/11–13/20]

Amplification retains the source of supplementation#

Ashby's power-amplifier discussion states what is being supplemented. The crane driver's small movement controls a much larger flow of energy, supplied elsewhere. From the designer's account, the output does not exceed total supplied energy; from the user's immediate task, the ability to control the larger output is consequential. Both descriptions can be correct because they account for different boundaries. His analogy for regulatory amplification depends on keeping that distinction visible. [W001, §§14/1–14/3]

One example makes the borrowed capacity explicit: someone unable to correct hundreds of mains-voltage disturbances per second can select a suitable stabilizer from a catalogue. Choosing the product uses the manufacturer's design capacities and the apparatus's continuing response. The person's choice and the ensuing regulation have different alternative sets and time scales. The example demonstrates the logical possibility of obtaining much more regulation than the chooser can perform directly, while openly acknowledging the manufacturer's contribution. [W001, §14/5]

The water-bath example compares an assumed quantity of selection involved in making a thermostat with repeated corrections over a year. Ashby presents a large amplification on that informational account and then explicitly says there need not be amplification in every case. The practical comparison includes the cost, in some sense, of making the machine against doing the job personally. The units used for selection do not automatically measure financial expense, energy, skill or maintenance. Those further quantities require the particular comparison. [W001, §14/5]

His twenty mechanics and two thousand rooms are especially relevant to the work retained by automation. The alternative to manually regulating every room is to make and maintain machines that regulate them. Supplementation comes from other contributors to design and manufacture and from the environment, which supplies current temperature and humidity directly to conditioners rather than through the mechanics. The mechanics become regulators of the regulatory machinery. Ashby also says these relationships need not form one simple hierarchy. [W001, §14/5]

Conant and Ashby: what the “good regulator” result optimizes#

Roger Conant and Ashby's 1970 article asks a different formal question. Given regulatory events R, events S in the reguland, and an outcome determined by the two, it defines an optimal regulator for its theorem by minimal outcome entropy. The distribution of S and the joint outcome mapping are given; conditional probabilities of regulatory events given S are varied. Its simplest optimal regulator associates each relevant S event with one R event, a mapping from S to R. “Model” has that mapped-event sense here. It does not initially mean a predictive computer simulation stored inside a controller. [W050, PDF pp. 8–9]

The proof's operative move is to eliminate unnecessary conditional randomization. Where two actions available for one S event would generate different outcomes, shifting probability can lower outcome entropy, contradicting optimality in the conditions used. Where different actions give the same optimal outcome, one can choose a single action without changing optimality. Repeating this selection yields a deterministic conditional mapping. The paper's simplifying uniqueness assumption on the optimal outcome distribution is explicit. The argument establishes a mapping within that optimization. [W050, PDF pp. 8–9]

The authors themselves state that equally optimal regulators may retain unnecessary complexity. Thus their theorem does not literally establish the strongest reading of the title, that every successful regulator must have the simplest model relation. Moreover, minimum entropy is not a complete valuation of outcomes: one constant bad outcome can have zero entropy. [W050, PDF pp. 2–4, 8–9]

Virgo and colleagues: a model can be an attributed interpretation#

Nathaniel Virgo, Martin Biehl, Manuel Baltieri and Matteo Capucci's 2025 paper explicitly challenges the inference from Conant and Ashby to every good regulator having a nontrivial internal model. Their new theorem uses deterministic discrete-time coupled machines, a chosen agent/environment boundary and a good set of joint states. A regulating set is nonempty, lies within the good set and is forward-closed: starting in it, the coupled evolution stays in it. Existence of that set establishes regulation from appropriate joint initial states, not recovery from every arbitrary disturbance. [RGC-W036, §§2–2.1]

They then associate an agent state with the set of environment states paired with it in the regulating set. This can be interpreted as a possibilistic belief: it identifies what remains possible, without assigning Bayesian probabilities. Their consistency condition allows forgetting, so the newly attributed possibilities can be broader than the tightest update consistent with the action and observation. The lemma identifies this consistency with forward closure; the theorem adds nonemptiness and inclusion within the chosen good set. The model interpretation is constructed from the dynamics and the observer's choices. It is not an extra causal component that must already have been designed inside the agent. [RGC-W036, definitions 3.1–3.3, lemma 3.2, theorem 3.4]

Their doorstop example makes the qualification concrete. A singleton agent state and singleton action and sensor spaces admit a constant interpretation even if the environment and selected good set are complicated. The complicated description can belong to the observer's account, while the doorstop has no corresponding rich internal state. The authors therefore reject the inference that effective regulator design must always begin by building an explicit model. They distinguish such a trivial interpretation from cases with rich ongoing interaction, and leave more precise measures of that distinction for further work. Their suggested relation to the free-energy principle is qualitative and explicitly unresolved. [RGC-W036, §3.2 and discussion]

The deterministic model maps an environment state and action to the next environment state and sensor value. Its proposed stochastic extension is left for further work. [RGC-W036, definitions 2.2–2.3, §2, fig. 1]

Powers: retain the controlled perception and changing reference#

William Powers's 2009 primary summary of perceptual control theory gives another account of what repeated feedback can accomplish. The driver compares a perceived relation between car and road with a reference for how that relation should be. Steering changes as the discrepancy changes. A crosswind can require varying steering even while the car's visible path remains nearly constant. The repeated correction can therefore be active precisely where an observer sees little change in the controlled result. This is the mechanism Powers uses to challenge a description of behavior as a fixed sequence of responses computed in advance. [SG-W027, steps 6–9]

When the driver takes an exit, the reference changes. The lower process need not oppose every departure from the earlier lane position; it acts to bring perception toward the new reference. Powers's hierarchy gives higher systems the role of varying reference perceptions for lower systems, which retain the work of adjusting actions against immediate disturbances. His explanation separates specifying a desired result from specifying every muscle movement. It is especially relevant to how an arrangement can leave detailed action to an ongoing lower process while retaining a higher-level goal. [SG-W027, steps 8–9, 11]

Powers's reference concerns perception. Matching perception to a reference does not by itself establish correspondence to every external fact.

S05 Robustness and control: disturbances, criteria and mechanisms#

The scope of a favorable response#

The accounts in this section ask different questions about maintaining or recovering performance. Some characterize exact adaptation in a biochemical model, some optimize protection against declared uncertainty, and others reduce controller updates or describe organized physiological responses.

Yi and colleagues: integral feedback in a chemotaxis model#

Tau-Mu Yi, Yun Huang, Melvin Simon and John Doyle reconstruct the robust perfect adaptation of the Barkai–Leibler bacterial chemotaxis model through integral feedback. The pertinent variable is approximately total receptor methylation. Its rate of change can be expressed as a methylation contribution minus a term proportional to receptor-complex activity. At a stable steady state that rate is zero, so the activity returns to a value set by the ratio of those rates. If the relevant rates remain independent of ligand level, a changed ligand input does not change that steady-state activity. This is the selected structural reason for adaptation in their model. [W012, pp. 4650–4651]

Integral feedback is more specific than feedback in general. The accumulated error supplies a state that continues to influence the regulated process. A constant present error and a controller whose state retains accumulated history are different situations. The authors' description explicitly requires stability of the closed loop; an algebraic steady-state relation alone does not establish that the dynamics actually approach it. [W012, integral-control derivation and fig. 2]

They also identify four biochemical assumptions needed for the reconstruction: the demethylating action concerns active receptors; specified kinetic parameters and rate ratios are independent of the relevant methylation/occupancy distinctions; activity of the unmethylated form is negligible; and bound CheR does not depend on ligand level. Relaxing these assumptions can spoil exact adaptation. The authors inspect biological evidence for their relevance rather than hiding them behind the word robust. [W012, pp. 4650–4651, assumptions and discussion]

Yi and colleagues reconstruct the model introduced by Barkai and Leibler in Robustness in simple biochemical networks. [W033, through W012]

Cannon: constancy can require ongoing cooperation#

Walter Cannon's 1929 Organization for Physiological Homeostasis defines homeostasis for an open living system whose automatic adjustments keep disturbances of internal conditions within relatively narrow limits. He deliberately distinguishes this from using equilibrium in the simple closed physicochemical sense. His choice of “homeo” also permits variation rather than rigid identity. The selected explanation concerns coordinated physiological reactions, including organs and material supplies, rather than an immobile substance that stays correct without activity. [W062, pp. 399–404]

That distinction makes the apparent absence of change informative only when its means are understood. The selected postulates describe agencies acting or ready to act, stronger resistance to a disturbance, and simultaneous or successive cooperation among factors. Cannon calls these propositions tentative and conditional, acknowledges pathological failure and substantial gaps in knowledge, and distinguishes their status from a strict equilibrium principle. His expectation that further governing agencies will be found is a research position, not proof that every instance has already been mechanistically explained. [W062, pp. 424–426]

Sterling and Ramsay/Woods: anticipation does not settle the terminology#

Peter Sterling's allostasis account challenges a version of homeostasis centered on preserving a constant internal milieu through feedback error correction. He argues that regulation instead adjusts conditions to support survival and reproduction, using prediction and coordinated effectors. In the selected description, prior knowledge and current sensing help anticipate required resources; experience updates what can serve as prior knowledge later. Anticipation therefore retains acquired information, sensory input and action. [GL-W028, selected abstract and predictive-coordination discussion]

Sterling's broader article connects that argument to efficiency, behavior and proposed medical implications. These are his model and proposals. A response need not wait for a large harmful departure if relevant demands can be anticipated and effectors prepared. The adequacy of those predictions remains consequential.

Douglas Ramsay and Stephen Woods dispute the idea that anticipation alone requires abandoning homeostasis. Their selected 2014 discussion argues that contemporary homeostatic models can already accommodate anticipatory responses and errors of prediction. They also criticize using homeostasis for virtually any return of any variable to a former value, because that stretching can obscure its physiological scope. The disagreement is about concepts and mechanisms, rather than a simple contest between a modern predictive model and a uniformly static predecessor. [GL-W029, introduction and Scope of Homeostasis]

Their suggested distinction turns attention to underlying effector loops. They discuss persistent overcorrection, continuing effector activity after an initiating disturbance is gone, and competition among effectors as candidates for an allostatic explanation. They explicitly call their suggestions speculative and open to revision. Observing a changed temperature or other regulated value alone is therefore insufficient to decide which account applies. [GL-W029, Scope of Homeostasis and conclusions]

Carlson and Doyle: optimization can expose an unanticipated fragility#

Carlson and Doyle's highly optimized tolerance account uses a percolation template to distinguish structured design from random configurations near criticality. Occupied clusters are separated by vacant barriers; a spark damages the cluster it reaches. Optimizing expected yield requires a distribution of spark locations and a set of constraints. In the selected example, more protective cuts are placed where hits are more probable, producing smaller clusters there and larger clusters in less frequently hit regions. A high-performing arrangement is specialized to the risks it was designed to face. [W026, preprint pp. 1– 3]

This specialization explains a vulnerability as well as a benefit. Change the hit distribution or place a defect in a barrier and damage can spread differently. The source explicitly considers a tree occupying a location that should be vacant in a separating barrier: a small structural defect lets fire pass into neighboring regions. Adding protection against such flaws or multiple sparks can be possible at a cost in yield. The favorable performance and the sensitivity to what was omitted are consequences of the same specified design comparison. [W026, p. 3]

The authors emphatically say the simple model is not a realistic representation of a particular system and is only remotely related to forest management. Their broader engineering/biological comparisons are their interpretive extension. The model therefore offers a concrete mechanism and a caution about inference from a power-law distribution. Self-organized criticality and optimized tolerance remain different explanations in the source's comparison. [W026, pp. 3–4]

Bertsimas and Sim: robustness is chosen against a stated uncertainty class#

Dimitris Bertsimas and Melvyn Sim's robust discrete-optimization framework introduces a tunable degree of conservatism. Instead of requiring an exact distribution for every uncertain coefficient, it uses nominal values, permitted deviations and a declared uncertainty structure. Their selected mixed-integer formulation treats uncertain constraint coefficients as bounded, symmetric and independent, while uncertain costs have a specified range. Unknown distributional detail consequently does not mean all assumptions about uncertainty have been removed. [W060, §§1–2.1]

Protection parameters control how conservative a solution is relative to the uncertainty being represented. A stronger protection requirement can change the feasible choices or objective value; choosing the budget is part of the modeled decision. The article gives tractability results for specified problem classes and transformations. Its relevance is the explicit separation of information that can be dispensed with from bounds, structure and computation that remain. [W060, selected robust-formulation discussion]

Tabuada: an event trigger still has to be detected#

Paulo Tabuada's 2007 control-task paper studies execution of a stabilizing control task when plant state makes another update necessary, instead of at a fixed periodic rate. Between updates, an input is held constant; the difference between the last sampled state and current state grows into a measurement error. A trigger limits that error relative to a state-dependent bound so that an appropriate Lyapunov function continues to decrease. The draft separately accounts for time to sense, compute and update actuators: with nonzero delay, execution must start early enough to keep the required bound. [TA-W013, draft PDF pp. 3–4]

Its positive lower bound on inter-execution times is conditional on input-to-state stability with respect to measurement errors and specified Lipschitz/Lyapunov assumptions, for initial states in the stated compact set and sufficiently small implementation delay. Those conditions make the schedule feasible within the model rather than allowing update times to accumulate arbitrarily closely. The discussion of co-schedulability then retains other processor tasks and scheduling assumptions; fewer control executions are useful only in an arrangement that still meets those obligations. [TA-W013, theorem 3.1 and co-scheduling discussion]

The practical discussion is especially revealing. A trigger based on a difference between current and previous control-law values could require repeatedly computing the very control law whose executions one wants to avoid. The measurement-error version instead allows a simpler comparison that can be implemented in separate hardware. The activity is reduced or relocated on a specified resource account; monitoring has not vanished. [TA-W013, §7.2]

Anta and Tabuada: compute the next occasion from current information#

Adolfo Anta and Tabuada's 2008 self-triggered account addresses the continuous-monitoring demand of event triggering. When the current state is measured or estimated for a control update, that information and the model can also be used to determine when the controller should execute again. The next occasion is thus computed at the current one. The selected introduction frames this as a trade between resources allotted to control and achieved performance, including processor and communication demands. [TA-W014, introduction]

Their developed conditions concern state-dependent homogeneous and polynomial systems, with the relevant dynamics, desired performance and current measurement explicitly involved. Continuous trigger

tests may be avoided while predictor/model computation and a correct representation of the operating conditions remain. [TA-W014, introduction and §§2–3]

Self-triggering predictive control and feasibility#

Patent CN116627039B presents a self-triggering predictive-control proposal by Wang Mengzhi, Zhao Chengcheng, Yang Zeyu and Che Xin. Its abstract constructs a continuous-time networked model, solves a finite-horizon optimization, constructs a candidate feasible sequence at a later time and uses a cost-function deviation to select an update occasion. This gives the claimed reduction in updates a substantial computational setting: optimization and feasibility reasoning are part of the proposal, rather than work removed by the label self-triggering. [TA-W039, abstract and claims]

The patent record dates the application to 2023 and publication to 2026. Reduced computation is a proposed effect of the control scheme, rather than a measured deployment result.

Shraim: reacting to each fluctuation can add variation#

Mustafa Shraim's author report of an educational catapult exercise distinguishes reacting to ordinary variation as though every observation signals a new special cause from failing to investigate a genuine special cause. Its three scenarios run the process without adjustment, ask volunteers to adjust toward a target, and then repeat after collaborative improvements to the operating method. The report says informal repeated adjustment produced the most variation, while standardizing how the catapult was held and launched reduced it. A slip-of-hand observation in the first stage was retained and identified, rather than erased as ordinary noise. [W095, 2019 author report]

The example concerns the response to the type of variation and a changed work method. Its relevance is the bounded observation that more corrective activity can worsen a process when its basis is wrong, while deliberate work on the process can improve it.

Doyle and Csete: constraints that permit flexibility#

John Doyle and Marie Csete explicitly connect engineering, biology and neuroscience through architecture. In the selected clothing example, component constraints, outfit requirements and protocols jointly determine which combinations are useful. A wardrobe can permit many interchangeable outfits while excluding an even larger set of arbitrary heaps. The common restrictions enable a kind of flexibility by making components compatible. [UX-W042, Architecture as Constraints That Deconstrain]

They also distinguish minimal function under ideal conditions from robustness to broader conditions. Paper can be made into a garment, but that does not give it the endurance and protection of a layered textile architecture. Their discussion retains hidden technologies, layered relationships and control over different time scales. Even familiar outfit protocols do not automatically guarantee fit or suitability: people still try things on and choose for weather and activity. [UX-W042, Layered Architectures Simplified and following discussion]

Further sources on constraints and adaptation#

Nagumo's 1942 account of solution curves remaining within a region is developed in S54. [W044]

S109 Electrical power networks and coordinated operation#

Scheduled exchange and physical flow#

On 4 November 2006, E.ON Netz took the two circuits of the 380 kV Conneforde–Diele line out of service at 21:38 and 21:39. The outage was arranged to let a ship pass under the crossing of the Ems. The operators’ analyses before the outage indicated that their grids could accommodate the change. An agreed schedule specifies exchanges between systems, but actual power flows through the connected network. The UCTE investigation reports that flow on a different line, Landesbergen–Wehrendorf, rose by more than 600 MW after the switching and exceeded 1,200 MW. [T11-W001]

Landesbergen–Wehrendorf linked the E.ON Netz and RWE control areas. As loading rose again after 22:02, E.ON Netz dispatchers looked for a switching action to relieve it. At 22:10:11 they coupled two busbars at Landesbergen, joining parts of the substation they expected would redistribute the flow away from the loaded line. The investigation’s subsequent simulation estimated that this action instead raised current on the line by 67 A. At 22:10:13, the distance protection at the Wehrendorf end automatically disconnected it. Figure 3 shows the changes in power flow before the trip. Figure 5 puts the manual switch and the automatic trip on the same timeline. [T11-W001]

The report traces further protective trips as the surviving lines took on the changed flows. By about 22:10:29, the network had separated into western, northeastern and southeastern areas operating apart. Frequency fell in the western area, which had lost imports, and rose in the northeastern area, which had lost exports. The switching intended to relieve one line had been a dispatch decision. The trips and the initial frequency responses unfolded through the equipment and the resulting balance of generation and demand in each area. Times are those reported by UCTE. [T11-W001]

Separate responsibilities in a second regime#

The joint United States and Canada report on the 2003 blackout gives a different example of the division of work between a local operator and a regional reliability coordinator. It found that FirstEnergy’s failed control computers and alarm system helped leave its operators unaware of deteriorating conditions. MISO, the reliability coordinator, had its own limitations. It lacked correct data for the state estimator, the tool it used to infer the condition of the wider network from the measurements available to it. The task force called for stronger real-time tools and backup capabilities for both control areas and reliability coordinators. [T11-W002]

Energizing a network in stages#

顾雪平 and colleagues describe restoration beginning with a source that can start without outside electricity. It energizes a path to equipment that requires auxiliary power to start. Operators can then restore additional paths and admit load in steps. A carefully chosen load can help stabilize an energized island, while cold load pickup can cause a sudden increase in demand and constrain how much can be reconnected at once. In the parallel approach reviewed by the authors, operators restore regions separately and then synchronize them. The authors discuss how available starting sources, voltage and frequency control within each region, and the ability to synchronize across boundaries bear on the choice of regions. [T11-W003]

Reserves before a disturbance#

The Balance Management Task Force’s 2003 account distinguishes responses by how they are activated and what they accomplish. In England and Wales it describes a primary response delivered within 30 seconds to arrest a sharp fall in frequency, and a secondary response delivered from half a minute to 30 minutes to restore frequency. Its reserve tables separately describe fast reserve from hydro generation, which the operator could instruct manually. The first services respond on the timescale of the frequency disturbance. The fast-reserve entry describes capacity the operator could call on. [T11-W004]

S54 Stability, maneuverability and recovery#

Engineers can change both how a system moves and how deviations are corrected. Geometry, actuator response, sensory information, permitted operating regions and arrangements for handling failure enter those choices. The historical accounts below develop particular ways of allowing useful motion while maintaining a task, detecting an approaching limit or preparing a different response when ordinary operation fails.

Associated foundations appear in S03 on essential variables and regulation; S01 and S37 on locomotion and body–controller relations; S25 on coordination and metastability; and S43 on ecological resilience and viability. The accounts here add aircraft design and testing, experimental movement analysis, mathematical confinement and decision procedures, and the organization of response near capacity limits.

Walker: a maneuverable aircraft requires a supporting control arrangement#

Laurence Walker's 1997 test-pilot account describes the X-36 as a 28-percent-scale demonstrator of a tailless fighter configuration. Removing conventional tail surfaces promised reductions in weight, drag and cost, alongside a different problem of control. Canards, split ailerons, flaps and thrust vectoring supplied the means of changing motion. The control system offered different gains for landing, ordinary airborne operation and the demonstration of fighter response. The aircraft was divergent in pitch and yaw, so favorable handling depended on the controlled aircraft and its supporting arrangements. [SM-W001, pp. 1–5]

Moving the pilot to the ground removed familiar visual, sound and bodily cues. Walker describes compensating through displays, downlinked audio and the cockpit layout. The head-up display was matched geometrically to the camera image. An air-relative velocity symbol was intended to reveal developing divergence or sideslip early, because the remote pilot could not feel lateral acceleration or normal loading. That information still required calibration: after the first landing revealed an error in the predicted airflow near the sensor, the team used a different velocity reference for subsequent landings until the correction was incorporated. [SM-W001, pp. 3–5, 7–8]

Even handling test cards became an engineering problem. Looking down could permit a substantial attitude change without a bodily sensation warning the pilot. A tray immediately below the main display let him remove completed cards while continuing to watch the aircraft's attitude. The team also shielded the pilot from distracting activity and separated his communication channel from engineers' discussions. These arrangements kept information and attention available for controlling a responsive aircraft. [SM-W001, p. 6]

The small demonstrator used a single flight-control channel, accepting less redundancy to reduce cost. A speed restriction was chosen to reduce the danger of structural failure following control failure, so that an onboard parachute could recover the intact aircraft. The team rehearsed procedures and tested the data links through towing, lifting the aircraft and carrying it beneath a helicopter. Qualification, operating restrictions and a recovery device supported a configuration whose ordinary controlled behavior could otherwise conceal its dependence on the link and control system. [SM-W001, pp. 1–2, 6–7]

On the second flight, the data link weakened and the aircraft entered its programmed lost-link mode. Its nearest steering point lay behind it, initially taking it farther from the ground station before it returned toward a designated orbit. Walker reports bank angles beyond those previously flown and a response more aggressive than the team's simulation had shown. Control was regained and the aircraft landed. Subsequent testing located a temperature-sensitive amplifier problem: satisfactory behavior at the tested

low and high temperatures had concealed a failure between them. The event exposed a gap in the supporting tests while exercising a prepared autonomous recovery function. [SM-W001, pp. 8–9]

Testing also changed the control design. In the second phase, revised control laws and better estimates of aerodynamic behavior improved stability margins and produced Level 1 handling ratings in all axes. The report's rolling tests compare time to change bank angle against programme goals, with and without thrust vectoring. Walker reports strong agility alongside the improved controlled handling. His account relates the reported performance to successive configurations, measurements and corrections. [SM-W001, pp. 9–11, figs. 5–6]

A later X-36 account: reconfiguration after an effector failure#

Christian Gelzer's 2014 NASA history describes the completed 1997 programme of thirty-one flights, extending beyond the twenty-two-flight stage reported by Walker. It also reports two separate RESTORE research flights in December 1998. In those flights, neural-network reconfiguration software operated alongside the original control laws. Simulated control-surface failures were introduced in flight, and the software compensated sufficiently for the aircraft to continue being flown safely. The reported intervention changed the allocation of control after an effector became unavailable. [SM-W002, Project Summary; Accomplishments]

Kuznetsov and colleagues: small commands can expose a critical control limit#

I. P. Kuznetsov, A. A. Parshin, L. V. Khaletsky and V. Yu. Shitov's 2014 article develops actuator requirements for a prospective maneuverable aircraft with an aerodynamically unstable configuration. Their object is the coupled aircraft, flight-control system and actuator. Dead zones, friction, backlash and other nonlinearities can change how an actuator responds even to small commands. Persistent oscillations in that coupled system can then exceed angle-of-attack or normal-load limits. Selecting a control law requires attention to the physical transfer of its commands into movement. [SM-W007, pp. 2– 4]

Their model separates a linear airframe-and-control-law part from an actuator response that varies with input amplitude. The unstable airframe changes the gain problem: the authors identify a lower as well as an upper stability boundary. They compare families of actuator frequency responses with the response required by the remaining loop. An approximate construction estimates the amplitude and frequency of possible self-oscillation. Requirements on aircraft pitch and normal loading are carried backward into permissible actuator-input oscillation, taking the tighter restriction where the criteria differ. [SM-W007, pp. 4–13, figs. 1–3]

The worked comparisons concern small-input behavior. A linear approximation can fit an actuator over one range while missing the effect of a hydraulic dead zone or mechanical play at much smaller inputs. The article compares calculated and experimental frequency responses for the RPD-1B actuator and shows why its small-signal behavior can fail the specified whole-loop requirements. At these small inputs, a command can be too small to produce the assumed proportional response. [SM-W007, pp. 13–17, figs. 4 –6]

The proposed improvements alter the component itself. Reducing initial dead zones, changing the early slope of hydraulic response and controlling backlash improve the relevant transfer characteristics. Comparisons with SPM-6B responses and calculations of play in the transmission and feedback-sensor coupling make these interventions concrete. A later design uses a direct-control multichannel electrohydraulic amplifier and a linear electric motor to improve low-input behavior. The authors report actuator development and response measurements; their evidence concerns the component and modeled loop requirements. [SM-W007, pp. 17–23, figs. 7–11]

Scholz and Schöner: preserve the task without fixing every component#

John Scholz and Gregor Schöner's 1999 article asks which variables a movement-control system stabilizes. Their elementary geometric example uses an arm with three angular coordinates and a hand position described by two coordinates. Several combinations of angles can place the hand at the same location. Movement among those combinations changes the parts while preserving the chosen result. They call the corresponding family of configurations an uncontrolled manifold, using control operationally to mean selective stabilization relative to that task variable. [SM-W004, pp. 289–292, fig. 1]

Their procedure turns that idea into a test. Investigators choose a candidate task variable and a geometric mapping from body configuration to its value. A local linear approximation separates configuration changes that leave the variable unchanged from changes that alter it. Deviations across repeated trials are projected into those two sets of directions. The comparison adjusts for their different numbers of dimensions. Greater variability in directions preserving the task variable than in directions disturbing it supports the hypothesis of preferential stabilization within this model. [SM-W004, pp. 291, 294–295]

The experiment analyzed nine participants rising from a chair under normal conditions, with stiff ski boots restricting ankle movement, and with a narrow support beneath the feet. A sagittal-plane model connected segment angles with center-of-mass, head and hand positions. Trials were aligned by movement phase, and ten with consistent rising durations were selected for analysis. The center-of-mass hypothesis showed substantial variation among configurations that preserved its position, with less variation in directions that changed it.
