Body segments could therefore vary across successful performances while exhibiting an organized relation to the global task. [SM-W004, pp. 293–299, figs. 7–8]

The head-position analysis gives a less obvious result. Horizontal and vertical head positions could show similar absolute variability, yet their relation to segment configuration differed. Near extension, some angle changes have little effect on head height. A stable-looking height can consequently reflect geometric insensitivity, while a similarly variable horizontal position exhibits preferential stabilization. Combining both coordinates into one outcome can hide the difference. The mapping from component motion to task outcome is part of what the method investigates. [SM-W004, pp. 300–304, fig. 12]

The experimental restrictions changed the inferred structure less broadly than the authors had expected. Their explanation concerns a chosen model, candidate task variables and fluctuations at corresponding movement phases. It offers a procedure for asking what is stabilized and what variation remains compatible with it. Kelso's coordination and metastability account in S25 supplies a neighboring treatment of collective patterns and continuing autonomy. [SM-W004, pp. 302–304]

Huang and Ahmed: maneuverability and balance under uncertain targets#

Helen Huang and Alaa Ahmed's 2011 experiment combined a forward-lean task with a lateral balance demand. Eleven young adults used their center of pressure to move a cursor toward a target. A narrow beam beneath a balance board reduced the sideways base of support. In one block, the target could unexpectedly shift forward or backward during the movement. Reaching the target and keeping the board level imposed related demands, while the target changes tested how rapidly participants could redirect their movement. [SM-W003, pp. 2, 8–10, fig. 1]

The authors gave maneuverability and stability operational measures. Mean time to reverse the forward– backward motion after a backward target jump declined from 0.395 seconds in early successful trials to 0.371 seconds in later ones. A separate comparison held final target distance constant: the lateral stability margin, calculated from beam width and sideways center-of-pressure excursion, declined from 1.77 centimeters in late trials of the unchanging-target block to 1.64 centimeters in late no-jump trials within

the uncertain block. Smaller margins were associated with a lower probability of keeping the board level. [SM-W003, pp. 2–5, figs. 2–4, table 1]

Eight of eleven participants exhibited the described more-maneuverable, less-stable pattern. Others did not show that combination. During earlier practice on a wide support, responses became faster without the corresponding loss of margin. The wide-support work always preceded the narrow-support work, and the principal movement estimates used successful trials. The reported tradeoff therefore belongs to the task comparisons, support conditions and individual responses the study actually examined. [SM-W003, pp. 3–6, 8–10, fig. 5]

The experiment also tested a proposed explanation. The authors expected reduced muscle coactivation to accompany increased maneuverability. Surface recordings did not show a statistically significant uncertainty-phase change in the measured muscle activity or coactivation that matched the behavioral shift. Narrow support did increase some muscle activity and lateral-pair coactivation relative to wide support, but that was a different comparison. The expected within-task coactivation mechanism remained unsupported by these measurements, despite the observed change in movement strategy. [SM-W003, pp. 3–4, 6–9, figs. 6–8]

Nagumo: having an admissible continuation and confining every solution#

Mitio Nagumo's 1942 article asks when solution curves of an ordinary differential equation remain in a chosen region as the independent variable advances. He distinguishes two properties. A set can allow at least one short continuation from each of its points while a stronger property requires every solution beginning there to remain inside for as long as it stays in the specified ambient domain. The difference matters when the assumptions do not supply a unique solution. His term for the stronger property, attributed to Hukuhara, is a set that is majorant to the right. [W044, §§1–2, pp. 551–552]

For the weaker local property, Nagumo gives an approximate-step criterion. Within the specified relatively closed set, with a continuous vector field, one can find an arbitrarily nearby later point whose secant slope approximates the field at the starting point to an arbitrarily small prescribed tolerance. His proof constructs chains of increasingly accurate steps and obtains an integral curve through a limiting process. The existence of those local steps supports the existence of a continuation remaining in the set. [W044, §2, pp. 551–553]

His treatment of the stronger property uses an auxiliary scalar function called a subintegral. Such a function does not increase along any solution. For the relatively closed ambient domains with local admissibility in both directions that he specifies, confinement is characterized locally by a suitable subintegral that is zero on the selected set and positive outside it. Starting at zero and remaining nonincreasing precludes reaching a positive outside value. The function has the stated continuity and Lipschitz properties in the state coordinates; the local neighborhood and ambient-domain conditions belong to the characterization. [W044, §§3–4, pp. 553–556]

The final comparison results use a scalar bounding equation and a scalar function of the vector system to describe further regions of confinement. The resulting regions permit motion within them; their coordinates need not remain at an equilibrium. [W044, §5, pp. 557–559]

Bonneuil and Saint-Pierre: compute which choices preserve a route to a target#

Noël Bonneuil and Patrick Saint-Pierre's 1998 paper develops a decision model from Fredrik Barth's account of fishing captains. Captains can search for new opportunities or follow known ones; catches, running costs and recruitment relations affect their prospects. The authors use this reported setting to

investigate how a changing situation permits some strategies and rules out others. Their contribution is a formal and numerical model drawing on the anthropological description. [SM-W006, §§1–2.1, pp. 43–45]

The state description includes financial loss in a worst-case scenario, expected catch at known locations and the probability that no better catch will be discovered. The modeled control is the population's mean probability of exploring. A captain chooses an individual action that contributes to that mean; a lone captain does not directly set the collective quantity. Search, exploitation and the choices of others consequently enter the decision problem together. The authors supply a catch-distribution model and a target specifying an acceptable terminal situation. [SM-W006, §2.2, pp. 45–49]

Their winning domain consists of states from which at least one modeled trajectory can reach the target while respecting constraints. A viability kernel instead concerns the possibility of continuing within a constraint set indefinitely. For the target-reaching reduction under their stated assumptions, including an empty original viability kernel, the authors add zero velocity at the target so that reaching it permits remaining there. Computing the modified kernel then supplies the required domain. [SM-W006, §§3.1– 3.2, pp. 50–54]

The numerical procedure gives the region an operational construction. Start with the constraint set and remove states that have no permissible next step into the currently retained set. Repeat that elimination, then refine the discretization under the stated compactness, convexity and regularity assumptions. The fishing model poses an applicability problem at zero expected known-site catch, where the required compact-image condition fails. The authors work first above a positive cutoff, establish the needed properties there and prove convergence of the resulting domains as the cutoff approaches zero. The computation requires this repair to the model's boundary behavior. [SM-W006, §§4.1–4.3, pp. 55–60]

Knowing the domain still leaves a decision rule to obtain. The authors approximate the correspondence of viable controls and examine a selected feedback rule. In their numerical interpretation, less favorable initial financial circumstances can require more exploration. Underestimating the probability of finding no better catch can postpone necessary action. Their reachable-set calculation also includes destinations outside the winning domain: arriving somewhere does not ensure that the target remains attainable from there. The displayed approximate feedback depends on how closely it follows a selection of the exact rule. [SM-W006, §§4.4–5, pp. 61–64, figs. 5–7]

Cargo-aircraft criteria: protection must retain a usable response#

The Civil Aviation Administration of China's 2020 trial standard for high-risk cargo fixed-wing unmanned aircraft provides prescribed design and demonstration criteria. Its scope is primarily regional cargo operations under high-risk conditions. The stability provisions address flight-control augmentation, required weight and center-of-gravity combinations, and degraded control-system states. Transitions among flight states and modes are to be smooth and convergent, with damping assessed relative to the intended flight path. The standard calls for relevant flight-test evidence alongside calculations and simulation. [SM-W009, HY.1–2, HY.171]

Its envelope-protection clause requires limits appropriate to the flight phase and maneuver while retaining response to intentional dynamic maneuvers within those limits. Damping and overshoot must suit the relevant motion. When several protections or internal control restrictions operate together, they must avoid residual oscillation, adverse coupling or unfavorable priority effects. The boundaries and their priorities must be declared. Specifying separate limits therefore leaves the interaction among their control actions to be designed. [SM-W009, HY.334]

The emergency capability has another stated purpose: reducing the consequences of critical failures for third parties. It can involve flight termination, emergency recovery or their combination. The clauses address protection against unintended operation, power for the function and, where applicable, the

dimensions of an expected recovery site. Emergency response can consequently mean ending ordinary flight. [SM-W009, HY.1365]

Communication and procedures remain part of that capability. The standard requires information about data-link range and integrity, addresses latency, and calls for a declared lost-link strategy with an attempt at autonomous reacquisition. The flight manual is to describe normal, abnormal and emergency procedures, including recovery capabilities. These are specified functions, information and tests for the covered aircraft class; the standard is a normative account of what a design should provide. [SM-W009, HY.1585–1587, HY.1707–1711]

Woods: prepare the capacity to respond near saturation#

David Woods's 2018 theory of graceful extensibility concerns how systems serving human purposes sustain adaptation as resources remain finite and circumstances continue to change. He organizes the argument into ten proto-theorems about saturation, interdependent adaptive units and changing constraints. He explicitly leaves their formal status and explanatory testing for further development. Within that proposed synthesis, graceful extensibility is the ability to extend response capacity when surprise challenges the boundary of previously adequate behavior. [SM-W008, §§1.2–1.4, 4]

Woods distinguishes base capacity for familiar variations from the potential to mobilize or generate a response near saturation. His construct, capacity for maneuver, concerns the relation between demands and capability available to meet them. Being poised to adapt does not require continually changing plans. It includes recognizing when the current approach still fits, maintaining it when appropriate and revising it when circumstances cease to fit. Preparations made before disruption can supply response options that are difficult to create during a fast cascade. [SM-W008, §2.2.1]

The preparations have costs and can be removed by ordinary performance pressures. Reserves or relationships useful during an unusual event may look idle when assessed only through routine operations. Conversely, a large, poorly targeted investment after a failure can require resources disproportionate to its contribution and become unsustainable. Woods argues for targeted reserves and arrangements that rebalance ordinary and extended capacities. His discussion makes placement, readiness and the ability to deploy resources consequential alongside their amount. [SM-W008, §§2.4.1– 2.4.2]

Neighboring units can extend or constrict a unit's response. A local attempt to meet one objective can increase another unit's difficulty; waiting for serial authorization can consume the time in which coordinated action is needed. Woods describes initiative and reciprocity as parts of a response: recognize that a plan no longer fits, act without waiting for a new tasking, and donate limited effort to a neighbor in trouble. Donation imposes an immediate cost while future assistance remains uncertain. Initiative also needs coordination if it is to avoid fragmenting the response. [SM-W008, §§2.3.1–2.3.3]

His reported transportation-firm case during Hurricane Sandy, drawn from Deary's study, makes the reorganization concrete. The firm changed priorities, relaxed usual cost-control processes for safety, formed weather-impact teams and temporary local command centers, increased horizontal coordination and moved authority toward points of action. Those changes sacrificed some ordinary economic and process criteria while making different responses possible. [SM-W008, §2.4.3]

S06 Information, coding and production coordination#

Shannon: recover a selected message from alternatives#

Claude Shannon's 1948 A Mathematical Theory of Communication begins with a particular engineering problem: reproduce at one point a message selected at another. A system must be prepared for the possible selections, rather than only the message that happens to be sent. Its source, transmitter, channel, receiver and destination have different roles. The transmitter makes a suitable signal from the message; the receiver reconstructs the message from that signal. [W025, introduction]

The paper expressly sets semantic aspects aside for this engineering problem. That choice permits analysis of the alternatives and the transmission process without requiring the theory to establish what a recipient understands, believes or values. For equally likely alternatives, a logarithm of their number gives a convenient measure; base two expresses it in bits. Four equally likely messages correspond to two bits in that counting sense. [W025, introduction; arithmetic illustration]

The opening also makes coding a material and procedural operation. A telephone transmitter converts sound pressure into current; a telegraph code supplies a pattern of dots, dashes and spaces; more elaborate systems sample, quantize, encode and interleave. The abstract channel is one part of the process. The source's framework explains how differently constituted communication arrangements can be analyzed under common specified questions. [W025, introduction, communication-system description]

Reliable transmission is a capacity result with a coding obligation#

In the selected noisy discrete-channel result, Shannon relates a source's entropy rate to channel capacity. Below the relevant capacity, suitable coding can make the frequency of errors or remaining equivocation arbitrarily small under the model. The result is stronger than saying every bit must travel perfectly in isolation. A receiver can use a suitably organized longer signal to recover what was sent despite particular corruptions. The construction depends on the channel/noise model and the rate being considered. [W025, theorem 11]

Shannon's following discussion is unusually important for interpreting that accomplishment. The proof does not generally supply a straightforward practical method for constructing the ideal code. Appropriate redundancy must combat the particular noise structure, and approaching the ideal generally introduces delay. A longer sample gives the receiver a better basis for deciding which original signal caused the received one. The selected passage thus presents reliable transmission together with the work of coding, decoding and waiting that makes it possible. [W025, §14]

Redundancy serves two distinct roles. Statistical redundancy in a source can permit more compact representation; suitably retained or introduced redundancy can also help recover a message when the channel is noisy. Shannon's English-language example concerns contextual constraints assisting reconstruction, rather than establishing that all repetition should be removed. An arrangement that optimizes one objective can change the other. The desired rate, tolerated error and available delay must remain specified before a coding improvement can be assessed. [W025, §14]

Exchanging information to coordinate production#

In a 1999 conference paper, Stanley Reiter compares two tractor makers. One buys a gear train designed specifically for its tractors. The maker and its supplier exchange information and negotiate so that the gear trains arrive when the assembly schedule requires them. The other makes the gear train in a

separate unit of the same firm. Reiter observes that this unit and the tractor plant still face the same scheduling problem and may settle it by the same exchange of information. He contrasts this with divisions of an integrated petrochemical company exchanging intermediate products at transfer prices set to outside market prices. The examples distinguish the channel by which production decisions are coordinated from the ownership of the units making them. [DP-W001]

S33 Information acquisition, experiments and dual control#

Information for a specified decision#

The selected sources concern the information needed to estimate, decide or control. They also describe situations in which information is not a free input: obtaining it can require an experiment, a control action or a different distribution of knowledge among decision makers.

Fisher: reduction and the criterion of sufficiency#

In the definitions and §§2–4 of his 1922 paper, Fisher separates the population characteristics to be estimated from statistics calculated from a sample. This distinction addresses a practical ambiguity: a sample mean is an observed quantity, while the population parameter is what the statistic is meant to illuminate. He organizes statistical work around specification, estimation and distribution. Specification identifies a mathematical form for the hypothetical population; estimation uses sample data to estimate its parameters; distribution concerns how the resulting statistics vary across samples. [W058, definitions and §§2–4, printed pp. 309–317]

His criterion of sufficiency asks whether any other statistic calculated from the same sample can supply additional information about the parameter being estimated. The relevant reduction is consequently relative to a parameter and a statistical setting. It does not mean that the reduced statistic preserves every conceivable use of the observations. The observations may be compressed without losing the information specified by the criterion.

Fisher's separate criteria prevent several ideas from being treated as synonyms. Consistency, efficiency and sufficiency address different properties. An estimate can be evaluated for sampling behavior without thereby establishing that it contains all the relevant sample information. The historical discussion does not justify declaring every maximum-likelihood estimate sufficient. [W058]

The criterion concerns the statistical information retained for a specified model and parameter. Acquisition, computation, storage, explanation and use remain separate resource questions. A new model or question can require the original observations.

Blackwell's 1951 comparison: attainable losses#

In Comparison of Experiments, Blackwell represents an experiment by a set of probability measures corresponding to possible states or distributions. An observation is used to choose an action. Each action has a loss in each state, and a decision procedure produces a vector of expected losses. Comparing experiments therefore concerns what decision consequences can be attained using their observations, rather than the raw number of observations or their apparent descriptive richness. [W059, §§1–3, printed pp. 93–94]

The construction allows convexification and randomized mixtures of procedures. Its first theorem permits attention to closed convex action sets in the subsequent treatment. Randomized decision capability is part of the mathematical comparison; forbidding it changes the admissible procedure class and can change attainable losses. Blackwell presents equivalent decision criteria for the comparison, including formulations involving expected losses with state weights and worst-state loss. Their meaning depends on the specified class of decision problems.

The standard-experiment construction is especially relevant to information reduction. Blackwell associates an observation with a vector of normalized densities and shows that the corresponding standard experiment has the same attainable loss set in the stated setting. A decision rule on the reduced

representation can be composed with the transformation of the original observation; the converse uses conditional expectation and the convex action set. Thus the claim is not merely that a summary looks informative. It specifies a decision equivalence and the machinery supporting it. [W059, §§4–5, especially theorem 3, printed pp. 94–96]

Blackwell's 1951 summary distinguishes sufficiency-based comparison from the general converse and reports a converse for dichotomies. His later Equivalent Comparisons of Experiments appeared in 1953. [W029; W059]

Börgers: a readable finite reconstruction of dominance#

Börgers's December 2023 notes provide an operative scholarly reconstruction in a finite-state, finite-outcome setting. An experiment P is a Markov matrix: each row gives the distribution of its possible observations in one state. An action is represented by its losses in the states. A decision rule maps observations into actions, and the resulting risk vector gives expected loss state by state. This makes the comparison inspectable in terms of matrices and feasible decisions. [GL-W024, PDF pp. 1–3]

The central garbling condition is PM = Q, where M is a state-independent Markov matrix. It says that the observations of Q can be generated by taking observations of P and applying an additional randomized transformation that does not require knowledge of the true state. A decision maker with P can therefore reproduce the decision procedure available with Q: first carry out the transformation, then apply the Q-based rule. The transformation does not create hidden access to the very state the decision maker is trying to infer. [GL-W024, proposition 1 and explanation, PDF pp. 3–6]

The notes relate this condition to attainable risk vectors and to decision-value comparisons. Their second proposition gives equivalent conditions expressed through decision problems and their values. This gives an explicit bridge from a relation between observation systems to what an actor can achieve.

The notes develop the Blackwell tradition, including Blackwell and Girshick, in a finite setting with convex action possibilities and randomized procedures. [GL-W024, PDF pp. 1–9]

Brooks, Frankel and Kamenica: information already held can change the comparison#

The introduction and early definitions of the March 2024 manuscript distinguish an experiment from a signal. An experiment specifies how data relate to the truth; two separately specified experiments do not determine the joint informational content of their observations. Their use of a signal adds the joint relation to other information. The difference matters when information overlaps or becomes useful only in combination. [W071, introduction and §§2–3.2]

Their newspaper example makes the issue concrete without requiring a theorem proof. If a reader already receives one newspaper, another copy of it need not add as much as a different newspaper. A third publication can also alter the comparison because its reporting overlaps with one source or complements another. An ordering established for sources in isolation need not answer which additional source is more valuable for a reader with existing information.

The authors study comparisons robust both to the decision maker's preferences and to other information the decision maker may possess. Their announced reveal-or-refine condition requires that an observation from the favored signal either reveal the truth or refine what the other signal conveys. [W071]

Information value depends on the knowledge already in place. Two sources can be substitutable or complementary in ways not captured by their separate state–observation distributions.

Saldi and Yüksel: who is allowed to know what#

The introduction to Saldi and Yüksel's review presents information structures as restrictions on which observations each decision maker can use. Their example has several agents, each choosing an action from local information, possibly with an additional independent randomization device. A team cost depends on the underlying state and the agents' actions. The admissible policies must respect the local information rather than draw on an omniscient observer's knowledge. [TA-W004, introduction]

Their proposed probability-theoretic and topological approach studies the distributions induced over states, measurements and actions—strategic measures—and the geometry of feasible decision or control policies. The introduction distinguishes questions of existence, approximation, convexity and numerical bounds. An apparently favorable solution obtained by relaxing the information restrictions need not be implementable by the original agents.

These information structures specify local knowledge, admissible action and a team cost, making an information boundary part of the problem formulation. [TA-W004]

Wittenmark: an action can both control and probe#

Wittenmark's Adaptive Dual Control explains why immediate control and learning about a process can be linked. His stochastic formulation specifies a process model, admissible causal controllers and a loss over a horizon. The model structure and the driving process distribution are assumed known, while some parameters are unknown or changing. The history of inputs and outputs supports parameter estimation. The chosen control signal can affect not only the next output but also the quality of future estimates. [AFC-W012, pp. 1–4]

A certainty-equivalent controller inserts current parameter estimates as though they were the true values in a controller designed for known parameters. A cautious controller additionally responds to uncertainty in those estimates. In the one-step formulation, caution reduces controller gain when parameter uncertainty is high. This can be sensible protection against an unreliable estimate, yet it can also weaken the excitation that supplies information about the process.

Wittenmark describes a resulting turn-off possibility: smaller control signals yield less information; uncertainty can increase; control signals are then reduced further. His integrator example distinguishes the certainty-equivalent controller's difficulty near a zero estimated gain from the cautious controller's tendency toward diminishing action as uncertainty rises. [AFC-W012, pp. 4–6]

Dual control deliberately takes the informational effect of action into account over a longer horizon. An action can have a current cost while improving the basis for later actions. The chapter's summary stresses that the exact optimal problem is computationally intractable in general practice and motivates simpler suboptimal controllers with active probing features. Adding a term that rewards information is not automatically enough: for the intended dual effect it must depend on the control signal being selected and on the quality of the estimates. [AFC-W012, summary and dual-control discussion]

Bayesian design: a limited but explicit decision framing#

The abstract of Chaloner and Verdinelli's review frames experimental design as a decision problem in which the chosen design maximizes expected utility from the experiment. It establishes a relevant orientation: the experiment is selected for an anticipated decision or inferential purpose rather than because more data are inherently better. [AFC-W016]

Statistical and decision criteria#

The accounts above preserve distinct achievements: a parameter-specific sufficiency criterion; attainable-loss comparisons; a finite garbling reconstruction; a qualification involving correlated prior information; admissible local knowledge; and the informational effect of control action. Each gives a different way of making information operationally precise.

S74 Diagnostic testing and the choice of antimicrobial treatment#

Making susceptibility a dependable measurement#

Antimicrobial susceptibility testing connects a laboratory observation to a choice among treatments. William Kirby's 1985 retrospective described why the convenience of placing antibiotic disks on an inoculated plate had initially exceeded the comparability of the results. Laboratories varied the medium, inoculum, disk content and interpretation of the boundary around a disk. A clear zone could therefore look precise while reflecting different procedures. Kirby recalled the work that led to the standardized method published in 1966 and its later collaborative evaluation and adoption. [TD-W010]

A disk creates a concentration gradient as the drug diffuses into the medium. The inhibition zone can be related to the concentration required to inhibit growth, with zone diameter inversely related to the logarithm of the minimum inhibitory concentration. The relationship becomes interpretable when the procedure is controlled. Standardization made the convenient measurement useful across laboratories: the question was no longer merely whether a visible zone appeared, but what a zone obtained under specified conditions indicated about susceptibility. [TD-W010]

From growth measurement to a clinical category#

The 2025 recommendations of the Comité de l'antibiogramme de la Société française de microbiologie show how much of that interpretive structure remains in a modern standard. Medium, inoculum and test conditions are specified so that a measurement can be compared with an applicable breakpoint. A heavier inoculum, for example, can produce a smaller zone. Without control of that feature, an apparent change in susceptibility may instead be a change in how the test was performed. The recommendations join the measurement procedure to the conditions under which its result has meaning. [TD-W011]

The raw diameter or minimum inhibitory concentration is then interpreted for an organism–drug combination. The categories distinguish susceptibility at standard dosage, susceptibility at increased dosage or exposure, and resistance. The French recommendations discuss increased dosage in relation to EUCAST's increased-exposure terminology, which includes how drug reaches the site of infection. A categorical result therefore already incorporates assumptions about achievable exposure. It is not a context-free property of a drug considered in isolation from the organism and treatment conditions. [TD-W011]

Deciding whether to prescribe#

Jochen Cals and colleagues' 2009 trial examined a different decision: whether adults with lower respiratory tract infection should receive an antibiotic in primary care. Twenty practices and forty general practitioners participated, with 431 patients. A factorial design tested point-of-care C-reactive protein measurement and enhanced communication skills as separate interventions. CRP is a marker of the host's inflammatory response. The approximately three-minute measurement supplied evidence for interpreting the presentation; it did not identify an organism or determine which antibiotic would inhibit it. [TD-W012]

The test was introduced with interpretation training and a run-in period. The communication intervention taught eleven tasks addressing such matters as the patient's concerns, expectations and understanding of the illness's likely course. In the consultation, a clinician could establish why the patient had come, discuss the symptoms and test result, explain what recovery might involve, and reach a prescribing decision. The trial consequently tested changes to the use of information as well as the availability of information. [TD-W012]

Antibiotic prescribing at the first consultation was 31% among patients in the CRP-testing comparison and 53% without CRP testing. The corresponding communication comparison was 27% versus 54%. At twenty-eight days, the proportions receiving antibiotics remained lower: 45% versus 58% for CRP and 38% versus 63% for communication. Recovery and satisfaction did not differ detectably between the groups; median recovery took twenty-two days. The combined-intervention cell had particularly low prescribing, but the interaction was not statistically significant, so the study's factorial main effects provide the clearer account of what was established. [TD-W012]

Smedemark and colleagues' 2022 Cochrane review placed biomarker-guided prescribing in a larger primary-care evidence base. Twelve CRP trials included 10,218 participants, of whom 2,335 were children; one procalcitonin trial included 317 participants. CRP-guided care reduced initial prescribing, with a risk ratio of 0.77 and a 95% confidence interval from 0.69 to 0.86. The review rated that evidence moderate certainty and found substantial variation across trials. Prescribing within twenty-eight days was also reduced, with a risk ratio of 0.81, supported by high-certainty evidence. [TD-W013]

Recovery changed little. Deaths were too few to provide a precise assessment of mortality, for which the evidence was low certainty. These outcomes describe different consequences of the intervention: fewer prescriptions, the course of recovery, and uncommon serious events. The review's primary-care procalcitonin evidence should also be distinguished from inpatient studies using repeated procalcitonin measurements to stop treatment already underway. [TD-W013]

Pathogen testing and ordinary prescribing practice#

A rapid streptococcal antigen test gives a more targeted answer than a general inflammatory marker. Anna Maria Bonet-Esteve and colleagues' 2021 report studied its introduction for children aged three to fifteen with suspected streptococcal infection. Twenty-seven pediatricians participated; 557 children were eligible and 519 were followed. Adding the rapid test to the ordinary clinical pathway reduced antibiotic prescribing from 88.5% in the control group to 45.5% in the testing group. All positive tests and relatively few negative tests led to prescriptions. The test altered the treatment decision by distinguishing children within a clinically similar presenting group. [TD-W015]

The investigators also followed adherence by telephone. Among those prescribed antibiotics, adherence was 68% in the control group and 62.9% in the test group, a nonsignificant difference. A test that made prescribing more selective did not thereby establish improved completion of the prescribed course. The two outcomes concern different parts of the treatment process: deciding who receives an antibiotic and what happens after that decision. [TD-W015]

Sydenham and colleagues' 2021 register study examined how testing and prescribing were associated in ordinary general practice. It covered 783,252 antibiotic courses in nine Danish municipalities from 2013 through 2017. Diagnostic tests were associated with 43.4% of courses, using a window extending seven days before and after a prescription. CRP use increased over the period, while overall point-of-care testing remained stable and the mixture of tests changed. The study records practice patterns at scale. Because the association window included tests after prescribing, it does not measure the proportion of prescriptions preceded by a diagnostic test, and its observational design does not by itself identify what testing caused. [TD-W014]

When a rapid panel leaves prescribing unchanged#

Alastair Hay and colleagues' 2026 primary-care trial supplies an informative contrasting result. A rapid molecular panel tested for twenty-three respiratory targets, nineteen viruses and four atypical bacteria, in about forty-five minutes. The study enrolled 552 patients across sixteen practices, with 276 in each group. Participants had to be willing to wait. Clinicians received information about the panel and

presentations, but the intervention did not include the decision and communication training used in the earlier CRP study. Typical respiratory bacteria were outside the panel's target set. [TD-W016]

Antibiotics were prescribed to 124 patients in each group, 45% of both. The odds ratio was 1.00, with a 95% confidence interval from 0.71 to 1.41. Prespecified subgroup analyses showed less prescribing when a virus was found, offset by more prescribing when no target was detected. A negative result on a panel dominated by viral targets did not establish a bacterial cause. The authors discussed how clinicians might interpret that absence of detection, while the randomized overall result remained no reduction in prescribing. Symptom severity met the study's noninferiority criterion. The trial demonstrates why a faster and more detailed result has to be assessed as part of the clinical decision in which it is used. [TD-W016]

Correcting treatment after a positive blood culture#

The RAPIDS-GN trial addressed patients whose blood cultures had already become positive for Gram-negative bacilli. Antibiotic treatment could then need correction: a resistant organism might require escalation, or a susceptible organism might permit a narrower drug. Banerjee and colleagues' report first appeared in 2020. Five hundred patients were randomized; the modified intention-to-treat analysis included 448, with 222 assigned to rapid testing and 226 to standard testing. This was a study of what happened after a positive culture, rather than of withholding initial treatment while waiting for a culture to grow. [TD-W017]

Both groups received antimicrobial stewardship review. A physician or pharmacist was paged when the Gram stain, identification or susceptibility result became available, reviewed the record, and telephoned the treating service when a treatment modification appeared appropriate. Scenario-based recommendations had been developed for the stewardship clinicians. The treating team retained the decision to accept them. In the rapid arm, organism identification and phenotypic susceptibility testing were performed on the rapid platform in addition to ordinary testing, and results entered the medical record. Thus the route from laboratory to medication included a named recipient, review and communication in both groups. [TD-W017]

Median time to identification was 2.7 hours with rapid testing and 11.7 hours with standard testing; susceptibility results took 13.5 and 44.9 hours respectively. The primary outcome, time from randomization to the first antibiotic modification, was 8.6 versus 14.9 hours. For modification of Gram-negative-active antibiotics specifically, the medians were 17.3 versus 42.1 hours. These clinical intervals include more than an instrument's running time. They describe when results became available and when treatment, as recorded in medication administration, actually changed. [TD-W017]

Among patients with resistant organisms, escalation occurred at a median 18.4 hours in the rapid arm and 61.7 hours in the standard arm. The trial did not detect significant differences in clinical outcomes. Its most direct demonstrated achievement was earlier adjustment within this culture-to-review-to-treatment pathway. That finding remains substantial even though faster adjustment and an improvement in mortality are different outcomes. [TD-W017]

The investigators' secondary analysis, first published in 2024, examined 386 patients with monomicrobial, on-panel organisms who had received empiric therapy. It classified treatment as undertreatment, optimal narrow-spectrum treatment or overtreatment at the initial zero-to-two-hour interval and again at twenty-four to twenty-six and forty-eight to fifty-two hours. The clearest impact occurred with resistant Escherichia coli, Klebsiella and Proteus, for which rapid results supported earlier escalation. Broad-spectrum treatment often persisted even when an isolate was susceptible to narrower options. [TD-W018]

For Acinetobacter, Citrobacter, Enterobacter, Serratia and Pseudomonas, the analysis found little effect on treatment, although the groups were smaller. The authors proposed that clinicians might treat escalation as more urgent than narrowing therapy, or hesitate to remove broader coverage under diagnostic uncertainty. Those were explanations they offered for the observed response. The analysis did not review patient-level clinical details to establish every reason for a choice. It identifies differences in the parent trial's treatment trajectories; it was not a separately tested rule for selecting patients prospectively. [TD-W018]

Laboratory speed and patient outcomes#

Anton-Vazquez and colleagues' 2021 Cochrane review examined rapid susceptibility testing in bloodstream infection. Its six randomized trials included 1,638 participants and covered phenotypic and genotypic approaches producing results within eight hours of a positive culture. Individual trials reported earlier treatment changes, but the mortality estimate was imprecise: risk ratio 1.10, with a 95% confidence interval from 0.82 to 1.46, supported by low-certainty evidence. The review did not establish either a mortality reduction or the absence of a clinically meaningful effect. [TD-W019]

The review distinguishes the test's turnaround, time to appropriate treatment, and outcomes such as mortality and discharge. Empiric treatment was already active against the pathogen for many participants, so an earlier result did not always rescue an inactive regimen. Studies also differed in how results reached clinicians and how stewardship was organized. Those differences form part of the intervention being evaluated, rather than merely background to a laboratory comparison. [TD-W019]

Designing the report that reaches the clinician#

西村翔's 2024 review develops susceptibility testing as a contribution to antimicrobial stewardship across specimen collection, analysis and reporting. A resistance marker can answer a useful question without supplying a complete susceptibility profile. This is especially consequential for Gram-negative bacteria with several possible resistance mechanisms. Phenotypic testing and molecular detection therefore provide different information, whose interpretation depends on what was actually measured. [TD-W020]

Selective or cascade reporting changes which tested options routinely appear on the clinical report. A laboratory can make a narrower set of appropriate drugs immediately visible while keeping additional results available on request or under specified circumstances. The policy requires communication with clinicians so that an omitted drug is not mistaken for an unperformed test or an unusable treatment. In the author's hospital account, restrictions on routine fluoroquinolone reporting were discussed, tried and then implemented in July 2018, with exceptions for specified organisms. Use fell by roughly half in the reported before-and-after experience. This was an implementation observation, rather than a randomized estimate of the effect of reporting alone. [TD-W020]

The 2016 expert consensus by 王辉, 宁永忠, 陈宏斌 and colleagues sets out the construction of a bacterial susceptibility report. It begins before the display of drug names: the laboratory must consider whether the isolate is clinically significant and recognize intrinsic resistance. Panels combine standard expectations with local needs and consultation. The consensus's required reporting group is a reporting category, not a declaration that every listed agent is the clinician's first choice. [TD-W021]

The report separates smear observations, culture findings and susceptibility results. Measurements such as minimum inhibitory concentrations or zone diameters are accompanied by interpretation under a stated standard; comments can explain a consequential finding. Urgent partial results should be communicated with their timing clear, and unexpected resistance may require confirmation. These details

let the recipient distinguish a preliminary observation from a completed interpretation and act on important information before every part of the laboratory process is finished. [TD-W021]

Deciding when enough treatment has been given#

The PROGRESS trial, first published in 2020, used repeated procalcitonin measurements to inform stopping antibiotics in sepsis. Of 266 randomized patients, ten withdrew permission to use their data, leaving 125 in the procalcitonin group and 131 receiving standard care. Patients had already begun treatment and were randomized within twenty-four hours. The intervention measured procalcitonin at baseline and reassessed from day five, with daily measurements when the stopping criterion had not been reached. [TD-W023]

The Methods specified stopping when procalcitonin had fallen by at least 80% from baseline or was below 0.5 micrograms per liter, subject to the patient's condition. Instability, including persisting fever or vasopressor requirements, could justify continuing treatment despite the marker. Thirteen patients who reached the biochemical criterion were considered unstable; ninety-six patients complied with the stopping advice. The protocol therefore coupled a repeated measurement with a clinical exception, rather than making a single laboratory value an unconditional instruction. [TD-W023]

Median antibiotic duration was five days with procalcitonin guidance and ten days with standard care. The primary 180-day composite counted new infections by Clostridioides difficile or multidrug-resistant organisms, or death associated with either kind of infection present at baseline. It occurred in nine of 125 and twenty of 131 patients respectively. Twenty-eight-day mortality was also lower, nineteen versus thirty-seven deaths, while the 180-day mortality comparison was not statistically significant. The study involved hospital wards and excluded circumstances requiring prolonged treatment and specified patient groups. Its result concerns a defined stopping strategy after treatment had begun, with its measured outcomes and follow-up periods. [TD-W023]

Organizing a result-to-action pathway#

Chen and colleagues' 2026 narrative review proposes an explicit framework for making rapid results actionable. Its four clocks distinguish analytical turnaround, the wider laboratory interval, the point at which a result becomes clinically actionable, and the delay from result to action. A short assay does not uniquely determine any of the other three. A result may be technically available while the clinician still lacks the interpretation, patient information or response arrangement needed to use it. [TD-W022]

The authors organize actionability around five domains: result type and certainty, patient risk, probability of resistance, capacity to respond, and the quality of stewardship. They propose notification, interpretive comments, patient-specific recommendations, documentation, audit and feedback as connected components. This is their organizing clinical framework, not a validated numerical score. Its practical emphasis is on a result reaching someone who can interpret it, choose an action and record the response. S33 develops earlier accounts of information and decisions; these clinical histories show the particular measurements, reporting forms and treatment pathways through which information was used. [TD-W022]

S35 Conditioning, regularization and inverse operators#

Several different ways of making a calculation manageable#

The mathematical sources in this section explain distinct relations between data, a problem, its representation and a computational procedure. Conditioning describes sensitivity of the problem. Numerical stability concerns error introduced by an algorithm. Equilibration changes scaling; regularization constrains or penalizes possible answers; learned operators use prepared data and models to approximate a map.

Higham: a condition number belongs to a problem and its data#

Higham's exposition defines a condition number as a measure of how sensitive a solution is to small perturbations of input data. The definition depends on the function or implicitly defined problem, the input, a norm and the choice between relative and absolute perturbations. A claim that a problem is well conditioned is therefore incomplete without the relevant data and measurement convention. The same physical task can be represented by different mathematical questions, and a condition number answers the question actually specified. [W089, author exposition, 19 March 2020]

For a nonsingular square matrix, the familiar quantity κ(A) = ‖A ‖ ‖A-1‖ measures sensitivity associated with inversion in the stated norm. Higham relates it to linear-system sensitivity and distinguishes whether A alone or both A and b are treated as data. Large sensitivity describes what small perturbations can do, rather than asserting that every perturbation realizes the worst case. His diagrams and examples distinguish that potential amplification from the particular response to a given change.

The resource implication appears explicitly in the article: calculating a condition number exactly can be as expensive as computing the function itself, motivating estimates and bounds. Nor does a large but finite condition number imply mathematical discontinuity. [W089]

Higham: numerical stability belongs to an algorithm#

Higham's separate account of numerical stability asks how errors introduced while executing an algorithm affect its result. Forward error measures departure from the intended answer. Backward error asks how much the input would have to change for the computed answer to be exact. A backward-stable procedure returns the exact answer to a nearby problem, where the scale of nearby is judged relative to the arithmetic. Forward stability instead evaluates the resulting error in relation to conditioning. Mixed stability allows small changes to both input and output. [W090, author exposition, 4 August 2020]

These distinctions explain why an algorithm can behave well while its answer remains sensitive. A small computational perturbation can be amplified by an ill-conditioned problem. Conversely, inspecting an answer's apparent plausibility does not establish a small backward error. Higham's discussion also makes the data boundary explicit: in a linear system, are the matrix, the right-hand side or both uncertain? In a nonlinear formula, are numerical coefficients fixed constants or uncertain data?

The rank-one outer-product example shows why the error model matters. Rounding its many entries independently need not produce a matrix that is exactly rank one. Requiring the computed result to be representable by perturbing only the original two vectors can therefore be too restrictive. The stability claim therefore depends on which input perturbations the error model permits. [W090]

Diamond and Boyd: equilibration without reading individual matrix entries#

Diamond and Boyd study row and column scaling that equalizes the corresponding norms. Their matrix-free method is relevant when a solver can multiply by a matrix and its transpose without convenient access to all its entries. They formulate a convex optimization problem and use a stochastic projected-gradient method with an unbiased gradient estimate. The approach replaces a demand for explicit matrix access with operations available through the computational interface. [MIO-W003, introduction and selected §§3.1–3.3]

Their condition-number result concerns a particular upper bound and, in the square nonsingular setting, its minimization over diagonal scalings. It is not a theorem that every diagonal scaling lowers the exact condition number or accelerates every solver. The optimization also uses a penalty to keep the scaling problem controlled. That penalty belongs to the scaling optimization; it should not be confused with regularization of the original inverse problem.

The selected LSQR example shows how the authors preserve the original task. They solve a scaled system, (DAE)z = Db, and recover the original coordinates by x = Ez. They assess accuracy using the original residual ‖Ax − b ‖, rather than only the residual in scaled coordinates. A small transformed residual is not allowed to redefine success without translation back to the starting system. [MIO-W003, selected §6.1]

Their experiment also counts preparation. Each equilibration iteration and each LSQR iteration involves one multiplication by A and one by its transpose, making their comparison in total matrix multiplications intelligible. They compare different amounts of equilibration before applying the solver. The reported improvement concerns the constructed numerical setup. [MIO-W003, selected numerical discussion, §7 and conclusion]

Hansen: regularization suppresses unstable detail by changing the reconstruction#

Hansen's selected teaching slides explain why directly using small singular values can greatly amplify noisy components of data. Truncated singular-value decomposition removes selected components rather than using the complete inverse expansion. The truncation parameter should respond to where data coefficients become dominated by noise, not simply to a singular-value cutoff considered independently of the data. [MIO-W002, slides 1–8]

The slides make the tradeoff explicit: smaller covariance is purchased with bias. Truncation can reduce the effect of noise, but its abrupt cutoff can introduce artifacts; computing a full singular-value decomposition can also be infeasible for large problems. The convenient formula therefore includes both an approximation choice and a computational prerequisite.

Tikhonov regularization replaces residual minimization by a balance between data fit and a penalty. In the standard form shown, the target is to minimize ‖Ax − b ‖2 + λ2 ‖x ‖2. A large λ can oversmooth the answer; a small λ can allow noise to dominate. The selected material treats the smoothing norm and the balancing parameter as choices that affect the result. The regularization term encodes a preference or restriction on acceptable solutions, rather than generating information absent from the measurements. [MIO-W002, slides 10–14; formulas and tradeoffs]

Reducing a solver's burden on an equivalent system differs from accepting a biased or restricted reconstruction.

Nelsen and Yang: learning a family of inverse maps#

Nelsen and Yang's 2025 survey distinguishes end-to-end inverse learning from learning selected components inside a conventional inversion procedure. In the first approach, observed data are mapped

directly to an estimated unknown or to a posterior distribution. In the second, learned priors, regularizers or other components enter an algorithm that still carries out inversion. Those arrangements locate the learned information differently. [MIO-W001, selected introduction, §§2.2, 4.1, 4.4 and 5.2]

Their mathematical setup writes data as y = G(u) + η, with G the forward map, u the unknown and η noise. The true inverse, when it exists on the specified admissible domain, is defined on the range of G. A learned estimator can be evaluated on a larger observation space, including noisy data outside that range. The survey emphasizes that identifying an admissible domain on which the forward map is injective and its inverse continuous can itself require difficult analysis. The training procedure does not make that domain question disappear. [MIO-W001, §4.1]

The selected formulation trains using pairs of unknowns and noisy observations, drawn under a specified distribution and noise model, and minimizes a selected loss over a hypothesis class. Consequently the training distribution, noise and metric are part of what the learned map is prepared to do. Approximation existence, successful optimization and reliable practical use are distinct matters. An expressive architecture is not by itself evidence that an actual training run has recovered the desired inverse.

Their discussion of electrical impedance tomography retains severe sensitivity: the cited stability relation can be logarithmic in the noise. Restrictions to suitable finite-dimensional sets can improve the stability statement, with constants and dimension dependence that matter. These results are reported through the survey. [MIO-W001, selected §4.3, including equation 4.24]

Amortization and the retained preparation#

For posterior learning, Nelsen and Yang describe approximating a data-to-posterior map so that a family of inverse problems can be addressed without retraining for every observation. They explicitly acknowledge potentially high upfront training and data-generation costs. Repeated fast evaluations can amortize that preparation. [MIO-W001, §4.4]

One described approach uses a hypernetwork to map the data to parameters of a second network representing transport from prior to posterior. The survey notes that this training task is difficult in practice and that higher accuracy may require subsequent fine-tuning or using the learned model as a preconditioner for a fixed observation. The learned map can thus serve either as an approximate answer or as preparation for an observation-specific calculation.

IPCC: tuning retains physical and observational constraints#

The selected IPCC assessment passage on model tuning describes a different modeling practice. Parameters for unresolved processes are not treated as arbitrary controls. Their acceptable ranges are constrained by mathematical consistency, physical considerations such as energy conservation and observational evidence. Component modeling groups make initial choices; assembling the components into an Earth system model requires refinement against predefined tuning targets. [GL-W089, chapter 1, §1.5.3.2]

Meeting predefined tuning targets precedes release for model comparisons. The resulting Earth system model combines governing constraints with parameters refined against observed behavior. [GL-W089]

Sensitivity, preparation and reconstruction#

Higham supplies definitions needed to describe sensitivity and computational error accurately. Diamond and Boyd provide a particular preparation method with an original-task residual and counted setup operations. Hansen explains restricted reconstruction and its bias–noise tradeoff. Nelsen and Yang survey

reusable learned maps and retained priors, training and accuracy work. The IPCC assessment describes constrained component tuning.

S55 Numerical fidelity and computational cost#

A numerical computation can use different amounts of arithmetic precision in different places. The accounts below explain how programmers and numerical analysts select those places, check the returned result and pay for correction or monitoring. Their tasks range from solving a specified linear system to accepting a measured change in an application’s output. The required answer and the means of judging it enter the procedure alongside the available arithmetic.

S35 develops conditioning, stability and preparation of numerical problems. Here the focus is the allocation of fidelity during computation: what work can become cheaper, what must remain accurate and what happens when the initial allocation proves insufficient.

Buttari and colleagues: a cheap factorization with more accurate correction#

Buttari and colleagues divide the work of solving a dense linear system, Ax = b, between two arithmetic formats. They convert the matrix and right-hand side to single precision, factor the converted matrix and obtain an initial solution. They preserve the original double-precision matrix. Each subsequent correction begins by calculating the residual, b − Ax, using that original matrix in double precision. The existing single-precision factors are then reused to solve for a correction, which is added to the solution in double precision. The analogous procedure uses Cholesky factorization for a symmetric positive-definite system. [CG-W001, §1.1, Algorithms 2–3]

The procedure places the cubic-cost factorization in the faster arithmetic while retaining more accurate residual calculation and solution updates, whose cost per refinement step is quadratic. It also retains two matrix representations and conversions between them. Single precision therefore describes a particular part of the computation; it does not replace the accuracy required of the returned answer. The paper's error analysis makes the result conditional on a sufficiently well-conditioned matrix relative to the correction arithmetic and an adequately stable correction solver. Low-precision errors must still permit refinement to make progress. [CG-W001, §1.1 and Appendix A]

Their implementation comparisons show why the size and architecture matter. On the conventional processors tested, the reported gains reach approximately 1.8 for the nonsymmetric solver and 1.5 for the positive-definite solver when problems are sufficiently large. For small systems, even a few correction steps can outweigh the cheaper factorization. The Cell results use a different comparison: the mixed-precision solver's achieved throughput is compared with the processor's double-precision peak, giving the reported factors of seven and eleven. The experiments provide implementation evidence for this division of arithmetic work; the graph labels and processor configurations specify what was compared. [CG-W001, §1.2, Table 2 and Figures 1–8]

Carson and Higham: correction accuracy and convergence are different requirements#

Carson and Higham make three arithmetic roles independently adjustable: factorization, storage of data and solution, and residual calculation. Their general analysis also distinguishes the effective accuracy with which a correction equation is solved. This fourth parameter is useful when a low-precision factorization supports a more accurate iterative correction. An algorithm can thus store its answer in single precision, factor in half precision and compute residuals in double precision. Their conditions distinguish the rate at which errors decrease from the accuracy eventually attainable. More accurate residuals can lower the final forward-error level without repairing a correction process that fails to converge. [CG-W002, Algorithm 1.1, §§2–4 and 7]

Their GMRES variant uses the low-precision factors as a preconditioner, rather than relying on their triangular solves alone to supply each correction. This can extend the class of systems for which the solution reaches working-precision accuracy. The procedure still needs the original matrix and accurate applications of the preconditioned operator. Half precision's narrow numerical range also requires attention to scaling; when the initial solve overflows, the authors describe starting refinement from zero instead. [CG-W002, §§6 and 8, Algorithm 8.1]

The experiments expose a limit that a count of outer refinement steps would miss. For one generated 100-by-100 system, three outer steps contain 91, 92 and 92 GMRES iterations. A different family, with one small singular value, reaches the required error level with seven GMRES iterations in total despite a very large condition number. Every inner iteration performs additional accurate work. The authors accordingly distinguish successful numerical correction from an economical implementation: enough inner iterations can erase the benefit of a cheaper factorization. These tests use MATLAB, including emulated half precision, to examine error and iteration behavior. The paper's potential speed advantage remains conditional on hardware and correction cost. [CG-W002, §§10–11, Figures 10.7 and 10.9]

Precimonious: search against an explicit acceptance test#

Rubio-González and colleagues turn precision allocation into a search over program variants. The programmer supplies a program, test inputs and an accuracy requirement. Precimonious identifies floating-point variables whose types can change and, where alternatives are supplied, calls that can use another mathematical-function implementation. It generates candidate programs, compiles and runs them, and retains changes only when the results pass the accuracy and exception checks and the program satisfies the performance requirement. Their modified delta-debugging procedure tests groups of changes and progressively refines them. It seeks a locally minimal retained set of higher-precision variables rather than exhaustively finding the best possible allocation. [CG-W003, §§2–3, Figures 3–4]

The acceptance test compares a candidate's output with the original program's output on the supplied inputs. This provides a practical engineering contract, but its reference is the original implementation rather than an independently established mathematical answer. The authors' additional summation example makes the distinction consequential: truncating an infinite series and accumulating roundoff introduce different errors. Arithmetic precision can also change the number of iterations before a program stops, so apparently changing only a variable type can change the amount of work actually performed. [CG-W003, §§3.4 and 4.3]

Their experiments connect precision choices to execution cost. In the arc-length program, the reported speedup reaches 41.7% at two selected error thresholds. Several other programs improve less, while three produce no accepted faster configuration at the tested thresholds. The conversion instructions introduced between formats can outweigh savings elsewhere. A more permissive accuracy threshold consequently need not lead this search to a faster program. The FFT case with the strictest tested threshold explores 663 configurations and takes 116 minutes and 51 seconds. At publication, the suggested changes also required manual mapping back into source code, although transformed intermediate code was generated automatically. [CG-W003, §4.2, Tables 1–3; §5]

The authors test the limits of their input selection directly. They tune the NAS benchmarks using Class A inputs and subsequently try Classes B and C. Several allocations that pass the original test fail these new cases; for the EP benchmark, failures remain even at the most relaxed tested threshold. Its EP performance figure also has a specific scope: the 33.2% headline concerns the Gaussian-deviate phase that was tuned, while the reported improvement for the whole program averages 14%. [CG-W003, §4.2, Table 4 and footnote 6]

FPTuner: allocate precision under a conservative expression-wide bound#

Chiang and colleagues require a precision allocation to meet an error target throughout a declared input domain. Their object is a real-valued expression with a fixed computational structure, not an arbitrary program. They model rounding at operations and conversions, use symbolic Taylor expansions to relate these errors to the expression's output, and obtain conservative bounds over the input intervals. The allocation is then an optimization problem: maximize a weighted count of lower-precision operations while satisfying the error constraint. [CG-W004, §§2–4]

The procedure includes a further check. Its allocation search initially uses first-order error terms. FPTaylor then checks the generated allocation with higher-order effects included. If the candidate violates the target, the procedure can add an allowance for those effects and repeat the search. The authors report that the candidates in their experiments passed this check immediately. Thus the fast search approximation and the conservative acceptance check perform different jobs. Bounds on conversion error are included, and conversion counts can also be constrained. Groups of operations can be assigned the same precision to support vectorization. [CG-W004, §§4.1–5, Figure 4]

Their measurements show why a rigorous accuracy constraint does not make the cost objective exact. The objective's weighted operator count is a guide to allocation, not a direct measurement of execution time or energy. On a Jetson TK1 board, the authors measure single/double-precision versions using current and voltage instrumentation. Four selected benchmarks save energy on average when moved from all-double to one mixed allocation, but other configurations consume more energy or take longer. In the jetEngine expression, mixing formats increases register pressure and causes constants to be spilled and reloaded. The executed instructions defeat an apparent saving visible in the arithmetic allocation alone. [CG-W004, §6.3, Table 5 and Figures 7–8]

A separate timing comparison replaces some software-implemented quadruple-precision work with hardware-supported double precision. Those results have a different baseline from the Jetson comparison, where both formats have hardware support. The all-double version is also insufficient for the stricter error contracts used in the quadruple/double study; its faster time cannot be treated as an accuracy-matched alternative. Tuning itself can take seconds or, in one reported case, twenty minutes, followed by the final verification. [CG-W004, §§6.1–6.3 and 7.1]

The scope of the conservative result remains explicit. FPTuner treats straight-line expressions over bounded input domains. The paper does not implement general treatment of branches and loops: rounding can change a branch decision, and bounding the resulting difference is a separate problem. The contribution is a developed allocation and checking procedure for its stated expression model, accompanied by measurements that reveal when the intended resource gain survives compilation. [CG-W004, §§7.2–7.4]

Green: calibrate the effect on the output and restore accuracy when needed#

Baek and Chilimbi's Green system supports two deliberate approximations: replace an expensive function with a supplied alternative, or stop a loop before its original end. The programmer supplies an output-quality measure, a target and calibration inputs. Calibration relates the approximation to both its output effect and its performance and energy costs. Generated code then selects among function versions according to input ranges or determines when a loop can stop. In the adaptive loop policy, it also observes whether further iterations continue to improve the chosen quality measure. [CG-W005, §§2–3, Figures 1– 3]

The reference computation remains part of the operating arrangement. During sampled recalibration, Green records the quality that an early termination would have produced and then continues the precise

computation so that the difference can be assessed. It can increase the work retained, select a more accurate function version, or relax an approximation that is more accurate than the target requires. For a function input range where no available approximation meets the criterion, it uses the precise function. These comparisons and changes have a sampling cost. [CG-W005, §§2.2.3 and 3.2, Figures 3 and 5–7]

Local acceptance also has to survive combination. In the option-pricing benchmark, the locally selected exponential approximation and logarithm approximation do not together meet the application's target. Green changes the logarithm choice from one polynomial approximation to a more accurate one. The resulting combined version has less than 0.8% loss under the chosen output measure, with reported performance and energy improvements of 28.5% and 28%, respectively. The authors retain the application-level comparison rather than assuming that acceptable individual substitutions add up to an acceptable program. [CG-W005, §§3.4 and 4.4, Figures 8 and 23–24]

The search-engine experiment specifies a different output criterion. It counts queries whose ordered top results differ from the precise backend's results; it does not measure human judgments of relevance. Tests use a production index and query logs, with crawling and index updates disabled. One adaptive configuration improves throughput by 21% and reduces joules per query by 14%, while 0.27% of queries produce a different ordered result. Whole-system energy is measured from the main power cable. [CG-W005, §§4.1–4.3, Figures 10–12]

An intentionally inaccurate calibration model exposes the time required for restoration. The chosen target allows 2% differing queries, but the initial cutoff typically produces about 10%. After each 10,000 queries, Green runs the next 100 precisely and uses their comparison to increase the retained search work. In this experiment it reaches the target after 180,000 queries. More frequent monitoring could accelerate adaptation while consuming more resources. The paper's claims about statistical quality rest on calibration and observed target tracking; this experiment makes the delay visible rather than establishing a bound on every query. [CG-W005, §4.3, Figure 14]

EnerJ: protect the part that must remain precise#

Sampson and colleagues distinguish permission to approximate from the requirement to preserve precise computation. EnerJ extends Java with types that mark data as approximate or precise. Approximate values can use less reliable storage or operations, and approximate objects can select a supplied alternative algorithm. Unannotated data remains precise. The type system prevents approximate information from flowing into precise state without an explicit endorsement by the programmer. [CG-W006, §§2.1–2.5]

That protection includes indirect routes. An approximate condition cannot silently determine a branch that changes precise state. Array indices and lengths remain precise, and the implementation does not approximate pointers. An endorsement permits a selected approximate value to cross this boundary. It does not repair or recompute the value; the programmer accepts responsibility for how the receiving computation uses it. A checksum, for example, can be calculated precisely over data whose earlier production was approximate. Precisely encoding or storing that data preserves the selected value rather than proving it was the right value. [CG-W006, §§2.2, 2.4, 2.6 and 5.1]

The paper states a noninterference property for a core language without endorsements: changing approximate values does not change its precise state. This is an isolation property. Approximate values themselves have no quantitative accuracy guarantee. The conference article develops the language rules, states the properties and describes the implemented checker. [CG-W006, §3]

Their resource study uses a simulated approximation-aware architecture. It combines reduced floating-point mantissas, less reliable operations and storage, and reduced memory refresh. The energy model counts instruction execution and SRAM and DRAM storage; instruction fetch and decode retain their cost.

Its parameters combine earlier measurements with values explicitly identified as estimates. The model omits implementation and switching overheads, including voltage-scaling latency. The article reports potential CPU/memory energy savings ranging from 7% to 38%, not measurements from constructed approximate hardware. [CG-W006, §§4–5 and 6.1, Table 2 and Figure 4]

Application quality varies independently of that range. Means over twenty simulated runs show relatively small losses under mild approximation, while FFT and SOR lose substantial fidelity at stronger settings. The programmer also has work beyond adding declarations. For the barcode reader, the authors changed an out-of-bounds image-coordinate response to return a white pixel, then endorsed approximate coordinates where they became array indices. This adaptation made the computation more tolerant of errors; it was not performed automatically by the type system. EnerJ's developed contribution is the explicit protected boundary, with application-specific approximation and acceptance still supplied around it. [CG-W006, §§6.2–6.3, Figure 5]

The mandatory and optional task portions in S57 address another way of reducing computational work: stopping a refinement or choosing a shorter procedure while still delivering an acceptable result. That account concerns task execution and scheduling; the procedures here specify arithmetic roles, output comparisons and protected computation.

S75 Algorithm selection, adaptive sorting and computing only what is needed#

Choosing a method for an instance#

Lars Kotthoff's 2012 survey organizes algorithm selection around problem instances, descriptive features, a set of candidate algorithms and a performance measure. Its account of the earlier Rice framework makes the selection problem explicit: map information about an instance to a method expected to perform well on it. The desired result might be a short running time, a high-quality solution within a budget, or success on a difficult search problem. An algorithm's favorable average over one collection of instances need not make it the best choice for every member. [TD-W024]

The survey distinguishes choosing one algorithm before execution from scheduling a portfolio and from responding to observations during execution. A static selector might use instance features measured in advance. A schedule can allocate time among solvers, while an online approach obtains further information as work proceeds. These arrangements offer different ways to use uneven performance. They also require decisions about which features to compute, how expensive those computations may be, and when to use a default instead. [TD-W024]

Feature computation is itself work that can be budgeted. A predictor that needs an expensive search to describe an instance may consume the time that its choice was supposed to save. Kotthoff discusses selection and feature costs as part of assessing the system, along with the chosen algorithm's performance. The engineering question is consequently concrete: what can be learned economically about this instance, and which decision can still be changed by learning it? The histories of numerical preparation and precision in S35 and S55 concern other ways in which the representation and conduct of a computation affect its performance. [TD-W024]

Different kinds of partial order#

Vladimir Estivill-Castro and Derick Wood's 1992 survey shows why “nearly sorted” needs a specified meaning. Straight insertion sort maintains an ordered prefix and inserts each new item by moving larger predecessors aside.
