Each such shift removes one inversion: a pair whose earlier item is greater than its later item. If there are I inversions among n items, the work is O(n + I). A sequence with only O(n) inversions can therefore be sorted in linear time by this method. The relevant quantity is the number of inverted pairs, rather than simply how many items look displaced. [TD-W025]

Consider two explanatory inputs. The sequence [2, 1, 4, 3, 6, 5, 8, 7] has four inversions and four adjacent descents. Straight insertion needs four shifts of larger predecessors. The sequence [5, 6, 7, 8, 1, 2, 3, 4] has only one adjacent descent, but sixteen inversions: every item in the first half exceeds every item in the second. It consists of two ascending runs, which a merge can combine with linear work. Generalizing the second construction to two equal sorted halves gives n2/4 inversions even though only two runs need merging. [TD-W025]

A linear scan can find adjacent descents and run boundaries. That does not make it a linear-time count of all inverted pairs. Different measures expose different opportunities: few inversions suit ordinary insertion, while a few long runs favor merging. The survey develops adaptive sorting through explicit measures of disorder and bounds relative to the number of inputs compatible with a given amount of disorder. It reports Mannila's formalization and examples of algorithms designed to meet such bounds. [TD-W025]

This analysis does not contradict the worst-case comparison bound for unrestricted sorting. If a comparison procedure must distinguish all n! orders of distinct keys, its decision tree needs enough

leaves to represent them, requiring Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. A restricted class can contain fewer possibilities, and an adaptive algorithm can do less work on favorable inputs while retaining a larger worst case elsewhere. Sortedness is itself recognizable in linear time by checking neighbors. The useful distinction is between the task's worst case and the work justified by the particular order already present. [TD-W025, TD-W026]

Using the key representation#

MIT's 2011 linear-time sorting notes contrast comparison sorting with methods that inspect keys as data. Counting sort assumes integer keys in a range of size K. It allocates positions or buckets for those keys, scans the n records to count or distribute them, and visits the key range in order. The time is Θ(n + K); a record-carrying bucket implementation also uses Θ(n + K) space. If keys represent ages from zero through one hundred, K is small. If two keys are zero and a trillion, the same direct range allocation is unattractive despite the small number of records. [TD-W026]

Least-significant-digit radix sort instead represents a key by d digits in base b and performs a stable counting pass for each digit, from least to most significant. Stability preserves the order established by earlier passes among records sharing the present digit. For an explanatory example, sorting 21, 12, 11 by units gives 21, 11, 12, retaining the order of the two records ending in one; a stable tens pass then gives 11, 12, 21. The bound is Θ(d(n + b)). It becomes linear in n under suitable restrictions on d and b. A small key range, a bounded digit representation and a favorable probability distribution are different assumptions, each supporting different methods. [TD-W026]

Making radix sorting practical#

Peter McIlroy, Keith Bostic and M. Douglas McIlroy's 1993 engineering study treats string sorting as a problem of using the bytes already present in keys. A most-significant-byte distribution forms piles by the next byte and recursively sorts each unfinished pile. Strings sharing a prefix then advance together to the next position; a completed string need not continue through later characters. This avoids repeatedly rediscovering a long common prefix through whole-string comparisons. [TD-W027]

The bookkeeping matters. Clearing or scanning every possible byte pile can dominate when only a few piles are occupied, so the authors examine ways to track the occupied range or piles. Small piles can be finished by an insertion method rather than paying the full distribution overhead again. Their “American flag” method counts pile sizes, computes their destination ranges, and cycles misplaced string descriptors into the appropriate ranges in place. Once a descriptor is placed, the displaced descriptor supplies the next item to move. This yields an in-place distribution without requiring a separate full array of descriptors, although the permutation is not stable. [TD-W027]

Recursion order also affects storage: leaving the largest pile until last limits the stack needed for the remaining work. The article combines these details with tests on actual workloads and attention to the sorting interface. Its performance gains belong to those implementations and data. The enduring substance of the account is visible in the connected construction: use a key's next byte, group a shared prefix, avoid empty-pile work, move descriptors through counted ranges, and switch methods where a smaller routine is preferable. [TD-W027]

Sampling and equal-key blocks#

Jon Bentley and M. Douglas McIlroy's 1993 account of a library sort began with inputs that defeated existing implementations. Organ-pipe patterns and arrays containing only zeros and ones exposed quadratic behavior. The replacement was developed for a general interface in which a caller supplies the comparison operation and records may be expensive to exchange. Comparisons, swaps and partition

bookkeeping therefore had different costs from those in an abstract count of unit-time operations. [TD-W028]

Pivot sampling varied with size: a middle element for small inputs, a median of three for larger ones, and a pseudomedian assembled from nine samples for still larger ones. The authors chose thresholds empirically rather than presenting a single sampling rule as costless at every size. Their partitioning also gathered equal keys so that, after rearrangement, the middle block contained items equal to the pivot. Only the less-than and greater-than blocks required recursive sorting. With an all-equal input, one partitioning scan could finish the problem. [TD-W028]

For an explanatory zero/one input, choosing zero as pivot collects the zeros into the equal block and leaves only the ones on the greater side. Sorting need not repeatedly partition the zeros as if they still had unknown relative ranks. The authors' split-end partitioning implements this treatment of equals while supporting the general library interface. The paper supplies an engineering account of robustness across troublesome inputs; it should not be conflated with later introspective sorting methods that add a worst-case fallback. [TD-W028]

Choosing which runs to merge#

Natural mergesort discovers ordered runs, but it still must decide which adjacent runs to combine and in what order. A merge of runs of lengths a and b costs in proportion to a + b. Repeatedly merging a long run with each small arrival can scan its contents many times. A suitable merge tree limits how often an item travels through successive merges while preserving the adjacency needed for stable sorting. This is the problem addressed by J. Ian Munro and Sebastian Wild's 2018 peeksort and powersort algorithms. [TD-W029]

Peeksort finds the run around the middle of an interval and recursively organizes work around the resulting boundaries. Powersort processes runs from left to right and assigns a power to the boundary between neighboring runs. The power records the first binary subdivision depth that separates their normalized midpoints. It represents where the boundary belongs in a nearly balanced tree without requiring the entire run sequence in advance. When a new boundary has a shallower power than a pending one, the deeper work is merged first. A stack retains the unfinished adjacent pieces. [TD-W029]

For run lengths L1 through Lr totaling n, the authors use the entropy H = Σ(Li/n) log2(n/Li). It reflects the distribution of run lengths: one long run and several tiny ones need not require the merge work of many equally sized runs. Their powersort analysis bounds total merge cost M by nH + 2n. The additive linear term makes the result nearly optimal in this cost model. The measured runtime also depends on the implementation of a merge, memory traffic and comparisons. [TD-W029]

Vincent Jugé's 2020 account of adaptive ShiversSort develops another economical policy. It uses levels derived from the integer parts of the base-two logarithms of run lengths and examines only the top three runs on its stack when deciding the next merge. Run-size comparisons determine whether an older pair should be combined before the newest run is allowed to remain pending. This small local view is used to control the larger merge structure. The paper separates the merge policy from preparation of short runs and from optimizations inside a merge. [TD-W030]

Number the pending runs from the stack's top, so R1 is newest, and let each level be the floor of log2 of its length. If either of the top two levels is at least the third, the policy merges R2 with R3. Otherwise, if the top level is at least the second, it merges R1 with R2; otherwise it admits another run. At the end it merges the remaining stack. For an explanatory stack with lengths 8, 4, 4 from bottom to top, the levels are 3, 2, 2. The two top runs merge to length eight, after which the two eights merge. The older eight is not scanned once for each arriving four. [TD-W030]

Jugé states an nH + O(n) merge-cost bound for the adaptive policy and compares it with earlier guarantees. A better coefficient in an entropy bound concerns accumulated merge work, not an identical percentage reduction in execution time on every machine or input. The account shows how a compact rule operating on a few stack entries can be the subject of a substantial global guarantee. It also preserves a distinction between the historically described TimSort merge policies and later implementations adopting powersort. [TD-W030]

Adaptation during the work#

The sorting design notes shipped with CPython 3.14.0, released in October 2025, connect run discovery with the work of sorting itself. The implementation detects natural runs, normalizes descending runs, extends short runs with stable binary insertion, and uses powersort to organize their merges. Its treatment of equal-key subruns allows normalization while preserving stability. These are details of this frozen release, which incorporates developments after the original introduction of TimSort. [TD-W031]

For example, [3, 2, 1, 3, 4, 5, 0] begins with a descending stretch. Reversing its first three items produces [1, 2, 3], after which the scan can extend the ordered run across the following 3, 4, 5. Recognizing order and acting on it are interleaved. There need not be a separate, completed diagnosis of the whole input before sorting begins. If a run is too short for efficient merging, binary insertion brings it to the desired working length. [TD-W031]

During a merge, galloping responds to a sustained winning streak by one run. Exponential search followed by binary search finds a block that can be copied together rather than comparing each item against the other run's next item. The threshold adapts so that useful streaks encourage further galloping and unsuccessful attempts discourage it. The implementation therefore uses information at several scales: runs in the input, their lengths and merge positions, and temporary dominance during a particular merge. [TD-W031]

A rank without a full order#

Manuel Blum, Robert Floyd, Vaughan Pratt, Ronald Rivest and Robert Tarjan's 1973 selection paper proved that the item of a specified rank can be found with a worst-case linear number of comparisons. Their PICK construction sorts fixed-size columns, selects representatives, recursively finds a representative of controlled rank, and uses it to partition the original candidates. The representative is chosen so that a guaranteed fraction can be discarded. If the sought rank lies above the discarded lower part, its rank is adjusted within the remaining part; if below, the upper part becomes irrelevant. [TD-W032]

The original construction develops its guarantee through column sizes and representative positions, including a basic analysis with columns of twenty-one. Its result is about finding a rank, not arranging all items in order or necessarily supplying the fastest practical routine for a tiny requested subset. Once a cutoff rank is known, the relevant side of a partition can be retained without sorting the other side. Ordering the retained items is a further task whose size may be much smaller than n. [TD-W032]

Keeping a small extreme subset#

CPython 3.14's heapq implementation gives a practical streaming alternative for a small requested k. To retain the largest k items, a min-heap of k candidates exposes the smallest retained item at its root. Each new item is compared with that boundary. If it cannot enter the retained set, it is discarded; if it can, it replaces the root and the heap is repaired. After the scan, only k candidates remain. The worst-case work is O(n log k), with O(k) retained storage, followed by O(k log k) if the retained set is sorted for presentation. For a fixed ten candidates, the scan is linear in n. [TD-W031]

The release's nlargest and nsmallest functions include useful boundary cases: a request for one uses an extremum operation, and a request at least as large as a known input size can use a full sort. The functions return their retained results in order. Their heap entries also carry an order field, preserving a defined treatment of equal keys. A custom routine that only needs the set can leave its heap unordered; it should not assume that a library function returning ordered results omitted the final sort. [TD-W031]

Local top-k results also admit a simple merge. Under a consistent total ordering, an item excluded from a partition's top k already has at least k items ahead of it in that partition, so it cannot enter the global top k. The global answer is therefore contained in the union of the local answers; another top-k selection over that union suffices. Equal keys require a shared tie rule if exact membership matters. This is a direct consequence of the retained-set rule, illustrated by disjoint candidate partitions, rather than a separate empirical performance claim. Scanning a filesystem can involve additional work to compute directory totals or identify shared files; selecting the largest measured candidates is the part explained by this algorithm. [TD-W031]

S37 Morphology, embodiment and physical computation#

The body changes the control problem#

The sources in this section examine how a body's shape, materials and dynamics affect behavior, perception and control. They disagree about when such contributions should be called computation.

Hoffmann and Müller: a design tradeoff, not an automatic transfer#

Hoffmann and Müller's 2014 paper considers a design space extending from relatively simple bodies with model-based control to complex, compliant bodies with distributed or model-free schemes. Conventional rigid-robot engineering often simplifies the body dynamics that a controller must manage. A soft or highly compliant body supplies richer dynamics that can help produce useful behavior, but can also be difficult to model faithfully. The contribution of morphology therefore cannot be evaluated solely by counting fewer instructions in an otherwise unchanged controller. [W007, relevant definitions and body–control discussion]

The paper distinguishes exploiting physical properties to simplify control from performing a computation. It also asks whether a model is required and how difficult that model is to construct. A body well suited to a task can make the task easier, while its high dimensionality and nonlinearity make accurate modeling harder. The proposed tradeoff includes the design and knowledge problem.

Their criticism of proposed morphological-computation measures is particularly pertinent. A measure that rewards little influence by the agent's actions can favor a system that is difficult to control. A measure that rewards strong natural dynamics need not favor the body that makes the intended task easy. The authors distinguish these properties from engineering usefulness. Physical dynamics can resist a controller as well as assist it, and the desired balance depends on the task and environment. [W007]

Müller and Hoffmann: control, perception and computation are distinct contributions#

The 2017 article examines characteristic cases including passive walking, self-stabilization and gecko adhesion, task-shaped visual sensing and physical reservoir computing. Its classification separates morphology that facilitates control, morphology that facilitates perception and morphology that performs computation under a defensible account of physical computation. A useful foot or leg does not necessarily calculate an output merely because its properties reduce a controller's difficulty. [W008, characteristic cases and conceptual analysis]

In a passive walker, the movement can result from the physical dynamics without an abstract computational level. In a sensing arrangement, geometry or the distribution of receptors can make task-relevant distinctions available before later processing. These mechanisms deserve explanation in their own terms. Calling them all offloaded computation can obscure what the arrangement actually does and what sensing or action remains.

Reservoir examples offer a more specific computational use of rich dynamics. Inputs perturb a physical system, and a trained readout extracts an output useful for a task. The article discusses a tensegrity body used to classify terrain, as well as arrangements with feedback and a readout producing a periodic command pattern. The trained readout, input coupling and interpretation of the output remain parts of these examples. [W008, physical-reservoir discussion]

Miłkowski: when physical assistance counts as computation#

Miłkowski's abstract and opening passages argue that physical implementation matters to computation generally, and that morphology facilitating control need not itself constitute computation. A special label should not suggest that ordinary physical computing is independent of its material substrate. This challenges the language of outsourcing computation to a body. [W054, abstract and opening]

Liu and colleagues: behavior generation and morphology-based intelligence#

The opening sections of Liu, Guo, Sun and Zhang's 2023 review place body, brain and environment in interaction. They organize a broader research area around behavior generation through morphology, learning-based morphology control and learning-based morphology optimization. The early sections are especially useful because they distinguish resembling an organism from actually exploiting a body's dynamics in control. A biomimetic shape can enable a new capability while still requiring a complex controller. [W011, printed pp. 1132–1137, §§1–2.2.2]

Their account of morphology uses shape, material and dynamic properties to affect behavior. The examples include passive walking and physical interaction that produces movement, with an emphasis on implicit physical processes rather than merely wearable or implanted digital devices. The review's vocabulary is broad: it often calls this contribution morphological computation. That choice is reported as the review's usage, alongside the stricter distinctions in the preceding papers.

The review also keeps learning and morphology in a two-way relation. Behavior can gather samples that support learning; learning can alter control; control can alter morphology; and optimization can change the designed body. These are different routes, not a single completed method. The wider device literature is mediated through the review. [W011, conclusion, printed pp. 1148–1149]

Chen and colleagues: controllability depends on the arrangement#

Chen, Yu, Zhang and Su analyze vibration controllability in an underactuated flexible manipulator. Their example separates two questions. First they examine state controllability of the corresponding rigid system under different actuator placements, disregarding elastic deformation. Then they investigate structural vibration controllability of the flexible system. The operative variables include both joint configuration and where actuation is supplied. [W009, model, analysis and conclusion, printed pp. 391– 398]

Their conclusion makes controllability conditional on configuration, placement and the vibration-controllability matrix. It also uses a minimum singular value and a modal-reachability indicator to distinguish configurations and relative difficulty. Thus fewer actuators or a flexible link do not by themselves determine whether a particular motion can be controlled effectively. The arrangement matters within the approximated model.

The paper's simulation supports comparisons within its planar manipulator example and associated generalization. The informative contribution is the explicit dependence of control capability on how physical degrees of freedom and inputs are connected. [W009]

Montúfar, Ghazi-Zahedi and Ay: capacity for embodied behavior#

A Theory of Cheap Control in Embodied Systems provides a more formal meaning of cheap control than a general appeal to simplicity. Its main finite, reactive sensorimotor-loop model has fixed body and world channels. A policy maps sensor states to action distributions; the induced behavior also depends on the embodiment. Distinct policies can consequently be equivalent at the level of behavior. A controller need

not represent every possible policy distinction when those distinctions have no effect on the specified embodied behavior. [UX-W041, methods, lemma 1 and main theorem]

The authors exploit this reduction to give a sufficient approximation result for a model class of conditional restricted Boltzmann machines. The main theorem bounds a sufficient number of hidden units using the relevant sensory support and the dimension of embodied behavior. It establishes representational capacity to approximate the specified behavior, rather than a universally exact minimum controller size. The fixed channels, finite variables and reactive policy setting are part of the result.

The experimental treatment shows why estimating the relevant support is itself a substantive task. The authors sample a target behavior, estimate frequencies and prune the data before estimating support and a behavior dimension. They acknowledge that support estimation is a research problem in its own right and state that their pruning choice preceded the reported experimental outcomes. The controller-capacity calculation therefore relies on empirical estimates and a declared treatment of sampling noise. [UX-W041, experimental support estimation and discussion]

The result supplies an explanation of how an embodiment can restrict the behavior space a controller must cover. Representational capacity does not establish how quickly a learning algorithm can find the corresponding policy. [UX-W041]

Langer and Ay, 2021: a controller measure need not measure behavioral importance#

In their 2021 study, Langer and Ay use simple simulated agents moving on a racetrack without touching its walls. Changing sensor length changes the relation between the body and environment. They optimize policies and analyze information flows among environment, sensors, controller and actions. This provides a controlled setting for asking how the complexity of a task is distributed across interacting parts. [UX-W022, abstract, §1.1 and §4 discussion]

Their discussion points out that the integrated-information quantity in a controller can be high even when that quantity has no behavioral relevance. Information flowing into and out of the controller must also be considered. An internal measure cannot, by itself, establish what the controller contributes to the task. The optimization can converge to different local optima depending on its starting distribution, yielding more than one reasonably successful strategy.

The discussion separates directly optimizing a policy from learning an adequate world model. A result about a prepared policy does not settle how the agent would acquire the knowledge needed to behave that way. This limitation motivates the later study. [UX-W022]

Langer and Ay, 2024: learning can temporarily require more controller complexity#

The later paper makes the acquisition problem explicit. Again using simulated racetrack agents and information-theoretic measures, it adapts an em-algorithm that alternates improvement of goal-directed behavior with updating an internal world model. It compares agents whose world model is supplied with agents that must learn one, and includes split-controller arrangements that cannot integrate information in the same way. [UX-W015, selected v3 introduction, learning results and conclusion]

In the reported internal-world-model agents, successful learning is associated with initially higher controller complexity, followed by a decrease as useful body–environment interaction increases. Agents supplied with an ideal world model do not face the same prediction-learning demand. The comparison locates a possible earlier burden behind an apparently simple eventual controller.

The split internal-world-model agents predict the next sensory state less well and, on average, perform only marginally better than random movement, with relatively few successful agents. The authors take

this as support for the importance of integrated controller processing during world-model learning. They also recognize alternative explanations associated with the simplicity of the task, including the possibility that a single wall-avoidance problem demands little once an appropriate policy is available. [UX-W015, selected PDF pp. 14–18]

The paper supplies evidence about this sensorimotor loop, prediction task and learning scheme. [UX-W015; UX-W022]

Wang and colleagues: responsiveness is not sufficient for their physical-computing definition#

The selected opening of Wang, Zhou, Kahak and Li's 2026 Perspective defines a physical-computing kernel in which encoded inputs evolve through physical interactions into decoded outputs, with the possibility of programming the input–output evolution. It distinguishes analog and algorithmic forms and names analog oscillators, physical reservoirs and physical algorithmic computing as strategies for soft robots. The paper explicitly treats its framework as a proposed definition rather than universal agreement. [W098, published PDF pp. 1–2]

A responsive material can change shape or properties under heat, light, magnetic fields or other stimuli. Such a response can help adaptation or simplify operation while failing to satisfy the paper's computing definition. The distinction gives a concrete test of terminology: material responsiveness alone does not establish encoding, decoding and programmability. [W098]

Xie and colleagues: count persistence as well as task achievement#

The energy-accounting discussion in Xie and colleagues' article argues that task scores alone can conceal important embodied costs. Their reserve-based formulation tracks an internal energy stock, expenditure during a time step and energy intake. It treats remaining above an admissible energy boundary as a persistence condition. Energy is the accounted physical quantity; viability is a condition assessed through that account, rather than a synonym for energy. [W099, selected Energy as a Common Currency section]

The source points to search, movement, docking, processing, conversion and storage as possible demands associated with obtaining energy. Maintenance and persistence costs can also distinguish agents that achieve the same immediate task. Environment structure can change intake or dissipation. The proposal is consequently a call for explicit comparable accounting.

In their illustrations and discussion of open challenges, the authors expressly avoid claiming one universal energetic model for organisms and robots. [W099]

Co-design of morphology and control#

Rosendo, von Atzigen and Iida built two-module robots and tested how closely they could move toward a target. Their joint search varied the orientation and offset of the modules along with the amplitude and angular offsets of their motion. In a second set of trials, they froze the body design at several points in the search and used the remaining time to tune only the controller. Controller tuning improved several of the poorer body designs. For the same design time, continuing to search both body and controller produced the higher best scores later in the trials. [W034, figs. 2–5]

Mechanical assistance, perception and control#

These sources provide detailed accounts of mechanical assistance, task-shaped perception, physical computation, controller-capacity bounds, learning and physical accounting.

S110 Materials processing, degradation and failure#

How a surface flaw enters the fracture question#

A. A. Griffith introduces his 1921 paper through a question about filing, grinding and polishing machine parts subjected to repeated loads. He examines stresses near scratches and develops an energetic account of extending a flaw. The argument connects a change in the crack with changes in the energy of the stressed body and the cost of creating new surfaces. His controlled specimens make aspects of that relation observable. They are distinct from the machine parts that motivated the inquiry. [T12-W001]

Properties of a particular processed material#

Chen, Zhang and Ritchie tested a silicon carbide ceramic whose grain boundaries were initially glassy. In the as-processed material, measured fracture toughness was 6.2 MPa√m at 25 °C and 4.3 MPa√m at 1300 °C. After annealing for 85 hours at 1300 °C, the corresponding values were 7.2 and 5.2 MPa√m. Microscopy showed that most grain-boundary films had crystallized. In the authors’ account of fatigue, cracks extend between grains while intact grains bridging the crack behind its tip oppose its advance. The processing comparison comes from fracture-toughness measurements. The crack-growth observations come from the cyclic tests. [T12-W002]

Service conditions and specimens#

中村眞実 examines stainless-steel weld metal in a high-pressure hydrogen setting. The dissertation describes a pre-cooler used in a 70 MPa demonstration station and gives a 77 MPa condition for hydrogen in the cooling pipe. Its earlier discussion treats other hydrogen charging and tensile tests with specified weld metals and treatments. Fracture surfaces and reduction of area supply observations under those conditions. The component establishes an operating context, while a test specimen provides a particular material, exposure and loading arrangement. [T12-W003]

Motooka and Kiuchi compare load-controlled fatigue crack growth for refractory materials in boiling nitric acid and in air at room temperature. The stress-intensity range provides the axis of comparison. They motivate the study through reprocessing equipment. The two test settings differ in both environment and temperature, so the comparison describes behavior under two combined sets of conditions. [T12-W004]

S46 General physical principles and cross-domain proposals#

Physical and explanatory quantities#

The sources propose physical accounts and connections across physical, biological and cognitive domains. Physical free energy, variational free energy, entropy production, assembly index and reduced descriptive dimension concern different objects and operations.

Prigogine: thermodynamic openness and internal production#

Prigogine's Nobel lecture connects thermodynamics, kinetics, spatial and temporal structure, fluctuations and microscopic irreversibility. Its physical Helmholtz free energy is F = E − TS, using energy, temperature and entropy. This quantity belongs to the thermodynamic account; it is not introduced as a generic cost function for organizations or as the variational quantity in a later cognitive theory. [SG-W045, lecture opening, equation 1.1]

The entropy balance distinguishes exchange with the environment from nonnegative internal production. An open system can maintain or increase internal organization while exchanging matter and energy. That does not suspend the entropy balance over an appropriate boundary. A visually ordered structure is not enough to determine the whole balance, and an internal decrease cannot be treated as a global disappearance of entropy.

The expression of production through fluxes and forces uses local-equilibrium assumptions. The minimum-entropy-production result requires narrower conditions, including a near-equilibrium linear regime with appropriate constant coefficients. The lecture does not justify extending that result to every open steady state or every self-organizing process. These distinctions are central to what the physical source can contribute. [SG-W045, opening thermodynamic development]

Structure can appear while entropy production increases#

The Bénard-convection discussion provides an explicit countercondition to the idea that self-organization always minimizes production. Beyond a threshold, the system develops macroscopic flow structure while entropy production increases. The order of the pattern and the direction of the production change therefore answer different questions. [SG-W045, convection example, PDF p. 5]

Near equilibrium, thermodynamic stability arguments can use a restricted relation between fluctuations and restoring behavior. Farther away, kinetics and the sign of excess-production terms become important. An autocatalytic reaction can supply a necessary feature for instability in the setup being discussed without being sufficient for it. Naming positive feedback does not establish that a transition occurs or that its result is beneficial. [SG-W045, PDF pp. 6–9]

The relevant lesson is source-specific: the operating regime and reaction mechanism determine which result applies.

The Brusselator retains maintained reservoirs and reaction conditions#

Prigogine's chemical-clock model makes its supporting arrangement explicit. In the stated simplified reaction scheme, external species are held constant and rate constants are normalized. The homogeneous stationary concentrations are X = A and Y = B/A. Under the model's conditions, the threshold B > 1 + A2 marks instability of that branch and the emergence of oscillatory behavior. [SG-W045, selected connected chemical-instability development]

These equations do not describe an isolated chemical device sustaining itself without resources. Maintaining the external species is part of the model. Adding diffusion introduces possibilities of spatial pattern, with system size, shape and boundary conditions affecting what occurs. A repeating chemical pattern can be generated through the arrangement and kinetics without a central agent specifying every oscillation, while its material and energy provision remain.

The lecture also distinguishes behavior along a branch from selection among branches near a bifurcation. Fluctuations and history can matter to which continuation occurs. Its discussion of relative fluctuations retains the conditions behind large-number approximations; nonlinear reaction behavior and critical correlations need not follow the simplest independent-particle picture. [SG-W045, PDF pp. 10–15]

Irreversibility is an argument with restrictions and open questions#

The later lecture examines the relation between reversible microscopic descriptions and irreversible macroscopic behavior. Prigogine discusses alternatives involving representation and coarse-graining, then develops his own operator-based approach. The proposed transformation is conditional on properties of the dynamics and is not claimed to be possible for every periodic motion. [SG-W045, PDF pp. 16–21]

One apparent printed sign error in equation 7.8 conflicts with the nonnegative quantity defined earlier. The conclusion retains open questions and a proposal for relating levels of temporality. [SG-W045]

Bruers, Maes and Netočný: the variable and reversal symmetry matter#

The selected 2007 preprint studies entropy-production principles in linear electrical circuits through Langevin descriptions and dynamical fluctuation theory. It relates minimum and maximum principles to the close-to-equilibrium structure of fluctuations, including the parity of the relevant observable under time reversal. The choice between a current-like odd variable and an even variable is not an interchangeable labeling choice. [W079, selected setup and §§2.2–3.3]

The discussion explains a known counterexample and qualifications concerning unequal temperatures. Its conclusion questions exact extension beyond the linear regime and argues that dynamics, not thermodynamics alone, must justify further generalizations. These are results and interpretations within the selected circuit analysis. [W079, selected conclusion]

Bejan and Lorente: flow access is their proposed general principle#

Bejan and Lorente's selected constructal account proposes that finite flow systems persisting over time evolve configurations offering greater access to their currents. It treats branching flow arrangements across animate, inanimate and engineered settings as instances of a design phenomenon. The authors distinguish the proposal from a fixed final optimum or an inevitable end configuration. [W082, selected §§1–4]

Their engine-and-brake discussion also resists reducing every case to maximizing or minimizing one entropy-production quantity. Flow can involve useful delivery and dissipation in different parts of an arrangement. Their proposed generality therefore differs from the claim that nature always chooses the least resistance.

Bejan and Lorente extend their proposed law through scaling arguments. [W082, selected passages and conclusion]

Friston: variational free energy concerns a model of observations#

The opening and Box 1 of Friston's 2010 review present variational free energy in relation to a generative model and an approximate density over hidden causes. The formulation provides a tractable bound related to the surprise of observations, with perception and action interpreted through changes affecting that bound. Its energy and entropy terms are defined in that probabilistic construction. They are not simply the E and TS of the thermodynamic equation above. [W052, opening and Box 1]

Biehl and colleagues, and the response: a scoped mathematical dispute#

Biehl, Pollock and Kanai examine particular arguments connecting stochastic dynamics, Markov blankets and an inference interpretation. The selected critique identifies additional assumptions needed for some mathematical steps and gives counterexamples to a free-energy lemma taken at face value. It also questions the relation between a variational density and an ergodic conditional density, and notes that changing what parameterizes a density changes its interpretation. [W055, selected overview, observation discussion and lemma counterexample]

Their critique targets the mathematical arguments linking dynamics with inference, while leaving the wider free-energy programme open.

Friston, Da Costa and Parr's selected response distinguishes conditions on coupling, exact and approximate inference and flow on a manifold of conditional expectations. In their explanation, an average internal flow can be interpreted on a statistical manifold; an average flow on that manifold differs from each fluctuating internal trajectory. They defend the broader programme while addressing the assumptions highlighted by the critics. [W056, selected §§1–2 and 4–6]

The dispute concerns which assumptions support a Bayesian interpretation.

Assembly theory: a construction measure with specified building blocks#

Sharma and colleagues define an assembly space through elementary building blocks and permitted recursive joining operations. Previously assembled motifs remain available for reuse. The assembly index is the length of a shortest permitted construction path for an object; copy number adds information about how often a complex object occurs. The proposal links construction history, reusable structure and selection rather than describing complexity only by visual intricacy. [W084, selected printed pp. 321–325 and 327]

The measure depends on justified building blocks and allowed operations. A construction count is not automatically a person's cognitive burden or the full physical cost of making a molecule. The selected paper proposes empirical access, including molecular measurements.

Jaeger's selected critique distinguishes what assembly theory may characterize from what would be required to explain Darwinian evolution. [W085, selected discussion]

Constructor information: physical possibility includes alternatives#

Deutsch and Marletto's selected opening frames information through possible and impossible physical tasks. A constructor can perform a task repeatedly while retaining the ability to do so; a substrate undergoes the relevant transformation. The account emphasizes counterfactual alternatives: an actual state carries information in relation to other states it could have occupied. [W091, selected §§1–2, printed pp. 1–6]

The authors seek physical principles accounting for properties such as interoperability of information media. They explicitly present general principles as conjectures. The task-based formulation characterizes which repeatable operations are physically possible. [W091]

Wilson and Flack: a coarser description can have a specific explanatory role#

Wilson's renormalization-group lecture examines rescaling, fixed points and universality near critical conditions. Certain large-scale observables can become insensitive to some microscopic details under the relevant limiting description. The condition of being near the critical temperature and the class of system remain important. Universality is not an assertion that all physical systems behave alike or that their detailed design can always be ignored. [GL-W025, selected introduction and PDF pp. 10–11]

The account supplies an asymptotic physical explanation. Describing fewer relevant variables is different from showing that the actual system uses less energy or needs fewer controls.

Flack discusses endogenous coarse-graining: organisms or collectives can respond to relatively slow regularities, with feedback between aggregated descriptions and lower-level activity. The Santa Fe Institute's reconstruction presents this as collective compression and a possible account of downward influence. [TA-W041, through the Santa Fe Institute]

Multitime cognition and System 0#

Taniguchi and colleagues' selected quad-process proposal relates embodied dynamics, individual cognitive processes and language-based collective intelligence across time scales. It calls the collective symbolic layer System 3 and seeks to place it alongside Systems 0, 1 and 2. The account connects several research traditions and a philosophical interpretation of multiple rhythms of duration. [W051, selected §§2.2–2.4 and 3.1]

Collective predictive coding remains a hypothesis at this scope.

Haken, catastrophe theory and Bios: proposed transfers retain their prerequisites#

Haken's Can We Apply Synergetics to the Human Sciences? and his related 2017 article develop the conceptual account discussed in the shared-practice section. [W083, selected pp. 58–66; RGC-W038]

Golubitsky's selected opening to catastrophe theory distinguishes mathematical exposition from the difficulty of applying its assumptions. Classification of qualitative change in a mathematical setting does not automatically validate a social or biological application. Heuristics and proofs are kept distinct. [SG-W046, printed pp. 352–354]

Sabelli's Bios Theory of Innovation opens by relating recurrence and novelty within a proposed account of creative processes. The opening defers the empirical foundations of the proposal. [WME-W015, opening pp. 1–3]

Physical measures and cross-domain proposals#

The sources supply physical balances, operating regimes, construction measures, interpretive disputes and proposed connections across domains.

Part 3 Living, ecological, and flow arrangements#

These accounts address development, production, ecological persistence and representations of flows.

S28 Development, plasticity and constructed environments#

Arrangements have developmental and evolutionary histories#

These selected sources explain how stable responses, variable responses and environmental modifications arise or persist. Development within an individual, evolutionary change across generations and immediate ecological effects remain different processes.

Waddington: buffered development is conditional#

Waddington's 1942 article proposes canalization: a developmental reaction can produce a fairly definite outcome despite minor variation in the conditions along its course. The account includes tissue differentiation and the comparative constancy of wild-type outcomes. Such buffering is not absolute. Large abnormalities, late disturbances and pathological conditions can defeat it. [W032, 563–564]

He distinguishes an environmental influence that selects a developmental path from an influence participating in the processes that maintain it. These are conceptual alternatives rather than a rigid description of every real organ. Depending on how the alternatives are specified, the same influence can appear as a switch or as a modification within a path. The organism's developmental organization is part of the explanation of a response to the environment. [W032, 564]

The ostrich-callosity illustration supports a proposed evolutionary argument. If an environmental stimulus initially elicits a useful response, selection can favor the genetically influenced capacity to respond appropriately. If a relatively definite result is advantageous across variation in stimulus, canalization can develop. A different trigger, including a genetic one, can later activate the path. This is not inheritance of an acquired bodily change by assumption; it is a proposed sequence involving selection on developmental responsiveness. [W032, 563–565]

Timing and prior capability remain necessary. A replacement trigger needs to act before the environmental stimulus has already done the work for it. The developmental path must also be available and able to produce the response. Waddington's “normal” or “optimum” outcome belongs to this historical selection argument. [W032, 565]

Niche construction can leave a usable environmental legacy#

Odling-Smee and colleagues' selected practical guide distinguishes alteration of the environment from subsequent evolution in response to the altered conditions. Nests, burrows, webs, decomposition and changes to nutrient or other material flows can modify what later organisms encounter. Ecological inheritance names a legacy that persists and affects descendants' conditions, rather than genetic transmission alone. [TA-W020, PDF 3–8]

The distinction makes persistence and boundaries important. A constructed feature can decay, be counteracted or affect other organisms as well as the constructor. It can alter population dynamics without causing the evolutionary response attributed to it. Conversely, a lasting environmental change can modify selection after the original constructor has gone. The passages describe resource types, signatures and durability as matters to investigate. [TA-W020, PDF 3–8, 13]

The authors advocate recognizing niche construction as an evolutionary process in its own right. That is their theoretical position, not a settled conclusion established by the mere existence of environmental modification. Construction can also reduce fitness or produce effects negligible for the evolutionary question. A changed environment is not necessarily a better one for every participant. [TA-W020]

Outsourcing memory: a specified trade-off model#

Lee, Flack and Krakauer's selected revised model balances noisy present observations against memory that can become outdated. Their environment has a specified binary structure and persistence time. Longer memory can improve an estimate during a stable period while making adjustment after a switch slower. A useful memory duration consequently depends on the modeled environment and sensing conditions. [TA-W019, revised v2, model and results 1–2]

In the slow-environment regime examined, the authors derive a sublinear relation between optimal memory duration and environmental persistence under stated approximations. The result concerns their model and objective. Their separate metabolic estimate adds assumptions relating neural tissue, memory burden, size and lifespan. It is a model-based estimate. [TA-W019, results 2–3]

Active stabilization adds another option. Making the environment more persistent can reduce the new information required for adaptation. Their examples include persistent trails, caches, writing and maps. The relevant mechanism is that a maintained external regularity changes what an agent must continually estimate or encode internally. The construction and maintenance of that regularity remain activities. [TA-W019, result 4]

The model also exposes a distribution problem. Stabilizers pay for changing conditions, while other agents can enjoy the more predictable environment. Free riders can therefore exploit the benefit. The authors examine conditions involving monopolization and combine assumed costs of memory complexity, stabilization and sensing precision with adaptation error. The relative weights matter: changing them changes which strategy is favored. [TA-W019, result 4, equations 15–18]

Their local adaptive argument uses perturbative and convexity approximations. The discussion connects the model to institutions and social regularities as hypotheses about outsourced memory. [TA-W019]

The niche-construction dispute is about implications#

Scott-Phillips and colleagues' selected critical appraisal is an adversarial collaboration between an advocate and skeptics. The authors agree that organisms modify environments and that those effects can be consequential. They disagree about whether this requires a fundamental reformulation of evolutionary theory, how to define an evolutionary process and what explanatory role construction should receive. It is not a dispute over whether burrows or altered selection environments exist. [TA-W021, introduction and paired accounts]

Their dairy-farming example makes the distinction concrete. The standard account treats the changed nutritional environment as a source of selection on variation in lactose persistence. The niche-construction account emphasizes how the cultural practice generates and coevolves with that selective setting. The paired explanations and summary identify differences in emphasis and causal framing. [TA-W021, case study and summary table]

For gambits engineering, the informative point is the source's distinction between a demonstrated environmental feedback and a stronger claim about the reconstruction of theory. An arrangement's practical consequences can be examined while the wider theoretical interpretation remains contested.

Michod: group performance can constrain its members#

Michod's selected 2003 account asks how a group becomes a new evolutionary individual with heritable variation in fitness at the group level. Cooperation can benefit the group while imposing costs on participating cells. That creates potential conflict between levels. A conflict mediator changes the

opportunity for selection within or between groups, rather than merely announcing that the cells have a common interest. [TA-W023, PDF 1–2]

The simple model uses cooperating and defecting alleles and a life cycle from propagule to adult group and further propagules. Group fitness depends on adult size and functionality; cell replication can increase one while impairing the other. These assumptions make the level of the measure explicit. A faster-replicating cell and a more effective multicellular group need not be the same success. [TA-W023, PDF 2]

Propagule size, reproductive specialization, mutation processes and policing provide different possible mediators. A small propagule can reduce within-group conflict but also directly reduce adult group size under the model's conditions. Germ–soma specialization constrains reproductive opportunity for many cells while supporting the larger organism's functioning. Policing can require cooperating cells to spend time and energy monitoring defection. Conflict control is an activity or developmental constraint, not an automatically costless outcome of membership. [TA-W023, PDF 5]

Michod also notes that a mediator can restrict later evolvability, illustrated by a nonreplicative soma in Volvox. Greater current individuality is therefore not a guarantee of unlimited future potential. Cooperation and conflict in multicellularity also frame the abstract of Michod and Roze’s earlier 2001 article. [TA-W023, PDF 2, 5; TA-W022]

Costs of responsiveness require a careful comparison#

Van Buskirk and Steiner distinguish selection on the phenotype expressed in an environment from costs associated with the capacity for a plastic or canalized response. The mechanisms making a range of responses possible can have consequences even when a particular organism does not express the whole range. Plasticity and canalization can each be targets of cost comparisons; neither is presumed to be the cost-free baseline. [TA-W037, abstract and results/discussion]

Their meta-analysis reports twenty-seven studies and usually mild measured costs, with no simple general predominance of plasticity over canalization costs. Weak detected differences do not establish zero absolute costs. Shared costs, statistical detection and environmental stress remain relevant explanations in the account. [TA-W037]

The critical discussion in Auld, Agrawal and Relyea's article identifies another problem: correlation between trait values and plasticity can make estimated costs imprecise or biased. Bias can itself be environment-specific. They call for re-examining existing estimates, rather than concluding that all past estimates must be false. The passages also distinguish limits involving the range of developmental responses and the reliability of environmental information. [TA-W038, discussion of costs, bias and limits]

Its significant contribution here is a warning about what a comparison actually measures. The cost of producing one phenotype, the cost of retaining a response capacity and the failure to achieve an appropriate response are related but distinguishable questions. [TA-W038]

Developmental resources extend beyond the conventional organism#

Griffiths and Gray's selected introductory argument rejects a division in which genes form one fundamental kind of developmental cause and everything else forms another. Genes, cytoplasm and features of a learning environment are among interacting resources. Their proposed developmental unit comprises the resources producing outcomes stably replicated in a lineage, potentially extending beyond the conventional body boundary. [SG-W054, PDF 1–3, printed 277–278]

The parity claim is about reasoning and explanatory status, not equal numerical contributions from every resource or the absence of genetic specificity. Reproducing a developmental process still requires the relevant resources to be present and related appropriately. It identifies a broader boundary for asking how a recurring outcome is produced. [SG-W054]

S40 Biological organization, closure and autopoiesis#

Several meanings of closure#

The selected sources concern systems that produce, constrain or maintain conditions of their own activity. The term closure has different meanings in the sources: dependence among constraints, a production organization, closure of a reaction set and mathematical conditions for self-maintenance. None of these means that an organism or chemical system needs no external matter or energy.

Montévil and Mossio: constraints and the processes they shape#

Montévil and Mossio distinguish thermodynamically open processes from constraints acting on them. A constraint is a contingent structure or dynamics that changes the process while relevant aspects of the constraint remain conserved over the time scale considered. Its presence alone is insufficient: the effect must differ from the unconstrained case. Their vascular-system example concerns oxygen carried through a structured transport system rather than simply diffusing in its absence. [W013; GL-W026, 2015 article, §§2–3, definition 1]

The time-scale qualification matters. Conservation of a relevant property during a constrained process does not mean the structure lasts forever or never needs repair. A relatively persistent arrangement can shape many faster events while its longer-term production and maintenance depend on other processes. This is how the framework avoids treating every constraint as a permanently external boundary condition.

The paper's example of an inclined plane clarifies the difference. The plane constrains a sliding object, but that sliding does not normally produce or maintain the plane. Biological organization, in their proposed account, involves constraints whose continued existence depends on processes constrained by others in the organization. The system uses constrained thermodynamic flows in maintaining the constraints themselves. [W013, §§3–5]

Dependence, boundary and closure are specified rather than inferred from a cycle#

The authors ask whether any circular chain is enough and answer by defining dependence more carefully. Their framework distinguishes direct dependence from an indirect contribution through a longer chain of processes. Strict closure requires the relevant mutual dependence among constraints, rather than merely reciprocal benefit in a broad environment. Constraints outside the closed set and specified boundary conditions can still be necessary. Closure is consequently contextual, while thermodynamic openness continues underneath it. [W013; GL-W026, §§4–6]

The upper and lower boundaries pose an explicit problem for the framework. Descriptions of actual organisms are incomplete. The authors propose considering maximally closed systems within the available description, then examining how interacting systems can retain distinguishable organization. Their hunting-and-cooking example treats some collective dependencies as indirect and warns that loose cooperation need not satisfy strict closure. A team doing mutually useful work is therefore not automatically a biological closed organization under their definitions.

The authors state that their purpose is to characterize general features rather than supply a model capturing all the complexity of real organisms. Their later discussion retains the relation between stability and variation. [GL-W026, §§5–7]

The abstract of Mossio, Montévil and Longo’s 2016 Theoretical principles for biology: organization proposes organization as a principle for making biological objects intelligible and relates it to variation. [GL-W091, abstract]

Corti: causal conditions do not by themselves settle what ought to happen#

The selected part of Corti's critique examines a counterfactual argument for biological normativity. In the organizational account as he reconstructs it, a constraint must perform its role or the mutually maintained system will cease to exist. A further inference assigns what the constraint ought to do. Corti questions whether the causal premise is sufficient for that normative conclusion. [W047, counterfactual argument]

His comparison with a simple dependence relation makes the issue concrete. A condition can be necessary for an outcome without thereby acquiring a normative obligation to produce it. He then asks whether making the conditions internally generated and mutually dependent changes that inferential step. He accepts that closure can mark an important descriptive difference while disputing that the difference, on its own, establishes intrinsic norms.

Dittrich and Speroni di Fenizio: chemical closure is a property of a reaction set#

Chemical Organisation Theory begins with molecules and reaction rules. A closed set contains the products generated by reactions available within it. This is a different meaning from a physical seal around a container. The theory also distinguishes semi-self-maintenance, in which consumed types can be produced, from the stronger quantitative condition needed to maintain amounts. [W077, author preprint dated 1 December 2006, §§2.2–2.3]

The authors' small reversible example is instructive. Two molecular types produce one another, but both also decay. Having a route that produces each type is not sufficient to keep either at positive concentration. A diagram of reciprocal production can therefore conceal net depletion. Their self-maintenance condition uses the stoichiometric matrix and the existence of a compatible flux vector for which the relevant net production rates are nonnegative. The stipulated positivity of available reactions is part of that definition.

A chemical organization combines closure and self-maintenance in this formal sense. Its existence identifies a structural possibility under the reaction rules and flux conditions. It does not, without further kinetic information, establish that actual concentrations will approach a stable persistent state. An available feasible flux is different from the flux generated by a particular reaction-rate law and initial condition. [W077, definitions 5–11]

The later selected theorem relates fixed points of the specified dynamics to organizations under a mapping from concentrations to present molecular types. Threshold and reaction-positivity assumptions enter the construction. The direction reported is that the appropriately mapped stationary state is an organization, not that every formally feasible organization is a stable attractor. [W077, §3.2, definition 41 and theorem 42]

Varela, Maturana and Uribe: a production organization that realizes its boundary#

The early sections of Varela, Maturana and Uribe's 1974 paper characterize an autopoietic system through a network of component-producing processes. The components participate in generating the network that produces them and in realizing the system as a unity in a domain. Its boundary is consequently part of an ongoing production organization, rather than merely a wall placed around a collection of parts. [W081, printed pp. 187–191, §§1–7]

The distinction between organization and a particular material realization allows turnover without making the system an unchanging stock of molecules. The selected model and figures illustrate the proposed organization. Their role is conceptual demonstration in a specified construction. Reproduction is also not identical to the maintenance of such an organization; a system can be described in terms of its organization without making reproduction the definition of each operation.

Marletto: a recipe requires an executing and maintained constructor#

Marletto's selected constructor-theoretic argument asks what tasks the laws of physics permit, including accurate construction and reproduction under laws that do not contain a ready-made design for the task. Possibility is defined through arbitrarily good approximate constructors short of perfection. This differs from asking how probable a task is under observed evolution, or how much a particular implementation costs. [W092, §§2–3.1 and selected conclusions]

Her car-factory example separates a task-specific recipe from a more general vehicle that carries out its constituent operations. The recipe can be decomposed into subtasks permitted by the laws, with a modular programme specifying their organization. The task-specific information must be instantiated and preserved; the executing machinery must also remain capable of carrying out the operations. A stored recipe is therefore part of an architecture, rather than an alternative to physical execution.

Marletto connects accurate constructors, replication and maintenance in an architecture that joins a reusable recipe to machinery capable of executing it. [W092]

Hopfield: specificity can require an additional driven path#

Hopfield's 1974 kinetic-proofreading paper asks how biosynthetic processes can discriminate more accurately than a simple equilibrium recognition scheme would suggest. In the model, correct and incorrect substrates differ in their dissociation behavior. An additional reaction stage, driven away from equilibrium, creates an effective delay before incorporation. The more rapidly dissociating incorrect complex has more opportunity to leave before the final product forms. [TA-W017, printed pp. 4135–4137, reaction schemes 1–10]

The driving is essential in his analysis. Within the equilibrium constraint, merely adding the intermediate does not supply the desired improvement. Coupling to an energy source, such as phosphate hydrolysis, changes the available kinetic organization. The effective delay is a physical reaction mechanism, not a decision by an external inspector. Reactions that appear superfluous in a simpler description can serve a discrimination function.

Hopfield relates the mechanism to reported biosynthetic examples. The model shows why fidelity can retain additional pathways and free-energy supply. [TA-W017]

Galstyan and colleagues: spatial proofreading relocates part of the work#

The selected spatial-proofreading account uses gradients and spatial separation to create a discrimination opportunity. A bound complex must persist long enough during movement or diffusion to reach the region where product formation occurs. Different dissociation rates can then yield different success probabilities. The arrangement supplies a spatially organized delay rather than requiring the same local chemical architecture as the classical scheme. [TA-W018, selected model and gradient-maintenance passages]

The authors make the boundary of energy accounting explicit. An initial reported power calculation concerns the additional cost caused by proofreading's tendency to homogenize a gradient; it excludes the baseline cost of creating that gradient. Appendix B separately examines the continuing power needed to

counter diffusion even without the proofreading enzyme. [TA-W018, energy-cost discussion and appendix B]

The more realistic model describes a membrane-associated kinase and a distributed phosphatase maintaining an active-substrate gradient. At low enough enzyme activity, the gradient can persist and support proofreading. If activity overwhelms the maintaining mechanism, the gradient flattens and proofreading is lost. The selected parameter examples use experimentally constrained ranges, but the study remains a conceptual model rather than a demonstration that every proposed biological implementation uses the mechanism. [TA-W018, gradient-maintenance model]

Spatial organization can alter where discrimination work occurs, while successful use still depends on maintaining the spatial difference.

Synthetic Notch: a selected modular sensing–response account#

The summary and introductory material from Morsut and colleagues describe synthetic Notch receptors with replaced extracellular sensing and intracellular transcriptional modules. Binding an external ligand triggers release of a regulator, connecting a selected input to a selected cellular response. Their account reports pathways that do not share common signaling intermediates and can be combined to integrate cues, including Boolean response programmes. [GL-W060]

The engineered sensing interface uses receptor processing, transcriptional machinery and cellular resources to execute its response. [GL-W060]

Hypercycles: cooperative organization with vulnerabilities#

The selected 2016 PLOS Topic Page defines a hypercycle as a cyclic autocatalytic arrangement of self-replicating molecular types, each catalyzing a successor. Its historical motivation concerns an error threshold: imperfect copying can prevent a long sequence from retaining the information needed for more accurate replication. Coupled shorter replicators were proposed as a way of organizing a larger informational capacity. [SG-W047]

The review retains difficulties in the traditional ordinary-differential-equation model, including parasites and limits to stable cycle size. It also distinguishes an experimentally reported cooperative ribozyme network from a hypercycle in the strict sense. [SG-W047]

Maintained organization, productive closure and fidelity#

The constraint framework describes a conserved causal role and mutual maintenance; chemical organization adds reaction-set and feasible-flux conditions; autopoiesis concerns component production and realized unity; constructor theory examines task possibility and recipes; proofreading makes fidelity and supporting work concrete.

S50 Biological circuits, cellular organization and intervention#

From components to cellular behavior#

Biological circuits provide concrete cases of organization producing a capability: a temporary signal can leave a persistent expression state, a regulatory loop can generate repeated pulses, and the allocation of cellular machinery can change what an introduced construct achieves. Systems biology examines such behavior through molecular interactions, measurements and models. Synthetic biology also constructs circuits to investigate and use it. These traditions contain pertinent historical foundations for asking how a capability is produced, what sustains it, and what an intervention changes.

The accounts below move from experimentally investigated circuits to metabolic constraints, whole-cell modeling and selected recent computational approaches. Their objects include living cells, mathematical representations of cells, and the conduct of biological research. The experiments show particular realized behaviors; the models and reviews explain the questions, assumptions and methods through which those behaviors can be investigated.

Kitano on structure, dynamics, control and design#

Hiroaki Kitano's 2002 overview identifies four aspects of system-level understanding: structure, dynamics, control and design. A list of components supplies a different kind of knowledge from a network of interactions, and an interaction diagram supplies a different kind from the behavior of that network over time. His road-map analogy makes the distinction tangible: the map helps locate possible routes, while explaining traffic requires information about movement and interaction. Control asks how a state can be changed or stabilized; design asks how systems with desired properties can be constructed. [BC-W001, p. 1662]

The research cycle he describes makes a model's assumptions available for testing. Competing explanations can guide the choice of an experiment that distinguishes them, and disagreement with observation can require revision of the model. The needed measurements depend on that purpose: broad coverage, adequate temporal sampling and simultaneous observation of different molecular properties can matter differently. Kitano's account thus joins modeling to the organization of experimental work. He presents expanded control and design capabilities as ambitions supported by continuing advances in measurement, analysis and software. [BC-W001, pp. 1663–1664]

Alon on response time and persistence detection#

Uri Alon's 2007 review explains selected regulatory patterns through their dynamics and experimental investigation. Negative autoregulation occurs when a transcription factor represses production of itself. A strong promoter permits rapid initial accumulation; as the repressor approaches its threshold, it reduces further production. Relative to simple regulation reaching the same final concentration, the circuit can respond faster. The steady concentration and the route taken to reach it are separate properties. Alon also discusses reduced variation between cells and the possibility of noise amplification when feedback contains a long delay. [BC-W002, pp. 450–451]

A coherent feedforward circuit gives a different example. X activates Y, and both activate Z. When activation of Z requires both X and Y (an AND rule), it waits for Y to accumulate sufficiently. A brief input can disappear before that happens, whereas a persistent input permits expression. Turning X off can stop new Z production promptly even though Y remains. Alon describes experimental tests in the arabinose system and contrasts OR-like regulation in flagella, where either input can suffice and the delayed

transition changes. Timing therefore depends on the regulatory signs, the input rule and molecular kinetics as well as the wiring. [BC-W002, pp. 452–453]

Gardner, Cantor and Collins construct cellular memory#

Gardner, Cantor and Collins constructed a toggle from two genes whose protein products repress one another's promoters. When one side dominates, it suppresses production of its opponent and thereby sustains its own predominance. A temporary inducer weakens the active repressor, allowing the opposing side to accumulate and establish the other state. After the inducer is removed, mutual inhibition can retain the selected expression state. Their experiment thus separates the signal used to change state from the continuing gene expression that maintains it. [BC-W003, pp. 339–340]

The two arrows are only part of the design. Their model requires sufficiently cooperative repression and appropriately balanced effective synthesis rates. Six constructs shared the same basic configuration, but one had only one stable expression state. In one construct, the two culture states persisted for twenty-two further hours without inducer, under the reported growth conditions. These particulars explain what has to be arranged for a temporary input to leave a persistent cellular response. [BC-W003, box 1 and figs. 2– 4]

Elowitz and Leibler construct an oscillator#

Elowitz and Leibler's 2000 repressilator connects three transcriptional repressors in a cycle: LacI represses tetR, TetR represses cI, and CI represses lacI. Their design model permitted either convergence to a steady state or sustained oscillation, depending on expression, repression and decay parameters. To favor oscillation, the construction used tightly repressible promoters and degradation tags that shortened repressor lifetimes. Cellular protein destruction participates in producing the temporal behavior. [BC-W004, pp. 335–337]

A separate fluorescent reporter allowed the researchers to follow individual cell lineages. They observed oscillations lasting longer than a cell-division cycle and substantial variation in amplitude and period, including skipped or delayed cycles. At least forty percent of cells met their oscillation criterion in each of three movies. A population average would conceal important aspects of this behavior as cells lost synchrony. The experiment supplied a working synthetic oscillator whose irregularity was itself a subject for further investigation. [BC-W004, pp. 335–338]

Adaptation and a programmable sensing interface#

The chemotaxis account in S05 supplies another relation between organization and response. Yi and colleagues reconstruct exact adaptation through integral feedback: an internal state associated approximately with total receptor methylation changes with the difference between a methylation contribution and activity-dependent demethylation. At a stable steady state, its rate of change is zero. Under the specified biochemical assumptions, activity returns to a value independent of the changed ligand level. The continuing receptor-modification reactions support that response. [W012]

S05 explains the four biochemical assumptions and the stability requirement in detail. This is a response that returns an activity measure after a changed input, whereas the toggle experiment selects and retains an alternative expression state. The distinction gives a reader two concrete behaviors to investigate without using persistence as a single undifferentiated outcome. Their mathematical descriptions identify different states and different conditions for the reported result. [W012; BC-W003]

The selected synthetic Notch account in S40 describes replaced extracellular sensing and intracellular transcriptional modules. Ligand binding can release a regulator and connect a chosen external cue to a

chosen transcriptional response. The sensing interface is engineered while receptor processing and cellular execution remain involved. S40 develops the sensing interface and combined-cue response programmes. This example places an intervention at the connection between a signal and an existing cellular apparatus. [GL-W060]

Ceroni and colleagues measure the host's remaining capacity#

Ceroni, Algar, Stan and Ellis examine the burden imposed by introduced gene-expression constructs. Their capacity monitor uses a gene integrated into the bacterial chromosome that produces a fluorescent protein without an inducing signal. Its production rate provides an indirect assay of expression capacity remaining as another construct draws on cellular resources. Construct output, the monitor's output and cellular growth can then be compared. An introduced function enters a cell that already has demands on its expression machinery. [BC-W006, supplementary figs. 1–3]

Their translational resource model represents ribosomes moving along transcripts and returning to a shared pool. Stronger recruitment and slower elongation can change how much machinery is occupied. In the selected supplementary analysis, changing coding-sequence length or ribosome-binding strength changes both predicted output and remaining capacity. Tests with shorter antibody-fragment constructs captured important trends, while the model overestimated burden in some conditions. The comparison makes the object of improvement explicit: obtaining a desired product while retaining more host capacity. Its diagnostic is a measured reporter response supported by a specified model, rather than a direct inventory of every resource in the cell. [BC-W006, supplementary note 4 and figs. 9, 13–15]

Orth, Thiele and Palsson on feasible metabolic flux#

Orth, Thiele and Palsson's 2010 primer explains flux balance analysis through a stoichiometric matrix S and a vector of reaction rates v. Each matrix column records what a reaction consumes and produces. At steady state, Sv = 0 balances the represented metabolites. Upper and lower reaction bounds restrict the allowable rates, including exchange with the environment. These conditions define a feasible set that can contain many flux distributions without requiring a kinetic rate constant for every reaction. [BC-W005, box 1 and figs. 1–2]

Selecting a growth or production objective adds another commitment. Linear programming chooses a feasible distribution maximizing or minimizing a specified linear combination of fluxes. Biomass production can be represented by a reaction consuming measured proportions of precursor materials. The primer illustrates environmental intervention by changing oxygen-uptake bounds, and discusses alternative optima when several pathways attain the same objective.
