Market size and transportation costs help determine whether narrow specialization is viable. [UX-W001, “Job shops”]

The article's flow matrices distinguish a central coordinator from backward local signaling. In the latter, a downstream station signals readiness to its upstream neighbor, potentially through an empty container. Forward material transfers still occur. The conditional self-coordination claim presumes the initial stock and a compatible productive sequence; it does not mean that signals, replenishment or diagnosis have disappeared. The discussion also retains the need to find bottlenecks, rebalance tasks and ensure that workers can perform assigned work within the cycle. [UX-W001, “Synchronized flow production, ” fig. 7]

Its platform matrix separately displays rules, modules and system integration. Providers can work without direct lateral exchanges only insofar as the architecture actually makes their tasks separate and they follow common rules. There may be many integrators, including users. The article's comparison table describes platform efficiency as variable, a useful qualification against reading the sequence of paradigms as an automatic climb toward greater economy. [UX-W001, “Platform organizations, and ecosystems, ” fig. 8 and table 2]

The article finally discusses AI using its contemporary 2025 setting. It distinguishes the organizational work of developing and using systems from the unobserved internal steps of a model, and acknowledges that tasks and transfers may not be an adequate metaphor for those internal processes. This theoretical discussion marks the author's stated limit on extending the representation. [UX-W001, AI discussion and conclusion]

The valuation and scope carried by this account#

Baldwin asks how technologies and organizations create and capture value. Her notes define efficiency in terms of sustainable profit relative to investment, rather than simply lowest cost. This business criterion differs from physical resource use, human effort and welfare. [UX-W040, ch. 1 note 42; ch. 17 note 4; chs. 11, 16]

Baldwin explains why design rules can settle recurring questions, why some transfers are better left inside a transaction-free zone, how complementary investments favor coordination, and how separately exercisable options create value. [UX-W040, chs. 2–7, 11–17; UX-W008; SB-W005; UX-W001]

S111 Manufacturing variation, quality and experimental improvement#

From a chart signal to an investigation#

In his 1931 book, Walter Shewhart asks how fluctuations in the fraction defective might tell an investigator when to look for an assignable cause. Limits derived from previous observations give a basis for examining later points. In the example behind Fig. 6, he reports that the proportion of observations falling within the limits rose from 68 to 84 percent as causes were removed. The statistic counts points within the limits. Shewhart adds that even a point inside them can have an assignable cause. A chart supplies a signal for inquiry while the investigation establishes what changed. [T13-W001]

The NIST/SEMATECH handbook distinguishes the available specification width from the spread and centering of the process. A process can have room within the limits if centered yet put more pieces beyond one specification because its mean lies near that limit. The handbook treats capability estimates in the context of stable behavior and gives assumptions for converting them to expected reject fractions. Sampling uncertainty also affects the estimate. [T13-W002]

Designing for measurement and improvement#

仁科健 treats manufacturing as a recipient of the designer’s work. Design choices affect both ease of production and the ease with which an abnormal result can be detected. His exposition considers materials, equipment, operators, methods, measurement and surroundings. Finding a possible cause in the data leads to a further question about the technical relationship, for which he discusses experimental design. [T13-W003]

Sharma, Sahni and Sharma examine a measurement system whose burst test consumes the piece measured. Repeating a test under the same settings requires other pieces judged comparable, so variation within a batch enters the assessment of repeatability. The authors use a crossed gauge study as one part of evaluating the equipment and discuss examining unusual observations and repeating measurements under the same settings. Their case concerns the quality of the measurement system. [T13-W004]

Following a molding experiment into production#

สุรศักดิ์ ชุบไธสง and ระพี กาญจนะ studied silver streaking on injection-molded telephone part 1220402. They used a fractional factorial screen on eight candidate settings and then a central composite design to examine four factors. The combination they took forward used 97 MPa injection pressure, 240 tons clamping force, a nozzle temperature of 237 °C and injection speed of 30 mm/s. Screening, confirmation and later production supplied different observations. [T13-W005]

Their part-specific comparison records 1,092 affected pieces out of 32,357 before the change, 663 out of 42,878 during confirmation production and 723 out of 106,665 in later mass production. Those counts give about 33,748, 15,462 and 6,778 pieces with silver streaks per million. The observations concern one defect on one part across different production periods. The authors also call for monitoring other defect modes when applying the settings. [T13-W005]

S08 Form, context and overlapping use: Alexander's design argument#

What a form does in a specified context#

Christopher Alexander's Notes on the Synthesis of Form asks how a designer can organize more interacting requirements than unaided thought can easily manage. Its relevant argument connects the arrangement of a physical form, the conditions around it, practical correction, the representation of requirements and the invention of a design. [TA-W028, chs. 1–9]

Alexander's 1971 paperback preface revisits the 1964 argument. His separate A City Is Not a Tree develops a different account of overlapping relationships. [TA-W028, preface; TA-W029]

Alexander divides an ensemble into form and context. Form is the part the designer can change for the question at hand; context supplies the conditions with which it must fit. Fit belongs to their relationship. A property that works well in one situation need not work well in another, and the boundary can be drawn differently for another inquiry. The current inquiry nevertheless has to establish that boundary before judging the result. A kettle's ease of handling, for example, concerns the kettle in relation to human use, rather than an isolated geometrical property. [TA-W028, ch. 2]

Misfit makes the relationship easier to discuss. A particular difficulty can be noticed without possessing a complete positive description of the ideal form. Something burns a hand, obstructs movement, costs too much to maintain or fails under the conditions in which it is used. Alexander proposes organizing such identified failures and their interactions. He does not thereby claim that a finite list exhausts everything that might go wrong. Later chapters explicitly describe the list as a temporary, partly personal statement of the designer's view. [TA-W028, ch. 2; pp. 101–102]

This makes the choice of context consequential. A design may fit a market demand while fitting daily use poorly, or satisfy one participant's requirements while leaving another's out of view. The book's concern with what is included in an ensemble is therefore part of the relevant knowledge, not a preliminary detail that can be discarded once a graph has been drawn. A successful operation on the chosen representation still needs to be related back to the world it represents. [TA-W028, chs. 2, 5, 8]

Physical arrangement can supply several functions#

Alexander describes houses whose basic arrangements neglect sun, wind and the separation of incompatible activities. Fans, lamps, heating, ventilation or acoustic insulation are then added to handle problems individually. His criticism is that solving the problems separately can conceal the physical organization they imply together. The example proposes a contrast between arranging the form to fit several requirements and compensating afterward through peripheral devices. [TA-W028, pp. 29–30]

His Mousgoum hut example makes the combined-function account more concrete. Ribs reinforce the hut, guide rainwater and provide footholds during building. The footholds remain available when repair is needed. Construction access is built into the lasting form rather than supplied through disposable scaffolding. In Alexander's description, the same arrangement serves construction, use and maintenance, while siting responds to terrain and erosion. [TA-W028, pp. 30–31]

Practical knowledge is retained in that account. The person who builds also encounters the requirements of upkeep, and recurrent work can affect the initial form. Materials, environmental stresses and patterns of daily life constrain the result. The reported grouping of huts also reflects a particular social order. Its physical coherence does not, by itself, endorse the social relations described. [TA-W028, pp. 30–32]

The one-hole kettle supplies a later example of changed requirements permitting a different component arrangement. Filling, pouring, warning when boiling and avoiding a falling lid had previously been met

through several parts. Alexander argues that the requirements can instead have one physical center: a wide spout. But that possibility depends on noncorrosive metals and cheap, available descaler making a large cleaning-access opening less necessary. A part disappears from the kettle only because materials and maintenance provisions have changed. [TA-W028, pp. 128–129]

The example describes how a specific set of requirements changes when supporting conditions change. Manufacturing, supply and cleaning remain in the ensemble. [TA-W028, pp. 128–129]

Local correction, tradition and the rate of change#

The book contrasts what it calls unselfconscious and selfconscious design. These are the author's explanatory constructs, drawn sharply to examine mechanisms; the account is not a comprehensive anthropology of traditional and professional societies. In the first construct, users, makers and repairers remain close to the form and its failures. A noticed difficulty can lead quickly to a practical alteration. Continuing contact with materials and use preserves knowledge that need not first be translated into an elaborate verbal theory. [TA-W028, chs. 3–4]

Direct correction alone is insufficient in Alexander's explanation. If every change spreads through many relationships, a local improvement can reopen other failures. Tradition supplies resistance to needless alteration, keeping much of the arrangement stable while an urgent difficulty is corrected. Prompt response and restraint work together: the first detects and repairs a local misfit; the second limits the disturbance that the repair creates elsewhere. Relative independence among the relevant subsystems is important because it allows improvements to persist. [TA-W028, pp. 50–53]

The account also has a timescale condition. Adjustment has to proceed faster than the context changes. Otherwise a form can remain behind a moving target even though people continue correcting failures. A feedback arrangement that eventually settles under a fixed context does not thereby maintain fit under arbitrarily rapid social or material change. Alexander makes this condition explicit before claiming the advantage of local correction. [TA-W028, p. 51]

His model of linked binary misfit variables gives a simplified way to picture the issue. A variable indicates fit or misfit for a chosen requirement, and couplings allow change in one to disturb another. A highly coupled system can require a long search before all the relevant difficulties are resolved together. If correction can proceed in more restricted groups, gains can be retained locally. [TA-W028, ch. 3]

The numerical light-switching illustration conflates an individual waiting time with the time for an entire collection of independent lights to be off. The latter depends on the joint state of the collection. The illustration therefore does not establish its stated whole-system timing comparison. [TA-W028, chs. 3–4]

Professional design changes these relationships. Specialization can separate the designer from use and repair; feedback can be delayed; a professional culture can reward novelty; and contexts can change rapidly. Alexander argues that the designer must then work through an internal picture of the problem. If that picture organizes the requirements badly, the eventual form may preserve the picture's simplifications rather than the dependencies of actual use. [TA-W028, ch. 5]

The criticism is especially directed at broad verbal headings. Economics, acoustics and safety may be convenient compartments for thought, while a concrete feature participates in several of them. Such categories can hide relationships across their borders and make the wrong combination look natural. [TA-W028, ch. 5]

The governing notes widen the cost question. Maintenance, depreciation and social overheads can be missed when a narrow concept of economics stands in for the cost of a form. The book explicitly locates relevant costs in activities beyond the purchase or construction of the object. [TA-W028, p. 206, ch. 5 note 22]

Embedded adjustment still requires knowledge and invention#

One of the book's notes discusses making an ensemble more self-organizing. Governors, automatic regulation of dams or production lines, administrative arrangements and potentially physical urban organization are proposed as ways to take some burden off repeated selfconscious control. This is an unusually direct statement of the issue relevant to gambits engineering: an arrangement can make some adaptations occur through the ensemble's own operation. [TA-W028, pp. 207–208, ch. 6 note 6]

The same note immediately restricts the proposal. Such devices apply in special, limited situations, and designing them can demand an even greater grasp of the ensemble. Unfamiliar circumstances still require inventiveness. Alexander also credits conceptual thought with the ability to develop possibilities that would not emerge through ordinary local correction alone. [TA-W028, pp. 207–208]

Its main text explains why general design is not a solved selection procedure. Automatic selection would require an adequate way to generate alternatives and to express all criteria in a symbolism that permits testing them. For general physical design, Alexander says these conditions are not available. Imagination, experience and encounters with the world remain necessary. His mathematical proposal is intended to help organize the problem confronting that inventive activity. [TA-W028, pp. 74–75]

Requirements, interactions and a program for thought#

Alexander represents the selected requirements by a set M and their interactions by links L. Binary classification concerns whether a stated kind of misfit is present; it does not require the underlying physical quantity itself to have only two values. A quantitative property can be judged against an acceptable condition. The procedure is generally satisficing: it seeks to remove specified difficulties, rather than discovering a unique global optimum over every conceivable human aim. [TA-W028, ch. 8]

M is explicitly incomplete. The designer draws on observed failures and anticipated ways a new design might fail. Another designer can identify different issues or give different issues priority. Alexander describes the proposed structure as organizing a person's view of a problem. The method does not make that view objectively complete, ethically neutral or automatically shared by all affected people. [TA-W028, pp. 101–102]

The links also require judgment. Correlations among existing products can express temporary habits rather than necessary relations. Alexander distinguishes conflicts that seem nearly definitional, conflicts related to physical processes and associations arising from contingent current choices. A cheap kettle's hot handle might reflect the materials then used, not an unavoidable conflict between low price and safe handling. Treating that association as necessary could freeze a past design limitation into the new program. [TA-W028, pp. 107–108]

He proposes causal interpretations rather than blind reliance on correlations in a sample of existing forms. Those interpretations are still relative to the domain of possibilities the designer can conceive and to the adequacy of the model used. This is why representing a requirement network already consumes knowledge and why a mathematically neat partition cannot substitute for checking the chosen interactions against the design situation. [TA-W028, pp. 107–110]

The graph is then analyzed into groups whose internal interactions are dense relative to their external interactions. The hierarchical decomposition becomes a program: a way to concentrate on connected parts of the problem and then combine their implications. It is meant to direct attention toward substantive functional relationships rather than familiar headings. The tree represents the proposed organization of the design inquiry; it is not yet a completed physical artifact. [TA-W028, chs. 6, 8–9]

Constructive diagrams connect the analysis to form. A diagram expresses both a physical relationship and the functional forces it is meant to resolve. The designer invents and combines these diagrams, moving between proposed arrangements and the requirements. Conflict among diagrams may require revision, and a promising physical idea can expose a mistaken conception of the context. Synthesis remains a creative, revisable activity. [TA-W028, chs. 7, 9]

The book's notes explicitly say that a functional program can admit many forms. Even if the analysis usefully identifies a related group of requirements, it does not uniquely deduce the arrangement that must realize them. The kettle example shows an inventive recognition of a physical center under changed supporting conditions. [TA-W028, ch. 7 note 11, p. 210; pp. 128–129]

What the formal appendix contributes#

The mathematical appendix states a restricted problem: decompose binary stochastic variables under specified assumptions so that information transfer among subsystems is small. It introduces a constructed distribution, simplifies the marginal probabilities and works through a weak-correlation treatment. At the retained second order, a graph-cut expression becomes relevant. The later normalization compares partitions of different types against a random-graph reference. These are mathematical choices within the proposed approximation, not direct measurements of construction cost or cognitive effort. [TA-W028, appendix 2, pp. 174–192]

The approximation requires several conditions. Higher-order interactions must be absent or sufficiently small for the approximation; marginal scope has been deliberately simplified; and the graph must represent the relationships relevant to the question. The notes explicitly distinguish the artificial state distribution from the actual frequency of good and bad forms among real design alternatives. A favorable graph score therefore cannot be read as the probability that a village, building or device will work. [TA-W028, ch. 8; appendix 2; p. 215, appendix 2 note 8]

The entropy expressions on pp. 184 and 186 have an inconsistent sign. The stated random-cut variance omits a finite-population factor; within a fixed graph that factor does not alter the partition ranking in the ordinary nondegenerate case, but it matters to literal variance calibration. The all-singleton boundary of the displayed normalized expression also needs a special convention. [TA-W028, appendix 2, especially pp. 184–190]

The proposed search uses hill climbing. Reaching a stable local arrangement under such a procedure is not a proof that no better partition exists. Nor does a favorable partition at one level guarantee the best set of finer partitions. The connected design account must therefore remain distinguishable from a globally optimal decomposition algorithm. [TA-W028, pp. 190–192; SB-W011, main argument and selected appendices]

An especially important missing step is acknowledged by Alexander himself. The same design question could be described with another set of variables. He says that a secure foundation would require an invariance result showing that the implied physical components survive such a change of representation, but he has not proved it. Without that result, the procedure cannot guarantee representation-independent discovery of the physical constituents of a successful form. [TA-W028, p. 215, ch. 9 note 8]

The village example: several requirements meet in an arrangement#

The worked example describes an Indian village of roughly 600 people through 141 requirements. It groups them into a program and develops diagrams concerning cattle and fuel, agricultural production and distribution, communal life, and domestic life. The example shows the passage from a set of stated

needs to proposed physical combinations. It is a worked design proposal, not a report that an implemented village achieved the desired outcomes. [TA-W028, appendix 1]

Water collection, irrigation, roads and protection are treated together. An elevated bund can hold water and support a route protected from floods; the collector and distribution arrangements are related to slope and fields. The design combines functions whose separate treatment could require disconnected works. But water availability, sluices, maintenance, land organization and cooperation remain conditions of operation. Drawing a multipurpose feature does not supply those conditions by itself. [TA-W028, appendix 1, especially pp. 152–165]

The cattle and fuel proposals likewise connect material flows. The diagrams consider keeping cattle, handling manure and using the resulting resources in relation to domestic and agricultural needs. Their relevance lies in the attempt to arrange several recurring tasks together. [TA-W028, appendix 1, cattle/fuel and agricultural diagrams]

The domestic compound combines security, water distribution, shared activities and possibilities of change. In the proposed arrangement, a surrounding wall also carries water, and nearby washing, trees, sitting places and paths are placed in relation to recurrent activity. The text argues that a protected shared area could support women's movement and cottage work differently from secluded individual houses. These are the author's design hypotheses concerning social effects; their success is not established by their appearance on the diagram. [TA-W028, pp. 170–172]

Some requirements also expose unresolved institutional and normative questions. The program includes personal landholding, cooperative cultivation, maintenance responsibility and local rivalries. It includes the social fact of caste separation alongside reforming aims. A graph can register interactions among these statements without settling who should have authority, which arrangements are just or how incompatible demands should be changed. Alexander's proposed physical synthesis does not demonstrate that the relevant ownership, political and social agreements have been achieved. [TA-W028, appendix 1, especially pp. 162–163, 170–172]

The 1971 preface changes the emphasis#

In the later paperback preface, Alexander gives priority to constructive diagrams, now called patterns. He says the elaborate formal procedure for discovering independent diagrams is unnecessary. Designers can develop them from experience by examining interacting forces and then combining and improving the resulting patterns. This is a shift in the author's emphasis, stated years after the book's original argument. [TA-W028, 1971 preface]

He objects strongly to a study of design methods detached from practice and warns that blindly following a method will not make someone a better designer. He nevertheless retains a condition of dense internal and relatively weak external interactions for the patterns he recommends. The preface directs attention back to useful physical relationships and the practice of shaping forms. [TA-W028, 1971 preface]

Alexander’s later preface retains diagrams and interacting requirements while rejecting the necessity of the original algorithm. It qualifies the earlier method without abandoning the design problem developed in the book. [TA-W028, 1971 preface and chs. 6–9]

A City Is Not a Tree: preserving overlapping systems of use#

The separate essay A City Is Not a Tree examines the simplification of urban relationships into nested or disjoint units. Alexander amended the 1965 article for its 1966 reprint. A tree here is a structure of sets, not a botanical analogy: units can be contained within larger units or remain separate, but cannot

partially overlap in the way Alexander wants to preserve. A semilattice permits overlapping units while also including their common part in the collection. [TA-W029, pp. 1–5]

The drugstore, newsrack and traffic-light example explains what makes an urban unit. People waiting at a red light notice headlines and may buy a newspaper. The rack, sidewalk and light provide a relatively stable physical receptacle for changing flows of people, papers, money and electricity. Their coherence arises from an activity that crosses the boundaries of isolated objects. The traffic light need not have been designed for newspaper sales to participate in the system Alexander describes. [TA-W029, p. 3]

This is a precise reason why drawing a city as a set of single-purpose containers can miss something important. One location can participate in several activities, and one person's relationships can cross several administrative or spatial divisions. The essay's networks of friends, catchment areas, pedestrian movement and institutional uses show how actual groupings need not respect a single neighborhood tree. Their intersection may support a useful combination rather than represent an error to be removed. [TA-W029, pp. 5–14]

Alexander's urban-plan examples argue that imposed separations can break such relationships. The relevant object is the living system that uses the built receptacle. Organizing for visual simplicity or administrative convenience can move costs onto users whose activities cross the new boundaries. [TA-W029, pp. 5–14]

The essay is not a demand to mix everything. Separation of children from fast traffic can be appropriate; the problem is prescribing separation without examining the relevant functions. Alexander also distinguishes formal organizational hierarchy from the more changeable patterns of influence he reports through Banfield. [TA-W029, discussion of pedestrian/traffic systems and organizational influence, pp. 11 –14]

Most importantly, he admits that he cannot yet show a satisfactory plan for the desired modern city. Overlap for its own sake can produce chaos. The right relationships depend on changing functions, so copying the appearance of a historical city will not necessarily reproduce useful organization. The Nicholson painting and its multiple groupings supply an image for thought, not empirical proof that a corresponding urban design will perform well. [TA-W029, pp. 16–17]

Alexander reports psychological grouping experiments. The substantive urban challenge can be stated without them: a representation that excludes partial overlaps may destroy relationships that matter to use. The essay leaves the task of discovering and realizing the appropriate overlaps unfinished. [TA-W029, pp. 14–17]

The book proposes a hierarchy for organizing a chosen design problem; the essay attacks an imposed urban tree that severs significant overlaps. Their shared set-theoretic vocabulary serves these different constructions. The sequence contains both a decomposition programme and a challenge to disjoint urban organization. [TA-W028, chs. 6–9; TA-W029]

Habraken: levels of form and the distribution of control#

N. John Habraken's The Uses of Levels asks a related but distinct question: which parties control decisions at different levels of the built environment? The text is the 2002 reissue of a 1988 keynote. It distinguishes urban structure, building or support, infill and furniture. Lower-level changes can vary within higher-level provisions. But a diagram of physical levels does not identify control until responsibilities have also been assigned. [GL-W021, selected primary text, pp. 9–14, 16–17]

Design control and control during use require separate descriptions. Professionals might design a building whose subsequent management belongs to an outside organization or a collective of users. A resident might control only furniture, or might also control infill. Sites-and-services and core-house

arrangements distribute the work differently again. Habraken explicitly says that his model does not identify one universally superior strategy. Circumstances affect which division of responsibility is suitable. [GL-W021, pp. 9–11]

Technical systems can cross levels. In his wall and sewage examples, an individual, a collective and a municipality may control different portions of a system, and the distributions need not be identical for the two technologies. This makes the responsibility question more precise than a choice between central control and user freedom in the abstract. The relevant parties and the actual system have to be identified together. [GL-W021, pp. 11–12]

The support/infill proposal allows repetitive shared support while users choose and change individual layouts. Habraken argues that separating infill can support industrial production, installation efficiencies and continued improvement of the infill systems. Variety at the dwelling level need not require a separately invented support for each dwelling. [GL-W021, pp. 12–14]

Professional expertise remains essential in this account. Users need clearly defined responsibilities, and professionals need skill in organizing parties and coordinating their relationships across levels. Habraken says that misunderstandings of levels and poor coordination can cause problems regardless of the project's budget. More freedom of local choice therefore does not mean less need for understanding how the shared provisions work. [GL-W021, p. 16]

Habraken's synopsis of The Structure of the Ordinary, edited by Jonathan Teicher, distinguishes orders of form, territorial control and shared understanding, extending the subject beyond physical geometry. [GL-W092, author synopsis]

Gabriel: attempting to recover the decomposition#

Richard Gabriel's 2023 essay reconstructs the early design method through attempts to recover the published village decomposition and through the HIDECS program history. Gabriel reports difficulties with the interaction data, notation, goodness measures and the relation between the presented decomposition and the programs. His investigation makes the reproducibility of the worked formal example a substantive issue rather than treating the printed tree as a self-validating result. [SB-W011, pp. 1–25; selected appendices D–H]

He reports fifty asymmetries in the printed interaction table: a listed relation in one direction is not reciprocally listed where symmetry is intended. His initial inclination was to add the missing reciprocal relation. He later concluded from the program material that the input treatment instead removed such inconsistent relations. Which repair is made changes the graph that the algorithm receives. These are Gabriel's reported findings and historical reconstruction. [SB-W011, main reconstruction; appendices B, F]

The search procedure supplies a second challenge. A succession of favorable binary splits can fail to give the best finer-level partition. Gabriel describes how later program variants addressed holistic grouping and allowed overlaps, and he reports that his attempts did not reproduce the exact published decomposition. His account therefore separates several procedures that a casual reading might compress into one successful computer method. [SB-W011, main argument, especially §§1.5–1.9; selected appendices D, G, H]

Gabriel identifies difficulties in reconstructing the published decomposition, obtaining a global partition through local search, and relating the published account to the program variants. Notation problems in his alternative formulas also leave their numerical rankings uncertain. [SB-W011, main argument and appendix D]

Steadman: intentional craft and the biological analogy#

Philip Steadman's 2020 retrospective explains how his research into biological analogy developed partly through criticism of Alexander. He reads the early design account as depending on an analogy between the adaptation of organisms and the gradual adjustment of vernacular forms, while explicitly recognizing that this is his interpretation rather than Alexander's own description. He argues that organisms are not simply molded by environmental forces and that craftspeople deliberately introduce changes. Cultural variation is not equivalent to blind genetic mutation. [SB-W012, retrospective essay]

For gambits engineering, the intentionality objection matters because inherited forms can embody judgment and practical understanding. Treating a working tradition as an automatic product of environmental selection can conceal who noticed the failure, proposed a change and maintained the result. Steadman contrasts an ambition to generate an optimal solution automatically with scientific knowledge and simulations that help designers compare ranges of choices. His retrospective favors the latter use of research. [SB-W012, discussion of Alexander and architectural science]

Alexander's text complicates the strongest version of the criticism. It expressly reserves invention for designers, acknowledges the flexibility of conceptual thought and allows multiple forms for a program. Steadman’s essay retrospectively examines his own intellectual work. [SB-W012; TA-W028, pp. 74–75, 207–208, 210]

Zhao and Jiang: design agency and implementation institutions#

Zhao Botao and Jiang Hong's 2024 article interprets Alexander's urban-design work across a later trajectory. Their relevant criticism is that an approach centered on constructive design agency can underestimate the regulations, finance and institutional arrangements that condition implementation. A proposed spatial process does not secure those arrangements simply by offering a coherent design logic. [SB-W013, §§1–2 and later discussion]

In their interpretation of Alexander’s 1987 work, Zhao and Jiang resist describing his later development as an abandonment of constructive reasoning in favor of mysticism. Their account emphasizes design agency alongside the institutional conditions of realization. [SB-W013]

Form, correction and overlapping use#

The relevant material teaches several distinct things in detail: a form can combine construction, use and maintenance functions; prompt local correction depends on knowledge, restraint and time; a graph can organize selected interactions without exhausting a problem; and a built environment can support overlapping uses that a disjoint plan conceals. Habraken separately shows how physical provisions and control responsibilities can be distinguished. [TA-W028; TA-W029; GL-W021]

S108 Structures, ground conditions and construction sequences#

What supports a slab while it is raised#

The National Bureau of Standards investigation of the L’Ambiance Plaza collapse describes construction by lifting slabs. Floor slabs were cast near ground level, post-tensioned, raised by hydraulic jacks and secured to columns at the required elevations. During lifting, the jacking equipment and its connection to the slab carry loads that the final connection is intended to carry after attachment. The investigating report describes equipment, construction sequence and witness accounts as evidence from which to reconstruct the condition at collapse. [T10-W001]

How movement changes with excavation stage#

刘征 and 罗志琪 describe a large semi-top-down excavation near an existing 48-storey building. The staged work gave them reason to observe deformation while support conditions were changing. At point CX14 they report 38.9 mm at completion of the base slab and 48.4 mm at the later construction stage identified in Fig. 9. Most of the other points had final cumulative maximum displacements of 30 to 38 mm. The point, direction and construction stage matter to interpreting the values. The later reading concerns a different condition of the excavation and its supporting structure. [T10-W002]

Changing support during continued use#

The French engineering account of reinforcing ground below existing structures distinguishes treating the ground from transferring support through underpinning. Its Fig. 32 example uses temporary jacks and then sliding supports, followed by readjustments. The same account describes micropile arrangements for places where access is restricted. A transverse support can pass through a load-bearing wall and transfer its load to two vertical micropiles. What carries the load changes during the intervention. The example describes a sequence adapted to an existing structure and its ground conditions. [T10-W003]

The Federal Highway Administration’s bridge preservation guide connects inspection to decisions about maintenance and rehabilitation. It treats severity and the quantity of affected elements as relevant to the choice of action. Deterioration or loss of support can prompt more frequent monitoring, restrictions or closure. Its condition descriptions are institutional guidance for making those decisions. The excavation study instead provides measurements taken while a particular construction sequence was under way. [T10-W004]

S10 Coordination avoidance: the invariant, the operations, and the merge#

When local transactions compose safely#

Peter Bailis and colleagues ask when database transactions can execute without blocking coordination while preserving stated application invariants. Their framework makes the answer depend on the combination of an invariant, a transaction set, and a merge operation. The result concerns a declared database model. [W005, §§3–4]

The model represents a database state through versions of data items. A transaction operates on a logical replica, a partial view of versions, and changes to committed state are subsequently shared through merge. A logical replica is not necessarily a separate physical server. In the initial model, merge is set union: the resulting state includes the versions present on either side. The authors assume merge is associative, commutative, and idempotent for their discussion. Those algebraic properties describe how merges combine; they do not determine what application states are acceptable. [W005, §3]

Four requirements for coordination avoidance#

An invariant is a predicate that says whether a state is acceptable. The initial state must satisfy it. Global validity requires replica states to remain valid, including states reached by merging independently produced changes. Checking a transaction's immediate local result is therefore only part of what has to be established. [W005, §3, definitions 1 and 4]

Transactional availability is deliberately nontrivial. Under the stated access conditions, a transaction eventually commits except when its own abort operation or a violation of a declared invariant over its replica justifies aborting. Always refusing transactions is not an available solution in this definition. Convergence also rules out permanently isolated valid histories as a substitute for sharing state: without new writes and indefinite communication delay, servers eventually agree on versions of items they both store. [W005, §3, definitions 2–3]

Coordination-freedom concerns the progress of concurrently executing transactions. A transaction's progress depends on the versions it reads, rather than blocking synchronization with work performed for another transaction. This does not mean there is no communication. The model explicitly retains subsequent propagation and merge; an implementation may also communicate to provide a chosen durability level. Removing synchronous coordination between concurrent decisions is a more specific claim than eliminating every kind of network work. [W005, §3, definition 5 and discussion]

Reachability and the common ancestor#

The key property, invariant confluence, is defined over reachable states. A state is reachable in the relevant sense when transactions and merges can produce it through a history whose intermediate states satisfy the invariant. The criterion considers two such states with a common ancestor and asks whether their merge is also valid. Both reachability and common ancestry matter. The definition does not require arbitrary states that happen individually to be valid to merge safely, even when the permitted transactions could never have produced their divergent histories. [W005, §4.1, definition 6]

The source states a necessary-and-sufficient result: within its model, global invariant validity can coexist with coordination-freedom, transactional availability, and convergence exactly when the transaction set is invariant-confluent with respect to the invariant. The paper provides a proof sketch and directs the reader to a technical report for the full proof. [W005, §4.2, theorem 1]

Explanatory illustration: a property that survives union#

The following small example illustrates the paper's model and distinction. It is an explanatory construction for this monograph. Suppose the state is a set of records, and the only permitted transactions add records with nonnegative ages. Let the invariant require every stored age to be nonnegative. Start from the empty valid state. One history adds Alice, aged 30; another adds Bob, aged 40. Each result is valid, and their union is valid because each record in the union came from a side that met the same requirement. [W005, §§3–5, model and attribute constraints]

The reasoning extends over the specified add-only transaction set: none of its operations introduces a negative-age record, and taking unions does not introduce a record absent from both inputs. This explains why the property in this example is preserved through the permitted divergent histories and merge. It does not say anything yet about unique identifiers, correct billing, or other requirements that were not included in the invariant.

Change the invariant and the answer changes#

Now give the records identifiers, retaining set union as merge. Let the application invariant require that no two different people share an identifier. Two histories diverge from the same empty ancestor. On one replica, a transaction sees identifier 7 unused and inserts Alice with identifier 7. On the other, a transaction sees it unused and inserts Bob with identifier 7. Each local state satisfies uniqueness. Their merged state contains two different records with the same identifier and violates it. The local commit checks have not made the independent decisions composable. [W005, §§3–5, uniqueness discussion; explanatory illustration]

Idempotence does not repair this outcome. Unioning the already merged set with itself changes nothing. Alice's record and Bob's record are distinct elements; the duplicated application identifier does not make them the same version for set union. A stable, repeatable merge can therefore preserve an unacceptable result. The example shows why an algebraic merge property and an application invariant must not be substituted for each other.

Under the theorem's combination of obligations, the non-confluent pair prevents the unrestricted coordination-free conclusion for these operations and this invariant. One cannot save all the obligations simply by refusing to merge forever or by aborting every otherwise locally valid transaction. A different allocation operation, invariant, or representation would pose a different question and needs its own analysis. The paper's distinction between choosing a specific identifier and choosing some identifier is important for precisely this reason: uniqueness is not an unconditional verdict that every conceivable identifier-allocation design requires the same coordination. [W005, §§4.1–5]

Correctness still depends on what was specified#

The authors explicitly limit the framework to the invariants and operations supplied. If those requirements are incomplete or wrong, satisfying them need not satisfy the application's actual purposes. Specifying the requirements is itself substantive work. The framework can identify a possibility or an impossibility under its assumptions; it does not select every implementation, determine the relevance of every business rule, or demonstrate a net lifetime saving. [W005, §4.3]

Whether the local decisions compose safely depends on the allowed histories and the invariant under the chosen merge. The worked example exposes the temptation to infer application validity from idempotence alone. The answer depends on the specified database model and requirement.

What the coordination comparison actually compares#

Bailis and colleagues motivate their criterion by distinguishing serializability from application correctness. If each transaction is correct in isolation, an execution equivalent to a serial order supplies a powerful general guarantee. But not every interaction that conflicts at the read/write level compromises the application's selected invariant. Their proposal asks which combinations actually need synchronous coordination, rather than paying that cost for every general-purpose conflict. The distinction raises the specification from low-level interference to the application property that must remain true. [W005, §2]

Their measurements illustrate why that distinction can matter. An eight-server prototype comparison contrasts an optimized two-phase-locking implementation with execution without coordination. The latter avoids the locking bottleneck for its specified operations; distributed coordinated transactions suffer a much larger throughput drop as their scope expands. These are particular implementation and workload comparisons, supplemented by network-delay calculations using earlier trace studies. The paper explicitly notes that rare coordinating operations need not be a bottleneck and that disjoint read/write sets can allow a serializable database to perform similarly. The favorable case is therefore informative without establishing that removing coordination always improves the application's overall performance. [W005, §2, figs. 1–2]

The theorem and these measurements do different work. The criterion characterizes a possibility under the declared semantics; the benchmark measures particular costs under particular execution arrangements. Neither permits a correctness requirement to be silently discarded because avoiding it runs faster. Conversely, using a stronger general guarantee than the application needs can impose work that a more specific analysis could avoid.

Changing identifier allocation changes the problem#

The article's uniqueness discussion distinguishes “give this record this particular identifier” from “give this record some unique identifier.” In the latter case, replicas with known identities can allocate from disjoint portions of a namespace. Each then uses a space other replicas do not use; merging locally allocated identifiers does not introduce the collision caused by two replicas freely choosing the same value. The arrangement changes the allowed allocation operation and relies on membership information. The unrestricted-insertion counterexample above consequently does not refute this different design. [W005, §5.1]

This is a concrete example of prior structure changing a recurring interaction. The separated namespaces embody a constraint on which local choice can occur. Their suitability still depends on the actual identifier requirements and reliable handling of membership; a design requiring one particular shared identifier poses another task. The paper does not establish that choosing any identifier is an acceptable substitute in every application. Its result is strongest when the changed semantics remain explicit.

Referential integrity depends on the allowed updates#

For a foreign-key relationship, an inserted record requires a corresponding referenced record. In the article's non-destructive merge account, if every locally valid inserted reference has its target, union cannot make that target disappear. That argument explains a positive result for the specified insertions. Arbitrary deletion changes the situation: one history can add an employee to a department while another deletes the department. Each local view can meet its immediate requirements, yet their combined effect can leave a dangling reference. The condition is not simply “foreign keys are safe” or “foreign keys require coordination.” It depends on what updates and merge semantics are allowed. [W005, §5.1]

The source also considers cascading deletion and suitable propagation of related effects as different operations. Their treatment depends on the modeled semantics, not merely on attaching the word cascade to an implementation. It preserves the paper's reason for distinguishing the cases: validity can concern the visibility and persistence of related records as well as the immediate value in one field. Coordination requirements cannot be read from the invariant's name alone. [W005, §5.1]

Borrego and colleagues: a losing operation can become ineffective#

Dina Borrego, Nuno Preguiça, Elisa Gonzalez Boix and Carla Ferreira's 2025 No-Op approach maintains convergence and invariants through explicit conflict-resolution policies. In their music-data example, concurrently removing an artist and adding an album referring to that artist can threaten referential integrity. An update-wins policy can render the artist removal ineffective; a remove-wins policy can instead suppress the album addition. Both arrangements make a choice about which effect survives. They do not preserve both unrestricted effects while somehow making the conflict disappear. [W027, §§2–2.1]

The mechanism records operation calls and their causal dependencies in an execution graph. Concurrent calls remain unordered by causal edges. A winning call issues a block against an incompatible concurrent call, which is marked as a No-Op. When the other replica receives the relevant call, it can make the same determination. Replicas can therefore initially differ and subsequently agree after the required information is delivered. In the paper's update-wins trace, an artist removal that looked effective locally is later recognized as a No-Op. Immediate local appearance and eventual effective state must be distinguished. [W027, §2.1]

Their correctness argument assumes that every replica receives all updates, updates arrive in causal order, and a resolution policy exists for every conflicting pair. The claimed safe serializations and convergence retain those prerequisites. The workflow also retains programmers' responsibility for identifying conflicts and selecting policies. Verification of invariant preservation does not check that a chosen priority matches the programmer's intended meaning. A user-priority rule, for example, makes whose operation wins an explicit part of the arrangement. This remains a substantive semantic decision even when a formal check succeeds. [W027, §§2.2, 3.1]

The account is relevant alongside invariant confluence because it makes a changed obligation visible. Suppressing a losing effect is a particular concurrency semantics, not a counterexample to a theorem holding fixed the original transactions and its availability/validity obligations. Comparing the sources requires retaining what each permits to be discarded or made ineffective.

Bailis's dissertation: specification and mixed execution#

In the conclusion of his 2015 doctoral dissertation, Bailis describes four limitations of coordination avoidance. The invariant-confluence analysis has effectively assumed that program text and constraints are known in advance. A restricted safe language could permit some dynamic programming, but its usefulness still depends on admissible logic and complexity. This is an explicit condition on what has to be available before the runtime advantage can be established. [W057, ch. 8, printed pp. 185–186]

The same passage emphasizes complete correctness specifications. An invariant absent from the specification is treated as irrelevant to correctness. The programmer therefore bears a burden that does not disappear when the selected invariant is formally preserved. Bailis also describes the analysis and construction of algorithms as primarily manual, using proofs, rudimentary static analysis and design principles. [W057, printed p. 186]

Finally, the passage identifies mixed execution as an unresolved practical issue. Always coordinating whenever the criterion does not hold can waste opportunities; realizing the benefit may require combining coordinated and coordination-free semantics within one runtime. [W057, §8.2]

Sato: files and prior transactions supply state#

Ryo Sato's 1992 paper offers a state-space representation of business transaction systems, drawing its general system definitions from Mesarovic and Takahara. The selected opening pages treat operations such as orders, purchasing and bookkeeping as discrete events that can occur in parallel. Files retain accumulated past transactions, while internally set events also contribute to the state governing subsequent response. The proposed model therefore does not identify a business system only with a stream of current requests: its stored history changes how an incoming event can be handled. [SG-W035, printed pp. 184–187]

Sato's data-model definitions distinguish file types, attributes, keys and actual file contents, then formulate integrity conditions, including references between files. They supply a language for saying what information and constraints a transaction system contains. [SG-W035, definitions and prose, printed pp. 185–188]

S11 Convergence and self-stabilization: what local rules can establish#

Two questions about distributed behavior#

Edsger Dijkstra's self-stabilization paper and the replicated-data-type report by Marc Shapiro, Nuno Preguiça, Carlos Baquero and Marek Zawirski examine different global properties obtained through constrained local operations. Dijkstra asks whether a distributed state can enter a legitimate set from an arbitrary initial state and remain legitimate. The CRDT report asks when replicas that receive the same updates give equivalent answers despite asynchronous exchange. [W006; W061]

The permitted local actions replace some continuing global direction. Dijkstra specifies a scheduler and local interfaces. The CRDT report specifies update/merge properties and eventual delivery.

Dijkstra: recovery differs from preserving a good initial state#

In his 1974 two-page paper, Dijkstra begins with synchronization as preservation of legitimate global states. A system can be designed so that correctly admitted steps preserve legitimacy once established. That leaves another problem: an illegitimate state reached through an error may persist indefinitely. Self-stabilization adds recovery from any initial state admitted by the finite-machine model. Thus a local rule that keeps an already correct execution correct has not yet met the stronger requirement. [W006, p. 643]

His model places finite-state machines at nodes of a connected graph, with each able to inspect its own state and those of its neighbors. A privilege is a Boolean condition on that available state. When the privilege holds, its associated move is enabled. A central daemon chooses one present privilege, that machine changes state, and the process repeats. The central daemon models arbitrary relative speeds through nondeterministic choice of successive moves. Replacing it with a distributed daemon is expressly outside this short paper. “Distributed control” therefore does not mean the model has no global scheduling assumption. [W006, p. 643]

Legitimacy is a criterion on the joint state, although a node makes its move from local information. Dijkstra requires legitimate states to have at least one enabled privilege and to remain legitimate under every permitted next move. He also imposes conditions connecting the privileges and legitimate states. Self-stabilization then requires that some privilege is always present and that every allowed succession of daemon choices reaches a legitimate state after finitely many moves, regardless of the initial state. The quantification over allowed choices matters: one fortunate simulation is not the result being asserted. [W006, p. 643]

This is a recovery guarantee under fixed rules and scheduling semantics. Arbitrary initial state does not mean a continuing external agent can corrupt state at every step while the system is guaranteed to remain legitimate. Nor does an arbitrary corruption of the machine's transition rules fit the same model merely because its register contents were allowed to start arbitrarily.

The ring constructions retain an asymmetry#

Dijkstra supplies three ring constructions and says their full proofs and much of the discovery process are omitted from the article. In the K-state construction, the distinguished bottom machine advances its state cyclically when it matches its predecessor. Other machines copy their predecessor when they differ. The legitimate states selected for the ring have exactly one privilege present. The source's sufficient state-space relation is K greater than N for N+1 machines under the central daemon. The distinction of the bottom machine is consequential: this is not a construction of wholly identical nodes each executing an identical rule. [W006, pp. 643–644 and note 1]

A small legitimate trace helps explain the mechanism without purporting to prove recovery. Take three machines, four state values, and write the states in bottom-to-top order. Starting at (0,0,0), only the bottom machine's equality condition is enabled. It advances to 1, giving (1,0,0). The next machine now differs from its predecessor and copies it, giving (1,1,0). The third then copies, giving (1,1,1), where the bottom is again enabled. The single privilege has moved through the ring. This displayed trace illustrates behavior within the legitimate set; it does not establish the universal finite recovery assertion from all states or all daemon choices. [W006, K-state construction; explanatory instance]

The three-state and four-state constructions use different neighbor conditions, with special endpoint roles. Their presence shows that the short paper is offering concrete ways of meeting a global criterion with locally determined moves, rather than only naming self-stabilization. The constructions distinguish between closure of the legitimate set and convergence into it, together with the precise local-information and scheduling conditions used to demonstrate the possibility. [W006, p. 644]

For gambits engineering, the relevant material is consequently more specific than a slogan about self-repair. State and permitted relations can be arranged so that recovery need not require a separate controller to inspect the entire state and issue each corrective instruction. The construction nevertheless retains a selected notion of legitimacy, special rules, sufficient state space and an admitted order of moves.

Shapiro and colleagues: equal histories must give equivalent answers#

The 2011 INRIA report defines eventual convergence through both safety and liveness. Replicas with the same causal history must have equivalent abstract states, meaning their query operations give the same values. Updates must also eventually reach the causal histories of the other replicas. Identical answers obtained only by permanently ignoring some updates would not satisfy the combined condition. Nor does temporary disagreement before propagation automatically violate it. The property concerns histories and eventual communication in an asynchronous system. [W061, §§2.1–2.3]

The surrounding model allows network partitions and later recovery. A process can crash and recover while its memory survives. Byzantine behavior is excluded. These are substantial assumptions about what the arrangement must tolerate. [W061, §2]

The report gives two sufficient routes to convergence. State-based replication sends state, while operation-based replication sends operations. They place different requirements on the payload and communication. [W061, §§2.2–2.3, 3.1]

State-based merging retains order through the payload#

For a state-based convergent replicated data type, payload states form a join semilattice: any two states have a least state above both in the specified partial order. Merge returns that least upper bound. Local updates advance monotonically in the order. This supplies a way to retain all relevant progress while combining states. The order concerns the representation, rather than necessarily an increase in every visible application quantity. A type that supports a decreasing visible value may need a representation whose accumulated information still advances. [W061, §2.3.1]

Least-upper-bound merge is associative, commutative and idempotent. Changing the order of combining states, grouping several combinations, or receiving the same state again does not change the abstract combined result. These properties relieve the communication channel of some demands: individual messages can be duplicated, reordered or lost if sufficiently new state eventually reaches every replica, directly or through other merges. They do not remove the eventual-delivery requirement. A permanently missing update cannot be inferred from these algebraic properties. [W061, §2.3.1, proposition 2.1]

The proof's core comparison is between replicas with the same accumulated histories. Their respective merges contain the same updates, and commutativity of the least upper bound gives equivalent abstract states. Liveness supplies the eventual arrival needed to obtain those histories. The proof is therefore informative about how the obligations fit together. [W061, proposition 2.1]

A convergent scalar can still be the wrong counter#

The report's counter example shows why satisfying a convergence pattern is not enough to meet an arbitrary type specification. A single integer with merge by maximum and local increments forms a monotonic semilattice. Yet if two replicas start at zero and each increments to one, their maximum is one. If the desired counter should reflect both increments, that result loses one of them. The replicas can agree perfectly on an answer that fails the intended count. [W061, §3.1.2]

The state-based grow-only counter instead gives each source replica an entry in a vector. A replica increments its own entry; merge takes the componentwise maximum; query sums the entries. For two replicas, independent local states (1,0) and (0,1) merge to (1,1), and the query returns two. Receiving the same vector again makes no further change. Source-specific components preserve distinctions that a single maximum discarded. The explanation depends on the specified source identities and ownership of increments; arbitrary writers changing another source's entry would be a different operation set. [W061, §3.1.2, specification 6; two-replica explanatory instance]

This version also assumes the payload does not overflow and the set of replicas is known. It is a precise example of using a richer maintained representation to simplify combination. The vector retains additional state. The report states that its portfolio specifications favor clarity over efficiency and notes that equivalent representations can use less space. Choosing an actual representation and its maintenance still involves work beyond recognizing the semilattice property. [W061, §3 introduction and §3.1.2]

Operation-based replication has another channel obligation#

For an operation-based commutative replicated data type, operations not ordered by the required delivery relation must commute. Their permitted execution orders then give equivalent abstract states. The report assumes reliable broadcast that delivers operations in the order specified by the type. For the studied types, causal delivery is sufficient; some types can use weaker order if more pairs commute. The state-based tolerance of repeated state messages is therefore not a license to apply arbitrary operation messages twice without checking their semantics. [W061, §2.3.2]

Suitable operation algebra and delivery order replace a need to agree on a single order for all concurrent operations. The surrounding implementation still has to ensure that updates reach replicas and obey the chosen constraints.

Immediate updates, storage and later synchronization#

The report itself identifies costs beyond foreground synchronization. Some proposed designs grow without bound, and garbage collection can require a weaker form of synchronization. It treats that synchronization as off the critical path and not essential to liveness, rather than claiming the storage issue absent. It also discusses the need for synchronization for some less common operations as a direction beyond the main study. [W061, introduction]

The preceding coordination-avoidance account gives the separate application-validity question a concrete form. Idempotent union can preserve repeated-merge behavior while violating a unique-identifier invariant. Here, similarly, an integer maximum can converge while failing the intended total count.

Dijkstra's recovery property remains distinct again: agreement among replicas says nothing by itself about recovery from arbitrary corrupt initial states.

S12 Integration and expertise across boundaries#

A supplied component does not specify the whole obligation#

The sources address boundaries between firms and suppliers, applications and communication layers, flight crews and automation, and internet design under changing requirements.

Brusoni, Prencipe and Pavitt: knowing can extend beyond making#

Stefano Brusoni, Andrea Prencipe and Keith Pavitt distinguish a firm's production boundaries from its knowledge boundaries. In the selected discussion of complex products such as aircraft engines, the systems integrator can outsource detailed design and manufacture while retaining concept design and integration capabilities. Those capabilities coordinate suppliers' research, design and manufacturing and handle interdependencies at the product level. Buying the component consequently does not settle whether the buyer can also dispense with technological knowledge about it. [W068, abstract and discussion, pp. 617–618]

Their account gives two reasons overlapping knowledge can matter. A rapid advance in one technology can create an imbalance among component performances; an innovative opportunity at a specialized supplier can also make a different system architecture worth exploring. In either case, the assembler needs capabilities to recognize and work with the opportunity, including temporarily tighter links with outside knowledge. The authors call for cognitive overlap between assembler and supplier, rather than treating perfect separability as the definition of every useful supply relationship. [W068, pp. 617–618]

They describe this as a loosely coupled network organization: differentiated production and knowledge activities remain connected in ways that can change as technologies and products change. The selected conclusion also identifies limits. The empirical framework should be extended across sectors, and variables such as appropriability, past research investments and internal coalitions can affect make-or-buy decisions without being captured by their technological categories. [W068, pp. 617–618]

The source's substantive contribution is the explicit distinction between what is performed elsewhere and what must still be understood to integrate and change a complex product.

Saltzer, Reed and Clark: the endpoint must check the actual application result#

Jerome Saltzer, David Reed and David Clark's End-to-End Arguments in System Design asks where a function belongs among distributed-system modules. Its careful-file-transfer example identifies several places a transfer can go wrong: storage, programs, memory and transmission all participate. Making a communication subsystem highly reliable addresses only some of those opportunities. It cannot by itself check the complete application result, including the copy actually written at the destination. [GL-W030, author reprint pp. 1–3]

The alternative procedure retains an end-to-end checksum, comparison and retry/commit plan. After transfer, the destination reads its stored copy back, computes a checksum, and returns it for comparison with the original. Agreement permits the application to commit; disagreement can prompt another attempt. The proposed effectiveness depends on sufficiently rare faults, an appropriate checksum and a correct endpoint procedure. Repeated failures also indicate a need to repair the system, rather than retrying indefinitely while declaring reliability achieved. The detailed sequence shows what knowledge and action remain at the endpoint. [GL-W030, careful-file-transfer example]

The reported gateway incident makes the boundary problem concrete. Per-hop checksums protected transmissions but not data during internal copying in a gateway. A transient copying fault could therefore

alter data between those protected portions. Application programmers' inference that the network already guaranteed the whole required transfer was the mistake the account exposes. [GL-W030, pp. 3–4, A too-real example]

The argument does not make all lower-level reliability useless. Lower-level checks can substantially improve performance by reducing endpoint retries. The choice depends on error rates, relative costs and the application's obligation; an extremely unreliable lower level can make a theoretically correct end-to-end arrangement impractical. The selected source distinguishes completeness of the correctness function from helpful partial support. [GL-W030, pp. 3–4 and performance discussion]

Flight-deck automation: responsibility includes monitoring and procedure revision#

The recommendations of the PARC/CAST Flight Deck Automation Working Group frame the operational goal as flight-path management, rather than merely correct use of automated equipment. Their selected policy recommendation retains pilots' responsibility for that goal. The procedure-design recommendation emphasizes monitoring, cross-verification and allocating tasks between the pilot flying and pilot monitoring. These are identified parts of the supported operational arrangement, not residual activities that become unnecessary when automation is introduced. [GL-W083, recommendations 8–9]

The same passage calls for procedures to be updated using operational experience and research, and for investigation of when and why procedures are not followed. Retained expertise therefore includes learning from the interaction of people, procedures and equipment over time.

Clark and Blumenthal: stakeholders can change the architecture's problem#

David Clark and Marjory Blumenthal's September 2000 working paper revisits end-to-end arguments under a wider range of internet purposes. The institutional abstract identifies new stakeholders, including service providers and government interests, changed user motivations, and a tension between trustworthy overall operation and limited trust in individual users. An architecture chosen for one set of assumptions can therefore face a different task as its users and institutions change. This is the authors' proposed problem. [GL-W095, working-paper abstract]

Their stated concern is that accommodating emerging requirements could compromise support for new and unanticipated applications, one of the original architecture's valued features. That places benefits to one purpose beside possible restrictions on another.

S84 Specialization across abstraction boundaries#

An operating system can offer the same operations to many applications while fixing choices that matter differently to each of them. A file-copying program, a web server and a database can use familiar interfaces yet benefit from different arrangements of memory, storage and communication. The architectures examined here change which choices an application can make, which implementations it can replace and how those choices are protected. Their histories include both exposing lower-level resources and retaining interfaces while changing the work performed behind them.

Moving management into a replaceable library#

Dawson Engler, Frans Kaashoek and James O’Toole’s 1995 exokernel design separates protection of resources from their management. A small privileged kernel tracks ownership and controls access to physical resources. Library operating systems implement higher-level abstractions, such as virtual memory, interprocess communication and files. An application can use a library supplying familiar services or a specialized implementation suited to its task. Replacing a library need not require replacing the kernel. [XA-W001]

The authors identify several restrictions imposed by a fixed privileged implementation. A general replacement policy can be poorly matched to a database’s predictable access pattern. Hiding faults or timing information can obstruct an application’s own management. A new abstraction can require awkward emulation through an existing one. Their proposed change gives application software control of implementation decisions that would otherwise belong to the operating system. It extends the question of function placement developed in S12 to resource management. [XA-W001]

A secure binding separates authorization from subsequent use. When access is established, the system can examine the relevant ownership and permissions; later accesses can be checked through simpler hardware or software mechanisms. The kernel need not understand every higher-level purpose for which an authorized resource will be used. The design also exposes allocation and resource names so that an application can choose specific resources using information about their properties and availability. [XA-W001]

Control remains bounded by the kernel’s power to allocate and reclaim. Visible revocation lets a library choose which resource to surrender and adjust its own state. An abort protocol allows the kernel to reclaim resources when an application refuses to cooperate. Allocation denial and revocation can enforce quotas or other policies among competing applications. Moving management into a library therefore changes the application’s available decisions while preserving an authority that arbitrates access. [XA-W001]

Sharing disk data without prescribing one filesystem#

The later Xok/ExOS system makes protected sharing a concrete design problem. A library filesystem needs control of disk layout, caching and requests, but several libraries may access the same files. Partitioning the disk among applications would prevent useful sharing. XN, Xok’s storage substrate, instead protects blocks and metadata while allowing library filesystems to interpret and arrange them. [XA-W002]

Its buffer-cache registry records the association between a disk block and the physical page holding a cached copy. The data remain in application-managed pages. A library can inspect the registry to discover what is cached, but mapping a page requires corresponding access rights to the disk block. This arrangement permits reuse of cached data without giving every participant authority to modify it.

Libraries retain choices about replacement, prefetching and the division of their memory between cached files and other uses. [XA-W002]

Protection also concerns how metadata establishes ownership. XN uses deterministic metadata-interpreting functions to check whether a proposed update correctly tracks the blocks controlled by a filesystem object. It enforces ordering rules needed to prevent a crash from creating unauthorized access. For example, a persistent pointer must not expose uninitialized metadata, and a freed block must not be reused while old persistent pointers still refer to it. Libraries choose operations and schedules consistent with those rules. [XA-W002]

C-FFS supplies Unix filesystem behavior on this substrate, including access-control mappings and invariants such as unique names within a directory. ExOS supplies ordinary Unix abstractions through libraries. In the 1997 implementation, some shared tables were not yet fully protected; the ordinary-application experiments included extra calls to estimate the cost of checking writes to them. Those experiments showed comparable performance with conventional systems, including a 41-second workload total on ExOS/C-FFS against 51 seconds on OpenBSD/C-FFS. The specialized applications discussed next were measured without the newly developed XN substrate. [XA-W002]

Copying files without touching their contents#

XCP uses the exposed storage and cache interfaces to change how copying is scheduled. Given a list of files, it first enumerates and sorts their disk blocks. It can then issue large asynchronous reads in an order suited to disk access, rather than follow an application-level sequence of small reads and writes. Concurrent instances can have their disk schedules merged by the driver. [XA-W002]

While reads proceed, XCP creates destination files and allocates their blocks. As data arrive, it constructs large writes using the buffer-cache entries. The disk controller transfers data into and out of the cache through direct memory access; the CPU does not copy or examine the contents. Allocation, reading and writing overlap, and cached pages become the connection between the two sides of the copy. [XA-W002]

The authors report XCP running three times faster than cp using Unix interfaces on the same Xok/ExOS system. For resident files, avoiding CPU data movement contributes to the gain. For files on disk, large contiguous transfers and a schedule with fewer seeks also matter. The library filesystem makes it possible to combine operations around the copying task instead of expressing the entire task through the usual file-operation sequence. [XA-W002]

Coordinating an HTTP response across storage and networking#

Cheetah applies application knowledge across another boundary. An HTTP server receives a request, locates a document and sends it to a client. The XIO library and Cheetah implementation allow storage and TCP handling to be organized together around this task. Their optimizations concern the path from cached or stored document to transmitted response. [XA-W002]

Cheetah merges the file cache with the TCP retransmission pool. It transmits document data directly from cached pages, using precomputed checksums stored with the files. If a retransmission is required, the same cached data can supply it. Separate copies for file caching and retransmission become unnecessary. The arrangement joins knowledge of the stored object to the communication protocol’s requirements. [XA-W002]

Knowledge of the request also affects packet scheduling.
