Cheetah delays acknowledgment of a client’s request when it expects to include that acknowledgment with the response, reducing separate control packets. This matters particularly for small documents, where one packet is a substantial part of the

exchange. On disk, it groups files included by an HTML document near that document when possible, making related requests cheaper when the cache does not absorb most of the workload. [XA-W002]

The evaluation compares conventional OpenBSD servers, a base socket server on OpenBSD, that server using socket interfaces on Xok, and Cheetah’s specialized path. For documents of one kilobyte or less, Cheetah obtained approximately four times the throughput of the Xok socket-based implementation and eight times the best performance the authors achieved on OpenBSD. For larger documents, Cheetah delivered more than 29.3 megabytes per second with the CPU idle over 30 percent of the time, whereas the socket implementation reached 16.5 megabytes per second at full CPU utilization. The machines used 200 MHz Pentium Pro processors; the server’s available network bandwidth came from three 100 Mbit/s Ethernet connections. [XA-W002]

The external HTTP/TCP exchange remains recognizable while internal operations are coordinated differently. The paper reports that even its default socket and filesystem implementations benefited from changes such as packet merging and cached pointers to file blocks. Further specialization then used knowledge of the complete response. In this history, retaining a familiar interface and exposing another route for application-specific control were both productive choices. [XA-W002]

What the exokernel builders learned#

The authors’ later account distinguishes fast primitive operations from control over expensive work. Aegis had been heavily tuned for microbenchmarks; Xok had not. They nevertheless obtained strong application results by changing I/O and other substantial operations. They also describe a practical development advantage: a library can be edited, compiled, relinked and debugged without the repeated kernel reboot cycle. Another library operating system can remain available while the experimental one is developed. [XA-W002]

Designing a suitable protected interface still took repeated iterations. It had to expose enough control while preserving the invariants needed for sharing. Self-paging libraries also required careful treatment of circumstances in which the software responsible for obtaining memory itself needed memory. These were engineering problems encountered while constructing the systems, alongside the improvements their architecture enabled. [XA-W002]

The project’s distribution notes describe a system suitable for library-OS and application development, with restricted disk and Ethernet controller support, bugs and unimplemented features. They also distinguish source-history events and available snapshots. The release account presents the state of a developing system; the performance papers present particular implementations and experiments. [XA-W008]

Reusing a kernel by introducing an adaptation layer#

田崎創’s 2017 account of Linux Kernel Library begins with a reuse problem. Accessing a filesystem created under another operating system requires an implementation of its semantics. Reimplementing a large, evolving filesystem is substantial work; booting a complete guest operating system is another possible route. LKL makes existing Linux kernel functionality available as a library that a surrounding program can use. [XA-W005]

Its adaptation layer occupies the place normally used to accommodate a processor architecture. Instead of adapting Linux solely to a different CPU, it mediates between the kernel code and the surrounding execution environment. Time, scheduling and memory are supplied through that environment, and virtio supports transfers to external devices. This makes the same core functionality usable through several hosts. [XA-W005]

Applications can call the LKL system-call interface, use an interposition library that redirects calls, or follow a musl-based compilation route. The interfaces above and below the reused kernel make that kernel useful in a new setting. Here additional abstraction serves reuse: the design does not seek its benefit simply by removing intermediate components. [XA-W005]

The author examines the implementation with netperf against ordinary Linux 4.9.0, using two PCs connected through Intel X540-T2 10 Gbit/s Ethernet interfaces. Large TCP transfers exploit segmentation and checksum offload, limiting the reported throughput reduction to about ten percent. Smaller transfers lack the same batching advantage. The reported UDP deficit reaches 47 percent at a 1024-byte payload, while much larger payloads approach ordinary Linux performance. These measurements connect the reused functionality to the actual transfer sizes and processing path. [XA-W005]

Keeping familiar calls while selecting the machinery underneath#

Unikraft organizes a specialized system from selectable micro-libraries. Its 2021 account describes components with explicit dependencies and build configurations, so that the final image includes the functionality required for the application. Scheduling can be omitted for a suitable single-threaded or run-to-completion task. Locking primitives can similarly disappear when the configured execution circumstances do not require them. [XA-W003]

The memory-allocation design preserves a familiar external interface while opening choices underneath it. A POSIX-facing allocation interface supports existing application code. The internal ukalloc interface directs requests to an allocator backend, and a caller using that internal interface specifies which backend to use. Backends have their own memory regions and allocation functions. Boot code and application code can therefore use different allocators without requiring every ordinary allocation call to expose that choice. [XA-W003]

Application support uses native builds and compatibility components. A syscall shim connects libc’s required operations to implementations available in the image, allowing calls to become ordinary function calls. The paper reports 146 implemented system calls and additional work for glibc-specific compatibility. Its application evaluation uses manual ports of nginx and Redis, selected configurations and single-core virtual machines. Those workloads ran 70–170 percent faster than the Linux VM comparisons reported there; allocator choices and security-mitigation settings affected the differences. [XA-W003]

Startup measurements distinguish the guest from the virtual-machine monitor. A guest’s initialization can take far less time than the complete operation of launching it. The paper reports total startup of approximately three milliseconds with Solo5 and Firecracker, including their monitor overhead. Selecting and initializing fewer components contributes to the result. These are choices about the constructed system and its launch path as well as about application instructions. [XA-W003]

Lefeuvre and colleagues’ developer overview places this work within earlier attempts to make unikernels useful. They identify restricted application support, unfamiliar tooling, insufficient modularity and missing security mechanisms as obstacles. They also question the inference that a small image alone provides strong security. Their proposed development direction joins specialized execution to support for applications, actual protection mechanisms and familiar operational tools. [XA-W007]

Shortening a known path inside Linux#

Unikernel Linux takes a different starting point: retaining Linux and its ecosystem while allowing one application to be linked with the kernel. Raza and colleagues’ base model replaces system-call instructions with procedure calls but preserves much of the existing execution machinery. Application

and kernel code retain different stack and execution conventions. Ordinary user processes can run alongside the optimized application. [XA-W004]

The optimized application runs with supervisor privilege. Other processes are not protected from it in the manner that separate Xok applications are protected from one another; the UKL account uses external isolation where work requires that protection. Within this arrangement, developers can select further changes, including bypassing portions of entry and exit processing and choosing how stacks are handled. Preserving execution conventions supplies a working starting point from which more specific changes can be investigated. [XA-W004]

Redis supplies the developed application case. Profiling shows its read and write operations passing through generic dispatch before reaching TCP routines. Since the relevant Redis operations use TCP, a shortcut can invoke tcp_recvmsg and tcp_sendmsg directly. The authors report modifying about ten lines of Redis to use it. This changes the underlying path, rather than only the instruction used to enter that path. [XA-W004]

In the reported bare-metal experiment, the base model improved throughput by 1.6 percent over Linux. The bypass/return configuration improved it by twelve percent; adding the shortcut improved it by 26 percent. The 99th-percentile latency changed from 3.26 milliseconds for Linux to 2.54 milliseconds for the shortcut configuration. The comparison used matching kernel and library versions, with the specified security mitigations disabled on both systems. Its separate virtual-machine experiments produced different, smaller gains. [XA-W004]

The authors’ performance-counter analysis follows instructions, cycles, branches and caches. The shortcut configuration executes fewer instructions and branches and makes fewer cache accesses; the reduction in cycles is greater than the reduction in instructions. They interpret the changed path and improved cache behavior as important to the result. The experiment therefore develops the engineering beyond replacing a system-call instruction: it follows how application knowledge changes the work that remains in the execution path. [XA-W004]

Changing a working platform with its maintainers#

UKL’s implementation coordinates changes to Linux, glibc and application code. Configuration-specific changes keep the base kernel patch relatively small and allow normal configurations to remain available. The authors describe months of discussion with kernel developers at Red Hat and an October 2022 request for comments to the Linux kernel mailing list. Their comparison of patches records the files and subsystems affected, including the maintainers whose review and approval would be required. [XA-W004]

Richard Jones’s 2023 project account describes further work before another community submission: separating patches, preparing useful commit messages and checking Linux standards and tests. Demonstrating a useful configuration and obtaining its acceptance into a shared platform are separate parts of this history. The participating team could build and measure a coordinated optimization while still needing review of changes intended for wider incorporation. [XA-W006]

This account gives the organizational questions developed in S07 a particular engineering setting. Decisions about an experimental image, changes to an application and acceptance into a maintained common platform involve different participants and commitments. In Jones’s account, the subsequent work is to prepare the changes for review and demonstrate their usefulness with additional workloads and collaborators. [XA-W006]

S112 Requirements, integration and verification in systems engineering#

Requirements as an activity#

Jeanneret Medina, Baudet and Bonnal look back on the development of requirements engineering as an area of work. In their account, the early 1990s conferences mark the emergence of an identifiable research current. They point to Pohl’s distinction among specification, representation and agreement, and contrast that account with standards that enumerate analysis, verification, validation, communication, documentation and management. [T14-W001]

NASA’s systems engineering handbook describes technical requirements definition as an iterative process. Baselined stakeholder expectations and a concept of operations supply inputs. Requirements are elaborated from the product to lower levels and address relationships with other products, operators and maintainers. The handbook’s example of a specified force with a tolerance makes a condition checkable. The specification gives the test a criterion. The observed result comes from carrying out the test. [T14-W002]

A specified unit at an interface#

The 1999 Mars Climate Orbiter investigation traces a numerical mismatch through an interface. The specification required impulse in newton-seconds. A ground software application wrote values in pound-force seconds, and the downstream navigation process treated them as the required metric values. The unit conversion is about 4.45. The report identifies the application, exchanged file and consumer, and records responsibilities on the contractor and JPL sides as they existed in the project. The case shows the practical distance between establishing an interface requirement and producing effective evidence that exchanged values meet it. [T14-W003]

Change and acceptance evidence#

Ågren and colleagues’ interviews at two automotive manufacturers address the visibility of requirements change. A current baseline tells a reader what the requirements now say. The history of changes shows which requirements moved and gives people examining the consequences a way to trace the change. The study’s proposed improvements come from interviews and a second round of inquiry. [T14-W004]

The transport prototype acceptance report gives an example of evidence at a specified configuration. A script describes the expected result, and its steps are repeated at least 15 times. The test team observes displays or physical events and keeps logs for inspection after the run. Step pass rates concern those scripts and the configuration they exercised. The report distinguishes these acceptance checks from the later field evaluation. [T14-W005]

S29 Leveson: constraints, feedback and the organization of safety#

The connected safety account#

Nancy Leveson's Engineering a Safer World connects physical design, automated and human control, organizational responsibilities, regulation and change throughout a system's life. Its relevant contribution is an extensive account of preserving acceptable behavior while arranging the information, action and support that preservation requires. The connection is the author's applied synthesis. [UX-W021, 2012]

Leveson develops the framework in Engineering a Safer World, her 2004 accident-model article and a related 2009 formulation. [UX-W021; UX-W020; SB-W017]

Reliable components can participate in unsafe interactions#

The book distinguishes component reliability from system safety. A component can perform its specified function while its interaction with others violates a system constraint. A specification can also be wrong for the surrounding physical situation. Searching only for a failed part can therefore miss the conditions that made an otherwise expected action hazardous. [UX-W021, chs. 1–3]

An event sequence records what happened but can leave out what should have happened, why a control was missing, or which organizational process failed to maintain an assumption. Leveson's proposed account starts with constraints on acceptable behavior and asks how they are established and preserved. Physical barriers, software requirements, operating procedures, management and regulation can each contribute. [UX-W021, chs. 2–4]

The selected chemical-reactor example in the earlier article makes the interaction concrete. Cooling must be available when catalyst flow begins. Software following a locally stated instruction can still be unsafe if the instruction omits the relation between those operations. Executing the code as written is different from satisfying the necessary system-level condition. The example is Leveson's reconstruction. [UX-W020, 7–15]

Safety is also relative to losses judged unacceptable and to the environment and use considered. Several constraints can conflict. A train door, for example, should ordinarily remain closed while moving yet permit evacuation under different conditions. A useful safety account has to state those conditions and competing obligations. The vocabulary of constraints does not make stakeholder judgment unnecessary. [UX-W021, chs. 1, 6–9]

Actual feedback differs from evidence that a command was issued#

The control account distinguishes goals, action capacity, information about the controlled process and the assumptions through which a controller interprets that information. A command can be delayed, fail to execute or achieve only part of its intended effect. Information that power was applied to a valve is not proof that the valve reached its required position. The feedback must concern what the relevant constraint actually requires. [UX-W020, 13–16; UX-W021, ch. 4]

Direct physical coupling can supply information that a remote interface must reconstruct. Vibration, sound, temperature and the behavior of a mechanically connected gauge can reveal both the process and whether the display remains connected to it. Moving control to a remote electronic interface can improve capability while removing those incidental cues. Designers then have to decide what to represent and how the operator will obtain it under abnormal as well as routine conditions. [UX-W020, 14–15]

Delays occur in actuators, process response, measurement and communication. A controller's interpretation can be internally consistent but late or wrong about the actual state. The book's process-model analysis asks what each participant believes or assumes and how feedback changes that account. [UX-W021, chs. 4–5]

Leveson invokes Conant and Ashby to state a general requirement for controllers to contain a process model. The practical method can make hidden assumptions visible, but the universal inference needs the qualifications attached to the original result: its optimal-response premises do not establish that every successful passive constraint contains a rich internal representation. An observer's model of a controller is also different from a stored representation inside it. The original arguments are treated separately in the Ashby section. [UX-W020, 15–16; UX-W021, ch. 4]

Responsibilities can fall into gaps or overlap unsafely#

The development and operating control structures relate organizations as well as physical devices. Assumptions, requirements, reports, maintenance findings and changes must cross their interfaces. A nominal chart can omit who actually supplies or receives relevant information. Conversely, two controllers can each assume that the other has responsibility, or act incompatibly on the same process. [UX-W021, chs. 4–5; UX-W020, 17–25]

Overlap is therefore not always a remedy. The book's boundary-responsibility examples ask which controller handles the case at the edge of two domains and how their actions are coordinated. Removing an overlap can also leave a gap. The issue is the actual relation among responsibilities, knowledge, timing and action, rather than maximum integration or maximum separation in the abstract. [UX-W021, chs. 4, 8]

Asynchronous evolution names a further difficulty: one part changes while related parts retain assumptions about its earlier behavior. Software, equipment, procedures, training, contracts and regulation can change on different schedules. A previously acceptable arrangement can consequently become unsafe without one dramatic component breakdown. Maintenance of the relationships is part of safety work. [UX-W021, chs. 4, 12; UX-W020]

The friendly-fire chapter illustrates differences in local information, schedules, service expectations, liaison and interpretation. It reconstructs testimony and reports, preserving disagreements among sources. An unexplained identification-system failure prevents describing the whole event categorically as an accident without any component failure. The example's relevant contribution is how different local actions and understandings fit into a wider control structure. [UX-W021, ch. 5]

STPA begins with losses, hazards and a control structure#

Systems-Theoretic Process Analysis, STPA, first identifies the losses and hazards to be considered, relevant constraints and the control structure. Its four unsafe-control-action categories concern an action not supplied when needed, an action supplied unsafely, wrong timing or order, and an action stopped too soon or sustained too long. Timing and absence can therefore be analyzed alongside the occurrence of an explicit wrong action. [UX-W021, chs. 6–8]

The next task develops causal scenarios. Analysts examine controller assumptions, feedback, actuators, the controlled process, communications and environmental conditions that can lead to an unsafe action or prevent a necessary one from taking effect. The objective is to make design requirements and potential failures of their enforcement visible before relying on operation to reveal them. [UX-W021, ch. 8]

The analysis can begin early, with a coarse design, and be refined as decisions add detail. A new feature can remove one hazard while creating another. The model is revised with the design, rather than treated

as a document made once after the architecture has already been fixed. This gives analysis an active role in generating and comparing alternatives. [UX-W021, chs. 7–9]

Completeness remains bounded. Examining every listed control action does not prove that the list, the chosen boundary or the causal scenarios contain everything relevant in the real system. Some losses and interactions can have been omitted from the initial model. The book's comparisons with other analyses are author reports. [UX-W021, chs. 6–8]

A physical constraint can change the necessary response chain#

The high-energy door example starts with a requirement that opening the door must not expose a person to power. A design can detect door opening and command a separate interruption, requiring sensors, logic, action and timing. Alternatively, the physical circuit can pass through the door so opening it breaks that circuit. In the modeled example, the arrangement directly removes the identified exposure condition. Its physical integrity and other hazards still need consideration. [UX-W021, 224–225]

Adding an indicator offers another alternative: the operator can see whether power is present. That adds information but also a component that can fail and a display whose safe interpretation must be designed. The book explicitly says that each solution can introduce drawbacks and that the rationale for the choice should be recorded for later certification, reuse and maintenance. [UX-W021, 224–225]

The important distinction is between changing the set of possible physical interactions and asking a participant to detect and correct the same dangerous interaction. Either may be appropriate under particular obligations. Leveson's design process keeps the alternatives and their support requirements available for comparison, rather than identifying safety with a larger number of active checks. [UX-W021, chs. 8–9]

The robot example: a solution changes the problem#

The mobile robot's manipulator can destabilize its base. A sufficiently heavy base is a candidate physical solution, but added mass can worsen collision damage or impede manual movement in an emergency. A wider base can improve stability while preventing movement through doors and crowded spaces. These competing requirements constrain an apparently simple solution. [UX-W021, 257]

Deployable stabilizer legs offer another option. They must be extended before arm movement and retracted for travel. The change introduces additional hazards, synchronization requirements and feedback. An assurance that a motor was energized cannot replace evidence that the legs reached the required position; an obstruction could prevent full deployment. [UX-W021, 258–262]

The analysis can then change the decomposition. Combining the arm and leg controllers can reduce the communications needed to keep their assumptions consistent. This is an explicit example in which integration is considered to manage a strong coupling. [UX-W021, 261–262, figs. 9.3–9.5]

The example begins with a hazard, examines physical alternatives and environmental constraints, analyzes hazards introduced by a candidate solution, and revises the control architecture. Design and safety analysis inform one another through this sequence. [UX-W021, ch. 9]

Automation changes cognitive and contingency demands#

Automation can remove routine actions while leaving harder supervision, diagnosis and recovery tasks. Operators need opportunities to learn, practice and understand unusual conditions. An arrangement that performs ordinary work smoothly can still make an abnormal event difficult to recognize or handle.

Leveson therefore treats training, skill retention and useful feedback as design obligations, rather than assuming fewer routine interventions settle the comparison. [UX-W021, ch. 9]

Display design supplies a more specific economy. If an operator needs to know whether a variable exceeds a limit, a dial with a reference can reduce the extra processing required to compare an absolute number with a remembered threshold. Patterned displays can support recognition, while sequentially requested screens can require remembering one portion while seeking another. The claimed benefit concerns the actual decision task. [UX-W021, 304–305]

The book also preserves a trade-off: an effortlessly interpreted display may do less to develop the knowledge and thinking needed in abnormal conditions. It advocates involving operators, understanding the reasons behind established conventions, and evaluating the display in the work it supports. The design aim is appropriate information use with retained capability, not merely minimum momentary mental effort. [UX-W021, 304–305]

Intent specifications preserve why as well as what#

The intent-specification approach arranges information along intent, part–whole and refinement relations. It makes the rationale for a requirement available together with the requirement and its realization. A decision that appears arbitrary to a later engineer can have depended on an environmental assumption or a rejected alternative. Losing the reason can make maintenance and change hazardous. [UX-W021, ch. 10]

Refinement is not presented as an irreversible waterfall. Later findings can change earlier assumptions and choices. A specification can provide links among purpose, behavior, architecture, implementation and operation so that a revision can be examined for consequences elsewhere. The organization of information supports review and reuse; it still requires people who understand the domain and can judge the implications. [UX-W021, ch. 10]

Black-box behavioral specifications can serve as an interface between an integrator and contractors. The boundary hides selected implementation details while making required behavior and assumptions explicit. Reusing a component does not establish that its environmental assumptions remain satisfied in a new system. Those assumptions need ownership and revalidation; more documentation without such relationships is insufficient. [UX-W021, ch. 10]

The chapter's architecture-screening example uses severity and mitigatibility as comparative design information. Its ordinal scales are not calibrated probabilities or a complete quantitative risk model. Similarly, a promising operational alternative can shift demands to landing precision, infrastructure, communications or other supporting capabilities. Specifying an interface does not eliminate those external conditions. [UX-W021, ch. 10]

CAST reconstructs a wider control failure#

Causal Analysis based on Systems Theory, CAST, reconstructs events and then examines the control structure, constraints, context and decisions around them. It seeks explanations beyond a final error label. Information available somewhere in an organization may not have been observable to the relevant participant through the actual task and interface. An account must follow those relations rather than equate existence of data with usable knowledge. [UX-W021, ch. 11]

Citichem is a fictional teaching scenario. The chemical-overflow and Überlingen accounts are reconstructions from reports. Their practical value lies in making responsibilities and missing controls available for examination. Recommendation selection, priority and implementation remain judgment-laden. [UX-W021, ch. 11]

In the earlier 2004 article, Leveson reports completeness and analysis-effort advantages from informal evaluations and accident analyses. These evaluations compare the analyses rather than measuring a controlled resource intervention. [UX-W020, 26–28]

Designed constraints must survive operation and change#

Operational safety work includes review of planned change, detection of unplanned migration, audits, incident and problem reports, and feedback about the result. A constraint can be correctly designed and subsequently defeated by altered procedures, incentives, equipment or resources. The book asks who will notice and respond when an assumption no longer holds. [UX-W021, ch. 12]

The reporting example changes a small part of the work system. Instead of requiring a separate cumbersome report, a worker contacting those who can fix a problem can copy the safety function into an existing email. This can reduce the act of reporting. Acknowledgment, analysis, action and communication back to the reporter remain necessary; the extra copy is not the resolution. [UX-W021, 405]

Reporting incentives affect the data obtained. Fear of punishment, lack of confidence that anything will happen, confidentiality and time requirements can suppress reports. More reports can therefore indicate a changed reporting environment rather than a higher underlying hazard rate. The book also distinguishes a just culture from blanket immunity for gross negligence or deliberate disregard. The organizational purpose is useful learning and accountability in context. [UX-W021, chs. 12–13]

Generic indicators are not assumed to reveal every system's safety condition. Leading indicators should relate to the actual constraints and processes being maintained. Data collection has to be connected with interpretation and response. Training also needs to preserve reasons and assumptions, rather than only the memorized steps of a procedure. [UX-W021, ch. 12]

Authority, resources and insight require actual bearers#

Safety responsibilities must be matched with authority, resources and feedback. They occur at several levels and can differ by level. Leveson describes working groups as a means of preserving communication while maintaining review independence. Oversight can fail by becoming too entangled with the project or by withdrawing so far that it loses relevant understanding. [UX-W021, ch. 13, especially 435]

The book's warning about a transition from oversight to insight is concrete. A management-by-objectives label can conceal a reduction in personnel and budgets without anyone assuming critical tasks. Local interpretation of objectives needs competence and an actual process for satisfying the constraint. [UX-W021, 435]

Leveson argues for redesigns that improve safety and cost together, rather than treating their conflict as inevitable. Her account also addresses conflicting objectives, limited resources and negotiation. The related 2009 article seeks to reduce avoidable trade-offs. [UX-W021, chs. 8–13; SB-W017]

SUBSAFE illustrates a bounded, maintained institution#

The SUBSAFE account concerns watertight integrity and recovery from flooding. Other hazards, including fire, weapons and reactor safety, have other arrangements. Its assurance system includes material and fabrication evidence, design reviews, tests, calibration, maintenance, audits, training and reentry into controlled work processes. It is an extensive institutional architecture. [UX-W021, ch. 14]

The historical record reported for certified submarines is bounded by that purpose. The book's San Francisco collision account includes death and injuries even though the hull and recovery features performed. [UX-W021, ch. 14]

The example is informative because the design and operation are connected. An assurance claim depends on knowing materials, changes and test conditions and on continuing to enforce them. Certification is not a one-time substitute for maintenance or knowledge. The related 2009 source also identifies unusually favorable institutional resources, limiting simple transfer to a different setting. [UX-W021, ch. 14; SB-W017]

Interfaces can lose end-to-end ownership#

The satellite appendix traces a flight-constant entry through several organizations, formats and tests. A test can use a default rather than the actual flight data while participants assume the relevant assurance has occurred elsewhere. Many reviews do not compensate automatically for an unowned end-to-end process. [UX-W021, appendix B, 469–493]

Mergers, restructuring and staff departures also remove knowledge of why a process was designed as it was. The appendix describes lost history and rationale, no clearly identified process owner and misunderstandings about the coverage of testing. A filter was retained for consistency after a relevant need had changed. Some higher-level explanations remain speculative because the reports lacked data. [UX-W021, appendix B, especially 491–493]

The Walkerton appendix follows physical contamination controls together with monitoring, laboratory feedback, training and institutional change. The book explicitly distinguishes privatization itself from implementing a change without preserving notification and oversight. [UX-W021, appendix C, especially 514]

The system-dynamics appendix supplies another kind of account: qualitative reinforcing and balancing loops with delays. These diagrams identify hypotheses about migration and pressure. Signs alone do not establish exponential growth, equilibrium or instability without rate functions, parameters and conditions. [UX-W021, appendix D]

Related frameworks and a separate 2009 formulation#

La Porte's reconstruction of Perrow explains why interactive complexity and tight coupling can create conflicting demands for centralization and decentralization. A choice about authority depends on both dimensions. [UX-W004, through La Porte, printed 136]

Rosa’s 2005 symposium introduction compares normal-accident and high-reliability frameworks and calls for evidence from cases with and without accidents. Considering both challenges explanations built only from the selection of disasters. [UX-W016, abstract]

Leveson, Dulac, Marais and Carroll's 2009 article argues for examining concrete couplings and hazards rather than treating an industry label as sufficient explanation. Local decisions can be appropriate where coupling is reduced or where participants possess relevant knowledge and prepared responses. The account retains stakeholder judgment and goals in conflict. It is a related formulation by the same author group, with overlapping examples. [SB-W017]

SOHO: differences between analysts’ reconstructions#

Johnson and Holloway's 2003 SOHO analysis uses the same official report for two analysts. They identify useful systemic emphases but differ in model granularity and detailed classification. The comparison asks how analysts choose an appropriate representation, handle time and connect findings to recommendations. A framework does not mechanically determine all those judgments. [SB-W014]

They also acknowledge Leveson's response that constraints were underemphasized in their application. The criticism is therefore part of a methodological exchange, not a verdict based on an uncontested application. Their early concern about practical guidance should not be projected unchanged onto the later detailed 2012 book, which addresses temporal processes, actual versus nominal structures and operational change. [SB-W014; UX-W021]

A controlled method comparison reports a trade-off#

Abdulkhaleq and Wagner's 2015 study compared STPA, failure-mode-and-effects analysis and fault-tree analysis. Twenty-one students worked in three groups on three systems, with methods rotated. The results concern the requirements found and the effort of these participants, not observed future accidents. [SB-W015]

Reported mean recall was 0.443 for STPA, 0.326 for FMEA and 0.231 for FTA. Mean recorded time was 116, 94 and 88 minutes respectively. The method finding more requirements also required more time in this setting. [SB-W015, results and table 6]

The recall denominator was the union of reported requirements, not an independently known complete gold standard. Coverage also used a taxonomy partly drawn from Leveson. Group-level reports, novice participants, small sample and task ordering limit generalization. The paper's coverage table and prose disagree, as do its abstract and body about one applicability comparison. These inconsistencies make the corresponding coverage and applicability comparisons ambiguous. [SB-W015]

An application supplies conditional simulation evidence#

Liu and colleagues' 2020 differential-braking article models seven unsafe control actions and simulates selected scenarios using a cited aircraft model. It demonstrates how the approach is applied to specified control timing and state assumptions. It retains power, speed and torque sensing, position information, human response and the model's conditions. [SB-W016]

Its five-second threshold belongs to the stated dimensions, initial conditions and disturbances. It is not an operational rule or flight-validated universal limit. [SB-W016]

Information and coordinated pathways in selected practice sources#

The National Commission on Forensic Science's 2015 policy-development abstract asks which information belongs in a forensic assessment. A fact can support a conclusion about a suspect while being irrelevant to the inferential connection between an examined pattern and the requested scientific opinion. The proposed context management therefore concerns the arrangement and timing of information access, not simply less information in every task. Deciding relevance itself requires expertise. [GL-W063]

The document is an abstract of a developing proposal, not a final demonstrated intervention. Its reference to cognitive and contextual bias identifies the problem and intended principle. [GL-W063]

Rotter and colleagues' 2025 clinical-pathways review, reports fifty-eight studies and searches through July 2024. Stand-alone multidisciplinary pathways probably reduce in-hospital complications and length of stay, with moderate certainty; mortality, readmission and cost conclusions remain uncertain. Multifaceted implementations have less conclusive results. [GL-W058]

These findings are outcome-specific. A shorter stay does not establish every patient benefit or identify one coordination mechanism as the cause. [GL-W058]

The selected NHS England guidance, updated 23 July 2026, describes longer care packages joining prevention, personalized goals, team competence and continuing review, with funding arrangements intended to support them. The worked follow-up example illustrates planned work over time rather than episodic repair alone. It is an implementation design under a specific institutional arrangement, not comparative outcome evidence. [GL-W064, §§1.1–1.6 and worked example]

The forensic proposal addresses bias in evaluating evidence; the clinical-pathways review compares patient and hospital outcomes; the dental guidance organizes prevention and follow-up. They describe different activities within the conduct and assessment of care.

S30 Reliability, fault tolerance, and what fault experiments establish#

Reliability under disruption#

A system can contain unreliable components and still provide a useful service. Explaining how requires more than counting spare components or naming a recovery mechanism. The relevant literature specifies relationships among components, assumptions about failures, the service to be preserved, and ways of checking what happens under disruption.

Fault injection is especially informative because it intervenes in a system rather than waiting for a naturally occurring failure. It can reveal a weakness, exercise a recovery path, or test a bounded proposition about a model. The meaning of its result depends on what was changed, when the change occurred, the workload that exercised it, the observations collected, and the criterion of success. These dependencies are explicit in the sources considered below.

Von Neumann: reliability through an arrangement of fallible elements#

The reconstruction of John von Neumann's lectures develops the possibility of reliable computation using unreliable elements. A majority arrangement is a concrete part of the discussion. Its inputs are intended to represent the same state, while their errors are assumed independent in the relevant calculation. Agreement among several representations can then help preserve a correct result when an individual representation is wrong. The majority element can itself fail, so its error must also enter the account; counting additional representations alone does not settle the output's reliability. The source later explicitly calls a constant error probability independent of time and previous inputs unrealistic. Actual failure probabilities can vary with input, history, environment, and element. [W043, §§7–8, especially reconstructed pp. 23–24; §11.3]

Stott and colleagues: a modeled improvement can come from counting assumptions#

James Stott and colleagues examine a problem in transferring common-cause failure models and generic data from nuclear applications to aerospace. Redundant components can be affected together; their failures therefore cannot always be treated as independent events. The paper's selected methodological discussion goes further than this familiar warning. It asks what the recorded failures and testing arrangements actually allow an analyst to estimate. A test interval, an individual test episode, and a demand on the system are not automatically the same observational unit. The number of opportunities to detect failures changes how observed counts relate to the quantities in a model. [W065, §§3–5]

Their comparison distinguishes testing all members of a group in one episode from testing them in separate, staggered episodes. In the latter scheme, finding a failed component can lead to additional tests of the others. Those procedures affect the challenges and observations represented by the data. Using factors estimated under one interpretation with a model that assumes another can therefore alter the calculated risk without establishing a corresponding alteration in the physical system. The authors specifically criticize using mixed interpretations of generic data within one risk assessment or trade study. An alternative can receive a lower calculated risk because of the assumption assigned to it, then appear to earn that advantage as an analytical result. [W065, §§3–5]

The paper does not conclude that the actual testing schedule can never affect common-cause risk. It gives a possible real mechanism: separating test episodes may separate operators and thereby reduce some shared influences. Its point is that this causal difference is not captured merely by switching the parametric counting convention. Quantifying that benefit requires analysis of the relevant causes and coupling factors. The authors' recommendations concern the NASA modeling problem they address in

2010. The substantive lesson supplied by this source is how an apparent advantage of an arrangement can arise from the interpretation of evidence rather than an established change in the arrangement's failure behavior. [W065, §§5–6]

Hsueh, Tsai, and Iyer: the experiment includes a workload and an observer#

Mei-Chen Hsueh, Timothy Tsai, and Ravishankar Iyer's 1997 survey explains fault injection as an experimental approach to dependability evaluation. Its relevance extends beyond the act of introducing a fault. Their account distinguishes simulation during conception and design, injection into a prototype or operational system, and measurement of naturally occurring behavior in operation. Each supplies different evidence. A simulation can explore a design before implementation but embodies simplified assumptions. A physical or software intervention exercises an implemented system but represents the faults that the experimenter can emulate. Operational measurement observes real events and workloads but can require long collection periods and face changing field conditions. [AFC-W003, pp. 75–76]

The survey's experimental architecture makes these differences concrete. A target system runs a workload drawn from a workload generator and library. A fault injector applies changes selected from a fault library, including choices of type, location, and time. A controller organizes the experiment; monitoring and data collection record behavior; analysis interprets the observations. These are distinct functions even when some share a machine or program. The result is thus produced by a target-plus-experiment arrangement. The injector alone does not determine whether the relevant behavior was exercised or whether its consequences were observed. [AFC-W003, p. 76, fig. 1]

An introduced fault can produce an internal error without causing failure of the service being judged. The workload may not exercise a changed location. An internal error may be detected, contained, or masked before it affects the chosen result. Conversely, an incorrect result may escape a detector. The survey describes a Messaline device that senses whether an injected fault is activated and produces an error, and Ferrari experiments in which detection depended on fault type and on how frequently the affected routines were exercised. These details explain why the mere number of injections is an inadequate account of the experiment's outcome. [AFC-W003, pp. 77–80]

Selecting an injection technique also selects what can be reached and how the experiment may interfere with the system. Pin-level hardware methods can control particular physical intervention points and offer high time resolution, but do not literally reproduce every fault inside a chip. Contactless physical methods can reach internal behavior while providing less precise control over the exact time and location. Software methods offer access to applications and operating-system state without requiring the same specialized hardware, yet cannot reach every hardware location. Their added execution and instrumentation can disturb the workload or change the software structure. These are substantive differences in the relationship between intervention and object. [AFC-W003, pp. 76–79]

Timing matters to the observation as well as the intervention. A method with inadequate time resolution may miss rapid propagation even if it is adequate for a longer-lived memory error. The survey discusses combining software injection with hardware monitoring to address such cases, while retaining the extra cost and constraints of the monitoring equipment. Compile-time modification and runtime triggering likewise provide different control: placing a change in a program image differs from invoking an injector when a timer expires, a specified instruction is reached, or an exception occurs. The useful technique depends on the fault behavior and question being investigated. [AFC-W003, pp. 79–80]

The reported tool comparisons show why reach is consequential. In the cited MARS experiments, pin-level injection, heavy-ion radiation, and electromagnetic interference exercised different error-detection mechanisms. The methods were complementary in the surveyed results. Evidence about one chosen family of interventions cannot automatically establish coverage of error behavior that the family does not

produce. The survey also reports undetected incorrect outcomes in selected Xception tests; that observation remains attached to the tested processor units and setup rather than becoming a general percentage for all computers. [AFC-W003, pp. 78, 81]

Finally, the survey expressly distinguishes fault-injection findings from operational measures such as mean time between failures and availability. Choosing and injecting faults does not determine how often those faults occur in service. A collection of tests can investigate behavior conditional on specified interventions without providing the occurrence rates and representative exposure needed for an operational frequency estimate. A high pass rate across chosen injections therefore cannot simply be relabeled high field availability. The distinction is relevant even when the injections and observations are perfectly executed. [AFC-W003, pp. 75–76]

Alvaro, Rosen, and Hellerstein: choosing faults from an outcome's dependencies#

Peter Alvaro, Joshua Rosen, and Joseph Hellerstein address a difficulty that arises when a service can fail through combinations of disruptions. Selecting individual faults at random may quickly reveal shallow bugs while rarely reaching a particular sequence of message losses and crashes. Their lineage-driven fault injection, or LDFI, reasons backward from a successful outcome. It asks which events and messages supported that outcome and what combinations of allowed faults could remove all of the known support. This is a method for choosing informative candidate experiments. [AFC-W010, §§1–2]

The paper's historical Kafka replication example shows why a combination matters. In the described beta-version protocol, a leader becomes separated from other replicas. Those replicas are removed from the in-sync set; the remaining leader acknowledges a write without disseminating it, then crashes. The acknowledged write is lost. A nominal count of replicas does not describe the sequence that defeats the stated stable-write requirement. [AFC-W010, §1.1]

LDFI starts from the computational lineage of a good outcome: the sequence and dependencies through which it was obtained. Its MOLLY prototype turns information about uncertain communications into a logical problem for a satisfiability solver. A solution identifies a candidate combination of failures that could defeat the currently known derivations of the outcome. The system then performs a concrete execution with that candidate. This forward step is essential. A program may have a recovery path or alternative derivation that was absent from the earlier successful execution, so removing its known support need not actually make it fail. [AFC-W010, §1.2; appendix B]

The procedure alternates between those steps. A further successful execution can reveal additional support that the next candidate must defeat. An execution that violates the chosen assertion supplies a counterexample. When the specified search completes without such a counterexample, the authors give an assurance for the declared configuration and bounded model. Their soundness account depends on confirming candidate violations through execution rather than publishing every candidate generated by the solver as an actual bug. The completeness argument concerns coverage within its formal setting. [AFC-W010, §1.2; appendix B]

The bounds define the proposition being checked. The program, topology, inputs, and assertions are supplied. A logical end-of-time bound limits the execution length; an earlier end-of-finite-failures bound specifies when message loss ceases, leaving time for the program to respond; a separate bound limits permanent node crashes. The paper's example of six global transitions, message loss permitted during the first four, and at most one crash is an example of a particular failure specification. Byzantine behavior and crash recovery are outside the stated failure model. [AFC-W010, §2.1.1]

The abstraction of time has an additional effect. MOLLY evaluates the programs in a synchronous simulation with a deterministic ordering for successfully delivered messages. This focuses the analysis on faults and reduces the execution space, while potentially missing bugs that depend on asynchronous

ordering and timing. The paper explicitly says that this sacrifices completeness in the more general model. Similarly, the assurance relies on internal determinism: repeating the same faults must reproduce the relevant outcome lineage. Merely using the tool on an internally nondeterministic protocol does not confer the same completeness guarantee. [AFC-W010, §§2.1, 7]

Language and evidence requirements also remain. The method needs identifiable outputs, sufficiently fine-grained lineage, and control over the relevant communications. The prototype uses Dedalus programs to provide these facilities. Where a derivation depends on a fact's absence, the lineage analysis must account for why that fact did not occur. Appendix B describes different treatments of this issue, including an explicitly incomplete option that ignores such provenance. The assurance depends on these analysis conditions. [AFC-W010, §2.2; appendix B]

The evaluation is informative both for favorable cases and for a case that resists a blanket efficiency claim. In the reported Kafka model comparison, MOLLY found a counterexample in 38 concrete executions and 3.74 seconds; the random strategy averaged 1,183.12 executions and 133.30 seconds over 25 runs. For the three-phase-commit model, however, MOLLY took 55 executions and 9.60 seconds, while the random strategy averaged 40.60 executions and 6.24 seconds. These are source-reported measurements for the studied configurations. They show why fewer irrelevant candidate executions can be valuable, while also showing that the analysis is not uniformly faster for every example. [AFC-W010, §5, fig. 12]

The paper also distinguishes finding a counterexample from ruling out counterexamples within a bounded space. A random strategy may discover one quickly, yet an absence claim would require coverage it has not thereby provided. The reported examples of bug-free models compare MOLLY's executed tests with the much larger set of possible failure combinations under the chosen parameters. Their relevance is to the work required for that specified verification task. [AFC-W010, §5, figs. 11–13]

To see the boundary concretely, change the proposed application from the given inputs and message-loss/crash model to a new topology with recovery after a crash. The previously completed analysis no longer establishes the new proposition. The difference follows from the declared scope of the paper's model.

La Porte: efficiency and vulnerability in interdependent infrastructures#

Todd La Porte's selected chapter passage addresses large technical systems whose components and organizations are connected across locations. The examples include mutual dependence among electricity, telecommunications, transport, and water services. A disruption is not confined by the organizational ownership of the first affected component. He describes tight coupling as a source of efficiency in ordinary operation that can also increase vulnerability. Defensive management, stockpiling, and relationships with other organizations can then consume some of the efficiency the coupling was intended to provide. These are propositions in his organizational account of infrastructure protection. [UX-W005, pp. 135–137]

The same passage reports Charles Perrow's argument about conflicting demands for authority: tightly coupled operation can call for centralized coordination, while unexpected problems can require discretion among those closest to them. La Porte's surrounding discussion also makes the response depend on the character of disruption. Relatively predictable hazards support routinized preparation; purposive, changing threats can require other capabilities. Maintaining several modes of readiness creates organizational and budgetary demands that may be difficult to sustain after a conspicuous event has passed. [UX-W005, pp. 136–138]

An official practice account: resilience retains resources and responsibility#

The 2020 US interagency Sound Practices to Strengthen Operational Resilience supplies a further kind of source: an official practice formulation. The cyber-risk table describes governance, identification, protection, detection, response, recovery, and third-party risk management. It identifies data, personnel, devices, facilities, systems, and external providers as part of the dependencies of critical operations. Its account preserves a declared tolerance for disruption rather than promising uninterrupted performance in every respect. [SG-W029, selected body and table 1]

The table's detail is relevant because protection does not remove ongoing activity. It calls for training, maintenance, configuration management, monitoring, tested backups, exercised response and recovery processes, and independent oversight. Lessons from incidents are to inform later activities. Outsourcing likewise does not remove the firm's responsibility for risks associated with a critical operation: the formulation retains due diligence, contracts that allocate responsibilities, monitoring, and checks of a provider's ability to continue or restore service. These prescriptions describe organizational work that remains around the technical arrangements. [SG-W029, table 1]

Fault construction, observation and recovery#

The selected sources offer different answers to different questions: a conditional construction from fallible elements, an analysis of common-cause modeling, a survey of experimental apparatus, a lineage-guided search method, and organizational or official accounts of resilience.

S31 follows the subsequent work of analyzing a discovered weakness, changing an arrangement and retaining the change through chaos engineering and organizational learning.

S57 Preserving essential service under failure#

Insufficient capacity need not remove every useful function at once. The accounts here develop ways to retain an acceptable computation or service while relinquishing some work. Scheduling, application design, feedback control and incident response determine what survives. A further problem arises when the changed operation is difficult for its human supervisors to recognize.

S30 treats reliability and fault handling. The following sources concentrate on deliberately reduced service: how the reduction is prepared, selected and operated, and what its recipients lose.

Liu and colleagues: finish the mandatory computation#

Jane Liu and colleagues’ 1991 account of imprecise computation divides a time-critical task into mandatory and optional work. The mandatory part produces an acceptable result; optional execution improves its quality. A scheduler can stop the optional work when its time is exhausted and still return something useful. This requires a program designed to produce such a result. An arbitrary program interrupted before completion does not acquire that property merely because a deadline has arrived. [CG-W013, pp. 58–59]

The authors describe several ways to construct the task. In the milestone method, a computation records intermediate results with indicators of their error. Further execution improves the result, and the indicators let a recipient assess an early answer. A sieve method instead omits complete steps. Their radar example can omit an update to an estimate of background noise and reuse the earlier estimate. A third method provides two versions: a precise primary computation and a shorter, less accurate alternative. The alternatives make different forms of partial work useful. A half-executed sieve step or an unfinished alternate version may contribute nothing to the returned result. [CG-W013, p. 59]

Each construction has an implementation cost. Milestones require recording intermediate values. Sieve methods complicate scheduling when the optional steps must finish as units. Multiple versions need storage and a decision about which version can finish. The scheduler also needs bounds on mandatory execution. If all mandatory portions cannot fit within the available time, discarding optional portions cannot by itself make the task set feasible. The authors make mandatory feasibility a separate test before pursuing better quality. [CG-W013, pp. 59–61]

Their basic model includes ready times, deadlines, processing requirements, importance weights and precedence relations. Additional optional execution is assumed not to increase the result’s error. Several possible objectives remain: minimizing total error, limiting the greatest error, reducing the number of discarded optional tasks, or controlling delay. These choices produce different scheduling problems. Finishing by the deadline is consequently only one part of the specified service; the quality measure and the distribution of optional work also matter. [CG-W013, pp. 59–61]

The later queueing discussion distinguishes responsive service from a service commitment made on admission. A responsive scheme can reduce the service assigned to waiting tasks as congestion develops. It can clear an overload sooner, while changing what an already waiting task will receive. A guaranteed-service scheme decides on arrival which service a task will receive and preserves that decision. Tasks admitted before overload retain their promised full service, at the expense of slower clearance of the backlog. The authors develop these choices through queue models with specified arrival and service assumptions and identify further comparisons to be studied. [CG-W013, pp. 66–67]

Klein and colleagues: regulate optional application work#

Cristian Klein and colleagues’ 2014 Brownout system adjusts a cloud application’s demand by omitting optional response components. A parameter called the dimmer controls the probability that an optional component will execute. Individual requests sample that probability, while a feedback controller changes the parameter from measured response times. The application can thereby reduce the work required per request when its workload grows or its assigned processing capacity declines. [CG-W014, §§2–3]

The application must expose useful divisions of work. In their auction-site implementation, the researchers added a simple recommendation feature that could be omitted while the main response remained available. A script reads a small cached file containing the dimmer, decides whether to generate recommendations and reports response time to a local controller. The controller writes a replacement dimmer file and renames it atomically. This implementation makes the response path, measurement and actuation concrete: optionality is prepared in the code before the controller can use it. [CG-W014, §4]

Their bulletin-board implementation has two optional components, comments and recommendations. It first samples whether to include comments and then, if comments are included, samples again whether to add recommendations. With the same dimmer value for both independent trials, the probability of including comments is the dimmer value, while the probability of including both is its square. The researchers chose that dependency between features. It determines which combinations users can receive and how a controller setting changes the work performed. [CG-W014, §4]

The controller uses a simplified relationship between the dimmer and the maximum response time observed in a sampling window. It estimates changing gain online and applies feedback with protection against accumulated control action beyond the dimmer’s limits. Tuning changes the balance between fast response and sensitivity to noise or model error. If response time remains excessive with all optional work disabled, the requested operating point is infeasible: the controller has no further optional work to relinquish. [CG-W014, §3]

The experiments run an application stack inside a virtual machine on one physical machine, with the CPU as the bottleneck. Tests change processor resources, concurrent users, or both, and measure the time to receive a complete HTTP response. The controller reacts after observing the change, so transient violations remain. More conservative tuning recovers more slowly while reducing aggressive overshoot. The authors compare settings using a constructed revenue measure that awards one unit for a request and an additional half-unit for a recommendation. Their favorable comparisons concern that valuation and the tested workloads. The measurement was not customer sales. Extending the approach to applications distributed over several machines remained future work. [CG-W014, §§5, 7]

Meza and colleagues: maintain emergency feature controls#

Justin Meza and colleagues’ 2023 account of Defcon begins with an operational choice at Meta: reduce the work needed to provide a product by temporarily changing some of its features. Sending a message can remain available while an online-status indicator is omitted. A comment service can return comments while replacing model-based ranking with chronological order. Explicit switches, called knobs, select these changes in the affected control flow. The reductions alter what people receive while allowing the core request to proceed. [CG-W015, §§2.2–2.4, 3.2, pp. 609–612]

Product engineers identify candidate features and connect them to a shared configuration system. A testing framework measures resource savings and changes in user behavior. Operators use a portal showing those results and a command-line interface to activate groups of knobs. Knobs can span source files and binaries, identify an owner and belong to a degradation level. Keeping these definitions useful requires product teams to maintain them as their software changes. [CG-W015, §§3.1–3.3, pp. 611–612]

The actuation path is deliberately kept dependent on few other systems so that it remains usable during partial failures. Server changes can apply in seconds. Client changes can prevent requests from reaching servers, but configuration must first reach the devices. A push mechanism takes around thirty minutes across the client population. Periodic full configuration pulls require bandwidth and server resources; an emergency mechanism pulls selected configuration fields with manual intervention. The location of the switch therefore affects both the work saved and the time needed to obtain that saving. [CG-W015, §3.2, p. 611]

Ordinary operation is Level 4, with degradation knobs disabled. Levels 3, 2 and 1 were designed around target demand reductions of 5, 10 and 20 percent, with progressively greater product impact. These targets reflect Meta’s failure domains and expected disruptions. Responders inspect demand, tested savings and product effects, activate an appropriate level and continue monitoring. The reported October 2022 demand surge prompted successive activation of two levels, followed by withdrawal when the surge passed. This is a reported production response; the savings targets guide its preparation rather than guarantee a fixed reduction in every event. [CG-W015, §1, pp. 607–608; §3.5, pp. 613–614]

Savings cannot be inferred solely from the code that a knob skips. Tests trace changes into dependent services, including services without knobs of their own. Region-drain experiments also show that traffic relocation and cold caches change the comparison. Small controlled tests have a concurrent comparison group; larger exercises can instead use a modeled baseline built from forecast and backcast signals. Those estimates and the directly observed comparisons perform different evidential jobs in the account. [CG-W015, §§4.1–4.5, pp. 614–618]

Users bear some of the cost. One Level 1 product test reduced app usage time by 11 percent; combined tests increased reports of unexpected behavior. Alongside such outcomes, operators need current measurements, regression investigations, rehearsals and training. The paper describes continuing engineering and organizational work to keep the emergency option available. The existence of a switch is only the beginning of that preparation. [CG-W015, table 2, pp. 616–618; §5, pp. 619–620]

Sarter and Woods: recognize what the changed mode will do#

Nadine Sarter and David Woods’s 1995 article develops the human demands of supervising automation with many operating modes. A mode changes how a system responds to input. Transitions can follow an environmental event, a protection function or an earlier command without a new direct instruction. A supervisor needs to know which mode is active, which is armed for later activation and what conditions will cause a transition. A status indication may supply only part of that knowledge. [CG-W016, pp. 5–9]

Their account includes a part-task simulator study involving twenty airline pilots. The scenario introduced abnormal, time-critical events, including loss of the glide-slope signal during final approach. About half the pilots did not understand what that loss meant for the flight-management system; some had difficulty detecting the problem during the simulation. Only five knew when to expect the indication that go-around mode was available. The difficulty involved both recognizing a changed condition and anticipating which action would next become possible. [CG-W016, pp. 11–12]

The aborted-takeoff probe showed another distinction between knowledge and action. Sixty-five percent of participants were unaware that the autothrottle system controlled thrust in that situation. Only four of twenty managed the automation completely correctly, and one of those explained that he was following a procedure rather than understanding the active automation. Some pilots could describe relevant settings afterward without having used that knowledge during the event. The authors call attention to knowledge that remains inert when the situation requires it. [CG-W016, pp. 11–12]

Their proposed responses include feedback that makes present and future behavior more apparent and training that activates knowledge in context. An interaction history or an additional sensory channel

might help, but added information can also burden attention. Requiring consent before every change could keep people involved while making repeated checks automatic or interrupting other work. The article presents these as design directions requiring investigation. Its study explains a specific difficulty in operating changed automation; its proposals address the information and practice needed to use the remaining capability. [CG-W016, pp. 13–16]

S54 develops other accounts of control, reconfiguration and recovery. The present accounts concentrate on a selected reduction of service and on the knowledge required to operate when behavior changes.

S31 Chaos engineering and organizational learning#

Connecting experiments with changes in practice#

An experiment can identify an unexpected dependency without changing it. An organization can observe repeated failures without learning how to prevent them. The material selected in this section concerns the practices that connect intervention, observation, interpretation, and subsequent work.

The practitioner principles: make a claim about observable behavior#

The Principles of Chaos Engineering formulation defines a discipline of experimentation intended to build confidence in a system's ability to withstand turbulent production conditions. Its problem is not limited to a failed component. Interactions among functioning services can produce unexpected outcomes, while unusual events can expose weaknesses in fallback settings, retries, capacity, and dependencies. These are examples of the systemic uncertainty that the formulation proposes to investigate. [AFC-W004, definition and opening discussion]

The proposed experiment begins with a measurable output that indicates ordinary behavior, then states a hypothesis that this behavior will continue in a control and an experimental group. The experimental change represents an event such as a server crash or severed connection. Investigators try to disprove the hypothesis by looking for a difference in the measured behavior. The formulation's “steady state” therefore concerns a selected observational description over a period, rather than an internal state of each component. Throughput, error rates, and latency percentiles are among its suggested outputs. [AFC-W004, “Chaos in practice”; “Build a hypothesis around steady state behavior”]

The distinction between output and internal attribute is consequential. The experiment is directed toward whether the service continues to work under the chosen conditions. Merely confirming that a disturbance was introduced does not answer that question. Conversely, finding a weakness supplies a target for further improvement. In this formulation, discovery is followed by the opportunity to address the weakness; a disturbance by itself is not a repair. The underlying choice of measurable output remains part of what the experiment asks. [AFC-W004, “Chaos in practice”; advanced principles]

The advanced principles retain the surrounding engineering work. They recommend choosing realistic events by likely occurrence or potential impact, including non-failure changes such as traffic surges. They prefer production experiments because environment and traffic affect behavior. They also call for automation of orchestration and analysis, partly because repeated manual experiments consume labor. At the same time, they explicitly recognize possible short-term customer harm and assign responsibility for containing the experiment's effects. [AFC-W004, advanced principles]

Brier: connect stated probabilities with subsequent events#

Glenn Brier’s 1950 article begins with a practical objection to forecast verification: a scoring system can reward statements that serve the score better than the forecast’s users. A forecaster may learn to report something other than the probability they judge credible. Brier investigates a verification method for probability forecasts, asking how its incentives affect what the forecaster says. His categories must be mutually exclusive and exhaustive, with their assigned probabilities summing to one. The record therefore specifies both what outcomes count and how much confidence was assigned to them. [CG-W021, p. 1]

For each forecasting occasion, his score sums the squared differences between every category’s assigned probability and its observed indicator, one for the category that occurred and zero for the others. It then

averages those sums over the forecasting occasions. A perfect forecast scores zero; certainty in a category that does not occur scores two. His rain/no-rain example counts the errors for both categories. The article’s normalization consequently gives a range from zero to two. [CG-W021, pp. 1–2, equations 1–2]

The worked example links ten forecasts with the events that subsequently occurred. Their score is 0.19. A forecaster assigning the sample’s rain frequency, 0.3, on every occasion would score 0.42; using a climatological rain probability of 0.2 would score 0.44. The sample frequency is a benchmark calculated after observing the period, whereas a working forecaster must estimate such probabilities from available information. Brier uses the comparison to distinguish recognition of an average departure from climatology from discrimination among individual occasions. Both can contribute information. [CG-W021, p. 2, table 1 and equations 3–4]

Brier also groups a larger series of eighty-five forecasts by issued rain probability and compares those groups with observed rain frequencies. The relationship shows where the forecaster’s confidence needs adjustment. He says that this relationship alone does not establish usefulness: how often different probabilities are issued also matters. His closing account reports several months of experimental six-hour precipitation forecasts at the Weather Bureau. Some initial criticism concerned misunderstanding the method or disappointment at how little confidence the forecasts justified; he also leaves substantive questions about the scoring method for further investigation. [CG-W021, pp. 2–3, table 2 and conclusion]

Nosek and colleagues: preserve the plan and make changes inspectable#

Brian Nosek and colleagues’ 2018 account concerns the relationship between research questions, analysis choices and observed results. They distinguish predictions tested by observations from explanations generated after seeing them. Both activities contribute to inquiry. The difficulty arises when an explanation discovered in the data is presented as though the same data had tested an advance prediction. Their account joins reasoning biases with research incentives and the many decisions available when analyzing a dataset. [CG-W023, “Mental Constraints on Distinguishing Predictions and Postdictions”; “Standard Tools of Statistical Inference Assume Prediction”]

Their proposed preregistration mechanism deposits the questions, design and analysis plan in an independent registry before outcomes are observed. The registry preserves the record and makes it discoverable, sometimes after an embargo. A later report can then be compared with the plan, distinguishing planned tests, amendments and newly generated questions. The authors describe the case for preregistration as theoretically strong and supported by some correlational evidence, while explicitly saying that sufficient experimental evidence establishing superiority for reproducibility was not yet available. [CG-W023, “Preregistration Distinguishes Prediction and Postdiction”]

The practical examples retain the work required when research departs from its plan. A study may recruit fewer participants than intended or reveal violated statistical assumptions. Researchers can report amendments, their reasons and what outcomes had already been seen. Other possibilities include staged registration, blinded datasets, decision trees and standing procedures. These methods have conditions: an earlier stage may reveal the outcome intended for a later test, and a decision tree can formalize a biased stopping rule. Recording that rule makes it inspectable without improving its statistical properties. [CG-W023, challenges 1–2]

For existing datasets, the relevant separation concerns information access. Data may already exist while remaining unseen by the analyst. Conversely, earlier summaries or knowledge of correlated variables can influence a nominally new analysis. The authors therefore ask who has seen what and what has been communicated. They also describe splitting a dataset: exploration develops a prediction using one part, and registration precedes testing on a sealed part. Fast experimental workflows can use a related

sequence, treating initial experiments as exploration and then repeating a selected experiment with its design and analysis recorded in advance. [CG-W023, challenges 3–5 and 7]

The record must also extend beyond the successful attempt. In their example of a research program producing one positive result in twenty tries, registering every attempt does not prevent misleading selection if only the positive result is reported. Preserved, accessible registrations and outcomes permit examination of that wider history.
