諏訪晴彦, 森田大輔 and 三道弘明 distinguish the total amount of slack from its distribution. Their 2009 model begins with a resource-feasible baseline schedule, with fixed estimated processing times and constant resource availability. It then inserts dummy activities whose durations represent protective time. The sum of these durations is the chosen allowance K; allocating that sum is a further decision. [MG-W003]

The construction places a dummy before the first critical activity and after critical activities, including a terminal dummy. Critical work and affected successors are shifted to the right to accommodate these insertions. Later critical start times incorporate preceding dummy durations; ordinary activities start as early as their technological and resource predecessors permit in the changed schedule. Distinguishing the terminal dummy also separates the last real job's completion from the project's buffered due date. [MG-W003]

The objective concerns displacement from announced start times. Starting earlier can create inventory or other preparation costs; starting later can extend employment or disturb subcontracting arrangements. The model assigns early and late deviations their own weights. Buffer placement is judged through expected weighted displacement costs, so two schedules with the same K can have different consequences. The authors consider allocation rules based on position and successor relationships as well as uniform allocation. [MG-W003]

This formulation makes a concrete choice visible: how much protection to provide and where to provide it are separate scheduling decisions. A buffer's position changes which jobs move and which relationships absorb variation. The operating signals in Sood's account and the displacement-cost model address different parts of managing protective time. Work dependencies and coordination mechanisms receive broader treatment in S14.

S86 Forecasts, commitments and governing uncertain projects#

Authorizing a project involves more than estimating its tasks. Forecasts shape the commitment, people have reasons to present particular forecasts, and governing bodies decide whether the work still serves its purpose. Exploratory projects add another difficulty: the investigation can change what the project is supposed to accomplish.

Forecasting from completed projects#

Flyvbjerg's reference-class forecasting turns attention from the internal story of a proposed project to outcomes of comparable completed projects. The procedure identifies a reference class, establishes the distribution of its outcomes and locates the proposed project in relation to that distribution. The comparison must be appropriate to the kind of project and to the decision stage: an early estimate and an estimate made after detailed design answer different forecasting questions. [MG-W004]

The outcome distribution permits a decision about tolerated overrun probability. A budget based near the middle of a distribution accepts a different chance of overrun from one based at a higher percentile. Flyvbjerg illustrates the connection with a £100 million road estimate and a 32% uplift, producing £132 million. The uplift belongs to a specified reference class and risk tolerance, rather than being a general contingency percentage to attach to every undertaking. [MG-W004]

His Edinburgh Tram Line 2 account concerns an independent review before construction. It shows how an outside-view assessment can enter an authorization process. Its historical role is the review of an estimate at that stage, not a retrospective demonstration of the line's eventual cost. Independence matters because the people assembling a project's internal case may also be committed to getting it approved. [MG-W004]

Flyvbjerg distinguishes optimism bias from strategic misrepresentation. Better information can correct a sincere but unrealistic estimate; it has a different relationship to a forecast deliberately made attractive to secure approval. His proposals therefore concern incentives, scrutiny and accountability as well as the statistical procedure. The distinction explains why installing a forecasting technique and making an institution want an accurate forecast are separate interventions. [MG-W004]

The Heilmeier Catechism in research funding#

George H. Heilmeier recalled that he read and commented on each DARPA order before deciding whether to sign it. The director’s signature was the last step before funding. He described how staff critiqued one another’s proposals and agreed to use a common set of questions. Asked how many projects survived that scrutiny, Heilmeier said the more telling question was how many had changed during the discussions. [HCT-W001, pp. 180–181]

DARPA describes using the “catechism” to assess proposed research programs. It publishes the following eight questions. [HCT-W002]

1. What are you trying to do? Articulate your objectives using absolutely no jargon.

2. How is it done today, and what are the limits of current practice?

3. What is new in your approach and why do you think it will be successful?

4. Who cares? If you are successful, what difference will it make?

5. What are the risks?

6. How much will it cost?

7. How long will it take?

8. What are the mid-term and final “exams” to check for success?

Governing the undertaking beyond its initial approval#

Too and Weaver place project management within a governance framework linking project outputs to organizational strategy. The governing board supplies direction and remains accountable for governing the organization. Project managers exercise delegated authority to carry out work. Delegating a task does not make the governing responsibility disappear, while retaining accountability does not require the board to manage each operational decision. [MG-W005]

Their framework connects four elements: portfolio management, sponsorship, a project management office and project/program support. Portfolio management selects undertakings that support strategy and reconsiders those that cease to do so. Sponsorship maintains the connection between an undertaking and the organization that expects its benefits. The other elements supply oversight information and support for delivery. The authors present this as a conceptual construction drawn from management and governance literature. [MG-W005]

Continuing review changes the meaning of authorization. A project approved under one strategy or expectation need not retain its place indefinitely. Governing information must make it possible to consider the undertaking's continuing contribution, rather than merely whether its original schedule is being followed. Too and Weaver's account thus treats delivering the specified output and selecting the right continuing commitments as connected but different responsibilities. [MG-W005]

Organizing exploration before the project is fully specified#

Lenfle examines innovation projects for which a customer, goal or decomposition of work is not yet settled. The uncertainty extends beyond the time needed to carry out known activities. Investigation can alter the potential uses, technical questions and criteria by which an opportunity should be judged. A detailed development plan presupposes answers that this kind of project is trying to obtain. [MG-W006]

He gives the undertaking a provisional research program. It organizes related technical and use questions without pretending that the final product is already known. Tests supply occasions for learning and coordination: a deadline can require a team to produce knowledge rather than a completed feature. Exploring uses and technical possibilities together also avoids a sequence in which a technical answer arrives after the question about its value has changed. [MG-W006]

Legitimacy and evaluation are part of the construction. Without a recognized undertaking and criteria appropriate to exploration, investigations can appear to be disconnected studies competing for resources. The program gives them a common provisional purpose while allowing that purpose to be revised. The Usinor history developed in S62 supplies a related account of exploratory learning. Here Lenfle's contribution is the problem of organizing and evaluating such work when the usual specification-led project representation is premature. [MG-W006]

S98 Goal-setting: choosing aims, directing effort and revising commitments#

A goal can specify what an engineer is trying to construct, what an athlete attends to during performance, or what a manager rewards. It can also express an aim that someone accepts, revises or relinquishes. These uses bring different problems into view: constructing an adequate target, sustaining effort, learning how to act, recognizing a useful opportunity, and deciding whether pursuit should continue. Historical accounts of goal-setting address each of these problems through different models, procedures and kinds of evidence.

Constructing and adopting aims#

桑原哲郎 and 岸野哲's 1977 account begins before the target is fixed. An engineering problem does not always arrive with a satisfactory objective function awaiting optimization. The target itself must be constructed through inquiry into the system and its environment. They present this inquiry as a way of discovering causal regularities rather than restricting the goal to improvements under conditions already fixed. Their proposed reasoning follows effects from the system into its surroundings and the responses that return to it. Understanding those relations can change what it would be purposeful to accomplish. In this account, abstraction is part of discovering the target, rather than merely simplifying a target already supplied. [GS-W02]

The authors distinguish a creative phase and three execution phases. The creative phase abstracts the object, considers its wider relations and makes a judgment about purpose. The first execution phase introduces concrete conditions and asks whether the proposed account is effective; inadequacy can require returning to abstraction. The second works toward consistency between system and environment, including conditions left unexplained earlier. The third introduces economic and feasibility conditions and establishes the functions to be realized and the constraints under which conventional engineering design can proceed. Their table and diagrams distinguish phases by the determinacy of the target and the kind of judgment being made. The result is a proposed architecture for reasoning about an engineering objective, with revision built into its construction. [GS-W02]

Sheldon and Elliot's 1999 self-concordance model asks why people pursue the personal goals they have adopted. A person may act because the activity is enjoyable, because its importance is personally accepted, because failure would provoke guilt or self-reproach, or because other people demand it. Personally accepting an unpleasant but valued task differs from enjoying it, and both differ from acting under pressure. Self-concordance concerns these reasons for pursuit. It is therefore possible to specify the same outward achievement while having substantially different relationships to that achievement. [GS-W04]

Their model connects concordance with sustained effort and goal attainment. It then connects attainment with well-being through experiences of autonomy, competence and relatedness. A further relationship matters: concordance is expected to modify what attainment provides. Achieving a personally concordant goal should yield more need-satisfying experience than achieving a goal pursued for less personally accepted reasons. The account thus concerns both persistence toward an end and the experience of having reached it. [GS-W04]

In the first study, 169 students listed ten personal goals and rated their reasons for pursuing them. Repeated assessments over a semester followed effort and progress. The concordance index added intrinsic and identified reasons and subtracted external and introjected reasons. The reported associations were consistent with effort mediating attainment. The model begins with selected goals and commitment; its explanation concerns differences among adopted pursuits rather than the prior deliberation through which every possible end might be compared. [GS-W04]

Harald Seelig's operational account makes the component reasons especially tangible through exercise. Interest in the activity, acceptance of its value, self-reproach for failing to exercise and pressure from others can be examined separately. He explains that the difference index is a simplified global measure: inspecting the component profile gives more detail than the resulting score alone. The profile preserves distinctions between different combinations of reasons that a single total can conceal. [GS-W05]

Д. А. Леонтьев's account of self-regulation also gives the adoption of goals an active role. An aim may be supplied externally, but accepting it still involves the actor's selective judgment and responsibility. He contrasts the absence of personal criteria for selection with rigidity that makes an accepted goal impossible to relinquish. These are different problems: being unable to choose among demands and being unable to revise a choice once made. His discussion places both within the structure of activity and its correction. [GS-W10]

Directing attention, effort and learning#

In their 2002 retrospective, Locke and Latham explain four pathways through which goals affect task performance. Goals direct attention toward relevant activities, mobilize effort, prolong persistence and prompt the use or acquisition of task knowledge. Specificity reduces ambiguity about what counts as the required performance; difficulty supplies challenge. Knowledge, commitment and information about progress affect how those processes operate. The account explains why merely announcing a target can differ from giving someone a target that is understood, valued and connected to workable action. [GS-W01]

A particularly consequential distinction concerns performance and learning goals. A performance goal specifies the score or result to achieve. A learning goal concerns discovering or acquiring strategies for the task. When a task is unfamiliar and complex, a demanding score can draw effort toward immediate performance while the performer still lacks an effective method. The relevant work may instead be systematic strategy acquisition. Locke and Latham's discussion therefore distinguishes applying available knowledge from learning what action the task requires. Their account of commitment likewise includes the goal's importance and the person's perceived capability, rather than treating difficulty alone as sufficient motivation. [GS-W01]

Díaz-Ocejo and Mora-Merida's review distinguishes outcome, performance and process goals in sport. Winning a race is an outcome goal. Improving one's own previous time is a performance goal. Directing attention to a technical action is a process goal. The distinctions concern the content of the target and what the athlete can attend to or influence during execution. A process goal specifies an action to attend to, whereas a learning goal specifies knowledge or a strategy to acquire. [GS-W16; GS-W01]

The review reports more consistent support for goal-setting interventions in motor performance than for a uniform ranking of specificity, difficulty or proximity. Comparisons differ in who sets the target and how its difficulty is determined. Its discussion of proximity also raises flexibility: a commitment to a number of training sessions during a week permits adjustments that a rigid daily requirement may prevent when injury or another interruption occurs. The practical question is how the target organizes training under changing conditions, as well as how challenging it sounds when first stated. [GS-W16]

Frutuoso's sport-practice review develops a concrete coach–athlete account. Written goals are coupled with a strategy, a deadline, periodic evaluation and feedback. Goals are developed with the athlete, and the target actually pursued is compared with the one formally stated. Competition and training targets are distinguished; simultaneous aims need priorities and compatibility. Revision is part of the proposed practice. The inventory he describes elicits athletes' perceptions of goal-setting, while his recommended package brings formulation, execution and evaluation together as a coaching practice. [GS-W17]

From a desired future to situated action#

Oettingen, Pak and Schnetter's 2001 fantasy realization account distinguishes imagining a desired future from relating it to an obstructing present. Indulging in the future elaborates its attractive aspects; dwelling on the present elaborates difficulties. Mental contrasting brings the desired future and the present obstacle into relation. The proposed effect is expectancy-dependent commitment: determination strengthens when success appears feasible and weakens when it appears unlikely. The procedure is consequently concerned with selective commitment, rather than simply making every wish more motivating. [GS-W06]

Their first experiment involved 136 female students who named an important interpersonal problem, rated the importance and likelihood of a happy outcome, and listed positive aspects of that future and obstacles in the present. Contrasting instructions alternated elaboration of future and obstacle; comparison instructions elaborated one side alone. Immediate planning and perceived responsibility served as commitment indicators. The authors' general discussion reports the predicted expectancy-dependent pattern across their four experiments. Commitment here means determination to pursue the future, rather than a binary choice or a ranking of competing ultimate values. [GS-W06]

Gollwitzer and Sheeran's account of implementation intentions begins with a different difficulty: a person can intend an outcome yet fail to initiate the necessary action. Forgetting, missing an opportunity, initial reluctance and distraction pose different obstacles. Constructing an implementation intention involves identifying an instrumental response, choosing a feasible situation in which to perform it, and linking situation and response in an if–then plan. The selected response must serve the goal; the cue must be one the person can actually encounter and recognize. [GS-W07]

Their explanation has two parts. Specifying the situation makes its cue more accessible, and linking that cue to the response facilitates initiation without renewed deliberation at every encounter. Deliberate preparation is intended to make later action less dependent on a fresh decision. In a coupon-collection example discussed by Gollwitzer and Sheeran, location cues are connected with collecting the coupon; the account examines cue recognition and subsequent action, rather than intention alone. Their discussion also considers the strength and activation of the underlying goal. A pursuit already proceeding easily need not gain in the same way as one hindered by an initiation problem. [GS-W07]

Wang, Wang and Gai's 2021 meta-analysis evaluates mental contrasting with implementation intentions, or MCII, as a combined intervention. A desired future is related to an obstacle, and an obstacle-linked response plan is constructed. Included comparisons encompass MCII against no treatment and adding MCII to an intervention against that intervention without MCII. The review analyzes 24 independent samples or effect sizes from 21 reports, with 15,907 participants. Its random-effects estimate for goal attainment is g = 0.336: an average advantage of about one third of a standard deviation over the included controls. The 95% confidence interval of 0.229–0.443 expresses uncertainty around this pooled estimate. Heterogeneity I2 = 59.321% indicates substantial variation among study estimates beyond sampling error. [GS-W08]

The review's publication-bias diagnostics give different indications. Its trim-and-fill procedure estimates how the pooled result would change if apparently missing studies were included, yielding an adjusted g of 0.242. This is a sensitivity estimate based on that procedure's assumptions. Its pooled comparison evaluates the specified intervention against the included controls. Most comparisons do not isolate whether the combination outperforms each component separately. The delivery-mode analysis also has a different basis: it excludes two large online-course samples totaling 13,909 participants. Differences among delivery modes in that reduced collection are comparisons across studies, rather than randomized assignments to delivery modes within the full participant sample. [GS-W08]

Feedback and the people who manage goals#

野上真 and 古川久敬's 2010 review examines managerial action across goal formulation, execution and achievement appraisal. It distinguishes communicating or emphasizing demands, providing support through advice and feedback, and incorporating performers' views into decisions. These activities can occur at different points in the work. A manager can consult someone about the target, advise on the method, discuss progress during execution or involve the performer in appraisal. Each changes a different part of the goal-setting process. [GS-W03]

The review considers learning, satisfaction and organizational commitment alongside productivity and motivation. Advice about performing an unfamiliar task supplies something different from a report of the distance still remaining to a numerical target. Participation in devising a strategy also differs from participation in choosing the number. The authors find more developed evidence for support than for achievement demands and identify combinations across phases as a research question. Their summary table collects reported positive findings; their proposed complementarity among managerial actions is an interpretation and direction for research. [GS-W03]

Locke and Latham's discussion of participation similarly distinguishes a reasoned assignment from a terse command. Their account of the Erez–Latham collaboration examines what information and rationale accompany assignment, as well as whether the performer participated in setting the goal. Participation in developing task strategies can supply useful knowledge even when choosing the target is not the decisive motivational difference. Progress feedback gives the performer a basis for altering effort or strategy. The comparison therefore involves the interaction and information surrounding the target, as well as its nominal source. [GS-W01]

Леонтьев separates receiving feedback, comparing the actual state with a desired criterion, and correcting action. Information can be available without being received; an error can be recognized without producing a change of conduct. His conceptual structure distinguishes failure to begin acting from failure to notice a discrepancy and from failure to respond after recognizing it. Correction may concern the route being taken or the goal itself. These distinctions make it possible to describe several different failures that would otherwise appear simply as failure to attain a target. [GS-W10]

In Frutuoso's coaching account, periodic evaluation and feedback return attention to the goal actually being pursued. A formal agreement between coach and athlete does not by itself establish that training is organized around that agreement. Comparing stated and pursued aims, reviewing progress and revising the plan give the target an ongoing role in the working relationship. The accounts of participation and organizational strategy in S92 develop related questions about interpreting objectives and taking part in decisions. [GS-W17]

Revising, relinquishing and replacing goals#

Wrosch and colleagues' 2003 account addresses self-regulation when a goal becomes unattainable. Disengagement has two components: reducing effort and relinquishing commitment. Stopping an activity while remaining intensely committed to its outcome differs from releasing the commitment itself. Reengagement has its own components: identifying alternative goals, investing them with value and beginning their pursuit. The distinction permits someone to develop a new pursuit while the old commitment is still being relinquished. [GS-W09]

Participants rated how readily they could reduce effort and release commitment to an unattainable goal, and how readily they could find, value and pursue alternatives. The authors consider lost opportunities, changed life circumstances and competing demands on limited time and energy. These contexts give the problem a practical form: continuing to pursue one aim can interfere with pursuits that remain available,

while the absence of an alternative can make disengagement harder. Their framework distinguishes capacities for releasing and replacing goals rather than requiring a fixed sequence in which one must be completed before the other begins. [GS-W09]

The three samples comprised 115 undergraduates, 120 younger and older adults, and 45 parents of children with cancer or medically healthy children. Associations connected goal-adjustment capacities with aspects of subjective well-being. The authors identify the cross-sectional design and possible cohort differences as constraints on causal interpretation. The studies relate adjustment capacities to well-being; they do not supply a test for deciding that a difficult undertaking is objectively unattainable. [GS-W09]

Леонтьев's discussion of flexibility distinguishes changing a route from changing the desired destination. Recognizing a discrepancy can prompt either response. A goal that cannot be reconsidered can organize repeated action around a criterion that circumstances no longer support, while indiscriminate acceptance of new demands creates a different difficulty. His conceptual account places revision within self-regulation itself. The backward-planning accounts in S94 examine how means are derived from intended results; these adjustment accounts concern the possibility that the intended result will also change. [GS-W10]

Organizational objectives and the debate over targets#

Doran's 1981 formulation of SMART concerns making managerial objectives usable and communicable. Specific identifies an area for improvement. Measurable calls for quantity or an indicator of progress. Assignable identifies who will do the work. Realistic relates the intended results to available resources. Time-related specifies when results are to be achieved. The original A therefore concerns assignment of responsibility. His illustrative objective calls for developing and implementing an inventory system by December 31 of a designated year to reduce inventory costs by $1 million. The work is to take no more than 200 work hours and $15,000 in initial out-of-pocket expenditure. The example connects the intended result with a deadline and specified resources. [GS-W11]

Doran also allows abstract objectives and does not require every objective to satisfy every criterion or be quantified. Pairing the objective with an action plan matters to his account: writing an intelligible result and organizing its accomplishment are connected managerial tasks. He discusses managers' anxiety about commitments involving variables they cannot control and senior managers' role in communicating objectives. The proposal addresses formulation and coordination. [GS-W11]

Ordóñez, Schweitzer, Galinsky and Bazerman's 2009 critique asks what targets cause people to attend to and what selected performance measures leave out. They discuss a proofreading experiment in which explicit grammar or content targets are contrasted with an instruction to do one's best. Concentration on a specified dimension can leave the other dimension unattended. Their discussion of multiple goals likewise raises competition between quantity and quality: adding a second objective changes the demands rather than automatically resolving the allocation of attention. [GS-W12]

The critics also distinguish using dishonest means to attain a goal from falsely reporting that it has been attained. A target can organize conduct leading to a result, and a reward can depend on a report about that result; the two create different opportunities for misconduct. Corporate incidents illustrate their argument for examining risk and conduct alongside output. In their subsequent rejoinder, they distinguish using case histories to identify consequential questions from using them to prove causality and argue for studies that permit and measure broader consequences. [GS-W12; GS-W14]

Locke and Latham's reply contests inference from anecdotes, selective citation and the characterization of earlier research. Their stated position is that proponents had already described many of the pitfalls presented as neglected. The disagreement thus concerns both evidential standards and what the existing theory actually asserts. The proponents' earlier retrospective develops conditions involving knowledge,

commitment, rationale, participation and feedback; the critics ask whether investigations adequately capture consequences beyond the chosen performance score. [GS-W13; GS-W01; GS-W14]

文鹏, 任晓雅 and 陈诚's 2017 review separates target attributes, the setting process and target content. Difficulty and specificity concern attributes; participation and rewards concern how goals operate organizationally; result-oriented and process-oriented formulations concern content. The authors also distinguish violation of ethical norms from violation of an organization's internal rules. Conduct can serve an organization's immediate interests and still violate broader moral expectations. That distinction prevents organizational compliance from silently becoming the definition of ethical behavior. [GS-W15]

The review develops three proposed explanations. Goal shielding concentrates attention on an important target while other goals receive less attention. Organizational targets can thereby signal what is valued and where effort should go. Moral disengagement concerns justifying misconduct: treating the result as overriding other considerations can make deception seem acceptable, or an imposed target can encourage an actor to shift responsibility to the person who set it. The depletion account treats self-control as a limited resource. Demanding goals require effort and increase cognitive load; reduced self-control can then make conduct less consistent with internal standards. [GS-W15]

The review also examines studies involving unverifiable performance reports, nearly attained targets and moral justification. It records inconsistent findings and limited organizational-field evidence. The contrast between result-oriented and process-oriented content is presented as theoretically proposed, with direct tests still lacking in that comparison. The organizational debate extends from how an objective is written to what conduct is observed, what outcome is rewarded and what counts as an adequate explanation of the result. [GS-W15]

S99 Procrastination and beginning intended action#

When delay becomes procrastination#

Piers Steel’s 2007 review defines procrastination through the relationship between an intention, a delay and its expected consequences. A person voluntarily puts off an intended action while expecting the postponement to leave them worse off. The definition makes the prior intention consequential. Evidence that an action started late leaves open whether the person changed their mind, lost an opportunity or chose to wait because the task had become more favorable later. Steel discusses task aversiveness and the delay before a reward as different influences on the appeal of acting now. The histories of intentional waiting in S61 and S62 concern decisions in which postponement can serve a purpose. [T01-W001]

Recognizing delay in ordinary behavior#

Svartdal and colleagues asked how behavioral delay might be examined alongside a questionnaire. Among the routines they considered was bringing lunch from home versus buying it. Participants who generally brought lunch and those who generally bought it had mean Irrational Procrastination Scale scores of 2.71 and 2.99 respectively. The contrast associates a reported routine with a score. Classifying a particular postponement would require further evidence about what the person intended to prepare and what happened to that intention. [T01-W002]

Changing willingness to start#

童廷婷, 白幼玲 and 冯廷勇 investigated positive reappraisal among participants selected for high procrastination. Their report describes two groups of 34 and a week of experience sampling. They assessed willingness to execute the task, how aversive it seemed and the usefulness of the result. At post-test, the positive-reappraisal group reported greater willingness to begin the task and less aversion to it than the comparison group. In the authors’ mediation analysis, reduced aversion accounted for part of the relationship they studied, while increased perceived usefulness did not mediate it. [T01-W003]

Rozental and colleagues’ review pooled 21 comparisons from 12 studies, involving 718 participants. Against inactive controls, the pooled post-treatment difference on procrastination measures was 0.34 standard deviations in favor of treatment, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 0.11 to 0.56. Effects varied considerably among comparisons. Most studies assessed the outcome at the end of treatment. The cue-linked plans discussed in S98 specify when to initiate an action, while the reappraisal study above asks how the task feels when a person considers doing it. [T01-W004]

S94 Working backward from outcomes#

A proposition to be proved, a future to be examined and a performance to be demonstrated each give planning a possible starting point. The following accounts show how authors derive intermediate requirements, construct pathways and decide what evidence would establish an intended result.

S62 examines reverse business calculations and staged assumptions; S85 explains backward calculations in project scheduling.

Starting with the proposition to be established#

Stephanie Dick’s 2015 history follows mathematical heuristics into the construction of the Logic Theory Machine. The program began with a proposition to be proved and sought subproblems from which it could be deduced. It continued generating such subproblems until it could connect the chain to axioms; reversing a successful chain supplied the proof. A search could also fail to find the connection. Dick places Pólya’s working-backward heuristic within this history alongside other aids to discovery. Implementing the procedure on JOHNNIAC required representations and operations adapted to the machine. Her account makes the intended result an active part of the search: it determines which intermediate propositions would be useful. [PM-W001]

Regressing requirements and protecting goals#

Richard Waldinger’s Achieving Several Goals Simultaneously, issued as a technical report in 1975, addresses plans in which satisfying one goal can interfere with another. His procedure first constructs a plan for one goal, then modifies it to achieve the second while preserving required relations. Regression passes a desired relation backward across an action and asks what must have been true before the action for that relation to hold afterward. For an assignment X receives t, the desired relation P(X) becomes P(t) before the assignment. The substitution supplies a requirement that can be examined earlier in the plan. [PM-W002]

The three-block example shows why this operation matters. The target tower has A on B and B on C. Starting with separate blocks, the planner first puts A on B. A one-block-at-a-time arm cannot then put B on C while maintaining that arrangement. Passing the requirement that B be on C backward across the first action permits the planner to put B on C before placing A on B. Protection points identify relations that must hold at particular positions. Skeleton models retain selected facts and use regression to infer others as the plan changes. The action descriptions and protected relations make the modification inspectable. [PM-W002]

Backcasting, participation and the choice of a future#

Jaco Quist and Philip Vergragt’s 2006 account traces energy backcasting as an alternative to extrapolative forecasting and follows its extension into participatory sustainability work. Their proposed framework includes problem orientation, future visions, backcasting, elaboration of follow-up agendas, and embedding and implementation. Participation and iteration can change across these stages. In their historical reconstruction, Robinson’s earlier policy-analysis purpose and later stakeholder-oriented applications give backcasting different practical settings. [PM-W003]

Their SusHouse food-centre scenario illustrates how a vision enters further assessment. A neighbourhood centre for food preparation appeared attractive, but calculations using contemporary restaurant energy data suggested that energy demand might increase. The authors called for better data, and the workshop scenarios underwent environmental, economic and consumer assessment. The desirable image initiated

questions that subsequent investigation could alter. Their two food cases also had different follow-up histories: producing a vision and embedding subsequent activity were distinguishable achievements. [PM-W003]

Emilie Mutombo, Tom Bauler and Grégoire Wallenborn’s 2007 comparative report separates constructing a final image from constructing an evolution toward it. In their analytical grid, putting the final image first gives a backcasting order; putting the evolution first gives a forecasting order. Objectives, measures and monitoring remain further activities, with actual exercises often combining or overlapping the simplified stages. [PM-W004]

The report also examines how a destination is chosen. A vague image can accommodate apparently compatible principles; specifying it more precisely exposes different priorities and values. In its World Water Vision account, polarized conceptions remained unresolved and produced two reports. The staff report nevertheless supported initiatives by actors who adopted its vision. Participation could thus produce material for action without establishing one shared destination. The authors’ sequencing distinctions sit alongside this practical history of agreement and disagreement. [PM-W004]

Sebastian Bollien’s 2021 institutional account begins with a concrete future image and asks which events must precede it. Its example is peace negotiation between hostile parties: the backward questions concern conditions and timing that would make talks possible. Examining those requirements can lead to revising the image or moving it in time. The destination participates in the inquiry and can change as its prerequisites are examined. [PM-W012]

David Bengston, Lynne Westphal and Michael Dockry’s 2020 Backcasting Wheel places a preferred future at the centre of a diagram. Dimensions of success lead outward to signposts, opportunities and obstacles, and concrete management actions. Participants score importance and timing, and subsequent analysis organizes the results into action plans. The outward movement reaches earlier enabling actions, whereas a Futures Wheel explores later consequences of a change. [PM-W013]

Their Forest Service case involved two units preparing to share leadership and a headquarters. Mixed groups developed signposts, obstacles, opportunities and actions, scored them, and assigned leaders to urgent tasks. Participants later described the exercise as useful. Turnover interrupted continuity, leaving the eventual effect on the reorganization unresolved. The case records how an aspiration was translated into actions and assignments within a participatory exercise. [PM-W013]

Yusuke Kishita, Mattias Höjer and Jaco Quist’s 2024 comparison distinguishes participatory, goal-oriented and scenario-design approaches to backcasting. Implementation and stakeholder engagement receive a different emphasis from constructing goal-fulfilling future images. Their comparison retains those differences while developing the authors’ own design-framework questions about when, which, how and what. Backcasting continues to encompass different objects of design and different arrangements for involving participants. [PM-W014]

A backward tree and a forward storyline#

Haruna Wada and colleagues’ 2013 scenario-construction method starts with a target and builds a logic tree of events and actions that could lead to it. Key events divide the material into subscenarios. The writers then develop storylines forward from the present and turn them into scenario text. References and logical jumps are represented explicitly. [PM-W005]

Their worked target is an undesirable collapse of manufacturing in 2050. The tree separates inability to produce from inability to sell. When the resource branch is developed forward, substitution of aluminium for copper wiring introduces a possibility absent from the initial backward tree, one that could interrupt the collapse story. Backward tree construction and forward elaboration therefore perform different work

in the authors’ procedure. Selecting key events and judging the tree’s adequacy remain part of scenario construction; the paper discusses AND/OR operators as a subsequent improvement. [PM-W005]

Designing evidence of learning#

Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe’s Understanding by Design (1998) orders curriculum decisions around desired learning, acceptable evidence and then instruction. Their hypothetical teacher Bob James wants fifth-grade students to use nutrition knowledge to plan balanced diets. He specifies a three-day camp menu and an analysis of a hypothetical family’s diet as performances through which students can demonstrate that understanding. Quizzes supply evidence about prerequisite knowledge. [PM-W006]

These choices guide the teaching resources and activities: interpreting nutrition labels, scaling recipes, consulting a visiting nutritionist, and using a brochure, video and selected textbook passages. Assessment includes evidence gathered during learning through observations, dialogue and other tasks. The example changes the textbook’s role from an obligatory sequence to one resource among several. The authors acknowledge Tyler’s earlier objectives-based logic and supply filters, templates and design questions for putting such decisions into practice. [PM-W006]

Wiggins and McTighe’s 2011 guide distinguishes acquiring knowledge, making meaning and transferring learning. Evidence is chosen in relation to the intended result. Using knowledge independently in a new situation calls for a different demonstration from recalling facts. Their nutrition materials sequence analysis of a hypothetical family’s diet, feedback on misunderstandings and independent preparation of a camp menu. Instruction and practice prepare that performance. The GRASPS prompts make task design explicit through goal, role, audience, situation, product or performance, and standards. These are tools for designing a unit and inspecting its coherence. [PM-W007]

Wang Lingling’s 2023 account applies backward unit design to fifth-grade texts about Venice, Dutch pastures and the pyramids. Intended learning is expressed through performances such as explaining a place and preparing a travel guide. In a proposed tour-guide competition, groups choose locations, develop guide materials and presentations, and are judged on features of content and delivery. Further assessment concerns participation and cooperation. Wang’s exposition constructs the performance activity before separately discussing assessment evidence. The resulting account makes the product, audience and criteria visible within her formulation of unit teaching. [PM-W008]

Planning direction and predictions of completion#

Jessica Wiese, Roger Buehler and Dale Griffin’s 2016 experiments distinguish hours spent working from the calendar date on which a task is completed. Their four studies compare backward, forward and unspecified planning directions. In the fourth, adults nominated a multiday project with a deadline within two weeks, planned its steps and predicted when they would start and finish and how many work hours they would need. A follow-up asked what had happened. [PM-W009]

The initial analysed sample contained 187 participants; 125 reported completed projects and supplied the completion-bias analysis. Backward planners showed less average optimistic bias in predicted completion dates. The intervention shifted predictions without a corresponding reduction in actual completion time. Predicted work hours and starting-time bias had different results. The authors discuss attention to obstacles, additional steps and planning insights as possible processes, with variable support across their studies. [PM-W009]

Jooyoung Park, Fang-Chi Lu and William Hedgcock’s 2017 paper reports comparisons of chronological and reverse-chronological planning for personal goals, treating motivation, expectancy, perceived pressure and performance as distinct outcomes. Their 2018 corrigendum revises effect sizes, intervals

and portions of Study 3’s statistical reporting while stating that the interpretations stand; some corrected comparisons are marginal or nonsignificant. Their reported goal-pursuit findings concern different outcomes from Wiese and colleagues’ completion-time predictions. [PM-W010] [PM-W029]

Transforming computational planning problems#

Allen Ren, Brian Ichter and Anirudha Majumdar’s 2024 computational study examines graph paths, array transformations and block manipulation. A narrow passage near a goal can make searching from that end attractive. Simply asking their model to plan backward, however, performs worse. They instead flip the problem, plan forward in the transformed representation and convert the solution back. Directed edges must be reversed, and actions must have usable inverses for the relevant transformation. [PM-W011]

The experiments generate candidate plans, use model self-verification and apply an external task verifier. Combining ordinary and flipped planning improves success in their tested settings. Transforming the problem and checking the returned plan are substantial parts of the procedure. [PM-W011]

S95 Challenging plans before action#

A plan can depend on assumptions its proponents have not examined. Organized opposition, an assumed failure or an opponent’s next action can make those assumptions available for discussion. The historical accounts below describe what participants are asked to do and what the resulting arguments, reasons and decisions reveal.

S44 examines approaches to organizing inquiry; S86 discusses independent forecast review and project governance.

Exposing assumptions behind rival plans#

David McDonald, Gabriele Bammer and Peter Deane’s Research Integration Using Dialogue Methods (2009) reconstructs strategic assumption surfacing and testing through group formation, assumption surfacing and rating, debate, and attempted accommodation. Groups develop their positions and identify assumptions that trouble them in rival positions. The procedure makes the premises sustaining competing courses of action available for examination. [PM-W015]

Their Winterton example concerns an agency divided between finding business opportunities and recruiting cooperatives to pursue them, or helping people form cooperatives and then find opportunities. The groups identified different stakeholders and assumptions. Debate did not reconcile their positions, but participants agreed to gather information and conduct limited experiments. The reported action preserved the unresolved issue while making further investigation possible. [PM-W015]

The Pfeiffer Library’s 1998 robotics exercise provides a teachable implementation adapted from Mason and Mitroff. Participants receive the same automation proposal and form pro and con subgroups. They identify stakeholders, surface assumptions and rate their importance and certainty before presenting positions and debating damaging disagreements. Mixed groups subsequently propose integrative plans, retaining unresolved issues where agreement remains impossible. [PM-W016]

The stipulated Elmire case combines an attractive financial calculation for robot conversion with possible job losses, strikes, employee commitments and community reactions. It supplies participants with a situation in which assumptions about other people’s responses matter to the proposed investment. The exercise shows how those assumptions enter discussion and revision within the training design. [PM-W016]

Criticism, counterproposals and consensus#

George Wright and Gene Rowe’s 2011 review reconstructs the procedures compared by Schweiger and colleagues. In dialectical inquiry, subgroups develop opposing alternatives and debate their assumptions and recommendations. In devil’s advocacy, one subgroup offers a proposal and another critically probes its elements and recommendations. The returned material consequently differs: a rival proposal supplies another course of action to debate, while an organized critique identifies weaknesses in the proposal under examination. They contrast these conflict procedures with discussion directed toward consensus, without an assigned adversarial role. Their account also cautions that disagreement can turn toward personalities rather than factual issues. [PM-W028]

Charles Schwenk’s 1990 meta-analysis reports an overall advantage for devil’s advocacy over an expert-only approach. It reports no demonstrated superiority of dialectical inquiry over expert advice on relatively ill-structured tasks and no established winner between the two conflict methods. These reported conclusions address comparisons earlier reviews had interpreted differently. The task

qualification and comparator are part of the result: an advantage over expert-only advice answers a different question from an advantage over another organized-conflict procedure. [PM-W017]

Jerry Fjermestad’s 2019 review introduction frames a disagreement between organizational case and field studies and laboratory experiments. Active and passive participation, leadership and communication technology distinguish the settings. Groups whose participants merely receive an argument have a different experience from groups that construct and defend it. His framing also questions whether results from face-to-face work will carry into distributed computer-mediated teams. These distinctions direct attention to the organization of the comparison as well as the technique’s name. [PM-W018]

How participants interpret opposition#

Charlan Nemeth, Keith Brown and John Rogers’ 2001 experiment used a vacation-scheduling dispute in computer-mediated groups. The opposing participant delivered the same scripted arguments, while the conditions changed whether others understood her as expressing a minority belief or performing a devil’s-advocate role. After the discussion, participants generated possible solutions. [PM-W019]

The final usable pool was 94 female undergraduates, with smaller samples for individual measures. Perceived authentic dissent produced more alternatives and a stronger combined quantity/quality score than the consistent-role and control conditions. Mean quality alone did not differ significantly between those conditions. The manipulation thus concerns how participants interpreted the same opposition, while the separate measures distinguish producing more alternatives from improving their average quality. [PM-W019]

Explaining an assumed failure#

Deborah Mitchell, J. Edward Russo and Nancy Pennington’s 1989 experiments varied both the temporal setting of an event and the certainty of its outcome. Participants explained professional and personal successes or failures. The first experiment enrolled 114 MBA students; the second combined 76 MBA students with 32 paid students, with time recorded for the latter. [PM-W020]

In the dinner-party scenario, the same background was paired with success or failure presented as certain or possible and situated in the past or future. Certainty affected the number and episodic character of reasons more consistently than temporal framing. [PM-W020]

Gary Klein’s 2007 project premortem briefs a team on its plan and stipulates that the project has failed. Members independently write reasons for the failure, then contribute different reasons around the group. The manager considers changes in response. The exercise gives reservations a concrete occasion for expression before implementation. [PM-W021]

Klein’s software example concerns algorithms that would run too slowly on field laptops. A previously unmentioned shortcut was substituted after the concern surfaced. In his account, the change emerged from examining an assumed failure and identifying a specific technical reservation. [PM-W021]

Beth Veinott, Gary Klein and Sterling Wiggins’ 2010 study assigned 178 students to evaluate an H1N1 university response plan using a baseline, critique, pros/cons, cons-only or premortem condition. Participants rated confidence before criticism, after pooling concerns and after proposing improvements. The premortem condition showed a larger reduction in confidence followed by a larger recovery after improvements were considered. [PM-W022]

The paper reports confidence and subjective understanding; its overall understanding test was nonsignificant. Participants reviewed a supplied plan and did not implement it. [PM-W022]

Whose knowledge enters the review#

Guillermo Wippold and colleagues’ 2025 implementation premortem brings potential recipients into examining local conditions. In the Fade to Fitness example, recipients were recruited beyond the barbershop customers involved in shaping the original programme. After an overview and a stipulated failure, participants generated reasons individually, discussed responses and prioritized concerns. Transcripts were analysed through an implementation framework. [PM-W023]

The authors illustrate how limited shop space could lead to planning delivery during non-peak hours. The article explains that procedure and its contextual example, directing readers to a separate report for empirical findings. [PM-W023]

Giovanni Cunico, Nici Zimmermann and Nuno Videira’s study, first published online in 2023, addresses homogeneous groups whose disagreements may circulate only knowledge already present. Their New Devil’s Advocate is a prepared facilitator who temporarily represents absent stakeholders through documented information. Other facilitators maintain the process. A role-plot connects a stakeholder, evidence, a possible intervention and relevant model variables. [PM-W027]

In their UK housing-retrofit application, the first workshop left supply-chain and homeowner perspectives poorly represented. The team gathered information through three expert interviews, literature and earlier research, and prepared 45 inputs for two advocates. The role-plot paired each issue with a stakeholder, a way to raise it and possible model variables. One prepared intervention asked how household reluctance to borrow could affect renovation policy, connecting that concern to mortgage refinancing and the willingness to take loans. [PM-W027]

The resulting map incorporated relationships concerning installer skills, retrofit quality and performance, as well as household behaviour and perceived monthly savings. The authors traced 20 of the 45 prepared inputs into the map by comparing the role-plot, workshop transcripts and model changes. Their appendix shows how an input could be reformulated during modelling: household compliance with a retrofit measure became a link from behavioural compliance to measure performance. [PM-W027]

The two advocates participated very differently. The performer experienced in group model building supplied nearly all their interventions; the other, despite substantial topic knowledge, reported difficulty entering the discussion while trying to formulate contributions in the modelling language. The experienced performer occasionally returned to facilitation or joined a decision about model content. In one such instance, the facilitator asked the regular participants again whether they agreed to include the proposed variable. Transcripts and feedback thus reveal both how missing perspectives entered the model and how participants retained authority over its construction. [PM-W027]

Critical review and adversary perspectives#

The UK Ministry of Defence’s Red Teaming Handbook (2021) distinguishes critical review by a red team from adoption of an adversary or stakeholder perspective by a red cell. Its assumptions review identifies explicit and implicit assumptions in an estimate or plan, examines their support, asks when they might fail and considers what failure would change. Judgments about support and caveats are recorded for subsequent use. [PM-W024]

Argument mapping starts at a recommendation and traces supporting deductions, assumptions and assertions backward. Missing links and unsupported steps are marked. Reviewers then examine the chain forward to determine the consequences of flaws and the information needed to repair them. Red-cell work has a different information arrangement: separation from friendly planning and withholding privileged knowledge of friendly intentions help participants reason from the represented actor’s position. The handbook makes actor expertise part of that prescription. [PM-W024]

Héloïse Fayet and Amélie Férey’s 2023 institutional account distinguishes red cells modelling an opponent’s reactions, red teams questioning assumptions and defence foresight constructing fictional futures. Short brain games bring officials and external experts into roles, alongside more developed games and scenario efforts. The activities give participants different jobs and work across different time horizons. [PM-W025]

The authors also examine promotion incentives, hierarchy and personnel rotation. Critical perspectives have to be voiced, retained and used within an institution whose career and staffing practices influence those possibilities. Their account places the design of a session alongside the organization in which its results must circulate. [PM-W025]

Examining a course of action through a game#

Masahiro Kurita’s 2025 review compares traditional analytical wargaming with experiments that use repeated games as synthetic data. Human decisions, adjudication and consequences make the course of play responsive to participants. His review examines the tension between simplifying scenarios to isolate a variable and preserving the rich setting and interaction considered necessary for realistic choices. [PM-W026]

His account of the International Crisis Wargame describes teams of four to six acting as a fictional nuclear-armed state’s national security council. They choose responses to two separate crises. Repeated sessions vary whether their own nuclear command arrangements are vulnerable to cyberattack and whether they can attack the opponent’s arrangements. The principal material for analysis is the teams’ response plans. Play ends with the response decision, without a further exchange of actions between competing sides. [PM-W026]

SIGNAL uses a different design. Players representing three fictional states pursue economic, military and diplomatic objectives over five rounds. They negotiate and signal intentions, then take actions whose consequences are governed by rules. A player can depart from an earlier signal. This produces a sequence of interacting choices, rather than only a team’s response to a stipulated crisis. Kurita uses the two examples to show that experimental wargaming includes substantially different forms of play and data. [PM-W026]

The disagreement about immersion concerns those concrete choices. Fictional settings can help separate the variable under study from participants’ knowledge of real countries; removing subsequent interaction also simplifies comparison. Critics question whether such designs elicit decisions resembling those of actual policymakers. Kurita reports little empirical evidence establishing how much immersion is needed or which design features produce it. He treats the appropriate degree of simplification as an unresolved question for traditional analytical games as well as experimental ones. [PM-W026]

S53 Absorbing new resources and capabilities#

Acquiring equipment, finance or outside knowledge can leave substantial work between the acquisition and a useful result. People may have to learn unfamiliar operations, establish relationships, develop supporting services or change how decisions are made. The historical accounts below examine that work and the order in which it develops. Their interventions include organizing training, combining investments, distributing knowledge, adapting institutions and managing the pace of expenditure.

Baldwin's account in S07 explains complementary investments and transition costs; S14 develops changes in work design and information processing. Miller's overload discussion in S21 and the moving-constraint account in S44 address limits on increasing input. The sources here examine how the receiving capabilities themselves develop, including situations in which beginning an activity helps create the conditions for its further expansion.

Rosenstein-Rodan: training and investment beyond a single enterprise#

P. N. Rosenstein-Rodan's 1943 proposal for industrialization in Eastern and South-Eastern Europe treats training as an investment problem. A firm paying to prepare workers may lose them to another employer. The benefit of their acquired skills can exceed the return available to the firm that bears the training cost. He therefore considers training from the standpoint of the group of industries being created. Transport and housing enter the provision for bringing people into industrial work, alongside instruction itself. His proposed large investment unit would include this preparation among its capital costs. [AB-W003, pp. 204–205]

Complementarity also concerns the market for what new enterprises produce. In his hypothetical example, workers employed by one large shoe factory will spend their wages on many products, leaving the factory unable to rely on their demand alone. A group of industries producing the goods those workers require can generate demand for one another's output. The argument for coordinated investment thus includes relations among production, income and consumption. It asks why a project that looks unattractive by itself might contribute to a more valuable combined undertaking. [AB-W003, pp. 205–207]

Rosenstein-Rodan also questions a different proposal: build transport and power facilities and expect other industries to follow automatically. The region's existing transport provision and its intended productive activities affect what infrastructure is needed, where and in what quantity. His coordinated industrial programme is a proposed response to a particular reconstruction problem; the paper explicitly leaves detailed institutional implementation for later work. Training and complementary demand receive explanations, while the task of establishing the proposed investment organization remains to be worked out. [AB-W003, pp. 208–209]

Hirschman: developing the ability to invest#

In The Strategy of Economic Development (1958), Albert Hirschman distinguishes available savings and investment opportunities from the ability to connect them. Recognizing a project, obtaining cooperation and carrying it through require abilities that cannot be assumed to appear whenever finance becomes available. He argues that these abilities develop partly through practice in existing productive activities. An expanding sector can train people and create experience useful for further expansion. This makes the ability to undertake projects part of the development process itself. [AB-W004, pp. 35–38]

His schematic account allows the limiting factor to change. Initially, available or mobilizable savings may exceed what the existing productive sector can turn into investments. As that sector expands, its investing

abilities can increase until finance becomes the tighter restriction. Hirschman cautions that this transition need not occur at one neat date: skills and savings move imperfectly between sectors, so different activities can encounter the change at different times. He prefers investigating this developing ability to treating every difficulty as an obstacle to an assumed normal state in which all available finance would be absorbed. [AB-W004, pp. 36–39]

This interpretation also changes the role assigned to external capital. In his first situation, an outside investment can matter through skills, organization and ways of conducting an enterprise, as well as the money supplied. In a later situation, domestic managerial and entrepreneurial abilities may already outrun available savings, making finance itself more important. These are distinctions within his proposed account of development, with different implications for what a capital transfer must actually provide. [AB-W004, pp. 38–39]

Hirschman: choosing a sequence that elicits a response#

Hirschman's investment discussion compares expanding infrastructure before productive activity with allowing productive activity to advance far enough to create pressure for additional infrastructure. More transport or power capacity can reduce costs and attract investment. Conversely, existing producers facing costly shortages can press authorities to expand those services. The first route invites an activity through improved conditions; the second attempts to elicit action through a difficulty people already experience. His comparison depends on entrepreneurial response and on the responsiveness of the authorities responsible for infrastructure. [AB-W004, pp. 86–93, figs. 3–4]

His diagram separates the resources needed for a static least-cost combination from the decisions through which a country might reach a larger productive scale. He assumes, for that comparison, that infrastructure and directly productive activity cannot both be expanded at once. Infrastructure built ahead of demand supplies spare capacity whose value depends on subsequent use. Production expanded first can make the need for an additional road or power supply concrete enough to generate a decision that previously attracted little support. Those assumptions and induced responses, rather than a preference for imbalance as such, do the explanatory work. [AB-W004, pp. 86–90, fig. 3]

There is a technical minimum. Access and some supporting services must exist before an activity can operate at all. Prolonged neglect can also make expansion self-defeating: another factory may claim scarce services at the expense of existing firms, leaving little gain in aggregate productivity. The absence of an absolute barrier to building the new factory can conceal that displacement. Hirschman's discussion therefore distinguishes a shortage capable of provoking a useful response from one that continues to damage the productive system. [AB-W004, pp. 94–97]

He also allows experience to change the comparison. Investors who expect infrastructure providers to respond, and providers who anticipate growing demand, may act before an actual shortage or excess appears. Under those conditions, his alternative inducement curves permit coordinated expansion to sustain further investment. The same account that explains the possible usefulness of an uneven sequence also explains how learned expectations can reduce reliance on the difficulties that initially elicited action. [AB-W004, pp. 91–93, figs. 4a–4b]

Dierickx and Cool: expenditure flows and accumulated capabilities#

Ingemar Dierickx and Karel Cool's 1989 article distinguishes resources that can be traded from assets that develop through a history of activity. Trust, firm-specific knowledge and a reputation for reliable quality are among their examples. Current expenditure can purchase inputs to that history without immediately producing its accumulated result. Their stock-and-flow description makes the distinction

explicit: additions build an asset stock, while erosion diminishes it. A current research budget and accumulated technical know-how therefore describe different quantities. [AB-W002, pp. 1505–1506]

They call one possible property of accumulation time compression diseconomies. Increasing expenditure over a shorter period may not reproduce what a longer process would have developed. Their examples include crash research programmes and attempts to compress education. They also identify interconnectedness: building one asset can depend on another stock already in place. A service network, for example, can provide customer knowledge that contributes to technological development. These are proposed properties to investigate in particular accumulation processes, and the authors explicitly say that a process need not possess all of them. [AB-W002, pp. 1507–1509]

An accumulated advantage also needs maintenance and can be displaced by a different approach. Their Canon–Xerox illustration describes design capability substituting for a service network on which an earlier competitive position depended. The article's question is the sustainability of competitive advantage. Its conceptual examples explain why buying more inputs, accelerating expenditure, preserving an existing asset and developing a substitute are different strategic actions. [AB-W002, pp. 1508–1510]

Cohen and Levinthal: prior knowledge and the organization of reception#

Wesley Cohen and Daniel Levinthal's 1990 account names a firm's ability to recognize useful external knowledge, assimilate it and apply it commercially as absorptive capacity. Prior related knowledge helps people understand and connect new information. Their argument joins existing knowledge to effort and practice: information can be available without being intelligible or usable to its recipients. Research, technical training and experience in production can contribute to this capacity through different activities. [AB-W001, pp. 128–131]

Organizational reception involves more than employing several knowledgeable individuals. Someone encountering an outside idea must connect it with people who can evaluate or use it internally. A specialist at the boundary may translate unfamiliar material, but recipients still need enough related understanding to act on what is communicated. Where technical change is rapid and uncertain, the authors argue for a broader distribution of people able to notice relevant developments. Shared understanding supports communication, while excessive uniformity can restrict the different associations through which something new is recognized. [AB-W001, pp. 131–135]

They also explain why purchasing expertise may leave integration work unresolved. An external consultant or newly hired specialist can bring knowledge without possessing the firm's understanding of its own needs, routines and complementary capabilities. Maintaining some internal expertise helps participants interpret outside work and connect it with those particulars. Similarly, participation in a joint research venture leaves a firm with internal work if it is to use the venture's output. The authors distinguish knowledge related to ordinary activity, for which capacity may develop as a byproduct, from unfamiliar domains requiring deliberate preparation. [AB-W001, pp. 135, 148–150]

Their empirical discussion examines an indirect implication of this account: how learning conditions affect firms' research expenditure. It combines reported characteristics of technical knowledge with manufacturing business-unit data, rather than directly observing a completed absorption process. The R&D evidence reported in the article derives from their earlier work. Greater relevance of basic rather than applied science was associated with more research spending, as predicted when less targeted knowledge requires more internal effort to absorb. These spending patterns do not by themselves establish the causal effectiveness of the organizational practices described. Their closing discussion retains the difficulty of valuing indirect benefits when deciding how much to invest. [AB-W001, pp. 139– 150]

Noblet and Simon: making organizational practices observable#

Jean-Pierre Noblet and Eric Simon's 2008 study attempts to make absorptive capacity examinable through what firms do. They interview leaders of ten innovative companies, largely small and medium enterprises, using two appointments separated by two to four weeks and about thirty hours of interviews in total. Their literature-derived grid distinguishes acquiring, assimilating, transforming and exploiting knowledge. Indicators include alliances, shared understanding, research activity, changed routines and management support. They analyze meaningful passages in the interviews, with interpretation checked by another researcher. [AB-W007, pp. 9–12]

The reported practices give those categories substance. One leader describes joint research followed by a report and discussion that can change working practices. Others identify employees who scan external information or help colleagues find an outside application when their own work is blocked. The body of the paper emphasizes managerial openness, contact with final customers and trust. These concern willingness to reconsider an activity, opportunities to learn what a product must do, and relationships through which people exchange knowledge. [AB-W007, pp. 12–16]

Measurement itself becomes a practical issue. Interviewed leaders challenge patent counts as an adequate indicator for their firms because confidentiality, retained know-how and filing costs affect whether they patent. Noblet and Simon offer an exploratory operationalization based on leaders' accounts and call for further development of the instrument. Their practices and proposed indicators help identify what an investigation could observe, while the small selected sample and self-reports limit conclusions about their effects on growth or innovation. [AB-W007, pp. 13–16, appendices 1–2]

Picoli and Takahashi: similar equipment, different incorporation into work#

Florindo Rhaoni Picoli and Adriana Takahashi's 2016 study compares two public schools in Curitiba that received computer laboratories through Paraná Digital. Both received twenty computers in 2007 and had access to training and online manuals. The researchers collected interviews, documents and nonparticipant observations in 2013, reconstructing implementation since the programme began. They deliberately selected schools with contrasting levels of use and broadly comparable staffing, enrollment and location. [AB-W008, pp. 8–12]

At Professora Luiza Ross, earlier experience with a school computer laboratory helped staff approach the new equipment, although its Linux system differed from the software many already knew. Formal meetings and training were joined by informal exchanges during breaks. Staff discussed successful and unsuccessful experiences, tried the technology in practical situations and adapted how they worked. The authors associate these interactions with the transformation and use of knowledge obtained through the programme. [AB-W008, pp. 9–11]

At Santo Agostinho, staff also had some personal computer experience and access to the programme's support. The researchers nevertheless found little exchange about classroom use or change in teaching routines. The reported use was student internet research outside classes, without pedagogical guidance. The source's comparative coding locates the difference beyond initial introduction and understanding, in the sharing, experimentation and incorporation of knowledge into work. The knowledge-sharing account in S42 gives a neighboring treatment of support after transfer. [AB-W008, pp. 11–16; W088]

Picoli and Takahashi distinguish their observed knowledge-flow processes from a stronger claim about organization-wide learning. They say the latter would require deeper investigation of changes in culture, values and practice. Prior laboratory experience, space and other institutional differences also remain part of the comparison. The evidence develops an account of how people came to use supplied

technology; computer-use totals and staff reports do not themselves measure improvements in students' learning. [AB-W008, pp. 13–17]

Zhang and colleagues: imported technology and delayed innovation effort#

Zhang Jie, Chen Zhiyuan, Wu Shufeng and Sun Wenhao's 2020 article investigates the relation between foreign technology introduction and firms' own innovation effort. Its firm-level analysis uses the 2008– 2014 National Enterprise Innovation Survey database. The principal outcomes are spending on science and technology activity per science and technology worker, including a measure net of government funding. Technology-introduction expenditure is excluded from those outcomes. The study therefore examines changes in further innovation inputs rather than directly measuring inventions, productivity or operational mastery. [AB-W009, pp. 93–95]

The authors address reverse causation using an instrument based on government catalogues encouraging technology and product imports, matched to industries and lagged to allow for implementation. Their instrumental-variable estimates do not show a statistically significant contemporaneous increase in the spending outcomes. More consistent positive estimates appear for outcomes two years ahead. They interpret the delay through the work of learning, digestion and assimilation following a technology purchase. The estimates rely on the policy instrument's assumptions, while the learning process remains the authors' explanation of the observed delay. [AB-W009, pp. 94–98, tables 2–3]

Their theoretical model and subsequent comparisons also distinguish firms by position relative to industry leaders. The more consistent positive spending responses occur in the middle portions of their innovation-gap distribution. The reported tables are less uniform than a simple middle-only rule: one measure in the most distant group has weakly significant positive estimates. The model and the data comparisons make the initial capabilities and competitive setting relevant to the question, while the estimated delay and group boundaries remain properties of this investigation. [AB-W009, pp. 98–103, table 4]

Polterovich: institutions can change with acquired capabilities#

Victor Polterovich's 2009 account of building a national innovation system argues for intermediate institutions that help relax constraints on further development. His technological borrowing includes choosing a technology, obtaining rights, adapting it to local conditions, constructing prototypes and testing. The receiving activity can itself modify or improve what was acquired. Domestic scientific work remains important for adaptation, so borrowing and new knowledge creation are not mutually exclusive phases in his argument. [AB-W010, “Problem statement: seeking a strategy of intermediate institutions”; “Absorptive and innovative capabilities of a country”; “Transition to innovative development”]

A proposed institutional sequence changes as firms become able to do more.
