Polterovich reports the establishment of Korea's KIET in 1976 to support learning in semiconductor technologies and coordinate research. In the historical account he cites, the growth of corporate research led to a reorientation of that institution eight years later toward basic research supporting innovation. He uses the example to explain why an organization built to compensate for a missing capability can require a different role once that capability develops elsewhere. This is his report from the cited development literature. [AB-W010, “Main agents of technology imitation: the state and large firms”]

His account also examines interdependent investment. Refineries can hesitate over costly modernization while domestic equipment producers hesitate over supplying machinery without assured demand; downstream production may require changes as well. He proposes repeated interaction among public authorities, business, workers and consumers to coordinate expectations and investments. Indicative planning is an intermediate institution in this argument, capable of changing or receding as other

relations become adequate. His prescriptions concern catching-up development and its institutional conditions, and he expressly rejects a universal recipe for dividing resources between basic research and borrowing-based modernization. [AB-W010, “Escaping the trap: increasing absorptive capability through interactive planning”; “Transition to innovative development”; “Situation in Russia: approaches to modernization”]

Collier and colleagues: investing resource revenues requires an investment process#

Paul Collier, Frederick van der Ploeg, Michael Spence and Anthony Venables examine the use of resource revenues in capital-scarce economies. Their 2009 account distinguishes a high return on small additions to existing capital from the returns obtainable when investment expands rapidly. A spending increase can run into construction, skills and other domestic supply constraints. Prices then rise and other activities can be displaced. Some equipment can be imported, but productive, human and managerial capabilities are not all obtainable through an international purchase. [AB-W005, section 4.1]

The response they discuss includes changing the supply conditions. Investment in infrastructure and skills can support private production; administrative barriers, equipment-import delays and earlier underinvestment can otherwise restrict the response to new demand. They also distinguish technical and informational limitations from incentives that favor diversion or poorly chosen projects. A larger budget does not settle which of these difficulties a spending system faces. [AB-W005, sections 4.1, 4.5]

Their account separates ownership of the funds, control of aggregate spending and choice of individual projects. Transfers to citizens, public spending, domestic lending and foreign-asset accumulation allocate those functions differently. Passing project decisions to private actors can use their information and incentives, but the argument still requires channels that connect savers with productive investments. Their discussion of public expenditure separately examines honesty and efficiency, scrutiny before and after spending, and enforcement through authority, citizens, peers and professional conduct. [AB-W005, sections 4.2–4.5, tables 1–2]

Revenue volatility adds a different timing problem. A buffer of liquid foreign assets can protect spending from abrupt revenue changes, yet a fund large enough to stabilize everything can postpone valuable domestic consumption and investment. The authors consider allowing investment flows to vary while the accumulated capital stock changes less sharply. They also discuss designing construction-sector employment and financial commitments to withstand contractions. The capacity to manage an investment programme includes its response to lower revenues as well as to an initial expansion. [AB-W005, sections 5.1–5.3]

Their conclusion about a liquidity fund is consequently conditional on its role in the investment process. It can buy time for adjustment. It can also become counterproductive if saving overseas substitutes for developing the ability to invest effectively at home. Their proposed task is to restructure that process for a higher and more variable level of investment, with buffering as one instrument in the adjustment. [AB-W005, section 5.3]

S104 Consultancy and the client's capacity to act#

Inquiring into an engagement together#

Lambrechts and colleagues describe Edgar Schein’s process consultation as joint inquiry. A consultant and client consider an interaction while the participants can still examine how it unfolds. That work differs in purpose from a consultant’s report produced after collecting facts from others. The authors develop Schein’s account through their emphasis on relationships and on choices participants can author together. Their reconstruction gives process consultation a place among different ways of organizing a commission. [T06-W001]

Loizos Heracleous distinguishes interventions that ask a client to explain an episode from those that supply a concept or suggest an action. In his account of working with NASA, he describes a two-hour workshop on how to assess the value of the agency’s relationships with other organizations. The senior sponsor introduced the workshop and left. Heracleous supplied a framework for discussing the relationships, and participants used it to consider what criteria their agency could adopt. They did not finish choosing the criteria within the time allotted. [T06-W002]

The sponsor later expressed dissatisfaction with how little had been settled. The division leader and other participants told Heracleous that the framework had helped them think through the relationships and that they intended to use it in subsequent internal discussions. Heracleous decided against a further intervention. His account records the sponsor’s judgment and the participants’ intended next step. [T06-W002]

Work on both sides of the commission#

Isabel Boni-Le Goff examines management consultants in France through the demands of client service and the career pressures inside consulting firms. Consultants move across assignments and present work to clients while doing other work for colleagues and supervisors. The expectation of advancement or departure creates a second audience for their efforts. The account distinguishes what a client receives from the professional judgments governing a consultant’s career. [T06-W003]

Francesco Ciampi asks what knowledge is created during consulting and which organization can use it. His inquiry includes interviews with 15 medium and large Italian firms in 2015. Client learning and a consultancy’s ability to reuse what it learned are separate outcomes in this account. S53 addresses a related question about a recipient’s capacity to absorb outside knowledge. [T06-W004]

Following an intervention into operations#

In Bloom and colleagues’ field experiment in Indian textile firms, treatment and comparison plants both received a month of diagnostic consulting. The treatment plants received a further four months of intensive help putting recommended practices into use. One practice was to classify and record weaving defects daily. The authors illustrate how the resulting quality index could flag a faulty loom for discussion at the next day’s quality meeting, where it had previously been possible for such a problem to persist for weeks. [T06-W005]

After the implementation phase, the authors estimated that the treatment reduced the weighted quality-defect index by about 43 percent relative to the comparison, based on the intervention coefficient in Table II. They also reported lower yarn inventories and higher weaving output. The defect estimate is for the intervention package. Daily logging and review are among the practices the authors use to explain how it could improve quality. [T06-W005]

The authors also tracked practices at five other plants owned by treatment firms. By August 2010, adoption at those plants had risen by 17.5 percentage points. The authors report that firm directors copied practices from the plants that received the intervention. The researchers returned in 2011 to collect longer-run performance and management data. The trial’s comparison establishes an operational result, and the account of copying shows a specific use of the practices elsewhere within the firms. [T06-W005]

S58 Transfer and persistence of organizational capability#

A practice working in one place may be difficult to establish elsewhere. These accounts examine the transfer process, the work of reproducing an operating organization and the dependence of an individual’s performance on the setting. They ask what the receiving unit can do and what support makes that possible. S53 develops investment in receiving capacity; the material here follows particular attempts to transfer or reproduce capability.

Szulanski: transferring a practice through actual use#

Gabriel Szulanski’s 1996 study treated the transfer of a best practice as the recreation of coordinating relationships among resources. A practice could already work in one unit while remaining difficult to establish in another unit of the same company. He divided this process into initiation, implementation, ramp-up, and integration. The decision to transfer was followed by exchanges of resources and preparation, then by actual use and attempts to reach satisfactory performance, and finally by efforts to sustain routine use. A signed decision or a completed installation therefore did not exhaust the transfer process. [CG-W017, pp. 28–30]

Szulanski distinguished a transfer’s cost from the difficulty that people experienced while carrying it out. Costs could be hard to interpret without knowing what the same transfer would have cost in the absence of problems. Moreover, two equally expensive problems might place very different demands on an organization. One could be handled through established procedures; another could require senior managers and improvised coordination. His alternative was to examine the transfer’s “eventfulness”: the nonroutine problems that called for special attention. A company with established ways of handling an otherwise demanding transfer might experience it as relatively uneventful. The measure consequently concerned difficulty in relation to the organization undertaking the transfer. [CG-W017, pp. 29–30]

The four stages made that difficulty more specific. Before the decision to transfer, participants had to identify a need, recognize a promising practice, and investigate its suitability. During implementation they had to establish communication, prepare resources, and make adaptations. During ramp-up, actual use exposed problems that preparations had missed. The questionnaire asked, for example, whether trained people left, replacements were poorly qualified, changes introduced further problems, or support teams disbanded because other work intervened. Integration concerned maintaining the practice after satisfactory performance had first been achieved. Temporary workarounds could become habitual, unresolved problems could be displaced by daily pressures, or the recipient could reconsider adoption. These questionnaire items made visible several ways in which a transfer could remain incomplete after an apparently successful start. [CG-W017, pp. 28–30, 41–42]

The survey collected 271 questionnaires concerning 122 transfers of 38 practices in eight companies. Responses came from source units, recipient units, and third parties. The practices required coordinated work by multiple people; they included software-development procedures, drawing standards, appraisal, and activity-based costing. Szulanski measured difficulty partly through the problems participants encountered at each stage. His measures of the recipient’s ability to absorb knowledge included existing technical and managerial competence, clear responsibilities, and knowing whom to approach for help. The relationship between units was measured through the difficulty of communication and each side’s readiness to collaborate. These were organizational conditions of learning, rather than a count of documents delivered. [CG-W017, pp. 32–34, 41–43]

The strongest barriers in the survey analysis were limited recipient absorptive capacity, uncertainty about why the practice worked, and a laborious relationship between source and recipient. Motivational barriers were less prominent in this sample. The first analysis used 87 complete observations; excluding

an outcome measure increased the usable set to 142 and preserved the ordering of the three leading barriers. These were associations among survey measures, with transfers reported four to eight months after first use. Aborted transfers were difficult to include, and the design could not establish that changing a particular barrier would cause a corresponding improvement. Szulanski accordingly presented investment in learning capacity, relationships, and understanding practices as an alternative to relying only on incentives. [CG-W017, pp. 35–38]

The study’s unexpected result for retentive capacity also concerned timing. Its coefficient had the opposite sign from the one anticipated. Szulanski suggested that, only four to eight months after first use, some established routines might still preserve the old practice rather than the new one. Replacing them could itself be difficult. He offered this as a possible interpretation of a survey result, rather than evidence that retaining knowledge generally harms transfer. In interpreting the leading barriers, he instead stressed the recipient’s prior ability to understand and use the practice, uncertainty about its workings, and access to help from the source. [CG-W017, pp. 36–38]

Winter and Szulanski: reproduce the capability to operate#

Winter and Szulanski called a transfer broad in scope when it created or substantially changed the recipient organization’s context. Recreating an outlet capable of producing a service locally required more than relabeling goods received from a central supplier. It involved a collection of routines, people, equipment, supplies, and procedures. The central organization therefore needed knowledge of the features customers valued, the processes producing those features, the resources needed by those processes, and the environments where the combination could work. Their account distinguished copying the visible result from developing the capability to establish and maintain its production elsewhere. [CG-W018, pp. 732–733]

In Replication as Strategy (2001), Sidney Winter and Gabriel Szulanski distinguished a working example, or template, from the features that were both worth reproducing and reproducible elsewhere. Their term for knowledge of those features, how to create them, and suitable environments was the “Arrow core.” A successful outlet might also contain irrelevant details, a manager’s unrepeatable talents, or advantages peculiar to its location. Its success alone did not identify which elements a new outlet needed. The authors described learning through successive attempts, followed by a decision to stabilize a business model for wider replication. [CG-W018, pp. 731–736]

The template supplied something that a description alone could not: a functioning example to consult when a difficulty arose. Yet it could embody many things that a replicator should not reproduce. Winter and Szulanski offered a thought experiment about a successful local business whose profits might depend on an unusually capable manager or on local access to inexpensive skilled workers. They also used the example of a diner whose apple pie might travel well while its proprietor’s decorating tastes would not. Their question was which parts of a successful combination could be reproduced, at what cost, and in which other environments. This was the purpose of distinguishing the Arrow core from the actual outlet that served as a template. [CG-W018, pp. 733–735]

Their Banc One example concerned acquired banks being converted to common computer systems and operating procedures. A recently converted sister bank, selected for comparable systems and market conditions, supplied a working reference. Staff could visit it, receive training, and obtain temporary specialist assistance. A separate model bank provided a place to try new systems and procedures without disturbing an operating bank. The central organization’s job included selecting examples, training staff, and coordinating the conversion, rather than merely distributing software and instructions. [CG-W018, pp. 737–738]

Banc One Systems Corporation coordinated the conversion. In the authors’ reported history, departmental work initially proceeded with limited coordination and tacit procedures. The later creation of conversion management brought documentation, meetings across application groups and explicit attention to dependencies. Problems encountered during conversions became checkpoints and tasks. The organization doing the transfer developed alongside the transfers it carried out. [CG-W018, pp. 737–739]

The authors also examined combining selected features from different outlets. A proposed outlet might borrow one element from a St. Louis design and another from a San Francisco innovation. They argued that such a combination could introduce interactions absent from either original. The same employees might, for example, have to carry out both activities, creating conflicts over schedules and workloads. A mix of individually successful parts was consequently a different proposition from copying an operating whole. The authors allowed that new combinations could produce favorable interactions as well as problems. Their hypothesis favored guidance by a working template during exploitation; it did not establish that every combination or adaptation would fail. [CG-W018, pp. 735–736]

The authors proposed that using a working template, and initially copying it closely, could improve replication once early exploration had produced a satisfactory model. They also described the costs of this approach: copying irrelevant features, delaying improvement, and reproducing a design poorly suited to its new environment. Their precision-versus-adaptation argument was a set of hypotheses, illustrated by reported organizational experience. The Banc One account described 1970–1995 and did not establish a controlled comparison of replication methods. [CG-W018, pp. 735–739, endnotes 2, 7–8]

Huckman and Pisano: performance that depends on the setting#

Robert Huckman and Gary Pisano’s The Effect of Organizational Context on Individual Performance (2003) examined whether a skilled person’s performance could be carried unchanged between organizations. Their setting was coronary artery bypass graft surgery in Pennsylvania in 1994–1995. Many surgeons worked at more than one hospital during the same period, while nurses, technicians, anesthesiologists, and other resources were supplied by the hospitals. This allowed the researchers to compare a surgeon’s results across organizations without relying solely on a move from one employer to another many years apart. The underlying records covered more than 38,000 procedures by 203 surgeons at 43 hospitals. [CG-W019, pp. 1–10]

The principal regressions treated death in hospital following an individual procedure as the outcome. They included patient characteristics and clinical conditions, calendar-quarter effects, and measures of prior surgeon and hospital quality. The key comparison divided a surgeon’s case volume in the preceding quarter into procedures at the hospital where the current operation occurred and procedures at other hospitals. Using prior-quarter volume was intended to reduce reverse-causality concerns. A specification with hospital fixed effects checked whether the relationship survived a different way of accounting for stable hospital differences. The study did not randomly allocate surgeons or patients between hospitals. [CG-W019, pp. 11–18]

Higher volume at the current hospital was associated with a lower probability of death; volume at other hospitals had a much smaller, statistically insignificant association. In the first hospital-specific specification, a one-standard-deviation increase in local volume corresponded to a 0.34-percentage-point reduction relative to a predicted mortality probability of 1.8 percent. The corresponding estimate for volume elsewhere was 0.01 percentage points. The local and elsewhere coefficients differed at the 3 percent significance level in the first four specifications, including the hospital-fixed-effects comparison. These results concerned where a surgeon had recently performed procedures, rather than treating all of that surgeon’s experience as interchangeable. [CG-W019, pp. 17–18]

Huckman and Pisano considered two explanations for this hospital specificity. Familiarity with a hospital’s people and resources could improve coordination. Alternatively, a surgeon accounting for a large share of the hospital’s business might obtain preferential access to its resources. To investigate the latter explanation they added the surgeon’s share of the hospital’s procedure volume. Local volume retained its association with mortality, but the statistical distinction between local volume and volume elsewhere weakened to the 13 percent level. The share measure was only a proxy for influence and was correlated with local volume. The authors accordingly described the separation of familiarity and influence as suggestive. The data did not identify whether particular employees, team structures, or operating routines were responsible. [CG-W019, pp. 18–22]

Their staffing implications followed from this limited portability of measured performance. Hiring a highly skilled individual might not reproduce the results that person achieved with another organization’s complementary resources. The study also raised a question about dividing skilled workers among projects or units. Its evidence remained specific to cardiac surgery in this period. It could not distinguish learning to work together from a stable compatibility between a surgeon and a hospital. The authors’ estimates of the benefits from consolidating split practice were thought experiments under simplifying assumptions, rather than observed results from a consolidation program. [CG-W019, pp. 4–6, 19–22]

S07 and S12 develop neighboring accounts of organizational knowledge and retained expertise. The studies here concern the work of recreating a practice and the conditions under which demonstrated performance can be sustained in another setting.

S15 Institutions, messages and invested forms: what people can rely on#

Hayek: acting without knowing every cause#

F. A. Hayek's The Use of Knowledge in Society asks how an economic arrangement can make use of knowledge dispersed among people. The selected argument distinguishes scientific knowledge from knowledge of particular circumstances of time and place. Relevant knowledge is not already collected in one mind. The organizational question is how decisions can use it when needs, supplies and opportunities change. [W016, §§I–V]

Prices can communicate a relevant change without conveying its full history. In the tin example, people can economize on a scarcer input without each learning whether its scarcity arose from a new use or a lost supply. Changes in their demand affect other people and substitutes. The proposed economy concerns what a participant must know in order to adjust. [W016, §§IV–V, pp. 523–526]

Hayek explicitly resists the idea that a developed production apparatus makes important economic decisions necessary only at long intervals. Local adjustments continue. The price signal complements knowledge of available capacities and opportunities rather than replacing that knowledge with a complete centrally supplied instruction. [W016]

Ostrom: contingent commitment retains monitoring#

The selected passage from Elinor Ostrom's Governing the Commons concerns contingent commitments, observation and graduated sanctions. Participants' willingness to continue following rules depends partly on knowing that others generally do so. Monitoring makes behavior visible, while graduated responses allow the institution to address violations without treating every departure as a reason to abandon the whole arrangement. [W049, p. 186]

Local governance sustains cooperation by distributing responsibility for rules, monitoring, judging exceptions and applying graduated responses. [W049, p. 186]

Hurwicz: prescribed rules and feasible behavior differ#

Leonid Hurwicz's prize lecture But Who Will Guard the Guardians? connects mechanism design with information, feasible conduct and enforcement. Its selected opening sections examine information decentralization and limits of message exchange, while later selected sections distinguish the actions permitted by a rule from the actions people can actually take. A mechanism analyzed only over its prescribed legal strategies can omit profitable violations. [TA-W001, selected pp. 280–286]

The lecture calls the larger set the true strategy domain. Illegal actions can still have consequences. Enforcement matters because those actions are feasible; if violations were impossible, the enforcement question would have a different form. An equilibrium among permitted actions therefore need not be self-enforcing when a participant can move outside that set. The relevant institution includes the arrangements that affect the attractiveness and consequences of those departures. [TA-W001, p. 285]

Hurwicz's discussion of genuine implementation is correspondingly broad. His social-security illustration includes procedures for determining eligibility, calculating payments, collecting funds and authorizing the institutions that do the work. A desired allocation written in legislation does not perform those activities itself. Money, information and administrative capacity are part of implementation in this sense. The lecture distinguishes that meaning from narrower technical uses of the same term. [TA-W001, p. 286]

The argument is not that enforcement is universally impossible because guardians would require an infinite chain of guardians. The lecture uses that challenge to investigate how enforcement can be organized. [TA-W001]

Hurwicz and Reiter: informational requirements are design variables#

The introduction to Hurwicz and Stanley Reiter's Designing Economic Mechanisms treats the mechanism itself as a design variable. Given agents, an environment class and a goal, alternative decentralized arrangements can be compared by their informational requirements. Privacy means that an agent cannot simply observe another's private circumstances: information not directly observed has to arrive through an appropriate communication process. [TA-W002, introduction, pp. 1–6]

The introduction distinguishes realizing a goal when agents do not use information strategically from implementing it when they do. It also distinguishes recognizing an equilibrium from finding one. In a verification scenario, agents can respond to an announced candidate; unanimity of appropriate confirmations verifies it. That does not establish a practical process that discovers the candidate or reaches it dynamically within a deadline. [TA-W002, pp. 2–3]

The size of a message space supplies one way to compare mechanisms' information requirements. It is not a count of all resources involved in an institution. The introduction separately lists observation precision, communication, computation, losses from strategic behavior and enforcement. It describes cost comparison in a vectorial sense, and expressly says that computation is not treated formally in the book, although discussed in places. A smaller message space cannot therefore be presented as a proved minimum of every operating cost. [TA-W002, pp. 3–4]

Groves and Radner: the value of a restricted message exchange#

Theodore Groves and Roy Radner's Allocation of Resources in a Team studies decisions made after limited communication rather than assuming an adjustment process has run to completion. Enterprise managers observe local production information, and a resource manager observes available supply. The model asks which decision rules maximize expected total output under alternative information structures. A common objective is assumed; inducing truthful messages and obedience through incentives is set aside. [TA-W003, pp. 415–420]

In the selected quadratic model, a single price-and-demand exchange can have the same expected payoff as specified more informative one-stage messages. Theorem 2 compares a declared class: a resource message goes to enterprise managers, replies return to the resource manager, and communication among enterprises is prohibited. Additional information can have zero marginal value for the model's criterion even though the alternative message is more informative. That is the particular informational economy being described. [TA-W003, pp. 435–437]

The premises remain substantial. Quadratic production, the probability structure, the common expected-output objective and the timing and direction of messages matter. The introductory simple model assumes independent local variations and corresponding similarities among enterprises. The source explicitly distinguishes these results from the full-information comparator and observes that the optimal decisions need not maximize each enterprise's profit at a common price. It also leaves the optimal choice of information-processing technology outside the analysis. [TA-W003, pp. 416, 418–420]

Smith: exclusion as a limited-information interface#

Henry Smith's Property as the Law of Things proposes an architectural account of property through information costs. Specifying every possible relationship among every pair of people and every use of

resources would be difficult. A thing-based exclusion boundary can let outsiders respect a relatively simple instruction without learning all the uses and decisions inside it. [TA-W005, pp. 1691–1694, 1699– 1705]

His Blackacre example makes the mechanism concrete. An owner can choose among many uses without coordinating every choice with every neighbor. The law need not enumerate them all. Some activities, however, cause effects outside the boundary, such as nuisance, and require more detailed governance. Exclusion supplies a baseline; it does not settle every interaction. The ends still concern people's interests in using things. [TA-W005, p. 1704]

Different audiences need different information. Strangers can use a standardized boundary message. Potential transactors may need formal information about the interest offered. Insiders need richer arrangements for their own interactions. Notice, records and governance remain work. Smith also treats water and information as cases where interactions can make simple compartmentalization less adequate, rather than claiming all resources are naturally separable. [TA-W005, selected pp. 1699–1705, 1709– 1711]

The account explicitly draws on modularity arguments associated with Simon and Baldwin; those are the author's connections. Enforcement, competing uses and distributional judgments are not eliminated by the informational convenience of a boundary. [TA-W005]

Merrill: information savings do not exhaust ownership#

Thomas Merrill's response Property as Modularity agrees with much of the information-cost account. He finds modularity helpful for explaining why a property system presents different levels of complexity to strangers, transactors and insiders. A person outside the arrangement can rely on a relatively simple message while intricate relationships remain inside. [TA-W006, pp. 151–155]

His reservation is that a structural description can understate incentives and residual authority. Ownership includes the capacity to rearrange uses and claim the returns from doing so. Exclusion does more than reduce outsiders' information requirements: it can support initiative and continuing management. The critique therefore asks what the modular picture leaves less visible, rather than denying every informational advantage. [TA-W006, especially pp. 151–152]

The response is a reasoned criticism of explanatory emphasis. Smith's and Merrill's work has a partly shared authorship history. [TA-W005; TA-W006]

Diaz-Bone: invested forms extend coordination but retain interpretation#

Rainer Diaz-Bone's chapter reconstructs the economics of convention. It treats coordination as occurring in equipped situations that include material arrangements, categories, standards and conventions of evaluation. People do not arrive at each encounter without shared forms, but neither do those forms mechanically determine one interpretation in every situation. [GL-W031, chapter discussion]

Through Eymard-Duvernay and Thévenot, Diaz-Bone describes investment in cognitive as well as material forms. Organizations invest in means of recognizing relevant information, and those forms can extend coordination across time and space. A classification, label or standard can make future recognition and comparison possible without repeating all the original work of agreement. [GL-W031, investment in forms]

Plurality is integral to the reconstruction. Different conventions support different evaluations, and competent actors judge appropriateness, switch conventions, criticize one another or construct compromises. The approach rejects a single best method of coordination for all production, distribution

and consumption situations. Its treatment of law also includes enacted interpretation rather than treating law solely as an external constraint. [GL-W031, conventions, plural evaluation and law]

Diaz-Bone reconstructs the investment-in-forms argument of Laurent Thévenot's 1984 Rules and implements: investment in forms. [GL-W032, through GL-W031]

The abstract of Thévenot’s Organized Complexity presents the firm as an arrangement compromising among modes of coordination and evaluation. Plural requirements enter the description of the firm itself. [GL-W033, abstract]

Rules and standards: when specification work is done#

Louis Kaplow's Rules Versus Standards distinguishes giving legal content in advance from determining it later. Its repository abstract also separates that timing question from complexity and identifies promulgation, learning and enforcement costs. The relevant point is that moving a decision into an advance rule can change when and by whom interpretive work is performed; rule and simplicity are not synonyms. [GL-W043, abstract]

Lehavi's chapter excerpt develops the front-end/back-end tradeoff between advance specification and later interpretation or enforcement. [GL-W043; GL-W094, chapter excerpt]

A reusable provision can make later decisions easier. Its value depends on how often it can be reused and which differences between cases require fresh interpretation. [GL-W043; GL-W094]

Scharpf: a broker can reduce consultations without eliminating politics#

Fritz Scharpf's The Joint-Decision Trap Revisited examines mixed-motive bargaining, vetoes and the status quo in historical German and European arrangements. A compulsory negotiation system differs from one where parties can simply act separately if talks fail. Once an agreed rule binds them, a veto can prevent others from correcting it when circumstances change. Agreement and the absence of agreement therefore have consequences that a simple voluntary-exchange picture can miss. [SG-W025, selected body]

The central-proposer comparison identifies a possible organizational economy. With N participants and a salient concerns for each, the displayed all-channel comparison counts N(N−1)a2 impact examinations. A central agent's consultations are represented by Na. For fixed a, the first expression is quadratic, despite the text's exponential adjective. These are idealized consultation counts, not a measurement of the full cost of bargaining or a general proof of administrative efficiency. [SG-W025, printed pp. 850–851]

The broker still needs knowledge. The account describes extensive consultation with governments, interests and experts to identify constraints and develop proposals preferred to the status quo. The agent must be accepted as an honest broker, and a suitable mutually acceptable solution must exist. Its knowledge-gathering and design work have not vanished merely because every pair of participants need not perform the same comparison. [SG-W025, pp. 850–851]

Scharpf expressly says that the broker cannot solve an empty solution space. Preference diversity, transaction costs, political dynamics and compulsory commitments continue to limit agreement. His discussion qualifies pessimism about joint decisions rather than replacing it with an unrestricted case for centralization. [SG-W025, pp. 2–8, 16–17]

Signals, commitments and institutional boundaries#

These selected sources explain several forms of reliance: a scarcity signal, a monitored commitment, a restricted message, a property boundary, an invested classification, an advance rule and a broker's proposal. Their criteria and institutional premises remain different.

Across the accounts, the reader can recover which information may be omitted by a particular participant and where observation, interpretation, adjustment or enforcement must continue. [W016; W049; TA-W001; TA-W002; TA-W003; TA-W005; TA-W006; GL-W031; SG-W025]

S59 Expectations, public signals and reflexive feedback#

An announcement can matter because of what it reveals, because people can see that others have received it, or because it changes the consequences of acting alone. Prices, votes and other observable actions can themselves become information. The following accounts examine these processes through communication, investment decisions and the interaction between financial markets and institutions. They ask what participants can observe, what they infer, how they are evaluated, and how their responses change subsequent events.

Chwe: knowing that others received the message#

Michael Suk-Young Chwe's 1998 article starts with two coworkers who usually leave the bus together for a drink. On a crowded journey they become separated. A mutual acquaintance calls to invite them off at another stop. Each would enjoy joining the acquaintance, but mainly wants the other's company. Both may hear the invitation and nevertheless remain on the bus: neither is sure that the other heard it and will get off. The message has reached both people without supplying the assurance each needs to act. [EF-W003, pp. 49–50]

Knowing that the other heard is not always enough. One coworker may see the other look up but remain unsure whether the other has noticed that the invitation was mutually received. Chwe uses this progression to explain common knowledge: everyone knows something, everyone knows that everyone knows it, and the corresponding further levels hold. In the example, mutually observed eye contact supplies an immediate way to establish the relevant shared awareness. The communication problem includes what people know about one another's reception of the message. [EF-W003, pp. 49–50]

The dependence on joint participation matters. Chwe changes the example so that one coworker's partner is calling from the street. That coworker will get off regardless of what the other does. The remaining coworker then needs to know that the invitation was heard, but need not obtain the same assurance about mutual awareness. The original difficulty came from each wanting to participate only if the other participated. [EF-W003, p. 50]

Chwe applies this argument to the physical organization of public encounters. In inward-facing circles, people can observe others receiving a communication and reacting to it. His discussion of circular seating at Fort Worth's city hall emphasizes the audience's visual contact with one another as well as with the council. His reconstruction of revolutionary festivals similarly distinguishes the circle's symbolic meaning from the opportunity it gives spectators to see one another. Removing partitions or arranging sight lines can change this opportunity even when the spoken content remains the same. [EF-W003, pp. 58–59]

Publicity also enters his account of advertising. A buyer may value a product more when others use it, as with compatible computers or goods consumed together. Advertising on a conspicuously popular programme can inform viewers that many other viewers have encountered the product. Chwe compares advertising for 119 brands over three representative months of a network year. The eighteen brands classified as social goods appeared before larger audiences and paid substantially more per viewer than the other brands. The comparison is suggestive: the available brands were not a representative sample, classification was partly judgmental, and the social group was dominated by products aimed at men, particularly beer. [EF-W003, pp. 59–63, tables 1–2]

Chwe also addresses the apparent implausibility of indefinitely repeated beliefs about beliefs. People need not consciously recite an infinite chain. They can rely on familiar situations, recursive recognition or practical heuristics for judging shared awareness. He explicitly distinguishes such supports from a failsafe communication procedure. Common knowledge helps explain coordinated action without guaranteeing it. [EF-W003, p. 66]

Informational cascades: more followers need not mean more evidence#

Sushil Bikhchandani, David Hirshleifer and Ivo Welch's 1992 article examines a different reason for doing what others do. Participants decide sequentially whether to adopt an action. They observe predecessors' choices, but not their private information. Each also receives a private signal about whether adoption is worthwhile. The model's payoffs do not require a taste for conformity or a reward for agreeing with other people. Earlier actions matter because they may reveal information. [EF-W005, pp. 994–996]

In the article's elementary example, adoption has a known cost and an uncertain benefit, with two possible values. A signal is more likely to favor adoption when adoption is valuable. The first person's choice reveals that person's signal. The second combines this information with a new private signal, using a random tie-break when the two indications balance. After two preceding adoptions, the third person can find adoption preferable even after receiving an unfavorable signal. After two rejections the corresponding reversal occurs. With one adoption and one rejection, the third person's own signal again determines the choice. [EF-W005, pp. 996–997, table 1]

The consequential step is the loss of information in subsequent actions. Once someone chooses the same action regardless of the private signal received, observing that choice tells later participants nothing about that signal. Later people can then face the same informational balance and make the same choice. Many identical decisions may therefore rest on the information conveyed by only a few early decisions. They are not necessarily many independent confirmations of the action's merit. [EF-W005, pp. 998–1001]

The authors compare this with a setting in which previous signals remain observable. An individual may still choose against a private signal, but the signal enters the common information pool. Enough contrary signals can eventually reverse behavior. In the actions-only setting, signals arriving after the cascade begins remain hidden behind identical choices. The difference concerns what an observed action preserves about the reasoning or evidence behind it. [EF-W005, p. 999]

This also explains the fragility of a cascade. A public disclosure less informative than one person's private signal can make a long-established cascade unravel, because it need only counter the limited information that originally started the process. The crowd's size has not continually deepened its evidential basis. The article distinguishes disclosure before a cascade from disclosure afterward. An early noisy disclosure can change predecessors' choices in a way that reduces what later people learn from those choices; after a cascade has begun, new public information can add evidence without destroying information that later actions were still transmitting. These are results about the specified sequence and information structure. [EF-W005, pp. 1004–1007]

Scharfstein and Stein: the reputation gained by following others#

David Scharfstein and Jeremy Stein's 1990 model makes evaluation by other people part of the decision. Two managers consider investing in a cost-saving technology, with the first deciding before the second. Each receives a signal about the investment's eventual profitability. The outcome later becomes observable even if neither invests. Investment is available at a fixed price, so the model isolates reputation and inference without also determining a market-clearing asset price. [EF-W004, pp. 465–468]

Managers differ in their ability to obtain useful signals, but initially neither they nor the labor market know which managers have that ability. In the central case, capable managers receive correlated informative signals; other managers receive independent noise. An evaluator can therefore learn about ability from both the investment's eventual success and the similarity of the managers' decisions. Two managers making the same unsuccessful choice may have encountered an adverse circumstance that neither could have foreseen. A manager making an isolated unsuccessful choice has less of that explanation available. The authors call this sharing the blame. [EF-W004, pp. 466–469]

The second manager consequently has a reason to imitate beyond learning whether the investment will be profitable. Agreement can make that manager appear to have received the kind of information a capable colleague received. In the authors' herding equilibrium, the second manager follows the first even when a private signal points elsewhere. The information possessed by both firms need not be reflected in investment. Reputation affects future compensation, and maximizing that compensation can conflict with making the best present investment. [EF-W004, pp. 469–473]

This is a model of incentives within an evaluation system. Its managers need no explicit agreement to suppress private information. Nor does it require evaluators to be unaware of the incentive to imitate: managers' attempts to influence the inference about their ability occur within the equilibrium being analyzed. The definition of ability, what evaluators observe, the sequence of decisions and the dependence between informative signals all enter the original construction. [EF-W004, pp. 468–473]

The paper also develops countervailing incentives. Giving managers a material stake in profits can make sufficiently costly imitation unattractive. Rewarding relative standing can make merely matching another manager less appealing, because imitation prevents becoming the top-ranked performer. A broader conception of ability can reward finding a useful alternative rather than forecasting which of the same two choices will succeed. These changes affect what a manager gains by preserving a distinct judgment. [EF-W004, pp. 475–476]

The authors apply the argument to committee procedure. Sequential public voting may allow later members to echo the first speaker instead of contributing their information. Simultaneous written votes are one proposed response, although they can reduce valuable exchanges of ideas. Another is to let those with stronger reputational concerns speak first; under the conditions discussed, this can mean hearing younger members before established senior members. [EF-W004, pp. 477–478]

A later exchange clarifies what counts as herding#

Marco Ottaviani and Peter Sørensen's comment challenges the original claim that correlated prediction errors are necessary for reputational herding. They connect reputational imitation with statistical learning from predecessors' choices. An observed decision can change both the probability assigned to a favorable state and the reputational payoff associated with acting in that state. Relaxing a restriction on prior probabilities allows cases in which a later manager disregards private information even without the original form of conditional signal correlation. Their account gives learning and evaluation joint roles in the resulting decision. [EF-W009, opening argument; EF-W010, pp. 705–706]

In their 2000 reply, Scharfstein and Stein accept that result under the comment's broader definition, but distinguish it from a manager always following a predecessor. A sufficiently favorable prior can make even the first manager ignore a contrary signal. After an informative first action, the second manager can face similarly favorable odds and invest regardless of a new signal. In that case, the second manager could make the same choice even if evaluators could not observe the predecessor's action and could not tell that copying had occurred. The reply reserves the stronger sharing-the-blame interpretation for the mechanism in which visible agreement itself improves the evaluation. The exchange separates sometimes ignoring information, always copying another person, and benefiting from being seen to agree. [EF-W010, pp. 705–706]

Orléan: the resale price changes what it is rational to anticipate#

André Orléan's 1988 article, L'auto-référence dans la théorie keynésienne de la spéculation, reconstructs Keynes's distinction between estimating an asset's productive returns and anticipating its resale price. A person intending to hold an asset indefinitely has to consider its future income. A person expecting to sell also needs to consider the price another buyer will pay. The two valuations can be algebraically

compatible while depending on different activities of inquiry: examining productive conditions, or anticipating other market participants' judgments. [EF-W006, pp. 229–231]

Orléan emphasizes the institutional role of negotiability. The possibility of selling a financial claim does not make the corresponding physical investment withdrawable by the community as a whole. It does, however, expose the individual holder to changing market quotations. In the example he draws from Keynes, someone can judge an investment's long-term value to be thirty while expecting the market to value it at twenty in three months. Paying twenty-five now need not be attractive merely because the long-term assessment is higher. Expectations about a prospective transaction affect the sensible present action. [EF-W006, pp. 231–233]

Resources also affect whether a person can maintain a long-term position. Someone exposed to an unexpected need to liquidate cannot simply disregard an adverse current quotation, however confident that person is about eventual productive returns. Orléan uses this dependence to explain why attention to short-term market judgment can follow from the organization of a liquid market, rather than from a fixed personal disposition to speculate. In his interpretation, the same participant can be drawn into market-oriented anticipation by the conditions under which commitments must be financed and revised. [EF-W006, pp. 233–234]

Self-reference enters when the object being anticipated is produced by participants' anticipations. Each tries to anticipate the average judgment while recognizing that others are doing likewise. Orléan's discussion of Keynes's beauty contest gives this its recursive form: success depends on anticipating how other people anticipate the collective selection. A configuration of expectations can be validated by the price that those expectations help produce. Such validation answers a different question from whether investment is serving long-term productive requirements. [EF-W006, pp. 235–238]

Orléan presents this as a substantive reading of Keynes and a challenge to the organization of financial inquiry. He also finds formal resources in rational-expectations models that permit self-validating price paths in addition to a fundamental-value solution. His conclusion asks how conventions, institutions and forms of information beyond private competitive arbitrage can be understood. [EF-W006, pp. 238–241]

Morris and Shin: a public signal can coordinate a common error#

Stephen Morris and Hyun Song Shin's 2002 model gives public information two roles. It informs each participant about an underlying state, and it provides something each expects others to use. Participants want their actions to suit the state, but also want to be close to the actions of other participants. Each observes a shared noisy signal and a separate private signal. Their choices are made together rather than in the sequential chain used in an informational cascade. [EF-W008, pp. 1521–1526]

The equilibrium action places more weight on the public signal than a forecast concerned only with the underlying state would place on it. The reason is strategic: the common signal helps predict what others will do as well as what the state is. Higher-order expectations pull toward the information known to be publicly shared. The same property gives any error in that signal an unusually wide influence. Participants can all respond rationally within the model while reinforcing a common informational error. [EF-W008, pp. 1525–1530]

The welfare result depends on what is being evaluated. The authors construct the rewards for matching others as a zero-sum competition. Those rewards cancel when individual payoffs are added, leaving the average squared distance between actions and the underlying state as the social loss. Individually useful coordination therefore receives more weight in decisions than it receives in this welfare criterion. With a sufficiently strong coordination motive and sufficiently accurate private information, an improvement in a still-noisy public signal can worsen that criterion. [EF-W008, pp. 1524, 1528–1529]

Other cases in the paper preserve the value of information. When the shared signal is the only information available, greater accuracy improves welfare. Greater precision of private signals improves welfare in the central model. The authors also examine what changes when participants want to differentiate their actions rather than match them; the tendency to overweight public information then changes. Their disclosure problem concerns the interaction between signal precision, incentives and the stated objective, including the practical choice between early provisional information and later more accurate information. [EF-W008, pp. 1522–1523, 1529–1532]

Bacchetta and van Wincoop: finding a scapegoat in the price#

Philippe Bacchetta and Eric van Wincoop's 2004 article asks why market participants repeatedly change the importance they assign to particular macroeconomic indicators when explaining exchange rates. Its scapegoat is an observable economic variable given excessive weight through inference from the exchange rate. The model includes observed money supply and output, unobserved currency trades, and uncertainty about the persistence of economic conditions. Investors receive different private signals about the relevant persistence parameters. [EF-W001, pp. 114–116]

An exchange-rate movement is therefore ambiguous. It may reflect unobserved trading, or it may reflect information other investors possess about how persistent a change in money or output will be. Each investor rationally uses the price as a public signal alongside private information. The current price is partly an outcome of participants' expectations and partly evidence from which they estimate what those expectations contain. [EF-W001, pp. 115–116]

Consider the article's case in which money supply is unusually high and the exchange rate rises because of unobserved currency trades. An investor seeing a higher rate than expected can infer that other investors have information suggesting greater monetary persistence. Even investors whose own information gives little reason for that inference can revise their assessment because they do not know everyone else's signals. In the model, the private-signal errors average to zero, yet inference from the price produces a market-wide mistaken estimate. Everyone can think others possess supporting information that no one actually possesses. [EF-W001, pp. 116–117]

The resulting weight affects behavior and the exchange rate. Confusion amplifies the influence of the hidden trading shock and can increase both the actual and perceived importance of the visible monetary variable. Output can become the scapegoat under the corresponding conditions. The model also permits reduced weights, and its average weight can be correct across shocks while particular realizations produce substantial errors. Its result concerns the changing relation between observable conditions, private estimates and a price used as evidence. [EF-W001, pp. 117–118]

The short model limits information differences to one period and rules out bubbles in its later common-information setting. Its authors leave a fuller dynamic account to subsequent work. The operative explanation here is dispersed information and rational signal extraction; an observed indicator becomes influential because of what investors infer from the price, and that inference feeds into the price itself. [EF-W001, pp. 115, 118]

Soros: responses can change the conditions being interpreted#

George Soros distinguishes two functions of participants' thinking. The cognitive function attempts to understand conditions; the manipulative function attempts to influence events. In his account of reflexivity, these functions interfere because participants act within the reality they are trying to understand. Their interpretations influence conduct, while conduct changes the situation that will subsequently be interpreted. His 2013 symposium remarks distinguish corrective feedback from

reinforcing feedback and place interactions between authorities and markets alongside the more dramatic case of financial bubbles. [EF-W002, opening conceptual argument]

His 2009 lecture on financial markets gives a concrete credit mechanism. Easier credit encourages transactions and raises real-estate values. Defaults become less frequent, recorded loan performance improves, and lenders relax their standards. The increased apparent safety of lending is partly produced by the credit expansion whose safety is being judged. Treating collateral value as independent of credit availability misses this dependence. When the process reverses, forced liquidation can depress property values and weaken the collateral supporting remaining loans. [EF-W007, pp. 1–3]

In this account, a price is more than an inaccurate description of an independently fixed condition. Credit terms, transactions and collateral provide routes by which valuation affects what can actually be financed. Soros also discusses equity-financed expansion and the conglomerate boom: elevated expectations permit acquisitions that improve reported earnings, until performance can no longer sustain expectations. The credit example supplies the clearest operative sequence, while the conglomerate case illustrates his wider claim that different financing arrangements can transmit the interaction. [EF-W007, pp. 1–3]

Soros describes a boom as a real trend reinforcing a misconception about that trend. Tests can interrupt it; surviving a test can strengthen both confidence and the trend. He includes a period in which doubts grow while activity continues, followed by reversal and reinforcement in the other direction. He also says that corrective feedback can stop a reinforcing process before it completes this sequence. The account does not predict in advance whether a particular test will be survived. Soros acknowledges that he expected the 1997–1998 crisis to end a longer credit expansion and was wrong. [EF-W007, pp. 2, 4, 6]

Intervention is part of the feedback in his historical interpretation. Authorities rescue failing institutions and support activity; participants then interpret the resulting survival as evidence about the system. Soros argues that repeated successful rescues can reinforce confidence that markets are self-correcting even when official action was what prevented collapse. His proposed responses include varying margin and capital requirements and paying attention to credit availability, rather than treating control of the money supply as sufficient. He also distinguishes emergency support during a contraction from restrictions intended to limit a later expansion. [EF-W007, pp. 6–9]

The 2013 remarks extend his analysis to institutional rules. In his account of the euro, common treatment of government bonds in bank-capital and central-bank collateral arrangements encouraged purchases of higher-yielding debt. Converging borrowing costs contributed to divergent national economic trajectories; later recognition of default risk changed the pressures on indebted countries and on the authorities. The rules, interpretations and financing conditions developed together. This is Soros's application of reflexivity to a particular institutional history, where public authorities are participants rather than outside observers. [EF-W002, euro-crisis discussion]

Related accounts#

S15 develops the communication of dispersed knowledge through prices and institutional messages. S49 examines distributed action and expectations about others; S51 explains organizational silence and its reinforcing beliefs. The studies of common ground and collaborative memory in S56 concern how particular participants establish and retain shared understanding.

S16 Command, shared intent and retained control#

Acting together under uncertainty#

The relevant military literature asks how people can act together when no commander can know or decide every detail. Shared intent, training, delegated decisions, reporting, lateral relationships and intervention are different parts of the answer. The sources also ask when the organization itself should change.

Clausewitz: apparent simplicity and the resistances of execution#

The selected chapter on friction in On War describes why an organization that looks simple on paper becomes difficult to operate. It consists of people rather than one perfectly integrated mechanical part. Small delays, fatigue, uncertainty, weather and mistakes accumulate. An instruction can be intelligible while its execution still encounters circumstances absent from the diagram. [MIL-W036, book I, ch. VII]

The journey illustration makes the distinction accessible: expected transport can be unavailable, roads can be worse than anticipated and darkness can compound the delay. The point is the interaction of ordinary obstacles, not an unexplained mystical force. Clausewitz emphasizes experienced judgment and warns against expecting unattainable precision. Forceful will can also damage the organization while overcoming obstacles. [MIL-W036, book I, ch. VII]

Sunzi: disposition and collective potential#

The selected Art of War passage, traditionally attributed to Sunzi, directs attention toward disposition and

collective situational potential, associated with 勢, shi, rather than demanding the whole result from isolated individuals. Giles's 1910 translation and commentary use the image of logs and stones: shape, position and slope affect whether they remain still or move. The arrangement changes what effort can accomplish. [MIL-W027, ch. V, §§21–23 and commentary]

The received text and commentaries contain variant readings and different explanations of the passage. Across these interpretations, disposition and collective potential connect the configuration of circumstances with the effort required. [MIL-W027]

Implicit communication is prepared, not empty#

The Command and Control, MCDP 6, passage says that shared experience and a common outlook can permit implicit communication. People can interpret a brief indication through an established background rather than requiring every detail to be stated. The economy concerns explicit message traffic; interactive feedback remains necessary. It is a doctrinal explanation. [MIL-W001, selected printed 2-32 passage]

MCDP 6 was published in 1996 and amended by Change 1 in 2018. [MIL-W001]

The selected 2019 Army ADP 6-0 passages likewise tie delegation to competence, resources, shared understanding and trust. A commander can make fewer detailed decisions when subordinates understand the purpose and can act appropriately within it. Responsibility is redistributed; it is not enough to remove an approval step while leaving people without the capability or means to carry out the task. [MIL-W002, selected paras.1-26–1-41, 4-48–4-49]

Boyd: orientation grows through interaction#

John Boyd's Organic Design for Command and Control emphasizes implicit orientation and the relationships that make initiative coherent with a larger purpose. In the selected slides, orientation is shaped by heritage, culture, previous experience and unfolding circumstances; it also changes through interaction. It is a process of cross-reference, comparison and rejection, not merely a fixed instruction stored once. [MIL-W008, slides 7–23]

The proposed preparation exposes people with different abilities to varied situations in which they orient to one another as well as to events. Repeated shared experience can build similar expectations and trust. Boyd then argues that lower-level initiative can follow higher-level intent with less explicit communication. The source thus places substantial developmental work before the apparent ease of coordination. [MIL-W008, especially slides 13–18]

The warning against inward-looking formal arrangements is part of this argument. A procedure can become an obstacle if adherence cuts people off from changes in their environment. Yet the briefing's appeals to Gödel, Heisenberg and thermodynamics do not establish formal transfers of those results into organizations. Its organizational proposals are interpreted as a conceptual briefing, not a theorem derived from physics or logic. [MIL-W008, slides 20–23]

Logistics can require more than common intent#

Christopher Paparone and George Topic's 2014 article uses James Thompson's dependency distinctions to challenge a simple application of unity of command to the logistics enterprise. Pooled contributions can be coordinated partly by keeping activities from interfering. Sequential dependencies add requirements for order and transfer. Reciprocal dependencies mean that the output of one activity becomes another's input and vice versa. [MIL-W004, main argument]

The authors argue that reciprocal logistics relationships require continuing coordination across organizational boundaries. A common operational picture, lateral communication and trusted relationships support mutual adjustment. A single commander's statement of intent cannot specify every relevant interaction in a network shaped by industries, appropriations, transport, raw materials and political arrangements. This is a specific conceptual diagnosis of retained coordination work. [MIL-W004]

Paparone and Topic reconstruct Thompson’s 1967 Organizations in Action to explain these dependencies and challenge enterprise-level central regulation. [MIL-W005, through MIL-W004]

Van Creveld through later accounts, and Smith's criticism#

An MCDP 6 epigraph quotes Martin van Creveld's Command in War: a commander can increase information-processing capacity or redesign tasks and organization to reduce the information required. [MIL-W006, through MIL-W001, ch. 2 epigraph]

Christopher Smith's Network Centric Warfare, Command, and the Nature of War supplies a separate selected reconstruction of van Creveld's qualifications about technology and command. Smith criticizes narrow definitions of command and assertions of network advantage detached from context. More information or connectivity does not, in his argument, automatically resolve the human and organizational character of command. [MIL-W007, pp. 12–15, 64–68]

Power to the Edge: self-synchronization has conditions#

David Alberts and Richard Hayes's Power to the Edge proposes conditions under which participants can synchronize their activity without detailed central direction. The selected passage lists consistent

understanding of intent, good information and shared awareness, competence and trust. It explicitly retains command through congruent intent, authoritative allocation of resources and rules that guide action without dictating every detail. [MIL-W009, pp. 27–33]

The text also says that self-synchronization is not assumed appropriate when its conditions are absent. Its organizational proposal therefore differs from the claim that installing a network creates collective control. Responsibilities for information, architecture, preparation and resources persist, including in the selected later discussion. [MIL-W009, selected pp. 186–187, 208–210]

A passage in Alberts and Hayes's Understanding Command and Control distinguishes understanding from prediction. The SAS-085 overview develops the command-approach framework discussed below. [MIL-W010; MIL-W011]

SAS-085: changing the command arrangement is itself work#

The SAS-085 executive overview distinguishes decision rights, interaction patterns and information distribution as dimensions of a command approach. They can vary separately. Giving more people access to information does not, by itself, specify who may decide or which relationships carry coordination. The approach has to be described across those dimensions. [MIL-W011, selected pp. 9–15]

Agility includes recognizing when an arrangement no longer fits and being able to change it. That requires diagnosis, an alternative and a feasible transition, not simply permanent maximum decentralization. The group reports retrospective and simulation support. [MIL-W011]

The 2016 report on the 2014 Västmanland forest fire is a civil-emergency application of this programme. Its institutional abstract describes an initial mismatch in command arrangements and a case-analysis template. It demonstrates the scope of an application claim beyond combat. [MIL-W033, abstract and metadata]

Bousquet: a history of scientific images is not completed transformation#

In the abstract of Chaoplexic warfare, Bousquet relates military organization to scientific accounts of mechanism, thermodynamics, cybernetics, chaos and complexity. These provide the historical categories for his interpretation of changing images of order. [MIL-W018, abstract]

In Josefin Svensson's interview about The Scientific Way of Warfare, Bousquet describes scientific images of order and adaptation alongside a continuing tension between decentralizing ambitions and the hierarchical organization of state military institutions. [MIL-W019, through MIL-W020]

Stahel: doctrine, culture and historical practice do not coincide#

David Stahel's 2025 article examines the origins and application of Auftragstaktik and the problems of importing it into another institutional culture. A compact definition can hide differences in command level, available communications, personalities and organizational expectations. Stahel rejects a uniformly understood and practiced historical ideal. [MIL-W021, introduction and historical discussion]

Through Stephan Leistenschneider, he describes contested origins and early debates. Through Marco Sigg, he reports uneven practice across levels and periods. Better communications could permit close direction at lower levels, while higher-level autonomy could extend beyond the spirit of orders through rivalry and ambition. Initiative was not uniformly beneficial, and a culture emphasizing boldness had costs as well as capacities. [MIL-W021, reconstruction of historical studies]

Stahel also distinguishes the social and ethical purposes of later professional institutions from a purely functional reading of earlier military effectiveness. A historical technique cannot simply be imported as though its surrounding contract, authority and values were unchanged. [MIL-W021, conclusion]

Stahel reconstructs the mission-command histories developed in Sigg's Der Unterführer als Feldherr im Taschenformat and Leistenschneider's Auftragstaktik im preußisch-deutschen Heer. [MIL-W022; MIL-W023, through MIL-W021]

The supported historical qualification is more informative than a binary choice between always delegating and always directing. Stahel's account leaves an arrangement responsive to the operational circumstances and to the institution that can sustain it. [MIL-W021]

French, German and allied statements retain boundaries#

The selected French FT-05 passages distinguish command by detailed orders from command by objectives as complementary tendencies. Information collection does not remove uncertainty, and waiting for exhaustive information can itself obstruct decisions. Delegation can place execution where appropriate information can be acquired and used, while acute circumstances can lead to more centralized decisions. [MIL-W024, pp. 27–28]

Its subsidiarity passage retains systematic reporting and the commander's responsibility while warning against unnecessary intrusion into subordinate conduct. Local freedom exists within a wider relation of intent, reports and accountability. These are the source's doctrinal prescriptions. [MIL-W024, p. 38]

The selected German Agile Fehlerkultur passages similarly describe bounded independence under Führen mit Auftrag, with resources, training, responsibility and an acceptance of some errors. Nor does a modern discussion of Innere Führung establish that its social and legal assumptions are identical to every historical use of Auftragstaktik. [MIL-W025]

The selected 2022 allied land-doctrine passage makes trust earned and delegation conditional on capability, common training and professional understanding. Multinational cooperation can make that common background difficult. Sharing a doctrinal label cannot be assumed to supply the relationships and interpretation needed among organizations. The text is doctrinal prescription. [GL-W036, p. 43]

Command by veto: a prepared default with continuing oversight#

Alastair Cooper and Felicity Petrie's Mission Command at Sea and Command by Veto describes delegation within defined limits, with the delegating commander present physically or on a communication circuit. A trained delegate can proceed on a stated intention unless the commander modifies or vetoes it. Routine approval exchanges can therefore be reduced while the commander remains informed and able to intervene. [MIL-W034, definition and comparative argument]

The mechanism retains shared interpretation, competent delegates, explicit limits and attention. Authority may be delegated while accountability remains with the commander. The ability to act before a veto is useful only within the defined scope and appropriate timing. Silence in an unrelated, unobserved or misunderstood situation is not the same arrangement as the authors' command-by-veto construct. [MIL-W034]

The article connects changing communication and information capacities with changing command practice. Better information can support either more local action or a more active higher headquarters. It explicitly treats naval development on its own terms rather than reducing it to an identical land-doctrine history. [MIL-W034, conclusion and notes]

Duus: the bill for discretion is paid in preparation#

Anthony Duus's Paying the Mission Command Bill argues that trust rests on education, training, shared experience and execution. A hands-off posture without initial guidance, resources and appropriate supervision can leave a subordinate to discover the commander's intention only after expensive divergence. The relevant preparation is institutional as well as personal. [MIL-W035, selected introduction and trust/education sections]

Duus treats detailed and guided command as available within a spectrum, with circumstances and the relationship between people affecting the appropriate choice. His criticism is that terminology can hide the work needed to make discretion useful. This is a professional argument with historical illustrations. [MIL-W035]

Automation can remove interactions that were doing useful work#

The selected Re-Envisioning Command and Control passage proposes that repetition, communication in several forms, group ideation and reformulation can build understanding and trust. Efforts to automate apparently repetitive activity may remove some of the interactions through which that shared understanding develops. An activity can transmit content and also contribute to the relationship needed for later coordination. [MIL-W029, arXiv v2, introduction and framing]

The paper's human–AI organization is a research vision. [MIL-W029]

Civil incident organization and public accountability#

FEMA's 2017 National Incident Management System supplies a selected civil example of modular organization. Functions can be activated according to incident size and complexity; management responsibility is delegated, and unused elements can be demobilized. The arrangement changes the organization with the task rather than requiring every position to operate at every scale. [GL-W046, pp. 30, 90 (printed p. 81)]

Manageable span and modular expansion remain prescriptive principles. They depend on communications, experience and the relationships through which functions cooperate. [GL-W046]

Kevin Krupski's Who's the Boss? introduces another limit to importing an organizational model. He questions the wholesale transfer of a private-market principal–agent picture into civil–military relations, where public values and multiple principals matter. The selected discussion presents cultivated political and professional relationships as relevant to how accountability operates. [GL-W053, p. 28]

Krupski reconstructs Feaver’s monitoring argument while asking which purposes and constituencies an accountable command arrangement must serve. [GL-W053]

Common understanding, local decisions and accountability#

The selected sources offer substantive accounts of preparing common understanding, distributing decisions, preserving lateral coordination, monitoring defaults and adapting command relationships. They also expose the work of education, trust, resources, communication and accountability that a short instruction or a sparse organization chart can conceal.

S27 Voge, information costs and polycellular organization#

An original article and a chain of development#

Jean Voge's 1985 Crise, information et communication dans l'économie américaine connects organizational architecture with communication, selection, regulation and costs. The abstract of his 1983 article identifies the related information-economy inquiry, while later accounts interpret his 1997 Le complexe de Babel. [UX-W031; W094, abstract; RGC-W031, through UX-W028 and RGC-W030]

Hubert Landier's Polycellular Human Organisation develops this line of thought organizationally. Le Moigne's book review, the French Senate's discussion and Villiers's information-economy argument document other routes of development. [UX-W030; UX-W028; UX-W029; RGC-W030]

Voge: information work can offset productive gains#
