Voge's 1985 article divides material production from informational activity and asks how gains within material production can coexist with weak overall productivity. His proposed explanation includes rising organizational information and communication costs. Technical improvements to processing alone need not settle the issue if the organization creates increasing quantities of work to select, route and use information. The article concerns the arrangement of activity as well as its technical tools. [UX-W031, printed 39–47]

The historical macroeconomic argument uses a particular classification. In the notes Voge explicitly assumes, following Jonscher, that government information services such as education, research, documentation, regulation and administration should be treated with material final demand because material goods and services are their principal beneficiaries. That decision affects the resulting account. It is an assumption about classification, not an observed natural boundary dividing all beneficial information from overhead. [UX-W031, 46, notes]

The article's statistics, explanation of the early-1980s recovery and prediction of its duration are historical claims. The selected contribution is an explicit hypothesis about productive work and organizational demands, with its classification visible. [UX-W031, 39–46]

Branching and meshed communications differ#

Voge contrasts a branching communication structure with a cellular mesh. In the first, a downward message follows prescribed branches, while a message traveling upward follows a limited route through intermediaries. Selection is concentrated, and upper points can become bottlenecks. In the mesh, alternative routes and selective choices can exist at several points. The distinction is about where a choice of path is available. [UX-W031, 44–45]

His telephone comparison concerns particular quantities. He contrasts the number of switchable contacts needed for a caller to reach others, scaling linearly with subscriber count in the described pyramid and potentially logarithmically in the cellular arrangement. He separately contrasts operating costs as call volume grows. These are different measures. The comparison depends on switch design, ports, capacity, blocking, reliability and traffic. [UX-W031, 45]

The proposed organizational transfer decentralizes selection and supplies feedback at several levels. Voge favors interwoven serial and parallel processes and interactive dialogue instead of treating an organization solely as the execution channel for leaders' ideas. This is a connected architectural proposal. A communication diagram alone does not establish whether its human participants share purposes, possess relevant skills or can bear the assigned work. [UX-W031, 45–47]

The thermodynamic correspondence is a stronger claim#

Voge relates his economic account to thermodynamic models in which dissipative terms depend quadratically on forces or flows and useful power can peak at a particular point. He transfers the correspondence to informational production and a fifty-percent maximum. These are the author's analogies and proposed generalizations. Entropy production, dissipated power and monetary value are not treated here as interchangeable physical quantities. [UX-W031, 43–44]

Voge’s extension from a thermodynamic analogy to universal minimization of entropy production requires premises beyond the comparison. The architectural account instead specifies where information work occurs and how it can offset productive gains. [UX-W031, 43–47]

Landier's book: ideal types and actual informal work#

Landier's 2024 book revises material from the distinct 1987 L'entreprise polycellulaire through a later transdisciplinary framework. [UX-W030, prefatory material, PDF 13]

The pyramid and polycellular organization function as ideal types. Real organizations already contain informal relations, local improvisation and support work missing from their official diagrams. Landier's account of a strict pyramid says that employees often make it function by departing from impractical instructions. Each level can hide local accommodations from another because an intervention that appears rational above can be disruptive below. The actual coordination is richer than the formal reporting lines. [UX-W030, PDF 14–32, 51–59]

The proposed change therefore concerns both organization and representation. Calling an organization pyramidal can obscure the initiatives that sustain it; renaming it a network does not necessarily change its practices. Restructuring also encounters job losses, learning requirements, uncertainty and resistance tied to status or power. [UX-W030, opening chapters and PDF 57–59]

Landier draws the Voge argument directly from the 1985 article. His discussion of overflowing inboxes and intermediaries gives a contemporary-to-the-book interpretation of the same information-burden concern. The repeated thermodynamic and fifty-percent formulations remain dependent reception of that argument, not independent physical demonstrations. [UX-W030, PDF 57–59]

Proliferation, multiple routes and conditional autonomy#

The polycellular proposal has three connected principles. Units develop around a common project rather than simply filling a fixed chart. Communication has multiple possible paths. Local units retain operational autonomy conditional on effectiveness in relation to the shared project. The conditions distinguish the proposal from an arbitrary aggregate of independent teams. [UX-W030, PDF 60–64]

Multiple routes can permit communication after some failures, but require resources and appropriate surviving paths. Survival depends on node failures, loads and shared dependencies. The benefit must be specified against the disturbances and loads at issue. [UX-W030, PDF 62–63, fig. 9]

The autonomy principle explicitly retains central and intermediate responsibility. Management affirms the common project, monitors effectiveness and can intervene, reorganize or eliminate an ineffective unit. Apart from this corrective responsibility, it is meant to leave internal arrangements to the unit. Thus the proposal reallocates decisions. [UX-W030, PDF 64]

Development also involves initiative from the center and the periphery. A local unit can encounter possibilities unknown above, while broader management must be able to recognize and connect them. The intended organization depends on responses in both directions. [UX-W030, PDF 65–70]

Local knowledge substitutes for some directives#

Salespeople, technicians, buyers and production workers encounter different parts of an organization's environment. Their knowledge can be lost or delayed when every appropriate response must await a distant directive. Landier proposes local initiative because the person at the point of encounter can have relevant information unavailable to management. The argument concerns a particular distribution of knowledge and decision opportunity. [UX-W030, PDF 99–100]

The substitution increases other demands. Local members must know the organization's purposes and relate their actions to them. Internal communication, shared standards, selection and evaluation replace some detailed instructions. Landier also says the balance differs between activities such as accounting control and research. [UX-W030, PDF 99–102]

Common codes require work. When one level's information becomes unintelligible at another, the proposed responses include adopting a code, developing a compromise or negotiating a new relation. Surveys, audits, training and decoding support that adjustment. Disruption can destroy the organization or provoke intervention from outside it. [UX-W030, PDF 88–103, especially 94]

Leadership and arbitration remain functions#

Landier explicitly rejects the inference that local autonomy automatically gives an optimal outcome. Apparently equal relations can conceal age, status or other informal hierarchies, and conflicts can require legitimate arbitration. Participants can also have personal interests inconsistent with the common project, while relevant information is not automatically transparent. Removing an official supervisor does not remove these questions. [UX-W030, PDF 81–82]

His team-climate account associates better conditions with available leadership, opportunities for peer exchange and information situating the team in the wider organization. Worse conditions include inaccessible managers, absent exchange and deficient information. The passage supplies the author's practical account of retained support. [UX-W030, PDF 82–83]

Networks themselves also have several possible characters. They predate the Internet and can support secrecy, clientelism or coercion as well as cooperation. Technology can enable a relation without ensuring its purpose or quality. The book's political or organizational forecasts are proposals and interpretations. [UX-W030, PDF 73–87]

A common project is made and maintained#

Landier criticizes a corporate-project exercise that ends in slogans and a brochure. A management statement is not automatically the project of all participants. Bringing it to life requires taking seriously the perspectives of individuals, teams, establishments and the organization, together with capital providers, customers, suppliers and public authorities. Participatory development permits outcomes management cannot fully specify in advance. [UX-W030, PDF 112–123]

The process can take years as an identity develops. It is iterative across levels: a site can formulate a project before a corporate document exists, and local work can contribute to the broader formulation. The relation is therefore not simply a complete goal flowing downward through a chart. Negotiation, mediation, labor representation and continuing revision are part of the intended arrangement. [UX-W030, PDF 112–123]

The expressions A = f(C) and C = f(A) represent a mutual dependence between autonomy and coherence. Appropriate initiative requires room to act, while continued autonomy depends on effectiveness and

relation to the common purpose. The functions, units and empirical optimum are not specified. The notation states a conceptual dependency. [UX-W030, PDF 118–119]

The individual is also more than an organizational component. Family, personal existence and other commitments have purposes that cannot be absorbed without remainder into a corporate aim. Landier makes manipulation and sacrifice of participants ethical problems. His biological analogy is expressly limited by the status of human beings as subjects. [UX-W030, PDF 70–72, 117–118]

Institutional boundaries do not contain every capability#

Outsourcing can assign a function to a complementary organization rather than develop it internally. Landier's account retains the provider's viability and the reciprocal conditions of continued exchange. A client can weaken a supplier through its terms, but doing so can damage the wider productive relation on which the client depends. The local disappearance of a function is therefore not a disappearance of its provision. [UX-W030, PDF 69–70, 85–86]

Cross-firm cooperation has explicit conditions: transaction costs, continuity, confidentiality, trust, shared concepts and tools, and an appropriate institutional setting. Legal and public institutions participate in the supporting arrangement. A nominally independent network of suppliers still requires negotiation and may contain severe asymmetries. The book's expected gains are conditional organizational proposals. [UX-W030, PDF 85–86]

The time discussion identifies waiting, repeated reporting and conflicts among horizons as effects of architecture. Managers must bridge several time scales, and plans need adjustment. Its Toyota account retains stocks, signals, foreman regulation and learning between upstream and downstream activities. [UX-W030, PDF 104–111]

The broader societal discussion includes externalities and a reported generalized travel-time calculation that counts acquisition, earning and maintenance as well as movement. The particular historical calculation is mediated. Its relevance is the stated boundary of the account. Landier's planetary and human-care commitments remain normative positions. [UX-W030, PDF 124–139, especially 136]

Le Moigne's review of Babel#

The review of Le complexe de Babel praises its transdisciplinary reach and recommends the chapter on diminishing returns to information and human capital. Le Moigne emphasizes cooperative production of meaning rather than sheer proliferation of signs. He also objects that Voge gives some contemporary management fashions too much credit. [UX-W028]

The Senate section adds supporting institutions#

The pertinent section of the French Senate's 1998 report reproduces the contrast between pyramids and networks and relates it to the Internet. Its conclusion also retains trust, education, market and state regulation, public participation in infrastructure and substantial intangible investment. Technology, a public, enterprises and a culture must come together for a medium to develop. The report therefore does not explain a communication society by the network alone. [UX-W029, section 2]

Its expectations about democracy, peace, technological progress and European opportunity are historical institutional forecasts. [UX-W029]

Villiers: the fifty-percent result has assumptions#

Villiers's professional essay reuses Babel to examine information employment and productivity. It supposes a proportional relation Q/L = kXi, where Xi is information employment as a share of total employment, and assumes average wages grow proportionally with output per worker. With the chosen division between informational costs and material benefit, the account arrives at a maximum. These are explicit modeling premises. [RGC-W030, information-economy discussion and notes]

The treatment of final informational consumption affects the result. Changing what counts as an intermediate informational cost changes the claimed maximum. Aggregate output, per-worker normalization and wage coefficients also require clarification before numerical reuse. [RGC-W030]

S38 Logistics and sustaining coordinated operation#

Sustaining operation is a continuing activity#

These selected accounts examine the provision, movement, maintenance and information that allow other activities to continue.

MCDP 4: visibility requires interpretation#

The 2023 edition of Marine Corps Logistics separates demand visibility from supply visibility. The first concerns what forces need in relation to an operation; the second concerns the resources available, including equipment, units, infrastructure and supplies. The document emphasizes that data must be processed and analyzed to create shared understanding. A current snapshot is not equivalent to knowing whether anticipated demands can be met. [MIL-W003, printed pp. 2-6–2-8]

Its sustainability discussion places self-sufficiency and dependency on a spectrum. A force carrying or producing everything it needs can have autonomy over a specified period. An outsourced arrangement can reduce its footprint, but requires access to external providers. The doctrine expects combinations, chosen in relation to mission and context, rather than pure self-sufficiency or pure outsourcing. The external supply relationship remains part of the account even when the supported unit is smaller.

Simplicity is likewise described as a designed and maintained property. Clear command relationships, standardized interoperable procedures, fewer required actions and practiced methods can make execution more manageable. The document does not describe the logistical undertaking as intrinsically simple: planners still estimate needs using usage, equipment, personnel and mission information. It seeks actionable concepts without instructions for every eventuality. [MIL-W003]

Push and pull distribute anticipation differently#

In the selected distribution passage, a push system forecasts requirements and supplies them on a predetermined schedule. Its advantages include regularity and predictability; its limitations include the time required to adjust when requirements change. Forethought, planning and coordination remain necessary. A pull system responds to requirements submitted by the receiving unit. It can reduce provision of unneeded supplies, but the receiver must identify and communicate its requirements. [MIL-W003, printed pp. 2-26–2-27, figure 2-6]

The figure explicitly assigns anticipation to the provider under push and to the receiver under pull. Pull is therefore not an absence of anticipation. It depends on developed procedures, reliable communications and available packages. The doctrine also recommends combinations: routine requirements can favor scheduled support while unusual requirements call for requests.

The logistics snowball discussion addresses inflated requirements and habitual extras. Repeated across a force, such demands burden the system and can divert support away from more urgent needs. The proposed response includes disciplined requirement generation, training, trust and good habits. Emerging digital mapping or machine learning is presented as a possible improvement to visibility and responsiveness. [MIL-W003]

The selected education and training pages retain the institutional investment behind manageable execution. People learn how the system works, how to request support, how occupational fields interact and how logistics limits plans. Training introduces friction and uncertainty and develops initiative. The foreword identifies the document as guidance and distinguishes fictional scenarios. [MIL-W003, printed pp. 4-12–4-14]

Thorpe: define sustaining functions so they are actually assigned#

In the opening of Pure Logistics, Thorpe argues that the definition of logistics determines a division of labor. If that division is incomplete, functions may be omitted; if it overlaps carelessly, effort may be duplicated. His example is care of the wounded: merely possessing medical personnel does not ensure that their numbers, equipment and employment have been estimated for the proposed operation. Assigning a function makes it part of planning. [MIL-W016, 1917 work in the 1997 edition, printed pp. 9– 13]

This historical argument is relevant because it treats classification as consequential for preparation. It does not suggest that a label performs the function. The care still needs people, resources and an estimate related to the planned activity. The selected later organizational passage also debates where intelligence belongs: information serves strategy, tactics and logistics, and must be systematically supplied even when its bureau is located elsewhere. Functional use and administrative location need not coincide. [MIL-W016, printed p. 45]

Thorpe's broader organizational proposals are prescriptive historical arguments. Later favorable editorial comments in the edition are distinguishable from Thorpe's own text.

Eccles through a doctrinal attribution#

The MCDP introduction draws on Eccles's Logistics in the National Defense to connect a national economy with combat operations. It treats logistics as transforming resources and productive capacity into the material means for operations. [MIL-W015, through MIL-W003, introduction]

Kress: intrinsic versatility and structural flexibility#

Kress's 2000 article distinguishes versatility of assets from flexibility supplied by their deployment in a logistics network. Intrinsic flexibility concerns how many relevant demands an asset can serve and how many resources a support asset can handle. The palletized-load example separates a truck from a particular load, allowing a vehicle to switch among resource types. General-purpose maintenance capability supplies another kind of versatility, conditional on staff qualification, equipment and spares. [MIL-W013, printed pp. 44–49]

The intrinsic-flexibility index counts associations between assets and essential demand units. An essential demand unit pairs a supported unit with a resource it can actually consume. The association is not established by a generic name: a maintenance unit supports a particular vehicle type only if it has the capability to do so. The worked examples show how a change in transport or maintenance versatility changes the index. The index measures those defined associations, rather than the complete cost or effectiveness of every asset.

Structural flexibility concerns where resources are held and how they can flow. Kress represents source, intermediate and destination nodes, with edge capacities affected by transport and reliability. Because meaningful lateral flow at a command level is largely excluded in the model, the graph is essentially a tree. This is a substantive assumption. A result for that structure should not be presented as a theorem about an arbitrary network with extensive peer redistribution. [MIL-W013, printed pp. 45–47]

Holding supplies higher in a tree can postpone commitment to a particular subordinate unit. It preserves alternative destinations, provided reliable transport can deliver them in time. Concentration is therefore coupled to flow capacity and lead time. The paper's sufficient comparison of two systems sharing a graph explicitly includes the requirement that the relevant edge capacities not be worse in the more concentrated system. Rearward inventory without usable delivery is not the claimed mechanism.

The flexibility comparison can reverse#

Kress's structural-flexibility measure combines resource sufficiency and timeliness, with stated weighting across command levels. In its worked comparison, posture B is often favored, but not under every supply and demand condition. For one parameter combination the reported indices are 0.574 for B and 0.353 for A. With relatively abundant resources and lower variation in demand, the ordering reverses: the reported comparison gives 0.795 for A and 0.768 for B. [MIL-W013, printed pp. 52–53]

The paper explains the reversal. When both arrangements are highly likely to have enough supplies, the extra benefit associated with concentration becomes less important, while the time to deliver dominates the index. A resource-positioning advantage depends on which constraint binds.

These numbers belong to a constructed model with specified demand, timeliness and weighting assumptions. [MIL-W013]

Identifying and locating a convoy#

Kress illustrates convoy tracking by combining two kinds of data. Radio-frequency tags associate a convoy with its cargo. GPS receivers locate its vehicles. A map can then show where the convoy is and how it is moving alongside its destination and load. Tracking the vehicles answers where the convoy is. Identifying its load lets the logistician see which supplies are on the move. [MIL-W012, example 5.13]

RAND: sense and response retain prediction and command#

The selected RAND report combines prediction, responsiveness and command-and-control capabilities. Its future-work discussion calls for continuous monitoring of resources and process performance, estimates of changing campaign needs, assessment of plan feasibility and review of infrastructure configurations. The report places logistics information early in planning so proposed operations can be supportable. [MIL-W017, summary, printed pp. 9–10 and 79–81]

The selected passages require weighing support alternatives against time, capability, risk and cost. Near-real-time sensing is intended to alert decision makers to deviations before mission capability is affected. Metrics should concern outcomes rather than only outputs. The apparent responsiveness is consequently supported by maintained information, planning, thresholds, configuration and authority. It is a program analysis and proposal.

Shared standards and a shared system#

The official account describes joint support using common technical standards, interfaces, containers and pallets. Its examples contrast incompatible equipment interfaces with arrangements that can be combined across services. A further passage describes several services using a joint logistics information system during an exercise. The relevant mechanism is compatibility prepared in advance, together with

shared information during coordinated operation. [MIL-W026, sections 统一标准 and 共用系统]

The account reports implementation and exercises from an official organizational perspective. Common standards and systems require design, implementation and maintenance.

Fox: threat, environment and one's own organization#

Fox's conceptual essay divides contested-logistics challenges among the threat, the environment and the supported organization's own arrangements. It argues that the categories must be addressed together and calls for attention to transport possibilities, protection, deception and masking. The support system's

exposure is thus part of its usefulness: a technically efficient movement route can still be vulnerable. [MIL-W030, framing and conceptual support-boundary discussion]

The essay questions whether reducing or removing a movement demand could reduce opportunities for interference, while calling for theory as well as technology. This is a conceptual proposal with a hypothetical future vignette.

Sherbrooke: multi-echelon recoverable-item inventory#

Sherbrooke’s METRIC model compares where to hold spare parts in a system of bases and a depot. When an item fails, the base repairs it if it can. Otherwise the item goes to the depot for repair and the base requests a replacement from the depot. For costly parts with low demand, the model starts repair and replenishment one item at a time. It leaves out transfers between bases. [MIL-W031]

Sherbrooke’s program compares stocking plans by the number of requests expected to remain unfilled at a given inventory investment. It can evaluate an existing distribution of spares as well as compare alternatives, so the decision concerns where to stock a part as well as how many to buy. [MIL-W032] [MIL-W031]

A queueing benchmark for pooling#

Van Leeuwaarden, Mathijsen and Zwart's review explains resource pooling using an M/M/s queue. Jobs arrive as a Poisson process, service times are independent exponential variables, servers share a common service capability, and waiting occurs in an unbounded buffer in arrival order. Separate queues can leave one server idle while another has waiting jobs. A common queue removes that particular mismatch under the model's assumptions. [TA-W016, printed pp. 403–411, especially p. 405]

The quality-and-efficiency-driven regime adds capacity of square-root order above offered load as the system grows. Utilization can approach one while the probability of delay approaches a value strictly between zero and one, with mean delay decreasing at the specified scale. Proposition 2.1 states the asymptotic relation for the benchmark setting. Pooling therefore does not mean that every job avoids waiting, nor does high utilization alone establish good service.

The pooling result depends on the model's arrival, service, capacity and limiting assumptions. [TA-W016, introduction and proposition]

IMO: integrate navigation information while retaining integrity work#

The IMO e-navigation framework concerns harmonized collection, integration, exchange, presentation and analysis of marine information aboard ship and ashore. Its five solutions address bridge design, standardized automated reporting, equipment and information integrity, graphical integration, and communication of vessel-traffic services. These are distinguishable components of an intended reduction in administrative burden and improvement of navigation services. [GL-W082, definition and implementation-plan sections]

The plan remains subject to review as user needs, technologies and lessons change. The source states intended benefits rather than measured outcomes.

Positioning supplies and pooling capacity#

The sources explain sustaining operation through assigned responsibilities, versatile assets, retained alternatives, delivery capacity, compatible interfaces, shared information and controlled pooling. Kress's

ranking reversal shows how the advantage of a resource position depends on supply, demand and delivery time; the doctrine distributes anticipation across organizational roles.

S113 Maneuver warfare and disruption of coordinated action#

Firepower and the scale of operations#

В. К. Триандафиллов’s 1929 work examines changes in weapons and in the composition and movement of forces. In his account of cavalry, the capacity to move and the ability to fight mounted are different problems. The spread of automatic weapons changes what can be done in a mounted engagement and shifts the importance of the fire weapons a formation can bring. His argument is framed by the forces and operations of his period. [T15-W001]

The Marine Corps account of maneuver warfare#

The 1997 Marine Corps publication Warfighting describes maneuver and attrition as styles along a spectrum. Its account of maneuver emphasizes identifying and exploiting gaps and vulnerabilities, moving rapidly enough to exploit a changing situation and giving subordinates room to act under uncertainty. The discussion still gives combat power a place. Disruption is an intended effect on the opponent’s capacity to respond coherently. S16 explains the separate command question of how shared intent can support subordinate decisions. [T15-W002]

Cole Petersen examines the difficulty of carrying the maneuver and attrition distinction into strategy. His account traces part of the debate through Liddell Hart’s discussion of an indirect approach. A method of fighting can describe how a force acts in a particular engagement, while a strategic account has to explain the relationship of those actions to a wider object. Petersen disputes treating the two labels as complete competing strategies. [T15-W004]

Competing accounts of a campaign#

A Command and General Staff College study asks how to interpret the coalition campaign in the Gulf War. It contrasts an explanation centered on AirLand Battle maneuver precepts with one centered on firepower and attrition. The study concludes that the coalition used maneuver-warfare precepts in defeating Iraqi forces. The author’s judgment concerns the campaign as interpreted through AirLand Battle doctrine. [T15-W003]

The Defense Department’s 1992 report to Congress documents how different aircraft could supply parts of a single engagement. In the northern Persian Gulf, U.S. SH-60B helicopters provided electronic surveillance and radar capability, while British Lynx helicopters brought radar-guided missiles. The report describes this combination in operations against Iraqi vessels and distinguishes it from helicopter patrols for mines. [T15-W005]

Florian Waitl’s Army University Press study describes a different operation at the opening of the air campaign. Early on 17 January 1991, Task Force Normandy combined eight Army AH-64 Apache attack helicopters with Air Force MH-53J Pave Low helicopters. It destroyed two Iraqi air-defense command and control sites. In Waitl’s account, the strikes opened a corridor through the air-defense network for coalition aircraft. The chapter then traces the shift in targeting from the air campaign to preparations for the ground campaign, including strikes on communications, logistics and armored units. Waitl describes what destroying the sites enabled. The staff-college study’s judgment about maneuver and attrition concerns the campaign as a whole. [T15-W006]

S48 Burden, autonomy, power and evaluation#

These sources examine effort, authority, care, autonomy and alienation, asking whose purposes and experiences enter judgments of an economical arrangement.

Knowledge and power inside hierarchies#

Dosi, Marengo and Virgillito treat hierarchy as an arrangement of knowledge and power as well as a means of organizing production. In this historical and interpretive framework, authority can shape who knows what, whose decisions count, and which choices remain available to others. The organization of knowledge is therefore not necessarily independent of the organization of control. Making a worker’s local task simpler can coincide with relocating understanding and discretion into managerial routines. Productivity alone does not describe that redistribution. [W093, §§1–3]

Their comparison of Taylorism and Toyotism concerns different ways of using and organizing workers’ knowledge, rather than a simple contrast between an organization possessing knowledge and one lacking it. Participation in improvement and discretion over execution need to be read alongside the surrounding authority relations. The consequences of local simplification depend on who acquires the corresponding knowledge and power. [W093]

Tainter: complexity as a costly problem-solving investment#

Tainter’s selected introduction, definitions and discussion of problem-solving costs present social complexity as an investment made in response to problems. More elaborate organization can provide benefits, but it must also be supported. As solutions accumulate, the resources required to sustain institutions and specialized activities can become consequential to sustainability. In this argument a successful response to an immediate difficulty can create continuing obligations rather than simply remove a problem from the system. [UX-W006, printed pp. 91–94]

The relevant material is historical and organizational reasoning about returns and support requirements. Tainter expressly cautions about transferring ecological generalizations to societies. [UX-W006]

Work and care are different evaluative concerns#

Murphy and Parry examine household sustainability through work and care. Counting domestic activities as unpaid work can reveal effort hidden by monetary accounts, but the authors argue that this description can also lose personal and relational aspects of the activity. Their selected care discussion reconstructs scholarship in which maintaining people and their world is an ongoing relational activity. Who undertakes care, and whether adequate care occurs, are consequential questions in addition to the number of hours recorded. [GL-W006, care section]

Their integration discussion consequently does not equate a more equal division of household work with every possible improvement in care. Technology can alter expectations, standards and relations as well as the duration of a task. Its relevance is the more discriminating question: which work changes, whose work it becomes, and which quality or relation the proposed improvement is intended to preserve. Equal allocation and better care remain distinct normative goals. [GL-W006]

Administrative burden: three kinds of cost#

Moynihan, Herd and Harvey distinguish learning, psychological and compliance costs in citizen–state interactions. Learning includes discovering that a programme exists, determining eligibility and

understanding its procedures. Compliance concerns the actions required to meet those procedures, such as supplying information or satisfying process requirements. Psychological costs concern experiences such as stress, stigma or loss of autonomy associated with the interaction. These categories distinguish burdens that an account of administrative processing time alone can miss. [GL-W018, introduction and table 1, printed pp. 46–47]

The allocation of these costs between citizen and state can be political. A procedure that is inexpensive for an agency may require the applicant to assemble information, interpret requirements or repeatedly establish eligibility. Conversely, reducing citizen effort can require the agency to perform additional work. The authors also recognize that procedures can protect legitimate public values. “Minimum burden” is therefore not automatically the institution’s sole objective. [GL-W018]

What the administrative-burden review covers#

Halling and Bækgaard’s selected systematic-review passages distinguish government actions, citizens’ experienced burdens and subsequent outcomes. These are links in an explanatory account, not interchangeable observations. A formal requirement can exist without affecting everyone in the same way; an experienced difficulty does not by itself identify which state action caused it; an outcome can have several causes. The review identifies a larger research agenda while flagging missing causal links and questions about legitimacy. [GL-W019]

Its corpus comprises 119 English-language studies from 2012 to February 2023 within the administrative-burden framework. The authors note the predominance of Western settings. [GL-W019]

Relational autonomy: dependence does not settle the question#

The selected Stanford Encyclopedia account distinguishes causal from constitutive relational theories of autonomy. On a causal account, relationships and social conditions can develop or undermine a person’s capacity for autonomy. Support from parents, teachers or friends can enable agency; oppressive socialization can impede it. On a constitutive account, certain interpersonal or social conditions belong to what autonomy itself consists in, rather than merely explaining how it arose. The distinction changes what would count as an adequate explanation of a person’s autonomy. [GL-W040]

The selected discussion of stronger substantive and social-relational views also considers severely constraining relationships in which routine aspects of a person’s life remain under another’s control. Subjective endorsement alone need not settle the autonomy question for those theories. Other positions resist making every preferred way of life subject to the same substantive test. The entry presents a controversy, not a single established metric. Dependence on a person, institution or technical aid cannot simply be read as absence of autonomy. The quality and structure of the relationship matter within the competing accounts. [GL-W040, selected lines 246–260]

Alienation: technology and its social employment#

Leopold’s selected reconstruction separates objectification from alienation and distinguishes a criticism of technology’s social employment from a rejection of technology as such. Producing an object does not, merely because the product exists outside its maker, establish an objectionable separation. A theory of alienation must identify the relationship that has become problematic. Similarly, a machine’s technical capability does not determine the social relationship in which people use it. [GL-W049, objectification/fetishism discussion]

The entry’s selected later discussion raises problems of measurement and of connecting a diagnosis of alienation to a practicable account of unalienated production. This prevents a short circuit from “less

effort” or “more automation” to emancipation. Whether an arrangement improves control over activity, its products or its social meaning is a further question within the theory being discussed. [GL-W049, §§6.2 –6.3]

Peripheral case: coordinated roles in a traditional account#

China’s National Health Commission’s 2017 institutional description presents traditional Chinese medicine as treating a person’s condition holistically and tailoring formulations to that condition. Its selected account assigns differentiated roles within a formulation: a chief ingredient, an ancillary ingredient, an ingredient intended to reduce adverse effects, and one intended to coordinate the others. The source is relevant here as a public description of how a tradition conceptualizes an organized combination, rather than as evidence that every ingredient has the proposed effect. [GL-W061]

The NCCIH public evidence orientation distinguishes modalities and outcomes instead of validating traditional Chinese medicine as a unitary whole. It reports that some physical or psychological approaches may help particular outcomes, while results for herbal products vary; it also identifies contamination, substitution and other safety problems. The relevant lesson within this source is that an account of a coordinated formulation must remain distinguishable from evidence about specific interventions and harms. [GL-W062, selected effectiveness, safety and definition sections]

Effort, care, autonomy and power#

These source accounts leave their evaluative objects distinct. Task effort, allocation of knowledge, political control, experienced burden, adequacy of care, autonomy and alienation cannot be substituted for one another merely by calling an arrangement efficient.

S96 Negotiation: preparation, bargaining and agreements#

Negotiation can change the proposal under discussion, the alternatives available outside it and the parties' understanding of what they want. Reaching an agreement also creates questions about representation, implementation and continuing relationships. The accounts developed here examine these activities through practitioner methods, training exercises, reviews and experiments. Institutional bargaining and brokers have their developed account in S15; deception during negotiation is discussed in S93.

Preparation and the choice to negotiate#

Алла Стремовская's 2012 discussion makes strategy depend on the importance of substantive results and of the relationship with the other party. Avoidance, accommodation, competition and cooperation consequently have different purposes. Her account includes the possibility that someone already satisfied with their position has little to gain by entering a negotiation. A presidential candidate leading in the polls, for example, may decline an opponent's request for additional debates. Preparation includes identifying other parties' strategies and adjusting one's own conduct as the exchange develops. The article brings together earlier writers' approaches and examples. [NN-W007]

Aníbal Sierralta Ríos places commercial negotiation within institutions and their histories. People represent firms, states and other organizations whose policies, market positions and experience shape what their representatives can pursue. His account of negotiator education recalls the OEA–Brazil initiative CICOM and its contribution to training in Latin America. Preparation in this setting concerns the organization represented as well as the person speaking: institutional experience and commitments enter the encounter through the negotiator. His opening discussion gives these collective circumstances a place alongside the individual's conduct. [NN-W008]

Fisher and Ury: interests, options, standards and alternatives#

Roger Fisher and William Ury's Getting to Yes, first published in 1981, develops principled negotiation through four connected practices: separating interpersonal difficulties from the substantive problem, investigating interests behind positions, generating possible agreements and discussing standards for choosing among them. The parties can remain concerned about their relationship while examining a disputed question on its merits. Their method asks negotiators to discover what a demand is meant to accomplish, rather than treating the demand as the only possible expression of the interest. [NN-W001]

Their orange illustration makes the distinction concrete. Dividing the fruit appears to require a compromise until the parties discover that one wants the flesh to eat and the other wants the peel for baking. The uses differ, so an exchange can satisfy more of both parties' interests than equal division. Their interpretation of the Sinai settlement develops a larger example. They describe Egypt's concern with sovereignty and Israel's concern with security: returning territory while restricting military deployment addresses different interests within what initially appears to be an incompatible territorial demand. This is the authors' explanation of the settlement. [NN-W001]

Generating an option and judging it are distinct activities in their method. The discussion of objective criteria asks the parties to examine standards and the reasons for selecting them. In a disagreement about an insurance settlement, the relevant question can become the cost of replacing the destroyed car with a comparable one. In a disagreement about foundations, construction requirements provide a different kind of standard. The proposed change is in what the negotiators argue about: they can examine a basis for the decision instead of merely repeating how far they are willing to concede. Competing standards can themselves require discussion. [NN-W001]

The book's best alternative to a negotiated agreement, or BATNA, is developed through three operations. First, list possible actions if agreement fails. Second, improve promising possibilities into practical alternatives. Third, select the best available option. Thinking about a job in another city is a possibility; obtaining an offer there makes it an alternative against which a current offer can be assessed. The book similarly describes turning possible union action into operational decisions, such as obtaining authorization for a strike. Negotiating power in this account includes work performed outside the exchange. [NN-W001]

The resulting alternative supplies a basis for accepting or rejecting an offer. Fisher and Ury also ask negotiators to investigate the other party's alternatives, including whether that party overestimates them. If both sides have attractive alternatives, discovering that no agreement would improve their positions can itself bring the negotiation to a satisfactory close. Their treatment therefore joins the creation of possible agreements to the development of a feasible course of action without agreement. [NN-W001]

James White credits the book's search for mutual gains but argues that it neglects distributive bargaining, where an additional benefit to one party imposes a cost on the other. His labor-contract example distinguishes changing an insurance provider to obtain better services at lower cost from bargaining over wages that reduce the profits available to shareholders. Discovering a mutually beneficial adjustment does not, in his account, eliminate the subsequent dispute over distribution. [NN-W009, pp. 115–116]

White also questions the distinction between objective criteria and persuasive rationalizations. A seller may obtain different prices from buyers with different needs, while numerical tables for pain and suffering can give subjective judgments an appearance of objectivity. He regards standards as useful arguments, but disputes the suggestion that they generally remove the influence of bargaining power. His objection concerns the scope claimed for the method, alongside his appreciation of its practical techniques. [NN-W009, pp. 116–117]

First offers and the unfolding exchange#

John Oesch and Adam Galinsky's review manuscript examines four connected questions: who opens, how extreme the opening is, how it affects the final agreement and how participants subsequently evaluate the outcome. An opening can convey information about a bargaining position, signal an intention or establish a reference point. Their discussion of resistance to anchoring concerns the recipient's attention. Considering the opponent's alternatives or reservation point, or concentrating on one's own target, can direct judgment away from the initial proposal. They also discuss the possibility that an implausibly extreme offer undermines agreement. [NN-W004]

Wolfram Lipp, Remigiusz Smolinski and Peter Kesting's review of 119 articles distinguishes a first settlement proposal from anchoring, the judgment process that it may activate. A proposal can contain qualitative conditions as well as a numerical amount. Their process model connects antecedents and offer characteristics to the counterpart's response and to subsequent interaction. What the recipient knows and does consequently belongs within the explanation of an opening's effect. Economic results and subjective evaluations occupy different places among the outcomes considered. The review develops comparisons and open research questions across this literature. [NN-W003]

张真 and 皇甫刚 organize influences on integrative negotiation into contextual and process factors. Their contextual category includes cultural values, social motives and emotions already present when formal negotiation begins. Process factors concern the frequency and sequence of strategies and their use at different stages of the exchange. This distinction separates initial circumstances from conduct that unfolds between the parties, allowing a question about a tactic's use to include when it occurs and what precedes or follows it. [NN-W011]

苏勇, 程骏骏 and 吴展's review of cooperative negotiation argues that much of the research has remained dominated by linear and static models. They propose developing dynamic and relational perspectives on the mechanisms of cooperation. Their criticism concerns the way a research setting represents negotiation over time and among people in relationships. Their proposed direction gives the evolving exchange a different emphasis from a comparison of isolated strategies or average outcomes. [NN-W010]

Erica Boothby, Gus Cooney and Maurice Schweitzer's review likewise emphasizes interactions, evolving conversations and real settings. Its relationship discussion treats relational outcomes as part of what negotiation produces. Its cultural discussion includes adaptation and flexible exchange of information alongside knowledge of the setting. The authors also examine how simplified role-play paradigms shape available evidence. These accounts distinguish a settlement's economic terms from whether agreement is reached and from what happens to the relationship between the participants. [NN-W005]

Discovering trades and making an agreement operate#

The Organisation internationale du Travail's 2010 training manual makes differences in preference tangible through an exchange between Mariama and Abdoulaye. Mariama has a green sweet and two orange sweets, dislikes green and particularly wants yellow. Abdoulaye has a yellow sweet and two brown sweets, dislikes yellow and particularly wants green. Both also value variety. Exchanging the unwanted green and yellow sweets benefits both; exchanging an orange for a brown creates a further opportunity. The exercise asks participants to discover interests that a simple division of the stock would conceal. [NN-W002]

The manual carries the exchange into the work of establishing an agreement. Participants assemble acceptable options, prepare a draft and check whether the parties understand it in the same way. Responsibilities then require specification: who will do what, where, when and how. Evaluation, follow-up and procedures for difficulties make the agreement an operating arrangement. Partial, trial and time-limited agreements appear among the possibilities when a final settlement is difficult. Its labor-dispute setting also includes consultation with constituencies and assistance from third parties. [NN-W002]

Maurice Schweitzer and colleagues' handbook chapter distinguishes opportunity negotiations from disputes arising after loss or conflict. Preparation includes recognizing the setting, identifying issues, gathering information and considering alternatives and the counterpart. Its account of logrolling develops exchanges across issues valued differently by the parties. Bringing a start date into a salary discussion, for example, introduces a further dimension on which preferences can differ. Its phases extend through closing and subsequent behavior, placing continuing relationships and implementation within the subject. [NN-W006]

The handbook also distinguishes teams negotiating against one another from negotiation among several parties. A team can bring several participants to the interpretation and exchange of information. Several parties introduce additional questions about coalitions and whose agreement is required. Economic gains and relational outcomes remain separate matters in the chapter's assessment of group negotiation. These distinctions connect preparation and exchange to the people entitled to participate and to the rules under which a decision can be made. [NN-W006]

Decision rules and procedural fairness#

Bianca Beersma and Carsten De Dreu's experiments assign participants to represent a bakery, flower shop and grocer planning a joint market. They negotiate design, temperature and rental-cost allocation with private profit schedules. Their first experiment involves 90 students; the second involves 141. The instructions vary social motives, and the second experiment also varies the decision rule. Unanimity

requires all three parties to agree. Majority rule allows two to settle, making it possible to impose an agreement on the third participant. [NN-W025]

Under majority rule, prosocial groups report greater procedural fairness than egoistic groups; the corresponding difference does not appear under unanimity. Joint agreement points and participants' fairness ratings are distinct outcomes. The experimental construction makes the mechanism of exclusion concrete: the minority's consent has a different role under the two rules, while motive instructions change what the participants are encouraged to pursue. The available coalition is a feature of the task, distinct from what every group actually chooses to do. These experiments give a particular institutional form to the broader bargaining and veto questions developed in S15. [NN-W025]

S97 Building, maintaining and renewing personal and professional networks#

A relationship can provide companionship, belonging, advice or practical assistance. Its development involves encounters and communication over time, while changes of workplace, residence or activity can alter the opportunities for contact. The accounts here examine how people form relationships, sustain them and reconnect after an interval. Friendship and mutual support are purposes in their own right alongside professional access and advancement.

Encounters and the development of a friendship#

Claire Bidart describes sociability through repeated encounters that acquire a shared history. As a relationship develops, its participants cease to be interchangeable: knowing this person involves a history that another person does not simply replace. Her discussion distinguishes a network centered on an individual from the network of a collective. Specifying which relations are included is part of describing the network. This account gives particular relationships and their development a place within a picture that might otherwise appear to consist of nodes and connections alone. [NN-W018]

Jeffrey Hall examines friendship formation among 355 recently relocated adults and begins a nine-week longitudinal study with 112 first-year students. Participants identify acquaintances, report time and activities together and describe their closeness. Shared work or study does not carry the same association with closeness as chosen social time: leisure and everyday interaction help distinguish developing friendship from merely being present in the same workplace or classroom. The studies examine both the amount of time together and what people do during it. [NN-W013]

In the relocated-adult study, the logistic models put the probability of the casual-friend to friend transition above one half at approximately 164 hours together, and the friend to good/best-friend transition above one half at approximately 219 hours. These retrospective modeled estimates concern different relationship categories among the sampled adults, distinct from the students' longitudinal observations. They describe observed relationships between time and closeness rather than durations that guarantee friendship. [NN-W013]

岡田涼's review brings friendship research together with achievement goals, social goals, social cognition and self-determination accounts. His proposed model distinguishes motivation, conduct toward a friend and the relationship that develops through their interaction. Environmental conditions, including parent– child relations and classroom climate, and individual characteristics influence motivation for friendship. Motivation in turn encourages actions such as initiating conversation, helping and disclosing personal thoughts. The model places these actions between motivation and the closeness, satisfaction, trust and affection characterizing a friendship. [NN-W016, pp. 578–580, Figure 1]

The resulting relationship feeds back into later motivation while also contributing to adjustment and

mental health. 岡田 distinguishes possessing social skills from being motivated to use them: someone may know how to help or disclose appropriately without taking the initiative to engage. His discussion therefore follows the emergence of interaction, not just the qualities of an already established friendship. The review proposes this explanatory framework using findings primarily about schoolchildren and university students; it identifies developmental differences and tests of motivational intervention as questions for further research. [NN-W016, pp. 580–582]

Maintenance, motives and reciprocity#

Debra Oswald, Eddie Clark and Cheryl Kelly identify positivity, supportiveness, openness and interaction as dimensions of friendship maintenance. Across three studies they develop and confirm a measure and examine the interdependence of friends' behavior. Their findings connect both partners' reported conduct with dyad-level satisfaction and commitment. Maintenance in this account belongs within a reciprocal relationship: what one person does and what their friend does contribute to the relationship-level picture. The dimensions describe a family of maintenance behaviors rather than a count of how many contacts a person possesses. [NN-W014]

本田周二 studies relatively less intimate friendships, asking how motivation relates to communication, responses to conflict, satisfaction and mental health. Participants nominate a less-close friend of the same sex and answer questions about that relationship. Of 247 surveyed students, 211 remain in the analysis after exclusions. The study distinguishes motives arising from enjoyment or personal importance from motives involving obligation, anxiety or internal pressure. It also records communication through different media and responses to actual interpersonal conflict. [NN-W015]

In 本田's analyses, introjected motivation is associated with avoidance and self-concession in conflict and with lower relationship satisfaction. More autonomous motivation has few associations with the measured communication behaviors. The finding gives a particular difficulty in maintenance an explanatory home: continuing a relationship can involve pressure to retain it, and that pressure relates to how disagreements are handled. These are associations in the students' reported relationships. The reasons for continuing contact and the frequency or form of communication remain distinct parts of the investigation. [NN-W015]

李松, 刘峻君, 鲍秀琴 and 陈旭 review interpersonal gratitude in relationship maintenance. They distinguish buffering a relationship against threats from strengthening it after the threat has subsided. Their account also includes maladaptive maintenance, in which preserving a relationship conflicts with a person's wishes or social norms. They propose self- and other-evaluation as explanatory links and call for investigation at the dyadic level. Gratitude thus enters their account in both repair and further development of a connection, with the value of preserving the connection itself remaining part of the question. [NN-W017]

Professional contacts inside and outside an organization#

Hans-Georg Wolff and Klaus Moser's 2006 measurement work crosses two distinctions: contacts inside versus outside the organization, and building, maintaining versus using contacts. The resulting six subscales concern conduct, rather than network size alone. Three studies examine the proposed structure and validity. This formulation separates meeting a person from continuing the relationship and from seeking help through it, while keeping the organizational boundary explicit. Their later longitudinal investigation uses this measurement tradition to examine career outcomes. [NN-W019]

In the 2009 study, examples of the measured conduct include using company events to make contacts, catching up with colleagues in other departments about their work and seeking confidential business advice through those contacts. Building an internal relationship, maintaining it and making use of it consequently appear as different activities. External contacts receive the corresponding distinction. The three-wave analysis includes 235 participants using available repeated observations, a different number from the respondents present at the final wave. [NN-W020]

Networking is related to salary level and salary growth in this study. Career satisfaction is related to networking concurrently, with no corresponding satisfaction-growth effect. The different results matter

to the interpretation of professional success: income trajectories and satisfaction trajectories are separate outcomes. The study follows behavior and careers over time; its account does not reduce professional relationships to attendance at events or treat every favorable career measure as the same result. [NN-W020]

Tiziana Casciaro, Francesca Gino and Maryam Kouchaki distinguish deliberately instrumental professional networking from personal support and spontaneously formed relationships. Their experiments examine feelings of moral contamination, while a law-firm survey relates networking experiences to networking frequency and billable work. In that setting, relationships with clients and colleagues are consequential for work allocation. The study makes the experience of forming an instrumental tie part of the account of whether people engage in professional networking. [NN-W021]

The 2024 correction records an independent reanalysis of the available data for Studies 2–4; Study 1's original data were unavailable. In Study 3, eight participants began the survey twice but completed it only once, and the analyses used their complete entries. The correction also clarifies the office-location controls in models predicting billable hours; supplementary controls did not change the key findings. In Study 4, correcting a coding error involving two participants changes the interaction between networking content and power on cleansing-product preference to p = .072. [NN-W022]

Reconnecting after losing touch#

Daniel Levin, Jorge Walter and Keith Murnighan investigate the usefulness of dormant ties for work-project advice. They ask 224 Executive MBA participants to reconnect with two contacts after at least three years without communication, one formerly strong and one formerly weak. Participants select people who might help with an important current project, locate them, reopen communication and seek their advice. Ultimately, 129 executives complete both surveys. The comparison concerns the usefulness and features of these exchanges relative to current ties. [NN-W012]

Reconnected strong ties combine novel knowledge with retained trust and shared perspective in the authors' findings; dormant weak ties are also useful. A past relationship can retain something relevant to a new exchange while the participants have acquired different knowledge during their separation. The authors also examine contact selection in a further sample by asking participants to rank possible contacts and try lower-ranked choices. Their account describes purposeful selection and project-related reconnection. Its demonstrated outcome is useful renewed exchange, rather than sustained restoration of a close friendship. [NN-W012]

Mentorship and support communities#

Lillian Eby and colleagues' meta-analysis combines 116 independent samples comparing mentored and non-mentored individuals across youth, academic and workplace settings. Their definition involves a more experienced person taking an interest in and encouraging someone less experienced or disadvantaged. The review considers behavioral, attitudinal, relational, motivational, health and career outcomes. Associations are generally favorable and small, with differences across settings and outcome categories. [NN-W023]

Mentorship includes attention and encouragement extended to another person rather than only access sought for oneself. Its developmental and supportive outcomes differ from the salary and networking-frequency measures in the professional-contact studies. Sponsorship through advocacy and allocation of opportunities has its related account in S91, while S92 examines enrolling support for strategic work. [NN-W023]

Giovania Maesima, Lívia Gomes and Daniela Levandowski review 25 studies of internet use and interpersonal relationships. Their account describes online communication as part of existing relationships and as an entrance to new ones. Shared activity and support communities give the practices a concrete setting. Among the populations considered are parents of autistic children and people affected by cancer; exchanges can provide practical knowledge and a sense of belonging. These examples are the review's accounts of the studies it examines. [NN-W024]

The review challenges a simple division between online and offline relationships by examining particular media practices and communities. Communication can continue a connection across separation, support participation in a group or help a new relationship develop. The relevant conduct concerns what participants do together and what they exchange, as well as the medium available to them. Alongside Hall's relocation and university transitions, these accounts show relationships developing and continuing as the conditions for encounter change. Encounters and the pursuit of unexpected connections receive their complementary account in S83. [NN-W024]

S91 Acquiring, maintaining and contesting power#

Getting a proposal approved, controlling a resource and holding an office present different problems of influence. An office supplies certain rights; practical dependence can give someone influence well beyond those rights. Support may have to be assembled before a decision, renewed after it or protected against a rival. The accounts developed here examine how people acquire room to act, obtain cooperation, establish dependence and sustain positions of control.

Political skill and willingness to act#

Liam Maher, Aqsa Ejaz, Chi Lan Nguyen and Gerald Ferris distinguish the ability to act politically from the willingness to do so. Their review describes political skill through four connected capacities: understanding other people and situations, influencing interpersonal encounters, building networks, and appearing sincere. Social astuteness helps someone recognize an opportunity; relationships make resources accessible; interpersonal influence concerns using the understanding effectively in an encounter. Apparent sincerity concerns how the conduct is received. The same overt attempt to please a superior may be accepted as appropriate or dismissed as transparent flattery. [PWR-W001, pp. 6–10]

The distinction matters for interpreting a repertoire of influence tactics. Knowing a tactic's name does not establish an ability to perform it successfully, and possessing that ability does not establish a willingness to incur the relational or reputational risks of using it. The review follows political skill into relationships, reputation and evaluations by others, including supervisors and colleagues. These outcomes explain much of its relevance to careers: an employee's work is performed and assessed among people whose cooperation, information and judgments affect what becomes possible. [PWR-W001, pp. 5–10]

Dependence outside the hierarchy#

Michel Crozier's investigation of French factories gives practical dependence a concrete organizational form. Elaborate rules specify work, rights and relations between occupational groups. Seniority governs movement within a category, while recruitment from outside limits promotion between categories. Security and impersonal procedures reduce the personal discretion of supervisors. Yet machine breakdowns interrupt the otherwise regulated activity, and repairs depend on the maintenance workers. Production workers consequently experience dependence on people who are not their formal superiors. [PWR-W002]

Crozier asks why breakdowns become so consequential in these particular factories. When much of working life is specified beforehand, the events escaping the rules acquire exceptional importance. The maintenance workers control the response to one such uncertainty. Foremen object to the relationship but cannot resolve it through their own technical competence. Their position in the official hierarchy does not supply mastery of the practical problem on which production depends. [PWR-W002]

The maintenance group's position also has protection higher in the organization. An operations engineer possesses practical knowledge that formally superior engineers need, while his career prospects remain subordinate to theirs. Crozier interprets his support for the maintenance workers as protecting his own advantage. The resulting relationship runs across ranks: practical competence, dependence and backing reinforce a pattern that the official chart does not describe. Baldwin's strategic bottlenecks in S07 and Stinchcombe's occupational authority in S13 provide neighboring accounts of dependence and knowledge; Crozier develops the relations among the people occupying these particular positions. [PWR-W002]

Robert Greene's The 48 Laws of Power presents dependence as a deliberate objective. Its numbered prescriptions recommend keeping others in need of one's contribution and avoiding teaching them enough to dispense with one's services. Other prescriptions concern allowing a superior to feel secure, protecting reputation, controlling disclosure and taking credit for other people's work. These recommendations direct attention to different objects of political action: the distribution of capability, the attribution of achievement and others' beliefs about an actor. Greene treats preserving dependence and managing recognition as conduct to cultivate in the pursuit of power. [PWR-W004, laws 1, 3–7, 11]

Assembling support before a decision#

Jeffrey Pfeffer's Power Play begins with the difficulty of implementing an agenda among people who have competing purposes. Discretion over money, equipment, space or information can supply a means of recruiting support. Access to influential people can also be valuable. His account treats favors and resource distribution as ways of creating reciprocal support, alongside the substantive case for a proposed change. [PWR-W003]

Laura Esserman's efforts to change breast-cancer care illustrate several avenues of support operating over time. At the University of California, San Francisco, she sought more integrated care, easier enrollment in clinical trials and better collection of treatment information. When local changes met resistance, she continued building scientific and clinical visibility and relationships beyond the immediate organization. She also maintained relationships with patients and former patients, some of whom had substantial resources and connections. In Pfeffer's account, these activities kept adding advocates while parts of the program remained obstructed. [PWR-W003]

The account makes the construction of support part of implementing the clinical agenda. A relationship established outside the immediate dispute could become useful within it. Continuing on several fronts meant that resistance to one part did not stop every means of advancing. Pfeffer's reported case supplies this history of persistence and relationship building; the proposal itself was accompanied by efforts to acquire the practical capacity to carry it through. [PWR-W003]

大嶋玲未 and 廣川佳子 examine preparatory influence in new proposals within large Japanese firms. Their 2020 study draws on interviews with seven managers, analyzed using the KJ method. They identify

understanding the informal decision process, preparing the surrounding conditions and 根回し, or advance approaches to relevant participants. The managers needed to know who actually mattered, what concerns would arise and which parts of the approval process could be influenced through prior discussion. [PWR-W005, pp. 61–64]

The actions are specific. A manager might tell a key person about an impending proposal and ask which points mattered. Participants could develop a compromise before a formal confrontation, exchange concessions or speak beforehand to someone likely to obstruct the discussion. An intermediary could approach a person more effectively than the proposer could. Table 2 includes an account of asking a vice-president to supplement a presentation to the president where additional support was needed. The sequence of approaches and the choice of messenger form part of the work. [PWR-W005, Table 2]

Formal procedures continue alongside these activities. The managers' preparation sought both timely approval and cooperation once an approved proposal had to be implemented. The authors describe functions of coordinating intentions, avoiding stalled decisions and making subsequent collaboration easier. Their evidence concerns proposal situations in hierarchical firms. They also observe that short, single interviews may make improper political conduct difficult to disclose. [PWR-W005, pp. 68–69]

Opponents, superiors and subordinates#

Pfeffer describes incorporating opponents into an institution as one way of changing a conflict. In his university example, a committee, modest resources and an official role gave critics a stake in the organization they had been challenging. Their attention came to include sustaining the committee itself. Another example concerns helping rivals obtain attractive positions elsewhere: Willie Brown supported assembly rivals' moves to other elected offices. A departure could remove local opposition while giving the departing person an opportunity worth accepting. These cases concern changes in participants' positions and interests, as well as arguments addressed to them. [PWR-W003]

Fong Keng-Highberger, Zhiyu Feng, Kai Chi Yam, Xiao-Ping Chen and Hu Li study a different configuration: a middle manager situated between a superior and subordinates. Their account distinguishes coercive power over subordinates from relational empowerment supplied by a senior manager. They propose that Machiavellian middle managers can cultivate close upward relationships while using abusive supervision downward. The two relations concern different dependencies and different sources of power. [PWR-W006, §§2–3]

The proposed coercive mechanism involves the expectation of punishment. A subordinate may comply to avoid abuse, making the withholding of an undesirable consequence valuable. Upward closeness supplies a different route, through the superior's relational support and empowerment. Perceived threats to the existing hierarchy enter the authors' explanation of why both strategies may intensify. In the laboratory manipulation, subordinates challenged the middle manager's usefulness and threatened to report the manager to the senior manager. [PWR-W006, §§3–4]

The research combines a laboratory study with 338 students in Singapore, a multiwave and multisource field study in China, and a two-wave study of 716 managers from the United States and United Kingdom. The results did not support every proposed relationship uniformly. The association between Machiavellianism and abusive supervision appeared in the laboratory and US/UK study but not in the China field study. The authors' general discussion preserves that inconsistency alongside the broader support for their model. Laboratory responses to a manipulated threat and reports of relationships at work are distinct parts of the evidence. [PWR-W006, §§4–7]

Positions that control access#

Alexander Beresford's account of gatekeeper politics examines the African National Congress through party documents, interviews and observations around its 2012 centenary policy conference. Party or public positions can place their occupants in control of access to resources and opportunities. Granting or denying that access helps form relations of support and dependence. Rivals consequently compete over the positions through which distribution is controlled. [PWR-W010]

Beresford follows this relation into patronage networks, accumulation and factional struggles. Access is important to aspiring elites, but also to ordinary people seeking opportunities amid inequality, unemployment and poverty. The relationships are therefore sustained by several kinds of need. His account does not restrict patronage to kinship or inherited traditional authority: loyalties can run through modern party organization and become volatile as alliances and positions change. Holding the gate and fighting over who holds it are connected parts of the political process he describes. [PWR-W010]

This gives organizational reform a difficult setting. Integrity measures, political education and membership procedures address conduct within the party, while access to office and resources continues to support the relationships under examination. Beresford questions whether disciplinary measures alone can resolve that problem. He places gatekeeping within a broader political economy of patronage

and accumulation, explicitly resisting an interpretation of it as a uniquely African deviation. [PWR-W010, conclusion]

В. П. Пугачев's 2006 discussion of public human-resource management uses a narrower conception of micropolitics. He identifies sustained action to obtain, use and preserve power or resource-distribution positions for personal interests conflicting with official organizational purposes. Scarce resources, weak accountability, areas left to discretion and mismatches between individual and organizational interests help explain the opportunities for such action in his diagnosis. [PWR-W008]

Pugachev also recognizes defensive motives. Employees who experience injustice or neglect may seek protection for themselves and those close to them. His account follows increasing suspicion into additional preparation, safeguards and monitoring, with energy diverted into protecting positions and countering other people's moves. This adverse conception of micropolitics differs from the broader treatment of informal coordination in the proposal study. The difference concerns which activities the authors include in the category, as well as how they evaluate them. [PWR-W008]

Ezequiel Alpuche de la Cruz, José Luis Bernal López and Cesaire Chiatchoua examine organizational power through property rights, contracts and hierarchy. In their institutional account, ownership supports appropriation of the benefits attached to rights, while contracts organize exchanges and the allocation of resources among competing uses. Control is consequently embedded in legal and organizational forms as well as exercised through personal relationships. Their discussion connects these forms with bounded rationality, transaction costs and control of uncertainty. S15 develops the neighboring history of property and residual authority in greater detail. [PWR-W012]

Historical networks and room to maneuver#
